01 — Senior FE Roadmap, Skills Inventory & 12-Week Plan

What a senior FE owns · Targets by company · Daily / weekly / 12-week cadence

Merged from v1/01, v2/01, v3/00, and the 8-week plan. Treat this as the operating manual for your prep.

This doc is the spine. Every other doc (02–08) is a depth dive; this one tells you *what order to attack them in, how to measure yourself, and when you are done*. Read Part A to calibrate the bar, Part B to find your weak rows, Part C to pick targets, and Part D–F to execute. The progress tracker keys off the headings below — do not rename them.

Part A — Who is a Senior FE in 2026?

At FAANG-tier orgs in 2026, "Senior Frontend Engineer" (L5/E5/IC4) is expected to own end-to-end delivery of a meaningful surface, from architecture through ship, with measurable business impact. The bar is not "writes great React" — it is "ships a system the team can rely on for 18 months without rewriting".

Concretely, the level transition from mid (L4/E4) to senior (L5/E5) is a transition from *task ownership* to *problem ownership*. A mid-level engineer is handed a well-specified ticket and closes it. A senior is handed an ambiguous problem ("checkout conversion is down 3% on mobile"), decomposes it, decides what to build vs buy vs defer, writes the design doc, gets buy-in, ships incrementally behind flags, instruments it, and owns the metric afterward. The interview loop is designed to detect this. Coding rounds check that you can still execute; system design and behavioral rounds check that you can *own*.

What this means for your prep: you cannot pass a senior loop by grinding LeetCode alone. The differentiating signal is in the design doc you write in your head during a system-design round, the tradeoff you articulate without prompting, and the STAR story where you describe influencing a decision you did not have authority over.

Core competencies (the senior rubric)

PillarWhat "senior" looks like
CodeIdiomatic JS/TS, React 19, modern CSS. Reviews others productively. Refactors with intent.
ArchitectureOwns design of a multi-surface system. Articulates tradeoffs (RSC vs SPA, CRDT vs OT, edge vs node).
PerformanceHits Core Web Vitals on real users (p75 LCP < 2.0 s, INP < 200 ms, CLS < 0.1). Reads flame charts.
ReliabilityDesigns for failure. Error boundaries, retries, idempotency, graceful degradation are second nature.
SecurityCSP, Trusted Types, SRI, cookie hygiene, supply-chain awareness, no secrets in client.
AvailabilityAtomic deploys + one-click rollback, synthetic monitoring, multi-region SSR or fallback.
CollaborationMentors. Writes design docs. Drives postmortems. Influences without authority.
ProductPushes back on PM with data, but ships what users actually need. Knows the conversion funnel.

How interviewers actually map to these pillars — and where loops are won and lost:

RoundPillars probedWhere seniors fail it
Coding (DSA)CodeCan solve, but narrates nothing; no complexity analysis; freezes on follow-up.
Machine codingCode, Performance, ReliabilityBuilds happy path only; no a11y, no error/loading/empty states, no cleanup.
System designArchitecture, Performance, Reliability, AvailabilityJumps to a solution; never states requirements or tradeoffs; no failure modes.
BehavioralCollaboration, ProductStories are "we"-heavy, no conflict, no measurable outcome, no reflection.

Self-test for the whole rubric: *Pick the last non-trivial thing you shipped. Can you, in 90 seconds, state the problem, two design alternatives you rejected and why, the metric it moved, and what you would do differently?* If any of those four is blank, that pillar is your weak spot.

Part B — Skills Inventory (read row by row)

Mark each row Strong / OK / Weak. The Weak rows tell you where to focus first.

Scoring rubric so the marks are honest, not aspirational:

  • Strong = you can teach it on a whiteboard cold, including edge cases and at least one tradeoff, and you have shipped it.
  • OK = you can use it with docs open and recognize it in code review, but you would hesitate explaining it live.
  • Weak = you would need to study before an interview question on it.

Re-score every two weeks. A row only moves to Strong after you have done the "highest-leverage drill" listed for it at least three times across different days (spacing beats cramming for retention).

B.1 JavaScript core

  • Closures, lexical scope, hoisting, TDZ, IIFE.
  • Prototypes, classes, private fields (#), inheritance, mixins.
  • this binding rules + arrow vs function.
  • Event loop, task queue, microtasks, rAF, rIC, scheduler.yield.
  • Promises end-to-end: chaining, error propagation, AbortController, Promise.allSettled / any / race.
  • Async iterators + generators.
  • ES Modules vs CommonJS; tree-shaking; dynamic import.
  • Memory model: heap, stack, weak refs, GC.
  • Polyfills: should be able to dictate 10+ without an IDE (see Doc 02 Part 2).

Senior-level mastery means: you reason about *ordering and lifetime*, not just syntax. You can predict the exact interleaving of sync code, microtasks, and macrotasks; you know a closure captures a *variable binding* not a value; you know WeakMap/WeakRef exist to avoid leaks in caches keyed by DOM nodes; and you can write a hand-rolled promise/scheduler from scratch.

1-line self-test: Without running it, give the full output order of a snippet mixing console.log, setTimeout(…,0), Promise.resolve().then, and queueMicrotask.

Highest-leverage drill: Implement Promise from scratch (then/catch/finally/all/race/allSettled) passing the relevant Promises/A+ ordering cases. It forces the microtask model into muscle memory.

// The canonical event-loop ordering question. Output: 1, 4, 3, 2
console.log(1);                                   // sync
setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0);              // macrotask
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3));     // microtask
console.log(4);                                   // sync
// All microtasks (3) drain before the next macrotask (2) ever runs.

// Closures capture bindings, not snapshots — the classic loop trap:
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log('var', i)); // 3,3,3
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) setTimeout(() => console.log('let', j)); // 0,1,2
// `let` creates a fresh binding per iteration; `var` shares one.

B.2 TypeScript

  • Generics with constraints; conditional types + infer; mapped types; template literals.
  • Discriminated unions; satisfies; const generics; branded types.
  • Type-level utilities you can author: DeepReadonly, DeepPartial, UnionToTuple, RouteParams.
  • Performance: cardinality of unions, recursion depth, declaration merging.

Senior-level mastery means: you use the type system to make illegal states unrepresentable and to push errors to compile time, without turning the codebase into type golf that nobody can maintain. You know when satisfies beats a type annotation (preserves the literal type while checking the constraint), when a discriminated union beats optional fields, and when to *stop* and just write unknown + a runtime guard.

1-line self-test: Write RouteParams<'/users/:id/posts/:postId'> that resolves to { id: string; postId: string } using template-literal + recursive conditional types.

Highest-leverage drill: Author five utility types without an IDE: DeepReadonly<T>, DeepPartial<T>, RouteParams<S>, UnionToIntersection<U>, and a Result<T, E> discriminated union with an exhaustive match.

// Extract path params at the type level — a staple FE TS interview question.
type RouteParams<S extends string> =
  S extends `${string}:${infer P}/${infer Rest}`
    ? { [K in P]: string } & RouteParams<`/${Rest}`>
    : S extends `${string}:${infer P}`
      ? { [K in P]: string }
      : {};

type R = RouteParams<'/users/:id/posts/:postId'>;
// { id: string } & { postId: string }

// `satisfies` checks the shape but keeps the narrow literal types:
const routes = {
  home: '/',
  user: '/users/:id',
} satisfies Record<string, `/${string}`>;
// typeof routes.user is the literal '/users/:id', not string.

B.3 React + modern stack

  • Rules of React; reconciliation; commit phase.
  • Hooks: useState / useReducer / useEffect / useLayoutEffect / useTransition / useDeferredValue.
  • React 19: Compiler, use(), Server Actions, useOptimistic, useFormStatus, useActionState.
  • Server vs Client Component boundary + serialization.
  • Concurrency: Suspense, streaming, selective hydration.
  • Next.js 15: App Router, PPR, the four caches, edge vs node, parallel + intercepting routes.
  • State: TanStack Query (server), Zustand (client), Jotai (atomized), Signals (radar).
  • Forms: React Hook Form + Zod; native validation; Server Actions.

Senior-level mastery means: you can draw the RSC boundary and explain *what serializes across it* (props must be serializable; functions only as Server Actions; no class instances), reason about why an effect re-runs, and choose the right state tool by *where the data lives* — server cache (TanStack Query), URL, React state, or a client store (Zustand) — rather than reaching for useState reflexively. With the React Compiler shipping, you also know that most manual useMemo/useCallback is now noise, and you can articulate when it still matters (referential identity passed into non-React boundaries).

1-line self-test: Explain why moving a useState up a tree can fix a "form resets on parent re-render" bug, and when you would instead reach for key.

Highest-leverage drill: Take a CSR toy app and (a) split it into Server + Client Components, (b) replace ad-hoc fetching with TanStack Query including optimistic update + rollback, (c) convert one form to a Server Action with useActionState + useOptimistic.

// React 19 form: progressive-enhancement-friendly, optimistic, with pending state.
'use client';
import { useActionState, useOptimistic } from 'react';
import { addTodo } from './actions'; // a Server Action

function Todos({ initial }: { initial: Todo[] }) {
  const [optimistic, addOptimistic] = useOptimistic(
    initial,
    (state, text: string) => [...state, { id: 'tmp', text, pending: true }]
  );
  const [, formAction] = useActionState(async (_: unknown, fd: FormData) => {
    const text = String(fd.get('text'));
    addOptimistic(text);          // instant UI
    return addTodo(text);         // server reconciles; failure reverts optimistic
  }, null);

  return (
    <form action={formAction}>
      <input name="text" />
      <ul>{optimistic.map(t => <li key={t.id} data-pending={t.pending}>{t.text}</li>)}</ul>
    </form>
  );
}

Decision table for state tools (interviewers love hearing this):

Where the data livesUseAnti-pattern
Server, fetched, cacheableTanStack QueryManual useEffect + useState fetching
Shareable / bookmarkableURL (search params)Global store for filters/tabs
Local to one subtreeuseState/useReducerGlobal store for a modal's open flag
Cross-tree client UI stateZustand / JotaiContext with frequently-changing value (re-renders all consumers)

B.4 Web platform + CSS

  • Layout: flexbox + grid + subgrid; container queries; anchor positioning; :has().
  • Modern features: cascade layers, scope, custom properties, color-mix, color spaces (oklch).
  • APIs: View Transitions, Popover, Dialog, IntersectionObserver, ResizeObserver, MutationObserver.
  • Accessibility: WCAG 2.2 + ARIA patterns (combobox, listbox, tabs, dialog).
  • Browser internals: rendering pipeline (parse → layout → paint → composite); reflow vs repaint.

Senior-level mastery means: you reach for the platform before a library — a native <dialog> with the Popover API instead of a JS modal lib, container queries instead of JS resize listeners, :has() instead of parent-selector hacks. You know which CSS properties are composited (transform/opacity) versus layout-triggering (top/left/width), and you can name the a11y contract of a combobox (roles, aria-activedescendant, keyboard model) without looking it up.

1-line self-test: Which of transform: translateX() vs left: animates without a layout/paint, and why does that matter for INP?

Highest-leverage drill: Build an accessible combobox/autocomplete from scratch — no library — with full keyboard support (ArrowUp/Down, Enter, Escape, Home/End), aria-activedescendant, and a debounced async data source. This single component covers DOM APIs, a11y, and perf at once and is the most common machine-coding prompt.

/* Container queries: component responds to its own width, not the viewport. */
.card-grid { container-type: inline-size; }
@container (min-width: 480px) {
  .card { grid-template-columns: 120px 1fr; }
}

/* :has() — style a label based on its input's state, no JS. */
.field:has(input:invalid) > label { color: oklch(0.6 0.2 25); }

B.5 Performance + reliability + security + availability (FRSA)

  • CWV: LCP, INP, CLS targets + triage flow.
  • Bundle: code-splitting, tree-shaking, modern targets, replace heavy libs.
  • Image + font pipelines.
  • RUM + sourcemap upload + Sentry.
  • Error boundaries, fetch resilience, race-condition guard, optimistic UI.
  • CSP, Trusted Types, SRI, HttpOnly cookies, SameSite, HSTS.
  • CDN, atomic deploy + rollback, multi-region SSR, synthetic monitoring.

Senior-level mastery means: you optimize against *field data* (RUM p75), not lab numbers, and you have a triage flow per metric. LCP slow → find the LCP element, then preload it, kill render-blocking resources, fix priority. INP slow → break long tasks, useDeferredValue/startTransition, yield with scheduler.yield(). CLS → reserve space (width/height, aspect-ratio, font size-adjust). On reliability you treat the network as adversarial: every fetch has a timeout, an abort, a retry-with-backoff policy, and a race guard. On security you can write a CSP and know why unsafe-inline defeats it.

1-line self-test: Your INP regressed to 350 ms after a feature; name the three most likely causes and the tool you would open first.

Highest-leverage drill: Take a real app, capture RUM web-vitals, and ship *one measurable* win per metric (LCP, INP, CLS), proving each with before/after p75. Add a Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only header and read the violation reports.

// 1. Ship real-user vitals to your backend. This is what seniors instrument.
import { onLCP, onINP, onCLS } from 'web-vitals';
function send(metric) {
  navigator.sendBeacon('/rum', JSON.stringify({
    name: metric.name, value: metric.value, id: metric.id,
    rating: metric.rating, path: location.pathname,
  }));
}
onLCP(send); onINP(send); onCLS(send);
// 2. Race-condition guard + abort — the bug behind most "stale results" UIs.
function makeSearch() {
  let controller;
  return async function search(q) {
    controller?.abort();                 // cancel the in-flight request
    controller = new AbortController();
    const res = await fetch(`/api?q=${q}`, { signal: controller.signal });
    return res.json();                   // only the latest call resolves
  };
}

FRSA triage cheat-sheet:

SymptomFirst toolLikely fix
LCP > 2.5 sLighthouse / WebPageView filmstripPreload LCP image, drop render-blocking CSS/JS, fetchpriority="high"
INP > 200 msPerformance panel long-tasksBreak tasks, startTransition, virtualize, debounce
CLS > 0.1Layout Shift regions overlaySet dimensions/aspect-ratio, reserve ad/font space
Bundle bloatsource-map-explorer / bundle analyzerDynamic import, swap moment→date-fns/Temporal, drop polyfills

B.6 System design (FE)

  • RADIO framework.
  • Patterns: real-time fan-out, virtualization, offline-first, optimistic mutation.
  • CRDT vs OT.
  • 10 case studies: Figma / Google Docs, Twitter, Netflix, Notion, Drive, Slack, Stripe, Maps, Calendar, Autocomplete.

Senior-level mastery means: you drive the round with a framework instead of jumping to a solution. RADIO = Requirements (functional + non-functional, scale, devices), Architecture/components, Data model + API/entities, Interface/optimizations (perf, a11y, i18n), Optimizations/deep-dives + tradeoffs. You can compare transport (polling vs SSE vs WebSocket vs WebTransport), consistency models (OT vs CRDT for collaboration), and rendering strategies, and you proactively raise failure modes and offline behavior.

1-line self-test: For a collaborative editor, state when you would pick CRDT over OT and the concrete cost you pay for that choice.

Highest-leverage drill: Pick 2–3 cases (not 10) and perform them aloud end-to-end in 35 minutes each, including a data model sketch and at least two tradeoffs you raise unprompted. Depth on three beats shallow coverage of ten.

DecisionOption AOption BPick A when…
Real-time transportWebSocketSSE / long-pollBidirectional, low-latency (chat, cursors); SSE for server→client only
Collab consistencyCRDTOTP2P / offline-first, no authoritative server; OT when a server can serialize
Big list renderingWindowing/virtualizationPaginationContinuous scroll feel needed; paginate for SEO/bookmarkable pages
Mutation UXOptimistic + rollbackPessimisticHigh success rate, latency hurts UX; pessimistic for money/irreversible ops

B.7 DSA + machine coding

  • Patterns: sliding window, two pointers, BFS/DFS, DP, trees, graphs, heaps, tries.
  • Machine coding: carousel, autocomplete, infinite scroll, modal, toast, rating, tabs, pagination, drag-and-drop, wizard.
  • JS-only: deep clone, deep equal, currying, memoization, EventEmitter, LRU.

Senior-level mastery means: for DSA you recognize the pattern from the constraints (sorted → two pointers/binary search; "subarray/substring" → sliding window; "shortest in unweighted graph" → BFS) and you narrate complexity as you go. For machine coding the bar is *production-shaped*: loading/error/empty states, accessibility, cleanup of listeners/timers, no memory leaks, and a sensible component API — not just the happy path. Interviewers downgrade candidates who ship the demo but forget the AbortController, the Escape-to-close, or the focus trap.

1-line self-test: Implement an LRU cache with O(1) get/put and explain the data structures (hash map + doubly linked list, or insertion-ordered Map) before writing it.

Highest-leverage drill: Re-build the same five components (autocomplete, infinite scroll, modal, toast, tabs) once a week from a blank file, timing yourself to 30 minutes, each with full a11y + cleanup. Repetition is the entire game here — novelty is not.

// LRU in O(1): Map preserves insertion order, so the oldest key is Map's first.
class LRU {
  constructor(capacity) { this.cap = capacity; this.map = new Map(); }
  get(k) {
    if (!this.map.has(k)) return -1;
    const v = this.map.get(k);
    this.map.delete(k); this.map.set(k, v); // mark most-recently-used
    return v;
  }
  put(k, v) {
    if (this.map.has(k)) this.map.delete(k);
    else if (this.map.size >= this.cap) this.map.delete(this.map.keys().next().value);
    this.map.set(k, v);
  }
}

Machine-coding "done" checklist (apply to every component):

  • [ ] Loading, error, and empty states rendered (not just success).
  • [ ] Keyboard + screen-reader accessible (roles, focus management, Escape).
  • [ ] Effects clean up (listeners, timers, observers, aborts).
  • [ ] No race conditions on async (abort or sequence-guard).
  • [ ] Sensible, typed props API; no leaked internal state.

B.8 Behavioral + comms

  • STAR stories (12 universal).
  • Company-specific rubrics (Amazon LPs, Googleyness, Meta impact, Netflix judgment).
  • Negotiation script.
  • Take-home blueprint.

Senior-level mastery means: your stories are STAR with a heavy R (Result) stated as a metric, framed in "I" not "we", and each one quietly demonstrates a senior signal — ambiguity, conflict, influence without authority, or a mistake you owned. You can re-skin one real project into answers for "biggest impact", "hardest conflict", "failure", and "disagreed with a decision". You map stories to each target's rubric (Amazon Leadership Principles, Meta's impact/direction, Netflix's judgment/candor).

1-line self-test: Tell a 2-minute story where you changed a senior stakeholder's mind using data, ending with the measured outcome.

Highest-leverage drill: Write 6 stories, then record yourself answering 3 prompts per target company and cut each to under 2 minutes. Behavioral fails more senior loops than coding — this drill has outsized ROI.

STAR skeleton (fill one per story, ~150 words spoken):
S — context + stakes (1 sentence): why it mattered, what was at risk.
T — your specific responsibility (1 sentence): "I owned…".
A — 2–3 concrete actions, decisions, and the tradeoff you made.
R — the measured result + what you learned / would change.

Part C — Targets by company (where to aim)

Note: TC figures are rough medians (base + equity + bonus, US, levels.fyi-style) and move with the equity market — verify per offer before negotiating. Read the *onsite shape* column as your prep-allocation signal:

  • DSA-heavy (Google, Amazon, Meta): invest more in Doc 07 patterns + complexity narration. Amazon weights behavioral (LPs) as much as coding — prep 2 stories per relevant LP.
  • Machine-coding-heavy (Figma, Stripe, Airbnb, Linear): invest in Doc 07 components and shipping production-shaped UI fast. Figma's 75-min and Stripe's 90-min builds reward a clean component you can extend live.
  • Judgment / take-home (Netflix, Vercel, Linear): less LeetCode, more "show senior judgment". For Netflix, every answer should demonstrate the culture memo's bar; for take-homes, treat the README + tests + tradeoffs section as graded.
  • Fundamentals (Apple): expect deep JS/CSS/perf questions over framework trivia — Doc 02 and Doc 04 matter most.

Pick exactly three targets across at least two of these buckets so your prep is forced to be well-rounded, then weight your final two weeks toward your top choice's shape.

Part D — The 12-week plan (extended from the original 8-week)

Cadence assumption: ~1 focused hour on weekdays + a longer block on weekends (~10 h/week). If you have less, extend each phase rather than skipping rows. Every week ends with a Friday self-score on the Part B inventory; a row only moves up after the drill is done 3×. The "done" criteria below are deliberately binary so you can't fool yourself.

Phase 0 — Orientation (week 0, 3 days)

  • Run Doc 00 baseline (Lighthouse + RUM + JS error rate + bundle size + uptime).
  • Read this doc + Doc 00 Learning Path.
  • Pick 3 target companies + levels. Lock comp data.
  • Block 1 hour/day on calendar for prep, non-negotiable.

Daily deliverables: Day 1 — a baseline numbers doc (LCP/INP/CLS p75, JS error rate, bundle KB, uptime). Day 2 — Part B inventory fully scored Strong/OK/Weak. Day 3 — three locked targets with level + verified TC + onsite shape pasted in.

Done looks like: a one-page "starting state" with measured baselines, a scored skills inventory, three committed targets, and a recurring calendar block. If you can't see your weak rows at a glance, you're not done.

Weeks 1–2 — Fundamentals reset

  • Doc 02 (JS/TS) — read fully. 5 polyfill drills/day.
  • Doc 04 (Web Platform & CSS) — read fully. Build one demo per chapter.
  • Doc 03 Part 1 (React 19) — write 5 mini demos.
  • Daily: 30 min DSA.

Daily deliverables: 5 polyfills dictated from memory (cumulative list of 50+ by end of week 2: bind, call, apply, Promise.all/allSettled/race/any, debounce, throttle, curry, flat, Array.prototype.map/reduce, Object.assign, EventEmitter, deep clone/equal). One CSS/platform demo per chapter (container-query layout, :has() form, native <dialog>, View Transition). One React 19 mini-demo (useActionState, useOptimistic, use(), Suspense streaming, a custom hook).

Done looks like: you can write the top-10 polyfills cold in under 5 min each; B.1, B.2, B.4 each have at least one row promoted to Strong; 5 committed React demos in a repo. If you still need docs for bind or debounce, repeat the week.

Week 3 — Stack + state + AI

  • Doc 03 Part 2 (Next.js 15) — tiny PPR demo.
  • Doc 03 Part 3 (AI SDK) — streaming chat with one tool call.
  • Doc 03 Part 4 (state) — port one toy app to Zustand + TanStack Query.
  • Doc 07 — 2 machine-coding components.

Daily deliverables: a deployed Next.js app demonstrating Partial Prerendering (static shell + streamed dynamic hole). A streaming chat route with one tool/function call and visible token streaming. One toy app's data layer ported to TanStack Query (with optimistic update) + Zustand for client UI state. Two machine-coding components (autocomplete + modal) built to the B.7 checklist.

Done looks like: you can explain the four Next caches and the RSC serialization boundary aloud; the PPR demo shows a static shell with a streamed dynamic region; both components pass the machine-coding checklist (a11y + cleanup + states). B.3 has rows promoted to Strong.

Weeks 4–5 — Performance + reliability + security

  • Doc 05 — read fully.
  • Profile a real app; ship one INP / LCP / CLS win.
  • Add a CSP report-only on a real project.
  • Wire web-vitals beacon on a real project.

Daily deliverables: a profiling session with a saved flame chart + written diagnosis. Three shipped wins (one each LCP/INP/CLS) each with a before/after p75 screenshot. A Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only header live + a sample of collected violation reports. A web-vitals beacon posting to a real endpoint with a dashboard or log of real-user values.

Done looks like: you can run the FRSA triage table from memory; three metric wins are proven with field data (not Lighthouse lab); RUM is flowing and a CSP report-only is collecting violations. B.5 promoted to Strong.

Week 6 — System design (1)

  • Doc 06 — frameworks + cases 1–5 (Figma, Twitter, Netflix, Notion, Drive).
  • One case per day; speak aloud.

Daily deliverables: one recorded 35-minute walkthrough per case using RADIO, each with a data-model sketch and at least two tradeoffs raised unprompted. Day 1 Figma (CRDT, canvas rendering, cursors), Day 2 Twitter (feed fan-out, virtualization, pagination), Day 3 Netflix (preloading, adaptive media, image CDN), Day 4 Notion (block model, offline, sync), Day 5 Drive (uploads, chunking, conflict).

Done looks like: for at least two cases you can run RADIO end-to-end without notes, name the transport/consistency/rendering tradeoffs, and answer one curveball ("now make it offline-first"). Watch your own recordings and cut the rambling.

Week 7 — System design (2) + machine coding

  • Doc 06 — cases 6–10 (Slack, Stripe, Maps, Calendar, Autocomplete).
  • Doc 07 — 5 more machine-coding components.

Daily deliverables: five more recorded RADIO walkthroughs (Slack: presence + threads + unread; Stripe: secure embedded form + idempotency; Maps: tiling + viewport virtualization; Calendar: recurrence + timezones; Autocomplete: debounce + cache + a11y). Five components rebuilt from blank under 30 min each (infinite scroll, toast queue, tabs, rating, drag-and-drop) to the B.7 checklist.

Done looks like: 7–10 total cases performed aloud, with your strongest 2–3 polished to "interview-grade"; all 10 machine-coding components built at least once with a11y + cleanup. B.6 and B.7 promoted to Strong.

Week 8 — Behavioral + companies

  • Doc 08 — write 6 STAR stories.
  • Practice 3 questions per target company.
  • First mock interview (system design).

Daily deliverables: 6 written STAR stories (each <150 words, "I"-framed, metric in the Result). A mapping grid of stories → each target's rubric (Amazon LPs / Meta impact / Netflix judgment). Recorded answers to 3 questions per target, each cut under 2 minutes. One full system-design mock with a peer or mentor + written feedback.

Done looks like: every story has a measurable Result and shows a senior signal (ambiguity/conflict/influence/failure); each target's top-3 likely behavioral prompts have a polished spoken answer; you have written mock feedback with two action items. B.8 promoted to Strong.

Week 9 — Polish + mocks

  • Two mock interviews (1 coding + 1 system design).
  • Re-read Doc 08 Part 2 (negotiation).
  • Tune resume + LinkedIn; ask for referrals at target companies.

Daily deliverables: two mocks (1 coding with complexity narration, 1 system design) with written feedback and a fix list. A negotiation script you can recite (anchor, BATNA, competing-offers framing, "I'm excited — here's what would make this easy to say yes to"). A resume rewritten to lead each bullet with an impact metric; a LinkedIn headline aligned to target level. Referral requests sent.

Done looks like: mock feedback shows no repeat of week-8 weaknesses; resume bullets each lead with a measurable outcome; at least one referral in motion per target; negotiation script memorized.

Week 10 — Apply

  • Submit applications + referrals at target companies.
  • Continue daily routine.

Daily deliverables: applications submitted to all three targets (referral-first where possible). A tracking sheet (company, role, level, referrer, date, stage). Continued Part E daily routine so skills don't decay during the wait. A "batch" plan to cluster onsites.

Done looks like: all targets applied with referrals where available, a live application tracker, and an unbroken daily routine. Aim to time loops so onsites cluster in weeks 11–12 for offer leverage.

Weeks 11–12 — Onsites + offers

  • Cluster onsites within 2 weeks for parallel offer leverage.
  • Journal question themes after each loop.
  • Use Doc 08 Part 2 negotiation script on every offer.

Daily deliverables: the night before each loop, a 30-min warm-up (one polyfill, one DSA, one STAR rehearsal). After each loop, a journal entry of question themes + what to sharpen. On every offer, run the negotiation script — never accept the first number, always surface competing timelines.

Done looks like: onsites clustered for parallel offers; a post-loop journal feeding rapid iteration between loops; the negotiation script used on *every* offer (the single highest-ROI hour of the 12 weeks). Target outcome: a multi-offer position you negotiate from.

Part E — Daily routine

  • One polyfill OR type-level drill (Doc 02 / Doc 07).
  • One DSA problem (alternate easy / medium).
  • One system-design verbal walkthrough OR one machine-coding component (Doc 06 / 07).
  • Read one section of a category doc (15 min).
  • Re-rehearse one STAR story aloud (Doc 08).

Make the routine concrete so it survives a busy day. A ~60-minute template:

0:00–0:10  Polyfill or utility type from memory (rotate the list; no IDE help).
0:10–0:30  One DSA problem; say the pattern + Big-O out loud before coding.
0:30–0:50  Either a 20-min RADIO walkthrough OR a timed component rebuild.
0:50–0:58  Read one doc section; write one sentence of takeaway.
0:58–1:00  Speak one STAR story; check it has a measured Result.

Rules that make it stick: rehearse *aloud* (interviews are spoken, not typed); rotate so you revisit each topic every few days (spacing); and log a single metric per day (problems solved, components built) so streaks are visible. The routine is the floor, not the ceiling — the weekly phase deliverables are the real work.

Part F — Common prep mistakes

  • Treating each topic as one-and-done — repeat machine-coding components weekly.
  • Skipping behavioral until the week before. Behavioral fails more senior loops than coding.
  • Studying alone the whole time. Pair mocks accelerate growth dramatically.
  • Going broad without depth — pick 2–3 system designs you can perform brilliantly.
  • Ignoring negotiation prep. The hour spent on negotiation has the highest ROI of the 12 weeks.

Each mistake has a concrete countermeasure — install these as habits, not reminders:

MistakeWhy it sinks senior loopsCountermeasure
One-and-done topicsSkills decay; you freeze on a problem you "knew" a month agoWeekly rebuild of the same 5 components from blank, timed
Behavioral last-minuteSenior bar is judgment/influence; thin stories read as juniorWrite 6 stories by week 8; rehearse one aloud daily
Studying soloYou can't see your own blind spots or rambling≥1 pair mock/week from week 6; act on written feedback
Breadth over depthDepth on 3 designs wins offers; shallow on 10 wins nothingPick 2–3 designs, perform to "interview-grade"
Skipping negotiationLeaving 10–20% TC on the table for one unprepared hourMemorize the script; never accept the first number

Two additional senior-specific traps worth naming: (1) solving before scoping in system design — always state requirements and constraints first, even when you "know" the answer; interviewers grade the framework, not the destination. (2) happy-path machine coding — shipping the demo without states, a11y, or cleanup reads as mid-level no matter how fast you were.

Next: open Doc 02 (JavaScript / TypeScript) and start with the closures + event loop section. Begin Day 1.

Treat this as the operating manual for your prep. This doc is the spine. Every other doc (02–08) is a depth dive; this one tells you *what order to attack them in, how to measure yourself, and when you are done*. Read Part A to calibrate the bar, Part B to find your weak rows, Part C to pick targets, and Part D–F to execute. The progress tracker keys off the headings below — do not rename them. Part A — Who is a Senior FE in 2026? At FAANG-tier orgs in 2026, "Senior Frontend Engineer" (L5/E5/IC4) is expected to own end-to-end delivery of a meaningful surface, from architecture through ship, with measurable business impact. The bar is not "writes great React" — it is "ships a system the team can rely on for 18 months without rewriting". Concretely, the level transition from mid (L4/E4) to senior (L5/E5) is a transition from *task ownership* to *problem ownership*. A mid-level engineer is handed a well-specified ticket and closes it. A senior is handed an ambiguous problem ("checkout conversion is down 3% on mobile"), decomposes it, decides what to build vs buy vs defer, writes the design doc, gets buy-in, ships incrementally behind flags, instruments it, and owns the metric afterward. The interview loop is designed to detect this. Coding rounds check that you can still execute; system design and behavioral rounds check that you can *own*. What this means for your prep: you cannot pass a senior loop by grinding LeetCode alone. The differentiating signal is in the design doc you write in your head during a system-design round, the tradeoff you articulate without prompting, and the STAR story where you describe influencing a decision you did not have authority over. Core competencies (the senior rubric) Pillar What "senior" looks like Code Idiomatic JS/TS, React 19, modern CSS. Reviews others productively. Refactors with intent. Architecture Owns design of a multi-surface system. Articulates tradeoffs (RSC vs SPA, CRDT vs OT, edge vs node). Performance Hits Core Web Vitals on real users (p75 LCP < 2.0 s, INP < 200 ms, CLS < 0.1). Reads flame charts. Reliability Designs for failure. Error boundaries, retries, idempotency, graceful degradation are second nature. Security CSP, Trusted Types, SRI, cookie hygiene, supply-chain awareness, no secrets in client. Availability Atomic deploys + one-click rollback, synthetic monitoring, multi-region SSR or fallback. Collaboration Mentors. Writes design docs. Drives postmortems. Influences without authority. Product Pushes back on PM with data, but ships what users actually need. Knows the conversion funnel. How interviewers actually map to these pillars — and where loops are won and lost: Round Pillars probed Where seniors fail it Coding (DSA) Code Can solve, but narrates nothing; no complexity analysis; freezes on follow-up. Machine coding Code, Performance, Reliability Builds happy path only; no a11y, no error/loading/empty states, no cleanup. System design Architecture, Performance, Reliability, Availability Jumps to a solution; never states requirements or tradeoffs; no failure modes. Behavioral Collaboration, Product Stories are "we"-heavy, no conflict, no measurable outcome, no reflection. Self-test for the whole rubric: *Pick the last non-trivial thing you shipped. Can you, in 90 seconds, state the problem, two design alternatives you rejected and why, the metric it moved, and what you would do differently?* If any of those four is blank, that pillar is your weak spot. Part B — Skills Inventory (read row by row) Mark each row Strong / OK / Weak. The Weak rows tell you where to focus first. Scoring rubric so the marks are honest, not aspirational: Strong = you can teach it on a whiteboard cold, including edge cases and at least one tradeoff, and you have shipped it. OK = you can use it with docs open and recognize it in code review, but you would hesitate explaining it live. Weak = you would need to study before an interview question on it. Re-score every two weeks. A row only moves to Strong after you have done the "highest-leverage drill" listed for it at least three times across different days (spacing beats cramming for retention). Senior-level mastery means: you reason about *ordering and lifetime*, not just syntax. You can predict the exact interleaving of sync code, microtasks, and macrotasks; you know a closure captures a *variable binding* not a value; you know WeakMap / WeakRef exist to avoid leaks in caches keyed by DOM nodes; and you can write a hand-rolled promise/scheduler from scratch. 1-line self-test: Without running it, give the full output order of a snippet mixing console.log , setTimeout(…,0) , Promise.resolve().then , and queueMicrotask . Highest-leverage drill: Implement Promise from scratch ( then / catch / finally / all / race / allSettled ) passing the relevant Promises/A+ ordering cases. It forces the microtask model into muscle memory. // The canonical event-loop ordering question. Output: 1, 4, 3, 2 console.log(1); // sync setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0); // macrotask Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3)); // microtask console.log(4); // sync // All microtasks (3) drain before the next macrotask (2) ever runs. // Closures capture bindings, not snapshots — the classic loop trap: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log('var', i)); // 3,3,3 for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) setTimeout(() => console.log('let', j)); // 0,1,2 // `let` creates a fresh binding per iteration; `var` shares one. B.2 TypeScript Generics with constraints; conditional types + infer; mapped types; template literals. Discriminated unions; satisfies; const generics; branded types.
