02 — JavaScript + TypeScript Deep Dive (2026)

Fundamentals · Async · 10+ polyfills · Advanced TS patterns · 50 drills

Merged from v1/02 (JS fundamentals), v2/02 (TS + React-adjacent), and v3/10 (polyfills + advanced TS + 50 drills). One self-contained doc for everything JS/TS a senior FE must know cold.

Part 1 — JavaScript fundamentals

1.1 Closures and lexical scope

A closure is a function plus the lexical environment it was created in. Closures are how data is encapsulated and how callbacks remember context.

function counter() {
  let n = 0;
  return {
    inc: () => ++n,
    get: () => n,
  };
}
const c = counter();
c.inc(); c.inc(); c.get(); // 2
  • Common bug: forgetting let/const inside loops shares one variable; let creates per-iteration binding.
  • Memory: closures over large objects can prevent GC. Null out references when done.

Mechanism

Every function value carries a hidden internal slot [[Environment]] pointing at the *lexical environment record* active when the function was created — not when it is called. An environment record is a map of variable name → binding (a mutable cell), plus a pointer to its outer record. Name resolution walks this chain outward until a binding is found. The closure keeps the entire chain reachable, so the bindings it references survive after the outer function returns. Crucially, a closure closes over variables (bindings), not values — multiple closures over the same let n share one cell, which is why inc and get above see the same n.

var is function-scoped: one binding per function activation. let/const are block-scoped and, inside a for header, the spec creates a fresh binding per iteration and copies the previous value forward (CreatePerIterationEnvironment). That is the whole reason the loop fix below works.

Worked example — the classic loop gotcha

// BUG: var → single shared binding. All callbacks read the final i (3).
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i));
// Output: 3 3 3

// FIX: let → one fresh binding per iteration.
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) setTimeout(() => console.log(j));
// Output: 0 1 2

Why: with var, all three timer callbacks close over the *same* i; by the time any macrotask runs the loop has finished and i === 3. With let, each iteration's callback closes over its own j cell frozen at that iteration's value. The pre-let fix was an IIFE per iteration: (function(k){ setTimeout(()=>console.log(k)); })(i) — manufacturing a fresh scope manually.

Gotcha: a closure prevents GC of *everything reachable through the captured scope record*, even variables it never reads, because engines often capture the whole record. If a giant buffer and a tiny id share a scope and you return a closure using only id, some engines still pin buffer. Defensive fix: narrow the capture (const id = obj.id; return () => id;) or null the large var.

1.2 The this keyword

  • Method call: this is the object before the dot.
  • Function call (non-strict): this is global; strict: undefined.
  • new f(): this is the new object.
  • Arrow function: this is lexical (inherited from enclosing scope).
  • bind/call/apply explicitly set this.

Mechanism

this is not lexical for ordinary functions — it is bound fresh on every call by the call site, per these rules in priority order: (1) new → a brand-new object whose prototype is f.prototype; (2) explicit call/apply/bind → the given thisArg (boxed to an object in sloppy mode, left as-is in strict); (3) method call obj.f() → obj; (4) plain call f() → undefined in strict mode / globalThis in sloppy mode. Arrow functions have no own this: they capture this from the enclosing lexical scope at creation time and ignore all four rules above — call/bind cannot change an arrow's this.

Worked example

"use strict";
const obj = {
  val: 42,
  reg() { return this?.val; },
  arrow: () => this?.val,          // `this` is module/undefined, NOT obj
};
obj.reg();                          // 42  (method call → this = obj)
const f = obj.reg; f();             // undefined here `this` is undefined (strict plain call)
obj.reg.call({ val: 7 });           // 7   (explicit binding)
obj.arrow();                        // undefined (lexical this, captured outside obj)

Gotcha — lost this in callbacks. el.addEventListener('click', obj.handler) calls handler as a plain function, so this is the element (DOM) or undefined, not obj. Fixes: obj.handler.bind(obj), or define handler = () => {...} as an arrow class field so it captures the instance. The arrow-field trade-off: one closure per instance (not shared on the prototype), costing memory for many instances.

1.3 Prototypes and classes

class Animal {
  #name;                       // private
  constructor(name) { this.#name = name; }
  get name() { return this.#name; }
  static of(name) { return new Animal(name); }
}
class Dog extends Animal {
  bark() { return `${this.name}: woof!`; }
}

Mechanism

Objects have an internal [[Prototype]] (exposed as __proto__, read via Object.getPrototypeOf, set via Object.create). Property reads that miss on the own object walk the prototype chain until found or null. class is sugar over the prototype system: instance methods live on Dog.prototype, static members on the Dog constructor itself, and extends wires Dog.prototype.[[Prototype]] = Animal.prototype and Dog.[[Prototype]] = Animal (so statics inherit too). #name is a true private field — not a property — keyed by a per-class private name; access from outside the class is a *syntax* error, and #x in obj is the safe brand-check.

Worked example — chain resolution and super

const d = new Dog("Rex");
d.bark();                                   // "Rex: woof!"
Object.getPrototypeOf(d) === Dog.prototype; // true
Object.getPrototypeOf(Dog.prototype) === Animal.prototype; // true
d.hasOwnProperty("bark");                   // false — bark is on the prototype
Dog.of === Animal.of;                       // true — static inherited via Dog.[[Proto]]=Animal

class Cat extends Animal {
  constructor(n) { super(n); }              // MUST call super before using `this`
  describe() { return super.name; }         // super → Animal.prototype getter, `this`=instance
}

Gotcha: referencing this in a subclass constructor *before* super() throws a ReferenceError (the instance does not exist yet under the derived-class new-binding semantics). Also, class declarations are not hoisted like function (they sit in the temporal dead zone), and class bodies are always strict mode.

1.4 Event loop, microtasks, macrotasks

Single thread. Stack runs to empty → microtasks (Promise, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) → next macrotask (setTimeout, I/O) → rAF before next paint.

  • Promise.then callbacks are microtasks; setTimeout(fn, 0) is a macrotask.
  • Long task = > 50 ms on main thread = INP killer.
  • scheduler.yield() (2026) lets you split work without losing continuation; falls back to setTimeout(0).

Mechanism

One call stack, one message queue per task source, and a separate microtask queue. The loop: pick one macrotask (timer, I/O, message, DOM event) → run it to completion → drain the entire microtask queue (including microtasks queued *by* microtasks) → run rendering steps (requestAnimationFrame callbacks, then style/layout/paint) if it's time → back to the next macrotask. Microtasks therefore always run before the next macrotask and before paint. await x schedules the continuation as a microtask once x settles. Starvation hazard: an infinite chain of microtasks blocks rendering forever, while infinite macrotasks still allow paints between them.

Worked example — predict the exact order

console.log("A");
setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0);          // macrotask
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("C")); // microtask
queueMicrotask(() => console.log("D"));         // microtask
(async () => { console.log("E"); await null; console.log("F"); })();
console.log("G");
// Output: A E G C D F B

Why: synchronous run prints A, then the async IIFE runs synchronously up to await → E, then G. Now the stack empties. Microtask queue in enqueue order: C, D, then F (the awaited continuation was enqueued at the await). Drain → C D F. Only then the timer macrotask → B.

Gotcha: people expect await null to "do nothing" — it still yields a microtask even though null isn't a thenable, so F runs after the already-queued C/D. And setTimeout(fn, 0) is clamped to ≥4ms after 5 nested timers (HTML spec), so it is never truly immediate; use queueMicrotask or a MessageChannel for genuinely fast deferral.

1.5 Promises, async/await, AbortController

const ac = new AbortController();
try {
  const r = await fetch(url, { signal: ac.signal });
  if (!r.ok) throw new Error(r.statusText);
  return await r.json();
} catch (e) {
  if (e.name === "AbortError") return;
  throw e;
} finally { /* cleanup */ }
// Cancel after 5s
setTimeout(() => ac.abort(), 5000);
  • async functions always return a Promise.
  • await pauses ONLY the enclosing async function — not the whole runtime.
  • Use Promise.allSettled when you want all results, not first-fail.

Mechanism

A Promise is a state machine: pending → fulfilled | rejected, settling once, irreversibly. .then(onF, onR) registers reactions that run as microtasks after settlement; returning a thenable from a handler causes the chain to *adopt* it (flattening). async/await is generator-driven sugar: await e evaluates e, wraps it with Promise.resolve, suspends the function, and resumes (with the value, or by throwing the rejection) in a microtask when it settles. AbortController exposes a signal; abort(reason) fires the signal's abort event and sets signal.aborted. Web APIs that accept { signal } reject with a DOMException named AbortError (in 2026, with signal.reason as the rejection value). AbortSignal.timeout(ms) and AbortSignal.any([...]) compose signals declaratively.

Worked example — order and error propagation

async function f() {
  console.log(1);
  await Promise.resolve();
  console.log(3);          // resumes as a microtask
  return "done";
}
console.log(0); f().then(v => console.log(v)); console.log(2);
// Output: 0 1 2 3 done

Gotchas: (1) an unhandled rejection fires unhandledrejection; a .catch attached *later in the same tick* still prevents it, but a missing terminal .catch in production crashes Node. (2) try/catch around await catches async rejections, but try { somePromise(); } catch does not — you must await. (3) Forgetting return await inside try/finally can swallow errors or let finally run before the promise settles. (4) A synchronous throw before the first await in an async function still becomes a *rejected promise*, never a thrown exception to the caller.

1.6 Generators + async iterators

async function* pages(url) {
  let cursor = null;
  do {
    const r = await fetch(`${url}?cursor=${cursor}`);
    const j = await r.json();
    yield j.items;
    cursor = j.nextCursor;
  } while (cursor);
}
for await (const batch of pages("/api/list")) { /* process */ }

Mechanism

A generator function returns an iterator that is also iterable. yield suspends execution and hands a value out; .next(v) resumes, and v becomes the *result of the suspended yield expression* — making generators two-way channels (the basis of coroutine schedulers and how early async/await desugared via co). .return() and .throw() inject completion/exceptions at the suspension point, which is why try/finally inside a generator runs on early termination. An async generator yields Promises and is consumed with for await...of, which awaits each next(); it pairs lazy pull-based iteration with async I/O — ideal for paginated APIs and streams without buffering everything in memory.

Worked example — two-way communication and lazy evaluation

function* convo() {
  const name = yield "what is your name?";   // value sent via next()
  const age = yield `hi ${name}, age?`;
  return `${name} is ${age}`;
}
const it = convo();
it.next();          // { value: "what is your name?", done: false }
it.next("Ada");     // { value: "hi Ada, age?", done: false }
it.next(36);        // { value: "Ada is 36", done: true }

function* nats() { let n = 0; while (true) yield n++; } // infinite, but lazy
const g = nats(); g.next().value; g.next().value;       // 0, 1 — pulled on demand

Gotcha: the value passed to the first .next() is discarded (there is no suspended yield to receive it). Also, for await...of processes items sequentially (awaits each before pulling the next), so an async generator does not give you concurrency for free — fan-out needs an explicit pool (see Part 4). Always wrap the loop in try/finally or call .return() to release resources if you break early.

1.7 ES Modules vs CommonJS

  • ESM static; CJS dynamic.
  • ESM enables tree-shaking; CJS does not.
  • Dynamic import() returns a Promise; works in both module systems.
  • In 2026, Node fully supports ESM with .mjs / "type":"module"; many libs are ESM-only.

Mechanism

ESM has three phases: parse (collect import/export statically — bindings must be resolvable without running code), instantiate/link (allocate the module record, create *live bindings*, wire imports to exporters' cells), then evaluate (run module bodies in dependency order, top-level await allowed). Imports are live read-only views of the exporter's binding, not copies — if the exporter reassigns count, importers see the new value. CJS require runs synchronously and returns a *snapshot* of module.exports (a value copy at call time); circular requires can yield a partially-populated object. ESM's static structure is what enables tree-shaking and top-level await; CJS cannot be statically tree-shaken because module.exports is computed at runtime.

Worked example — live bindings vs snapshot

// counter.mjs
export let count = 0;
export function inc() { count++; }
// main.mjs
import { count, inc } from "./counter.mjs";
console.log(count); // 0
inc();
console.log(count); // 1  — live binding reflects the update
// `count = 5` here is a SyntaxError: imported bindings are read-only.

// Interop: default import of a CJS module gets module.exports
import cjs from "./legacy.cjs";        // cjs === module.exports
const { readFile } = await import("node:fs/promises"); // dynamic, returns a Promise

Gotchas: (1) ESM has no __dirname/require; use import.meta.url + new URL('.', import.meta.url). (2) You cannot require() an ESM-only package from CJS without await import(). (3) Named imports from a CJS module work via Node's static analysis but can fail for computed exports — fall back to import pkg from "..."; const { x } = pkg;. (4) Top-level await in a module makes it async and delays dependents' evaluation.

1.8 Memory and GC

  • JS uses mark-and-sweep + generational GC.
  • Leaks: detached DOM nodes held by closures, timers not cleared, global listeners.
  • WeakMap / WeakRef break GC cycles for caches.

Mechanism

Modern engines (V8) use a generational, mark-and-sweep/compacting collector. New objects go in a small *young generation* (scavenger, fast copying GC); survivors are promoted to the *old generation* (mark-sweep-compact, often incremental/concurrent to avoid jank). Reachability — not reference counting — defines liveness: an object is live iff reachable from a GC root (globals, the active stack, etc.). This means cycles are collected fine; the real leaks are *unintended reachability*. WeakMap/WeakSet hold keys weakly (entries vanish when the key is otherwise unreachable, and they're non-iterable); WeakRef + FinalizationRegistry give you weak references and best-effort finalization callbacks (never rely on their timing).

Worked example — a real leak and its fix

const cache = new Map();                 // LEAK: strong refs keep nodes alive forever
function track(node) { cache.set(node, computeMeta(node)); }
// even after node is removed from the DOM, the Map pins it → detached-DOM leak.

const wcache = new WeakMap();            // FIX: entry dies with the node
function trackWeak(node) { wcache.set(node, computeMeta(node)); }

// Classic listener/timer leak:
function mount(el) {
  const id = setInterval(poll, 1000);
  const onClick = () => {};
  el.addEventListener("click", onClick);
  return () => { clearInterval(id); el.removeEventListener("click", onClick); }; // cleanup!
}

Gotcha: the four most common FE leaks are (1) timers/intervals never cleared, (2) listeners on window/document not removed on unmount, (3) closures capturing large structures kept alive by a long-lived callback, (4) growing module-level caches with no eviction. WeakMap cannot be iterated and only accepts object keys — by design, since iteration would expose GC timing. Profile with DevTools "Detached elements" and heap-snapshot retainer paths, not guesswork.

Part 2 — Polyfills you must dictate live

State the contract, write the code, walk through edge cases (empty, sync vs async, this binding, errors). Then optionally talk perf.

2.1 Promise.all

Contract: takes an iterable of values/thenables; resolves to an array of results in input order once all fulfill; rejects immediately on the first rejection (fail-fast); resolves to [] for empty input. Non-thenable values pass through via Promise.resolve.

Promise.myAll = function (iter) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const arr = Array.from(iter);
    const results = new Array(arr.length);
    let pending = arr.length;
    if (pending === 0) return resolve([]);
    arr.forEach((p, i) => Promise.resolve(p).then(
      v => { results[i] = v; if (--pending === 0) resolve(results); },
      reject
    ));
  });
};

Edge cases: empty → resolve([]); order preserved via index i even though settle order varies; first reject wins and later settlements are ignored (a Promise settles once). Usage / complexity:

await Promise.myAll([1, Promise.resolve(2), Promise.resolve(3)]); // [1,2,3]

Time O(n) to schedule, settles when the slowest fulfills (or first rejects). Space O(n) for results.

2.2 Promise.race / any / allSettled

race: settles (resolve *or* reject) with the first settled input. any: resolves with the first *fulfilled*; rejects with AggregateError only if all reject. allSettled: never rejects; resolves to {status, value|reason}[]. Empty input: race hangs forever (nothing to settle — a known interview point), any([]) rejects with an empty AggregateError, allSettled([]) resolves [].

Promise.myRace = (iter) => new Promise((res, rej) => {
  for (const p of iter) Promise.resolve(p).then(res, rej);
});
Promise.mySettled = (iter) => Promise.myAll(Array.from(iter).map(p =>
  Promise.resolve(p).then(
    value => ({ status: "fulfilled", value }),
    reason => ({ status: "rejected", reason })
  )
));
Promise.myAny = (iter) => new Promise((res, rej) => {
  const arr = Array.from(iter);
  const errors = new Array(arr.length);
  let pending = arr.length;
  if (pending === 0) return rej(new AggregateError([], "all rejected"));
  arr.forEach((p, i) => Promise.resolve(p).then(res,
    e => { errors[i] = e; if (--pending === 0) rej(new AggregateError(errors)); }));
});

Usage / complexity:

await Promise.myRace([slow, fast]);                 // fast's settlement
await Promise.myAny([reject1, resolveLate]);        // resolveLate's value
await Promise.mySettled([ok, bad]); // [{status:'fulfilled',...},{status:'rejected',...}]

All O(n) scheduling. mySettled builds on myAll because mapping rejections into fulfilled wrappers means nothing ever rejects.

2.3 debounce (leading/trailing/maxWait)

Contract: coalesce a burst of calls; invoke once after wait ms of silence (trailing) and/or immediately on the first call (leading). maxWait guarantees an invocation at least every maxWait ms during a sustained burst. Preserve this and the *latest* args; expose cancel/flush.

function debounce(fn, wait, { leading = false, trailing = true, maxWait } = {}) {
  let timer, lastCallTime, lastInvoke = 0, lastArgs, lastThis;
  function invoke(t) { lastInvoke = t; fn.apply(lastThis, lastArgs); lastArgs = lastThis = null; }
  function later() {
    const t = Date.now();
    const since = t - lastCallTime;
    if (since >= wait || (maxWait && t - lastInvoke >= maxWait)) {
      return trailing && lastArgs ? invoke(t) : (timer = null);
    }
    timer = setTimeout(later, wait - since);
  }
  function debounced(...args) {
    const t = Date.now();
    lastArgs = args; lastThis = this; lastCallTime = t;
    if (!timer) {
      if (leading) invoke(t);
      timer = setTimeout(later, wait);
    }
  }
  debounced.cancel = () => { clearTimeout(timer); timer = null; lastArgs = null; };
  debounced.flush = () => { if (timer) { clearTimeout(timer); invoke(Date.now()); timer = null; } };
  return debounced;
}

Edge cases: trailing-only is the default (search-as-you-type); leading+trailing fires on both ends; maxWait prevents starvation under a never-ending burst. cancel drops a pending trailing call; flush forces it now. Usage / complexity:

const onSearch = debounce(q => fetchResults(q), 300, { maxWait: 1000 });
input.addEventListener("input", e => onSearch(e.target.value));

O(1) per call. Gotcha: never bind the args at schedule time — capture *latest* lastArgs, since the user's final keystroke is what matters.

2.4 throttle

Contract: invoke at most once per wait ms. Leading edge fires immediately; a trailing call fires once at the end of the window with the latest args. Use for scroll/resize/mousemove where you want a steady rate, not a single deferred call.

function throttle(fn, wait) {
  let last = 0, timer = null, lastArgs, lastThis;
  return function (...args) {
    const now = Date.now();
    const remaining = wait - (now - last);
    lastArgs = args; lastThis = this;
    if (remaining <= 0) { last = now; fn.apply(this, args); }
    else if (!timer) {
      timer = setTimeout(() => { last = Date.now(); timer = null; fn.apply(lastThis, lastArgs); }, remaining);
    }
  };
}

Edge cases: first call always runs (last = 0 → remaining <= 0); during the window only the last queued args fire on the trailing timer; resets cleanly afterward. Usage / complexity:

const onScroll = throttle(() => updateHeader(), 100);
window.addEventListener("scroll", onScroll);

O(1) per call. debounce vs throttle: debounce = "wait until activity stops"; throttle = "fire on a fixed cadence regardless of how long activity lasts."

2.5 curry

Contract: transform f(a,b,c) into a function callable as f(a)(b)(c), f(a,b)(c), or f(a,b,c). Invoke the original once enough args (default fn.length) are accumulated; preserve this.

function curry(fn, arity = fn.length) {
  return function curried(...args) {
    if (args.length >= arity) return fn.apply(this, args);
    return (...more) => curried.apply(this, [...args, ...more]);
  };
}

Edge cases: variadic functions need an explicit arity (fn.length ignores rest/defaults). Over-application (f(a,b,c,d)) forwards extra args to fn. Usage / complexity:

const add = curry((a, b, c) => a + b + c);
add(1)(2)(3);   // 6
add(1, 2)(3);   // 6
add(1)(2, 3);   // 6

O(arity) closures in the worst (fully-curried) path. Gotcha: placeholders (_) for skipping args require extra bookkeeping; mention you'd extend curried to scan for a placeholder sentinel.

2.6 Function.prototype.bind

Contract: return a new function with this permanently fixed to ctx and preset args prepended (partial application). When the bound function is used with new, the bound this is ignored and the freshly-constructed instance is used; the prototype chain must be preserved.

Function.prototype.myBind = function (ctx, ...preset) {
  const fn = this;
  function bound(...args) {
    return fn.apply(this instanceof bound ? this : ctx, [...preset, ...args]);
  }
  bound.prototype = Object.create(fn.prototype || null);
  return bound;
};

Edge cases: this instanceof bound detects construction so new (fn.bind(x))() ignores x; Object.create(fn.prototype) keeps instanceof working through the bound function. Usage / complexity:

function greet(greeting, name) { return `${greeting}, ${name}`; }
const hi = greet.myBind(null, "Hi");
hi("Ada");                       // "Hi, Ada"
function P(x){ this.x = x; }
const BP = P.myBind(null);
(new BP(5)).x;                   // 5 — bound this ignored under new

O(1) per call (plus arg spread). Note: native bind also sets bound.length/name and marks the result non-constructable in some cases — the instanceof trick is the canonical interview version.

2.7 deepClone (cycles + Map + Set + Date)

Contract: recursively copy a value so the clone shares no mutable references with the original; handle cycles (via a WeakMap of seen→clone), Date, RegExp, Map, Set, arrays, and plain/prototyped objects; preserve the prototype and symbol keys.

function deepClone(value, seen = new WeakMap()) {
  if (value === null || typeof value !== "object") return value;
  if (seen.has(value)) return seen.get(value);
  if (value instanceof Date) return new Date(value);
  if (value instanceof RegExp) return new RegExp(value.source, value.flags);
  if (value instanceof Map) {
    const m = new Map(); seen.set(value, m);
    value.forEach((v, k) => m.set(deepClone(k, seen), deepClone(v, seen)));
    return m;
  }
  if (value instanceof Set) {
    const s = new Set(); seen.set(value, s);
    value.forEach(v => s.add(deepClone(v, seen)));
    return s;
  }
  if (Array.isArray(value)) {
    const arr = []; seen.set(value, arr);
    value.forEach((v, i) => arr[i] = deepClone(v, seen));
    return arr;
  }
  const out = Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(value));
  seen.set(value, out);
  for (const k of Reflect.ownKeys(value)) out[k] = deepClone(value[k], seen);
  return out;
}

Edge cases: the seen map is set before recursing into children, so a self-referential object maps to its own clone (cycle-safe). Reflect.ownKeys includes symbol keys and non-enumerable keys (note: it copies values, not descriptors — getters become plain values). Usage / complexity:

const a = { d: new Date(), m: new Map([["k", 1]]) }; a.self = a;
const b = deepClone(a); b.self === b;        // true — cycle preserved

O(n) over all reachable nodes/edges. 2026 note: the built-in structuredClone() covers most of this (cycles, Map/Set/Date/ArrayBuffer) but drops functions, prototypes, and symbols — know when to hand-roll.

2.8 deepEqual

Contract: structural equality. Object.is for primitives (so NaN===NaN is true, +0!==-0); same constructor; same own keys (including symbols); recursively equal values; handle Date by timestamp.

function deepEqual(a, b) {
  if (Object.is(a, b)) return true;
  if (typeof a !== "object" || typeof b !== "object" || a === null || b === null) return false;
  if (a.constructor !== b.constructor) return false;
  if (a instanceof Date) return a.getTime() === b.getTime();
  const ka = Reflect.ownKeys(a), kb = Reflect.ownKeys(b);
  if (ka.length !== kb.length) return false;
  for (const k of ka) if (!kb.includes(k) || !deepEqual(a[k], b[k])) return false;
  return true;
}

Edge cases: Object.is handles NaN/±0 correctly; the constructor check rejects {} vs Object.create(null) and array vs object. To support Map/Set add branches comparing sizes then entries; to be fully cycle-safe, thread a seen pair-set. Usage / complexity:

deepEqual({ a: [1, NaN] }, { a: [1, NaN] }); // true
deepEqual([1,2], { 0:1, 1:2 });              // false (constructor differs)

Worst case O(n) but kb.includes(k) makes it O(n²) for wide objects — swap to a Set of kb for O(n). Gotcha: as written it lacks Map/Set and cycle handling — call that out and offer the extension.

2.9 memoize

Contract: cache results keyed by arguments so a pure function runs once per distinct input. Default key is JSON.stringify(args); allow a custom keyFn; preserve this; expose clear.

function memoize(fn, keyFn = (...a) => JSON.stringify(a)) {
  const cache = new Map();
  function memo(...args) {
    const k = keyFn(...args);
    if (cache.has(k)) return cache.get(k);
    const v = fn.apply(this, args); cache.set(k, v); return v;
  }
  memo.clear = () => cache.clear();
  return memo;
}

Edge cases: JSON.stringify is order-sensitive for object args ({a,b} ≠ {b,a}) and drops functions/undefined — pass a keyFn for object/array args. For single-object-arg pure functions, a WeakMap keyed by reference is leak-free and faster. Unbounded growth is the main risk — combine with the LRU below for eviction. Usage / complexity:

const fib = memoize(n => (n < 2 ? n : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)));
fib(40); // O(n) instead of exponential — memoized recursion

O(1) average lookup; O(key-size) to hash. Gotcha: memoizing impure or this-dependent functions returns stale results.

2.10 EventEmitter

Contract: on(ev, fn) subscribes and returns an unsubscribe function; once auto-removes after first emit; off removes; emit(ev, ...args) invokes all current listeners. A throwing listener must not stop the others.

class EventEmitter {
  #h = new Map();
  on(ev, fn) {
    (this.#h.get(ev) || this.#h.set(ev, new Set()).get(ev)).add(fn);
    return () => this.off(ev, fn);
  }
  once(ev, fn) { const w = (...a) => { this.off(ev, w); fn(...a); }; return this.on(ev, w); }
  off(ev, fn) { this.#h.get(ev)?.delete(fn); }
  emit(ev, ...args) { this.#h.get(ev)?.forEach(fn => { try { fn(...args); } catch (e) { setTimeout(() => { throw e; }); } }); }
}

Edge cases: Set gives O(1) add/remove and dedups identical listeners. The try/catch + deferred re-throw isolates one bad listener while surfacing the error to the global handler. once wraps fn and unsubscribes the wrapper first so re-entrancy is safe. Usage / complexity:

const bus = new EventEmitter();
const off = bus.on("tick", n => console.log(n));
bus.once("init", () => console.log("ready"));
bus.emit("init"); bus.emit("tick", 1); off();

O(listeners) per emit. Gotcha: mutating the listener set during emit — iterating a Set you also delete from (as once does) is safe in JS, but if you switch to an array, snapshot it ([...arr]) before iterating.

2.11 LRU cache (Map iteration order trick)

Contract: fixed-capacity cache evicting the least-recently-used entry on overflow. get/set are O(1) and both count as "use." Exploits that JS Map preserves insertion order and lets you delete+reinsert to mark recency.

class LRU {
  constructor(max) { this.max = max; this.map = new Map(); }
  get(k) {
    if (!this.map.has(k)) return undefined;
    const v = this.map.get(k);
    this.map.delete(k); this.map.set(k, v);  // bump to most recent
    return v;
  }
  set(k, v) {
    if (this.map.has(k)) this.map.delete(k);
    else if (this.map.size >= this.max) this.map.delete(this.map.keys().next().value);
    this.map.set(k, v);
  }
}

Edge cases: the oldest key is map.keys().next().value (first inserted); deleting then re-inserting on every access keeps insertion order == recency order. Updating an existing key must delete-first so it moves to the tail. Usage / complexity:

const c = new LRU(2);
c.set("a",1); c.set("b",2); c.get("a"); c.set("c",3); // evicts "b" (LRU)
c.get("b"); // undefined

O(1) per op. Alternative: the classic hashmap + doubly-linked-list implementation gives the same O(1) without relying on Map ordering — mention it as the language-agnostic version.

2.12 retry with exponential backoff + jitter

Contract: call an async fn; on rejection retry up to retries times with delay growing as 2^i * baseMs, randomized (full jitter) to avoid thundering-herd synchronization. Re-throw the last error if all attempts fail.

async function retry(fn, { retries = 3, baseMs = 200 } = {}) {
  for (let i = 0; i < retries; i++) {
    try { return await fn(); }
    catch (e) {
      if (i === retries - 1) throw e;
      const sleep = Math.random() * Math.pow(2, i) * baseMs;
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, sleep));
    }
  }
}

Edge cases: the last attempt re-throws instead of sleeping; full jitter (Math.random() * cap) decorrelates concurrent clients better than fixed backoff. Production hardening: cap the delay (Math.min(maxMs, ...)), respect an AbortSignal, and only retry idempotent/transient failures (network, 429, 503) — never a 400/validation error. Usage / complexity:

const data = await retry(() => fetch(url).then(r => { if (!r.ok) throw r; return r.json(); }),
                         { retries: 5, baseMs: 100 });

O(retries) attempts; total wall time bounded by the backoff sum. Gotcha: retrying non-idempotent POSTs can double-submit — add an idempotency key.

Part 3 — Advanced TypeScript

3.1 Generics with constraints

function pick<T, K extends keyof T>(o: T, keys: K[]): Pick<T, K> {
  return keys.reduce((acc, k) => ({ ...acc, [k]: o[k] }), {} as Pick<T, K>);
}

Mechanism: K extends keyof T constrains K to the *literal union of T's keys*, so the compiler knows each k indexes T and the return Pick<T,K> carries the exact selected properties with their original types — no any, no widening. The constraint is also the upper bound used when inferring K from the keys argument.

type User = { id: number; name: string; admin: boolean };
const u: User = { id: 1, name: "Ada", admin: true };
const r = pick(u, ["id", "name"]);   // type: Pick<User,"id"|"name"> = {id:number; name:string}
r.id;          // number ✓
// pick(u, ["xyz"]);  // ✗ Error: "xyz" is not assignable to keyof User
// r.admin;            // ✗ Error: Property 'admin' does not exist on the result

Prevents: passing a key that doesn't exist on the object, and reading a property that wasn't picked — both become compile-time errors instead of runtime undefined.

3.2 Conditional types + infer

type Awaited<T> = T extends Promise<infer U> ? Awaited<U> : T;
type Params<F> = F extends (...args: infer P) => unknown ? P : never;
type Ret<F> = F extends (...args: any) => infer R ? R : never;

Mechanism: a conditional type A extends B ? X : Y is the type-level if; infer U introduces a fresh type variable *captured by pattern-matching* the type being tested. Awaited recurses to unwrap nested promises. Conditional types over a naked type parameter also *distribute* over unions (T extends any ? ... : ... applies per-member). This is the backbone of the lib's ReturnType, Parameters, Awaited.

type A = Awaited<Promise<Promise<number>>>;      // number
type P = Params<(a: string, b: number) => void>; // [a: string, b: number]
type R = Ret<() => User>;                         // User
declare function call<F extends (...a: any) => any>(f: F, ...a: Params<F>): Ret<F>;

Prevents: hand-writing/duplicating a function's parameter or return types — they're derived, so they can never drift out of sync with the implementation.

3.3 Mapped types + key remap

type DeepReadonly<T> = T extends object
  ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> } : T;
type Getters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K];
};

Mechanism: a mapped type { [K in keyof T]: ... } iterates a key union, transforming each property; as remaps the key (here built from a template literal), and mapping a key to never deletes it (a filtering trick). readonly/? modifiers can be added (+) or removed (-readonly, -?). DeepReadonly recurses structurally to freeze nested objects at the type level.

type U = DeepReadonly<{ a: { b: number } }>;
// const x: U = ...; x.a.b = 1; // ✗ Cannot assign to 'b', it is read-only

type G = Getters<{ name: string; age: number }>;
// { getName: () => string; getAge: () => number }

Prevents: mutating a value meant to be immutable (e.g. Redux state) at any depth, and lets you derive an API surface (getters) from a data shape so they cannot fall out of sync.

3.4 Template literal types

type ExtractParam<S extends string> =
  S extends `${string}:${infer P}/${infer R}` ? P | ExtractParam<R>
  : S extends `${string}:${infer P}` ? P : never;
type Params = ExtractParam<"/users/:id/posts/:postId">;  // "id" | "postId"

Mechanism: template literal types pattern-match *string structure* at compile time; combined with infer they parse strings into unions/objects. Here ExtractParam peels one :param/rest segment at a time, recursing on R until no / remains, collecting each param name into a union.

type RouteParams<S extends string> = { [K in ExtractParam<S>]: string };
declare function navigate<S extends string>(path: S, params: RouteParams<S>): void;
navigate("/users/:id/posts/:postId", { id: "1", postId: "9" }); // ✓
// navigate("/users/:id", {});  // ✗ Property 'id' is missing

Prevents: calling a typed router/link with missing or misspelled URL params — the param object's required keys are derived from the path string literal itself.

3.5 Discriminated unions + exhaustiveness

type Result<T, E = Error> =
  | { kind: "loading" }
  | { kind: "ok"; data: T }
  | { kind: "err"; error: E };
function show(r: Result<User>): JSX.Element {
  switch (r.kind) {
    case "loading": return <Spinner />;
    case "ok": return <Profile user={r.data} />;
    case "err": return <Err msg={r.error.message} />;
    default: { const _e: never = r; return _e; }  // exhaustive
  }
}

Mechanism: every member shares a literal discriminant (kind); checking it in a switch/if lets the compiler *narrow* r to the matching member, so r.data is only accessible in the "ok" branch. The default assigns the remaining r to never — if you later add a kind and forget a case, r is no longer never and the assignment fails to compile.

// Adding `| { kind: "empty" }` to Result makes `const _e: never = r` error:
//   Type '{ kind: "empty" }' is not assignable to type 'never'.

Prevents: accessing a field that only exists on one variant (e.g. r.data while loading), and forgetting to handle a newly added state — the never check turns a missing branch into a build error.

3.6 Branded types

type Brand<T, B> = T & { readonly __brand: B };
type UserId = Brand<string, "UserId">;
type Email = Brand<string, "Email">;
function getUser(id: UserId) { /* … */ }
// getUser("123") fails; you must brand: const id = "u1" as UserId;

Mechanism: structurally, UserId and Email are both string, so TS would treat them interchangeably. Intersecting with a phantom { __brand: B } (a property that never exists at runtime) makes them nominally distinct — you can only obtain one through a deliberate cast or a validator. Zero runtime cost; the brand is erased.

function makeEmail(s: string): Email {
  if (!s.includes("@")) throw new Error("bad email");
  return s as Email;            // the ONLY place the cast lives
}
const e = makeEmail("a@b.com");
getUser(e);                      // ✗ Email is not UserId — IDs can't be mixed up

Prevents: passing a raw or wrong-kind string where a validated/identifier type is required — e.g. swapping a UserId and an OrderId, or using an unvalidated string as an Email.

3.7 satisfies + const generics

const route = { path: "/users/:id", method: "GET" } satisfies
  { path: string; method: "GET"|"POST" };
// route.method narrows to "GET", not the union
function freeze<const T>(x: T): T { return x; }
const xs = freeze([1, 2, 3]); // readonly [1, 2, 3]

Mechanism: satisfies checks a value against a type without widening it to that type — you keep the precise inferred literal types *and* get validation. Contrast with a : T annotation (widens method to "GET"|"POST") and as T (no checking, can lie). A const type parameter (<const T>) tells inference to keep literal/tuple types instead of widening (like an inline as const).

// With an annotation you'd lose the literal:
const r2: { method: "GET" | "POST"; path: string } = { method: "GET", path: "/x" };
r2.method; // "GET" | "POST"  — widened, less useful
route.method; // "GET" — exact, via satisfies

Prevents: silently introducing a typo or out-of-set value (method: "GETT" fails the satisfies check) while still preserving narrow literal types for downstream inference — you don't have to trade safety for precision.

3.8 Type-level utilities you should be able to author

type DeepPartial<T> = T extends object ? { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> } : T;
type UnionToIntersection<U> = (U extends any ? (k: U) => void : never) extends ((k: infer I) => void) ? I : never;
type Equals<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type LastInUnion<U> = UnionToIntersection<U extends any ? (x: U) => 0 : never> extends ((x: infer L) => 0) ? L : never;
type UnionToTuple<U, L = LastInUnion<U>> = [U] extends [never] ? [] : [...UnionToTuple<Exclude<U, L>>, L];

Mechanism: UnionToIntersection abuses contravariant function-parameter positions: a union of (k: U) => void types, when matched against (k: infer I) => void, forces I to be the *intersection* of all U (contravariance flips union→intersection). Equals compares two types for mutual assignability via identical conditional generic signatures — the canonical exact-equality check used in type tests. UnionToTuple repeatedly extracts the "last" union member (also via the contravariant trick) and Excludes it, building a tuple.

type _1 = UnionToIntersection<{ a: 1 } | { b: 2 }>;     // { a: 1 } & { b: 2 }
type _2 = Equals<{ a: 1 }, { a: 1 }>;                    // true
type _3 = Equals<string, string | number>;              // false
type _4 = UnionToTuple<"a" | "b" | "c">;                 // ["a","b","c"] (order impl-defined)
type Assert<T extends true> = T;
type _check = Assert<Equals<DeepPartial<{a:{b:number}}>, {a?:{b?:number}}>>; // compiles ⇒ pass

Prevents: these power type-level tests (Assert<Equals<...>> fails to compile if a utility regresses) and exhaustive transforms — e.g. proving two complex types are structurally identical, or materializing a union as a tuple to iterate it in another type.

3.9 Compile-time performance

  • Avoid > 100-member unions in hot paths.
  • Cap recursive depth; consider tail-recursion patterns.
  • Use type vs interface intentionally (interface enables declaration merging).
  • Prefer satisfies over as — keeps inference + validates.

Mechanism & practical guidance

The checker memoizes structural-relation results, but deeply recursive conditional/mapped types and large union cross-products explode the work it must do — manifesting as slow editor IntelliSense and tsc time, occasionally Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite (ts2589). Mitigations: (1) cap recursion (e.g. a depth-counter tuple [...D, 1] that bottoms out), and prefer tail-recursive accumulator patterns which TS optimizes for recursive conditional types; (2) avoid materializing large unions — operate on them lazily rather than UnionToTuple-ing 1000 members; (3) annotate exported function return types so the checker doesn't re-infer them at every call site; (4) interface for object shapes that may merge or be extends-chained (cheaper, cached, declaration-mergeable), type for unions/conditionals/mapped; (5) prefer satisfies over as to keep precise inference while validating.

// Bounded recursion guard — stops runaway instantiation:
type BuildTuple<N extends number, A extends unknown[] = []> =
  A["length"] extends N ? A : BuildTuple<N, [...A, unknown]>;
type Range5 = BuildTuple<5>["length"]; // 5 — terminates via the length check

Diagnose with: tsc --extendedDiagnostics (check Instantiation count, Check time) and tsc --generateTrace ./trace opened in a trace viewer to find the hot types.

  • Implement Promise.race; explain why empty input hangs.

  • Write curry that supports both curry(fn)(a)(b)(c) and curry(fn)(a,b)(c).

  • Implement deepClone with cycle support.

  • Implement memoize with custom key + cache eviction (LRU).
  • Implement EventEmitter with once + off + return-unsubscribe.
  • Implement retry-with-exponential-backoff utility.
  • Implement an LRU cache (Map iteration order trick).
  • Implement pub/sub with namespaces.
  • Build typeahead with cancel + race-guard.
  • Build infinite-scroll list with IntersectionObserver.
  • Build modal with focus trap.
  • Build a toast provider.
  • Build a star rating component.
  • Build a multi-select autocomplete with chips.
  • Build a kanban board with DnD and keyboard alt.
  • Build an accordion with proper ARIA.
  • Build pagination with ellipses.
  • Build a multi-step form wizard with URL state.

  • Build a virtual list for 100K items.
  • Build a tic-tac-toe with bot.
  • Build Snake on canvas.
  • Build a Sudoku solver UI.
  • Build a stopwatch with lap times.
  • Build a polling component with backoff and pause-on-hidden.
  • Type a state machine as a discriminated union.
  • Author DeepReadonly<T>.
  • Author DeepPartial<T>.
  • Author UnionToTuple<U>.
  • Author RouteParams<"/users/:id/posts/:pid">.
  • Author OmitDeep<T, K>.
  • Author Brand<T, "Email"> + a validator returning Branded.
  • Author Equals<X, Y> + a static assertion utility.
  • Author a typed fetch wrapper inferring response from URL pattern.
  • Author a typed event bus where on(name) infers payload type.
  • Type a Zod-like schema as a TS generic.
  • Implement useFetch hook with abort + retry + cache.
  • Implement an offline queue that retries on online.
  • Implement a Trie for autocomplete.
  • Build a Calculator with operator precedence.
  • Implement a Promise pool (concurrency cap).
  • Implement timeout(promise, ms).
  • Implement once(fn) — runs once, caches result.
  • Implement diff(a, b) returning JSON-Patch-style ops.
  • Implement structured-clone-ish for serialization.

Reference solutions for the trickier async/TS drills

// Promise pool — run tasks with at most `limit` in flight, preserve result order.
async function pool(tasks, limit) {                 // tasks: Array<() => Promise>
  const results = new Array(tasks.length);
  let i = 0;
  async function worker() {
    while (i < tasks.length) {
      const cur = i++;
      results[cur] = await tasks[cur]();
    }
  }
  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: Math.min(limit, tasks.length) }, worker));
  return results;
}
// timeout(promise, ms) — reject if the promise doesn't settle in time.
function timeout(promise, ms) {
  return new Promise((res, rej) => {
    const id = setTimeout(() => rej(new Error("timeout")), ms);
    promise.then(v => { clearTimeout(id); res(v); },
                 e => { clearTimeout(id); rej(e); });
  });
}
// 2026 alt for fetch: pass AbortSignal.timeout(ms) directly into the request.
// once(fn) — call through exactly once; cache and return that result thereafter.
function once(fn) {
  let called = false, value;
  return function (...args) {
    if (!called) { called = true; value = fn.apply(this, args); fn = null; }
    return value;
  };
}
// Trie for autocomplete — insert words, list completions for a prefix.
class Trie {
  #root = { children: new Map(), end: false };
  insert(w) {
    let n = this.#root;
    for (const ch of w) n = n.children.get(ch) || n.children.set(ch, { children: new Map(), end: false }).get(ch);
    n.end = true;
  }
  #node(prefix) { let n = this.#root; for (const ch of prefix) { n = n.children.get(ch); if (!n) return null; } return n; }
  complete(prefix) {
    const out = [], start = this.#node(prefix);
    if (!start) return out;
    (function dfs(n, path) { if (n.end) out.push(path); for (const [ch, c] of n.children) dfs(c, path + ch); })(start, prefix);
    return out;
  }
}
// Typed event bus — on(name) infers the payload type from a single event map.
type Events = { login: { userId: string }; logout: void };
class Bus<E extends Record<string, unknown>> {
  #h: { [K in keyof E]?: Array<(p: E[K]) => void> } = {};
  on<K extends keyof E>(k: K, fn: (p: E[K]) => void) { (this.#h[k] ??= []).push(fn); }
  emit<K extends keyof E>(k: K, p: E[K]) { this.#h[k]?.forEach(fn => fn(p)); }
}
const bus = new Bus<Events>();
bus.on("login", p => p.userId);   // p inferred as { userId: string }
// bus.emit("login", {});         // ✗ missing userId — payload type enforced

docs.search: 02 — JavaScript + TypeScript Deep Dive (2026) Fundamentals · Async · 10+ polyfills · Advanced TS patterns · 50 drills Merged from v1/02 (JS fundamentals), v2/02 (TS + React-adjacent), and v3/10 (polyfills + advanced TS + 50 drills). One self-contained doc for everything JS/TS a senior FE must know cold. Part 1 — JavaScript fundamentals 1.1 Closures and lexical scope A closure is a function plus the lexical environment it was created in. Closures are how data is encapsulated and how callbacks remember context. function counter() { let n = 0; return { inc: () => ++n, get: () => n, }; } const c = counter(); c.inc(); c.inc(); c.get(); // 2 Common bug: forgetting let/const inside loops shares one variable; let creates per-iteration binding. Memory: closures over large objects can prevent GC. Null out references when done. Mechanism Every function value carries a hidden internal slot [[Environment]] pointing at the *lexical environment record* active when the function was created — not when it is called. An environment record is a map of variable name → binding (a mutable cell), plus a pointer to its outer record. Name resolution walks this chain outward until a binding is found. The closure keeps the entire chain reachable, so the bindings it references survive after the outer function returns. Crucially, a closure closes over variables (bindings), not values — multiple closures over the same let n share one cell, which is why inc and get above see the same n . var is function-scoped: one binding per function activation. let / const are block-scoped and, inside a for header, the spec creates a fresh binding per iteration and copies the previous value forward ( CreatePerIterationEnvironment ). That is the whole reason the loop fix below works. Worked example — the classic loop gotcha // BUG: var → single shared binding. All callbacks read the final i (3). for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)); // Output: 3 3 3 // FIX: let → one fresh binding per iteration. for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) setTimeout(() => console.log(j)); // Output: 0 1 2 Why: with var , all three timer callbacks close over the *same* i ; by the time any macrotask runs the loop has finished and i === 3 . With let , each iteration's callback closes over its own j cell frozen at that iteration's value. The pre- let fix was an IIFE per iteration: (function(k){ setTimeout(()=>console.log(k)); })(i) — manufacturing a fresh scope manually. Gotcha: a closure prevents GC of *everything reachable through the captured scope record*, even variables it never reads, because engines often capture the whole record. If a giant buffer and a tiny id share a scope and you return a closure using only id , some engines still pin buffer . Defensive fix: narrow the capture ( const id = obj.id; return () => id; ) or null the large var. 1.2 The this keyword Method call: this is the object before the dot. Function call (non-strict): this is global; strict: undefined. new f(): this is the new object. Arrow function: this is lexical (inherited from enclosing scope). bind/call/apply explicitly set this. Mechanism this is not lexical for ordinary functions — it is bound fresh on every call by the call site, per these rules in priority order: (1) new → a brand-new object whose prototype is f.prototype ; (2) explicit call / apply / bind → the given thisArg (boxed to an object in sloppy mode, left as-is in strict); (3) method call obj.f() → obj ; (4) plain call f() → undefined in strict mode / globalThis in sloppy mode. Arrow functions have no own this : they capture this from the enclosing lexical scope at creation time and ignore all four rules above — call / bind cannot change an arrow's this . Worked example "use strict"; const obj = { val: 42, reg() { return this?.val; }, arrow: () => this?.val, // `this` is module/undefined, NOT obj }; obj.reg(); // 42 (method call → this = obj) const f = obj.reg; f(); // undefined here `this` is undefined (strict plain call) obj.reg.call({ val: 7 }); // 7 (explicit binding) obj.arrow(); // undefined (lexical this, captured outside obj) Gotcha — lost this in callbacks. el.addEventListener('click', obj.handler) calls handler as a plain function, so this is the element (DOM) or undefined , not obj . Fixes: obj.handler.bind(obj) , or define handler = () => {...} as an arrow class field so it captures the instance. The arrow-field trade-off: one closure per instance (not shared on the prototype), costing memory for many instances. 1.3 Prototypes and classes class Animal { #name; // private constructor(name) { this.#name = name; } get name() { return this.#name; } static of(name) { return new Animal(name); } } class Dog extends Animal { bark() { return `${this.name}: woof!`; } } Mechanism Objects have an internal [[Prototype]] (exposed as __proto__ , read via Object.getPrototypeOf , set via Object.create ). Property reads that miss on the own object walk the prototype chain until found or null . class is sugar over the prototype system: instance methods live on Dog.prototype , static members on the Dog constructor itself, and extends wires Dog.prototype.[[Prototype]] = Animal.prototype and Dog.[[Prototype]] = Animal (so statics inherit too). #name is a true private field — not a property — keyed by a per-class private name; access from outside the class is a *syntax* error, and #x in obj is the safe brand-check. Worked example — chain resolution and super const d = new Dog("Rex"); d.bark(); // "Rex: woof!" Object.getPrototypeOf(d) === Dog.prototype; // true Object.getPrototypeOf(Dog.prototype) === Animal.prototype; // true d.hasOwnProperty("bark"); // false — bark is on the prototype Dog.of === Animal.of; // true — static inherited via Dog.[[Proto]]=Animal class Cat extends Animal { constructor(n) { super(n); } // MUST call super before using `this` describe() { return super.name; } // super → Animal.prototype getter, `this`=instance } Gotcha: referencing this in a subclass constructor *before* super() throws a ReferenceError (the instance does not exist yet under the derived-class new-binding semantics). Also, class declarations are not hoisted like function (they sit in the temporal dead zone), and class bodies are always strict mode. 1.4 Event loop, microtasks, macrotasks Single thread. Stack runs to empty → microtasks (Promise, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) → next macrotask (setTimeout, I/O) → rAF before next paint. Promise.then callbacks are microtasks; setTimeout(fn, 0) is a macrotask. Long task = > 50 ms on main thread = INP killer. scheduler.yield() (2026) lets you split work without losing continuation; falls back to setTimeout(0). Mechanism One call stack, one message queue per task source, and a separate microtask queue . The loop: pick one macrotask (timer, I/O, message, DOM event) → run it to completion → drain the entire microtask queue (including microtasks queued *by* microtasks) → run rendering steps ( requestAnimationFrame callbacks, then style/layout/paint) if it's time → back to the next macrotask. Microtasks therefore always run before the next macrotask and before paint. await x schedules the continuation as a microtask once x settles. Starvation hazard: an infinite chain of microtasks blocks rendering forever, while infinite macrotasks still allow paints between them. Worked example — predict the exact order console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0); // macrotask Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("C")); // microtask queueMicrotask(() => console.log("D")); // microtask (async () => { console.log("E"); await null; console.log("F"); })(); console.log("G"); // Output: A E G C D F B Why: synchronous run prints A , then the async IIFE runs synchronously up to await → E , then G . Now the stack empties. Microtask queue in enqueue order: C , D , then F (the awaited continuation was enqueued at the await ). Drain → C D F . Only then the timer macrotask → B . Gotcha: people expect await null to "do nothing" — it still yields a microtask even though null isn't a thenable, so F runs after the already-queued C / D . And setTimeout(fn, 0) is clamped to ≥4ms after 5 nested timers (HTML spec), so it is never truly immediate; use queueMicrotask or a MessageChannel for genuinely fast deferral. 1.5 Promises, async/await, AbortController const ac = new AbortController(); try { const r = await fetch(url, { signal: ac.signal }); if (!r.ok) throw new Error(r.statusText); return await r.json(); } catch (e) { if (e.name === "AbortError") return; throw e; } finally { /* cleanup */ } // Cancel after 5s setTimeout(() => ac.abort(), 5000); async functions always return a Promise. await pauses ONLY the enclosing async function — not the whole runtime. Use Promise.allSettled when you want all results, not first-fail. Mechanism A Promise is a state machine: pending → fulfilled | rejected , settling once , irreversibly. .then(onF, onR) registers reactions that run as microtasks after settlement; returning a thenable from a handler causes the chain to *adopt* it (flattening). async/await is generator-driven sugar: await e evaluates e , wraps it with Promise.resolve , suspends the function, and resumes (with the value, or by throwing the rejection) in a microtask when it settles. AbortController exposes a signal ; abort(reason) fires the signal's abort event and sets signal.aborted . Web APIs that accept { signal } reject with a DOMException named AbortError (in 2026, with signal.reason as the rejection value). AbortSignal.timeout(ms) and AbortSignal.any([...]) compose signals declaratively. Worked example — order and error propagation async function f() { console.log(1); await Promise.resolve(); console.log(3); // resumes as a microtask return "done"; } console.log(0); f().then(v => console.log(v)); console.log(2); // Output: 0 1 2 3 done Gotchas: (1) an unhandled rejection fires unhandledrejection ; a .catch attached *later in the same tick* still prevents it, but a missing terminal .catch in production crashes Node. (2) try/catch around await catches async rejections, but try { somePromise(); } catch does not — you must await . (3) Forgetting return await inside try/finally can swallow errors or let finally run before the promise settles. (4) A synchronous throw before the first await in an async function still becomes a *rejected promise*, never a thrown exception to the caller. 1.6 Generators + async iterators async function* pages(url) { let cursor = null; do { const r = await fetch(`${url}?cursor=${cursor}`); const j = await r.json(); yield j.items; cursor = j.nextCursor; } while (cursor); } for await (const batch of pages("/api/list")) { /* process */ } Mechanism A generator function returns an iterator that is also iterable. yield suspends execution and hands a value out; .next(v) resumes, and v becomes the *result of the suspended yield expression* — making generators two-way channels (the basis of coroutine schedulers and how early async/await desugared via co ). .return() and .throw() inject completion/exceptions at the suspension point, which is why try/finally inside a generator runs on early termination. An async generator yields Promises and is consumed with for await...of , which awaits each next() ; it pairs lazy pull-based iteration with async I/O — ideal for paginated APIs and streams without buffering everything in memory. Worked example — two-way communication and lazy evaluation function* convo() { const name = yield "what is your name?"; // value sent via next() const age = yield `hi ${name}, age?`; return `${name} is ${age}`; } const it = convo(); it.next(); // { value: "what is your name?", done: false } it.next("Ada"); // { value: "hi Ada, age?", done: false } it.next(36); // { value: "Ada is 36", done: true } function* nats() { let n = 0; while (true) yield n++; } // infinite, but lazy const g = nats(); g.next().value; g.next().value; // 0, 1 — pulled on demand Gotcha: the value passed to the first
