03 — React + Modern Stack (Next.js + AI + State) 2026

React 19 · Server Components · Next.js 15 PPR · Vercel AI SDK · Zustand + TanStack

Merged from v2/02 (React + state) and v3/08 (React 19 / Next.js 15 / AI SDK). Self-contained.

Part 1 — React fundamentals refresher

1.1 Reconciliation + commit

  • Render phase: pure — builds the next fiber tree. May be paused, restarted (concurrent).
  • Commit phase: synchronous — applies DOM mutations + fires effects.
  • Keys identify reorders; never use array index for dynamic lists.

Mechanism. React keeps two fiber trees: current (on screen) and workInProgress (being built). Reconciliation diffs the new element tree against current using a heuristic that is O(n) instead of the O(n³) of a general tree diff. The heuristic rests on two assumptions: (1) elements of different *type* produce different trees — so React tears down and rebuilds rather than diffing across a type change; (2) key is a stable identity hint across renders. In concurrent mode the render phase is interruptible: React builds workInProgress in units of work and can yield to the browser between fibers (a scheduler checks shouldYield() against a ~5ms frame budget). Because render can restart, render must be pure — any side effect there can run twice or be thrown away.

The commit phase is a single synchronous, uninterruptible pass with three sub-phases: before mutation (run getSnapshotBeforeUpdate, schedule useEffect), mutation (apply DOM ops, run useLayoutEffect cleanups), and layout (run useLayoutEffect setups, swap current = workInProgress). Passive effects (useEffect) flush asynchronously after paint.

Why index keys break. With index keys, reordering or prepending shifts every element's identity, so React reconciles item[0]'s old state into the new item[0] — stale input values, wrong checkbox states, lost focus.

// WRONG — index key: deleting the first row keeps the deleted row's DOM state on row 0
{rows.map((row, i) => <EditableRow key={i} row={row} />)}

// RIGHT — stable identity survives reorder/insert/delete
{rows.map((row) => <EditableRow key={row.id} row={row} />)}

A staff-level point: when a list has no naturally stable id (freshly created client rows), generate one at creation (crypto.randomUUID()), not at render — generating in render produces a new key every render and remounts the component each time.

1.2 Hooks core

HookUseGotcha
useStateLocal component stateFunctional updater for stable updates from async
useReducerComplex state transitionsPair with discriminated union actions for TS
useEffectSide effects after commitCleanup runs before next effect + on unmount
useLayoutEffectRead DOM before paintSynchronous — blocks paint; rarely needed
useMemo / useCallbackMemoize expensive valuesMostly obsolete in React 19 (Compiler)
useRefMutable box that survives re-renderNot reactive; setting it does not trigger render
useTransitionNon-urgent update flagUse for state-driven view switches
useDeferredValueCheap throttle on expensive rendersBest for typing → large filter

State is a snapshot, not a variable. Each render closes over the state value it was rendered with. This is why batching multiple setCount(count + 1) calls in one event only increments once — they all read the same snapshot. The functional updater setCount(c => c + 1) reads the *queued* value, so three of them increment by three. The same closure-capture rule is the root cause of stale values inside setTimeout, event listeners, and async callbacks.

Effects synchronize, they don't "run on mount." Think of useEffect as: "keep this external system in sync with these reactive values." The dependency array is not an optimization knob — it is the set of values the effect reads. Lying about deps (omitting one to "run once") creates stale closures. If an effect should truly run once with no dependency on render values, it usually shouldn't be an effect at all (move it to a module, an event handler, or a ref-guarded init).

function SearchBox({ query }: { query: string }) {
  const [results, setResults] = useState<string[]>([]);

  // RIGHT — effect re-syncs whenever `query` changes; cleanup cancels the stale request
  useEffect(() => {
    const ctrl = new AbortController();
    fetch(`/api/search?q=${query}`, { signal: ctrl.signal })
      .then((r) => r.json())
      .then(setResults)
      .catch((e) => { if (e.name !== "AbortError") throw e; });
    return () => ctrl.abort(); // cleanup mirrors setup; runs before next effect + unmount
  }, [query]);

  return <Results items={results} />;
}

useRef is your escape hatch for values that must persist without driving renders (timers, previous values, imperative DOM handles). Writing ref.current during render is a Rules-of-React violation (impure); read/write it in effects or handlers.

1.3 Rules of React

  • Components are pure given props + state. Same input → same output.
  • Hooks called in the same order every render.
  • Never mutate props or state; always return new values.
  • Effects describe synchronization; cleanup mirrors setup.

Why purity is now load-bearing. Concurrent React may render a component, throw the result away, and render it again (e.g. when a higher-priority update preempts, or under <StrictMode> which intentionally double-invokes render and effects in dev). The React Compiler also depends on purity: it memoizes based on a static read-set analysis and assumes the same inputs produce the same output with no side effects. Break purity and the compiler can serve a stale memoized result.

The order rule exists because hooks are stored in a linked list on the fiber indexed by call order, not by name. A conditional hook shifts every subsequent hook's slot, so React reads the wrong state. eslint-plugin-react-hooks enforces rules-of-hooks and honest dependency arrays via exhaustive-deps.

// WRONG — conditional hook: slot indices shift between renders
function Profile({ id }: { id?: string }) {
  if (!id) return null;
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null); // sometimes called → state corruption
}

// RIGHT — hooks unconditional, branch on the value
function Profile({ id }: { id?: string }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);
  if (!id) return null;
  // ...
}

Mutation rule in practice: state.items.push(x); setState(state) does nothing — same reference, bailout. Always produce a new reference (setState(s => [...s, x])), or use Immer for ergonomic immutable updates.

Part 2 — React 19 (the staff-eng mental model)

2.1 React Compiler

Babel/SWC plugin that auto-memoizes components and hook values based on read-set analysis at build time. Default in Next.js 15.

// Before React 19
const Row = React.memo(function Row({ user, onSelect }) {
  const full = useMemo(() => `${user.first} ${user.last}`, [user]);
  const handler = useCallback(() => onSelect(user.id), [onSelect, user.id]);
  return <li onClick={handler}>{full}</li>;
});
// React 19 — write the obvious thing
function Row({ user, onSelect }: { user: User; onSelect: (id: string) => void }) {
  const full = `${user.first} ${user.last}`;
  return <li onClick={() => onSelect(user.id)}>{full}</li>;
}
  • Bailouts: mutate inputs, misuse refs, break Rules of React.
  • Still useMemo when: compiler bails, profile says, value crosses external system.

Mechanism. The compiler runs as a Babel plugin during build. It builds a control-flow graph of each component, infers which values derive from which inputs (props, state, hook returns), and emits code backed by a hidden memoization cache (conceptually a useMemoCache(n) array, one slot per memoizable value). At runtime each slot stores [lastDeps, lastValue]; if deps are referentially equal it reuses the value — exactly what hand-written useMemo/useCallback/React.memo did, but with correct, exhaustive dependencies humans routinely get wrong. It memoizes JSX too, so child elements are skipped when their inputs are unchanged.

Enabling and verifying (Next 15).

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from "next";
const config: NextConfig = { experimental: { reactCompiler: true } };
export default config;

Install eslint-plugin-react-compiler and babel-plugin-react-compiler. The ESLint rule flags code the compiler will skip *before* you ship. In React DevTools, compiler-optimized components show a "Memo ✨" badge — that's how you confirm a component was optimized rather than bailed.

Debugging a bailout. The compiler is conservative: if it cannot prove a transformation is safe, it leaves the component un-optimized (correctness over speed). Common causes: mutating props/state during render, reading or writing ref.current during render, calling a function it cannot analyze, or eslint-disable-ing a rules-of-hooks error. To debug: check the DevTools badge, run the compiler's health-check/logger, and fix the underlying purity violation rather than reaching back for manual memo. You still hand-write useMemo for genuinely expensive computations the compiler can't see across a boundary (value passed into a non-React system) or when profiling proves a hot path needs it.

2.2 The use() hook

Reads a Promise or a Context. Unlike useContext, callable conditionally.

async function ProductPage({ id }: { id: string }) {
  const product = use(getProduct(id));   // suspends; streams when ready
  return <ProductCard product={product} />;
}
function PriceTag({ showTax }: { showTax: boolean }) {
  const tax = showTax ? use(TaxContext) : null;
  return <span>{tax ? `${tax}%` : "no tax"}</span>;
}
  • Promise must be stable; memoize in parent or hoist to a cache.

What use actually does. use is not a hook in the linked-list sense — it can be called inside conditionals and loops because it doesn't allocate a persistent slot. When passed a Promise, it integrates with Suspense: if pending it *throws* the promise (suspending the nearest boundary); when it resolves React replays the render and use returns the value; if it rejects, the nearest error boundary catches it. When passed a Context it reads the value like useContext but is allowed in branches.

The stability gotcha. Because a suspended render replays, calling use(fetch(...)) inline in a Client Component creates a *new* promise every render → infinite suspend loop. The promise must be created outside render and be referentially stable. The clean pattern: create it in a Server Component (which doesn't re-render the same way) and pass it down.

// Server Component creates the promise once and passes it across the boundary
async function Page({ id }: { id: string }) {
  const userPromise = getUser(id); // not awaited here
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>
      <Profile userPromise={userPromise} />
    </Suspense>
  );
}

// Client Component unwraps it with use() — promise is stable (came from props)
"use client";
function Profile({ userPromise }: { userPromise: Promise<User> }) {
  const user = use(userPromise);
  return <h1>{user.name}</h1>;
}

This is the canonical "start fetching on the server, stream + unwrap on the client" pattern. use over useContext+useState+effect gives you conditional reads, automatic Suspense integration, and no waterfall.

2.3 Server Components vs Client Components

  • Server: never ships JS, can be async, reads DB/fs/env, no hooks/browser APIs.
  • Client ("use client"): ships JS, can use state/effects, cannot be async.
  • Composition: a Client Component can render Server Components only as children/props.
  • Props must be serializable across the boundary (no functions except Server Actions).

The mental model. Picture the tree split by a network boundary. Server Components (the default in the App Router — no directive needed) run *only* on the server during request/build. They execute, then *serialize their output* into a compact streaming format, the RSC Payload (Flight) — a description of the rendered tree, including holes where Client Components go and references to their JS chunks. The browser reconstructs the tree and only downloads/hydrates the Client Component islands. Server Component code and its imports (your ORM, secrets, markdown parser) never enter the client bundle. That's the whole value: zero-JS-cost data components, secrets stay server-side, the client bundle shrinks to interactive islands.

"use client" is a boundary, not a location. The directive marks an *entry point* into client land. Every module imported (transitively) from a "use client" file becomes part of the client bundle. Putting "use client" atop a big shared util pulls everything below it client-side. Push the directive down to the leaf that needs interactivity.

The composition rule everyone fails. A Client Component cannot *import* a Server Component (no server runtime). But it *can render one passed as children or a prop*, because by then the Server Component has already rendered to a payload on the server and is just an opaque slot:

// app/layout.tsx — Server Component
import { ClientShell } from "./client-shell";
import { ServerSidebar } from "./server-sidebar"; // async, reads DB

export default function Layout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return <ClientShell sidebar={<ServerSidebar />}>{children}</ClientShell>;
}

// client-shell.tsx
"use client";
import { useState } from "react";
export function ClientShell({
  sidebar, children,
}: { sidebar: React.ReactNode; children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(true);
  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={() => setOpen((o) => !o)}>Toggle</button>
      {open && sidebar}   {/* opaque server-rendered slot — no server code in client bundle */}
      <main>{children}</main>
    </div>
  );
}
// WRONG — importing a Server Component into a Client Component makes it Client too
"use client";
import { ServerSidebar } from "./server-sidebar"; // its DB import now ships to browser → error/leak

Serialization across the boundary. Props passed Server → Client are serialized via Flight. Serializable: primitives, plain objects/arrays, Date, Map, Set, BigInt, Promise, TypedArray, and Server Action references. Not serializable: class instances, functions (except Server Actions), Symbols, closures over server state. So a Date crosses fine (Flight handles it); a Mongoose document or a Prisma model with methods does not — map to a plain DTO first. A callback passed to a Client Component must be a "use server" action, not an arbitrary function.

Gotchas: Server Components can't use useState/useEffect/browser APIs (they run once, server-side). Client Components can't be async. Context providers must be Client Components — wrap once near the root and keep the tree below mostly server. import "server-only" in modules that must never reach the client gives a build-time tripwire.

2.4 Server Actions

// app/todos/actions.ts
"use server";
import { db } from "@/db";
import { todos } from "@/db/schema";
import { revalidatePath } from "next/cache";
import { z } from "zod";

const Schema = z.object({ title: z.string().min(1).max(200) });

export async function addTodo(_prev: unknown, formData: FormData) {
  const parsed = Schema.safeParse({ title: formData.get("title") });
  if (!parsed.success) return { error: "Title required" };

  const user = await requireUser();          // re-authenticate ON THE SERVER
  await db.insert(todos).values({ title: parsed.data.title, userId: user.id });
  revalidatePath("/todos");
  return { error: null };
}
// app/todos/new-todo.tsx ("use client")
"use client";
import { useActionState } from "react";
import { useFormStatus } from "react-dom";
import { addTodo } from "./actions";

export function NewTodo() {
  const [state, formAction] = useActionState(addTodo, { error: null });
  return (
    <form action={formAction}>
      <input name="title" />
      <SubmitButton />
      {state.error && <p role="alert">{state.error}</p>}
    </form>
  );
}
function SubmitButton() {
  const { pending } = useFormStatus();
  return <button disabled={pending}>{pending ? "Saving…" : "Add"}</button>;
}

What a Server Action is. A "use server" function is an RPC endpoint React/Next wires up automatically. The bundler replaces the imported reference on the client with a stub that POSTs a serialized call to the server; the server runs the real function and streams back the result *plus* any revalidated UI. Attach one directly to <form action={...}> and it works without JavaScript (progressive enhancement) — the form posts natively, the server handles it, the page re-renders. With JS, React intercepts and does it via fetch, enabling pending states and optimistic UI.

The security mental model — actions are public endpoints. Anyone can craft a POST to a Server Action. So: (1) always re-authenticate and re-authorize inside the action — never trust a user id from the client; (2) always re-validate input (Zod) — client form constraints are advisory; (3) treat closed-over variables carefully — values bound via .bind() are sent to the client encrypted, but don't bind secrets. Mutations belong in actions; reads belong in Server Components.

Cache invalidation is part of the action. After a write tell Next what to refresh: revalidatePath("/todos") (route-level) or revalidateTag("todos") (data-cache-level, surgical). Forgetting this is the #1 "I added a row but the list didn't update" bug. redirect() can be called at the end to navigate.

useActionState over manual useState. It wraps the action so React tracks the returned state and an isPending flag, and preserves the action's return value across the round trip — the idiomatic way to surface validation errors. Its signature: the action receives (prevState, formData).

2.5 New 19 hooks

HookPurposeReturns
useActionStateWrap an action to track state + pending[state, dispatch, isPending]
useOptimisticPredict state during in-flight mutation[optimisticState, addOptimistic]
useFormStatusRead parent form's pending state{ pending, data, method, action }
useRead Promise or Context (conditional)Resolved value, suspends if pending

useActionState(action, initialState, permalink?) returns [state, formAction, isPending]. Pass formAction to <form action={...}> or a button's formAction. The wrapped action's signature becomes (prevState, payload) => newState. Use it as the single source of truth for form result + error + pending.

useFormStatus() must be called from a component *rendered inside* the <form>, not the one that owns it — it reads the nearest parent form's status via context. That's why SubmitButton is a separate child. Returns { pending, data, method, action }; data is the in-flight FormData, handy for showing exactly what's submitting.

useOptimistic — full pattern, mental model, gotchas

Mental model. useOptimistic(realState, reducer) returns [optimisticState, addOptimistic]. While a transition/action is in flight, optimisticState reflects your *predicted* value (real + the delta you added). The instant the action settles and React commits the new *real* state (from a revalidation), the optimistic layer is discarded and optimisticState snaps back to truth. You never manually "roll back" — if the server rejects and real state doesn't change, the optimistic value simply vanishes on the next commit, reverting the UI automatically. That auto-revert is the whole point and the thing people miss.

Critical constraint: addOptimistic may only be called inside a transition (i.e. inside the action passed to <form action> or wrapped in startTransition). Calling it outside throws.

"use client";
import { useOptimistic, useRef } from "react";
import { addComment } from "./actions";

type Comment = { id: string; text: string; pending?: boolean };

export function Comments({ comments }: { comments: Comment[] }) {
  const formRef = useRef<HTMLFormElement>(null);
  const [optimistic, addOptimistic] = useOptimistic(
    comments,
    (state, text: string): Comment[] => [
      ...state,
      { id: `tmp-${crypto.randomUUID()}`, text, pending: true },
    ],
  );

  return (
    <>
      <ul>
        {optimistic.map((c) => (
          <li key={c.id} style={{ opacity: c.pending ? 0.5 : 1 }}>{c.text}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
      <form
        ref={formRef}
        action={async (formData: FormData) => {
          const text = String(formData.get("text"));
          addOptimistic(text);          // predict — inside the action = inside a transition ✓
          formRef.current?.reset();     // clear input immediately
          await addComment(text);       // server insert + revalidatePath → real state updates
        }}
      >
        <input name="text" required />
        <button type="submit">Post</button>
      </form>
    </>
  );
}

Conflict resolution. When the server returns the authoritative list (via revalidation), the optimistic temp item with id: "tmp-…" is replaced by the real row with the real id. If two users post concurrently, each client only optimistically adds *its own* item, and the revalidated server list reconciles ordering — last-write-wins on ordering, no lost writes (both inserts persist). If the action *throws* (server validation fails), real state never changes, the optimistic item disappears on the next commit, and you surface the error via useActionState.

Common wrong version: managing optimistic state with useState + manual rollback in try/catch. It works until a revalidation races your rollback and you get flicker or a stuck temp row. useOptimistic ties the optimistic lifetime to the transition, eliminating that class of bug.

2.6 Streaming + selective hydration

  • SSR HTML streams as ready (out-of-order).
  • Hydration is progressive; high-priority parts hydrate first.
  • User input tracked even before hydration.
  • Use Suspense boundaries to control granularity.

How streaming SSR works. With renderToPipeableStream (Node) / renderToReadableStream (edge), React sends the shell HTML immediately and, for any subtree wrapped in <Suspense> that suspends, sends the fallback inline first. When that subtree's data resolves, React streams the real HTML later in the response plus a tiny inline <script> that swaps the fallback for the content — out of order, so a slow widget never blocks the rest of the page's TTFB. This powers PPR and loading.tsx in Next.

Selective hydration. React 18+ hydrates Suspense boundaries independently and prioritizes by interaction. If a user clicks a not-yet-hydrated boundary, React records the event, hydrates *that* boundary first (jumping the queue), then replays the event — so clicks before hydration aren't lost; they feel slightly delayed rather than dropped. Boundaries hydrate in parallel rather than one giant blocking pass, which is why a heavy footer no longer stalls header interactivity.

// Each Suspense boundary streams + hydrates independently
export default function Page() {
  return (
    <>
      <Header />                                    {/* in shell, hydrates first */}
      <Suspense fallback={<FeedSkeleton />}>
        <Feed />                                    {/* streams when data ready */}
      </Suspense>
      <Suspense fallback={<SidebarSkeleton />}>
        <Recommendations />                         {/* independent boundary */}
      </Suspense>
    </>
  );
}

Granularity tradeoff: one boundary around everything = all-or-nothing (defeats streaming); a boundary per item = layout shift and overhead. Wrap at *semantic* chunks (feed, sidebar, comments) where each has its own data dependency.

2.7 Concurrent React patterns

  • useTransition + isPending — keep UI interactive during filter rerender.
  • useDeferredValue — throttle expensive renders driven by typing.
  • startTransition outside hooks — mark router nav as non-urgent.
  • Avoid: wrapping all setState in transitions; hides real lag.

The core idea: priority. Concurrent React can interrupt a low-priority render to handle a high-priority one (like typing). useTransition and useDeferredValue are the two public APIs to mark work as low-priority so the input thread stays responsive.

useTransition — you *own* the state update and want to mark it non-urgent. startTransition(() => setQuery(value)) keeps the old UI interactive and on screen while the expensive re-render happens in the background; isPending lets you show a subtle spinner.

useDeferredValue — you *receive* a value (often a prop) and want a lagging copy for the expensive part, without owning the setter. The input updates instantly; the deferred copy trails and powers the heavy list.

"use client";
import { useDeferredValue, useState, useMemo } from "react";

function Filterable({ items }: { items: Item[] }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
  const deferred = useDeferredValue(query);          // trails behind during fast typing
  const filtered = useMemo(
    () => items.filter((i) => i.name.includes(deferred)),
    [items, deferred],
  );
  const stale = query !== deferred;                  // show subtle "updating" state
  return (
    <>
      <input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} />
      <ul style={{ opacity: stale ? 0.6 : 1 }}>
        {filtered.map((i) => <li key={i.id}>{i.name}</li>)}
      </ul>
    </>
  );
}

When each: useTransition for view/route switches and tab changes you trigger; useDeferredValue for "type → filter a huge list" where you don't own the source; Suspense for *data not yet loaded*. They compose: a transition can wrap navigation that suspends. Anti-pattern: wrapping every setState in startTransition — it doesn't make work faster, just defers it, and over-using it hides genuine perf problems (real fix: virtualize, memoize, paginate).

Part 3 — Next.js 15 (App Router)

3.1 Why Next dominates 2026 senior FE JDs

  • Default React metaframework for production teams.
  • Brings RSC, Server Actions, streaming, edge runtime, ISR, PPR under one router.
  • Be ready to articulate tradeoffs vs Remix, SvelteKit, Astro, TanStack Start.

The honest comparison a senior gives. Next.js is the reference implementation of React Server Components and ships the deepest caching/streaming integration, which is why most production React teams default to it. Remix / React Router 7 leans into web standards (loaders/actions, Request/Response, no RSC-first model) and is excellent for form-heavy, progressively-enhanced apps. TanStack Start offers full-document SSR + type-safe routing with TanStack Query/Router DNA, appealing if your data layer is already TanStack. Astro wins for content sites (islands architecture, ships ~0 JS by default) and can host React islands. SvelteKit trades React's ecosystem for a smaller, faster runtime. The staff-level point: pick Next when you want RSC + streaming + a managed cache and accept the opinionated caching complexity; Astro for content; Remix/TanStack Start when web-standard simplicity or existing TanStack investment outweighs RSC.

3.2 Rendering modes

ModeWhenCacheLatency
Static (SSG)Marketing, docs, blogCDN forever or by tagBest (TTFB ~0)
ISR / on-demandCMS-drivenPer-tag revalidationBest with SWR
Dynamic SSRPersonalized, auth-gatedNo (per request)Worst — DB roundtrip
PPRMostly static with dynamic holesStatic shell cachedStatic TTFB, dynamic streams
Edge runtimeGeo-aware, lightweightPer request, runs at PoPLowest p95 globally

How Next decides. A route is static unless something opts it into dynamic rendering. Dynamic triggers: reading cookies(), headers(), searchParams, or a fetch with cache: "no-store" / next: { revalidate: 0 }. ISR is just static + a revalidate window (time-based) or revalidateTag/revalidatePath (on-demand) — the first request after expiry serves stale and regenerates in the background (stale-while-revalidate). Force a mode explicitly with route segment config:

// app/dashboard/page.tsx
export const dynamic = "force-dynamic";   // or "force-static"
export const revalidate = 60;             // ISR window in seconds
export const fetchCache = "default-cache";

3.3 PPR — Partial Prerendering

  • Build step renders static shell.
  • Request time: dynamic holes stream in via Suspense fallbacks.
  • Result: instant CDN TTFB + personalized content without blocking.
// next.config.ts — enable incremental PPR
import type { NextConfig } from "next";
export default { experimental: { ppr: "incremental" } } satisfies NextConfig;
// app/page.tsx
export const experimental_ppr = true;

import { Suspense } from "react";

export default function Page() {
  return (
    <>
      <StaticHeader />                          {/* prerendered into the static shell */}
      <Suspense fallback={<Skeleton />}>
        <PersonalizedFeed />                     {/* reads cookies(); the dynamic hole, streams */}
      </Suspense>
    </>
  );
}

The mental model — one route, two render times. PPR collapses the static-vs-dynamic decision from per-*route* to per-*component*. At build time, Next prerenders everything it can into a static shell, leaving holes exactly where a <Suspense> boundary wraps something that reads dynamic data (cookies, headers, uncached fetch). The shell serves from the CDN with near-zero TTFB; the dynamic holes render per request on the server and stream into their Suspense fallbacks over the same initial response. So you get static-page TTFB *and* personalization without choosing.

What's prerendered vs what streams: anything *outside* a Suspense boundary that doesn't touch dynamic APIs is in the shell (cached, instant). Anything inside a Suspense boundary that *does* touch dynamic APIs becomes a streamed hole. If a dynamic API is read *outside* any Suspense boundary, the whole route falls back to dynamic — so the discipline is: wrap every dynamic read in Suspense.

PPR × middleware. Middleware still runs on every request *before* the cached shell is served (it's at the edge, in front of the cache). Coarse auth/redirects in middleware compose fine with PPR — the shell is cached, middleware decides whether to serve it or redirect. Don't read per-user data in middleware to personalize the shell; personalize in the streamed hole instead.

3.4 The four-cache stack (Next 15)

  • Request Memoization — dedupes fetch() within one render.
  • Data Cache — persistent KV keyed by URL+options, invalidated by revalidateTag/revalidatePath.
  • Full Route Cache — rendered RSC payload + HTML.
  • Router Cache — in-memory client-side cache of prefetched segments.
  • Senior trap: "new comment not showing" → invalidate the cache AND check route is dynamic.
  • Tools: revalidateTag, revalidatePath, unstable_cache, cookies()/headers() to force-dynamic.

The four caches, by lifetime and location (the most-failed Next topic — know all four cold):

CacheWhereLifetimeKeyInvalidate
Request MemoizationServer, per requestSingle render passfn + argsautomatic (ends with request)
Data CacheServer, persistentAcross requests/deploysfetch URL + optionsrevalidateTag / revalidatePath / time
Full Route CacheServer (build/ISR)Until revalidatedroute + paramsrevalidatePath / redeploy
Router CacheClient, in-memorySession (seconds)route segmentrouter.refresh(), navigation, action

1. Request Memoization — within a *single* server render, two components calling fetch("/api/user") with the same args hit the network once; React memoizes the in-flight promise. Scope = one request. (Works for fetch; for non-fetch sources wrap in React's cache().)

2. Data Cache — Next's persistent server cache for fetch results, surviving across requests and deploys. Opt in/out per call:

// cached + tagged for surgical invalidation
const res = await fetch("https://api/products", { next: { tags: ["products"], revalidate: 3600 } });
// never cached (Next 15 default for fetch is no-store unless you opt in)
const live = await fetch("https://api/price", { cache: "no-store" });

For non-fetch sources (DB/ORM), use unstable_cache:

import { unstable_cache } from "next/cache";
const getProducts = unstable_cache(async () => db.query.products.findMany(), ["products"], {
  tags: ["products"], revalidate: 3600,
});

3. Full Route Cache — at build/ISR time Next stores the rendered RSC payload + HTML for static routes, served from CDN. Bypassed for dynamic routes.

4. Router Cache — the client keeps prefetched/visited RSC payloads in memory so back/forward and <Link> navigations are instant. The sneaky one: even after revalidatePath, a client that already has the segment cached may show stale UI until the Router Cache entry expires or you call router.refresh(). Server Actions auto-refresh the router cache for the current route.

Next 15 default change. In Next 14, fetch was cached by default; teams shipped stale data constantly. Next 15 flipped the default to no-store (uncached) for fetch, and GET Route Handlers and the Client Router Cache are also uncached by default. You now *opt in* to caching explicitly. Safer (no surprise staleness) but you must add revalidate/tags to benefit from the Data Cache.

The "new comment not showing" debug path: (1) did you revalidateTag/revalidatePath after the write? (2) is the route actually reading cached data, or is it dynamic and re-fetching? (3) is the *client* Router Cache serving a stale segment — do you need router.refresh()? You often need both server invalidation *and* a router refresh.

3.5 Edge vs Node runtime

  • Edge: V8 isolates, no Node APIs, no fs, limited packages. Use for: middleware, lightweight handlers, AI streaming proxies.
  • Node: full Node APIs, slower cold start. Use for: ORM, file uploads, heavy crypto.
  • export const runtime = "edge" | "nodejs".

Mechanism. The Edge runtime runs in lightweight V8 isolates deployed to every PoP (Vercel Edge / Cloudflare Workers style). Isolates have ~0ms cold starts and run geographically close to the user, so they win p95 latency for short, I/O-bound work. The cost: no Node built-ins (fs, net, Node's crypto API — you get Web Crypto), limited npm compatibility (anything depending on Node internals breaks), small bundle/memory/CPU-time limits.

Three good Edge uses: (1) middleware (auth redirect, A/B bucketing, geo headers), (2) streaming an LLM response (just piping a ReadableStream, no heavy compute), (3) personalization/redirects needing low global latency. Three good Node uses: (1) Prisma/Drizzle against a TCP database, (2) file/image processing and uploads (sharp, fs), (3) heavy crypto, PDF generation, or any library with native Node deps.

// app/api/chat/route.ts
export const runtime = "edge";       // stream tokens close to the user
// app/api/import/route.ts
export const runtime = "nodejs";     // ORM + file processing need Node APIs

Note: a database driver speaking HTTP (Neon serverless, Turso, Upstash) *can* run on Edge; a raw TCP driver can't.

3.6 Auth patterns 2026

  • Auth.js / Clerk / WorkOS / Kinde for OAuth.
  • Edge middleware does coarse auth (unauth redirects); fine-grained checks in Server Components/Actions.
  • Never trust the user object in a client component — re-verify on server before mutations.

Layered model. (1) Middleware (edge) does *coarse* gatekeeping — is there a session cookie? if not, redirect to /login. Keep it cheap: verify a signed/JWT session without a DB call (or hit a fast edge KV). No role checks here. (2) Server Components read the verified session to render the right data. (3) Server Actions / Route Handlers re-check authorization (may this user do this to this resource) on *every* mutation, because actions are public endpoints.

// middleware.ts — coarse auth only
import { NextResponse, type NextRequest } from "next/server";
import { verifySession } from "@/lib/session";

export async function middleware(req: NextRequest) {
  const session = await verifySession(req.cookies.get("session")?.value);
  if (!session) return NextResponse.redirect(new URL("/login", req.url));
  return NextResponse.next();
}
export const config = { matcher: ["/dashboard/:path*", "/settings/:path*"] };
// action — fine-grained authz at the mutation boundary
"use server";
export async function deleteProject(id: string) {
  const user = await requireUser();                       // authn
  const project = await db.query.projects.findFirst({ where: eq(projects.id, id) });
  if (project?.ownerId !== user.id) throw new Error("Forbidden"); // authz on the resource
  await db.delete(projects).where(eq(projects.id, id));
  revalidatePath("/dashboard");
}

The cardinal rule: the client user object is a UI hint only — anyone can forge a request. Authorization decisions live on the server, at the mutation, against the resource.

3.7 Parallel + intercepting routes

  • Parallel routes (@slot) for side-by-side UI.
  • Intercepting routes ((.)photo/[id]) for Instagram-style modal-over-page.

Parallel routes (@slot folders) render multiple independent route trees into one layout simultaneously, each with its own loading/error state and independent navigation. Great for dashboards (@analytics, @team) and for a modal slot.

Intercepting routes let a navigation render a route *in the current layout's context* instead of full-page. Matcher conventions: (.) same level, (..) one up, (...) from root. Combined with a parallel @modal slot you get the Instagram pattern: clicking a photo in the feed opens it as a modal overlay (intercepted), but a hard refresh or shared deep link renders the full photo page (the real route).

app/
  @modal/
    (.)photo/[id]/page.tsx   ← intercepts /photo/[id] when navigated from the feed → modal
    default.tsx              ← renders null when no modal active
  photo/[id]/page.tsx        ← full page on direct visit / refresh
  layout.tsx                 ← renders {children} and {modal}
// app/layout.tsx
export default function Layout({
  children, modal,
}: { children: React.ReactNode; modal: React.ReactNode }) {
  return <>{children}{modal}</>;
}

The magic: same /photo/123 URL, two presentations depending on *how* you arrived — soft nav → modal over feed; hard load → standalone page. Deep-linkable and shareable for free.

3.8 Bundle + image + font

  • next build --analyze for heaviest client bundle.
  • Dynamic import + Suspense for code splitting.
  • next/image with priority, sizes, fetchpriority.
  • next/font auto-subsets, removes CLS via size-adjust.

Cutting a bloated bundle (concrete playbook). (1) Run @next/bundle-analyzer to see the treemap — find the fat client modules. (2) Biggest App Router lever: move components to Server Components so their code never ships. A markdown renderer, a date library, a syntax highlighter used only for display belong on the server. (3) next/dynamic for genuinely client-only heavy widgets (charts, editors, maps) so they load on demand. (4) Replace heavy deps (moment → date-fns/Temporal, lodash → per-method imports or native). (5) Push "use client" to leaves so you don't drag shared utils client-side.

// Lazy-load a heavy client-only chart; ssr:false avoids shipping it in the initial payload
import dynamic from "next/dynamic";
const Chart = dynamic(() => import("./HeavyChart"), {
  loading: () => <ChartSkeleton />,
  ssr: false,
});
// Images: prevent CLS + prioritize LCP
import Image from "next/image";
<Image src={hero} alt="" priority sizes="100vw" />               // LCP image — eager, high fetchpriority
<Image src={thumb} alt="" width={64} height={64} loading="lazy" /> // below-the-fold — lazy
// Fonts: self-hosted, subset, no layout shift (size-adjust metrics baked in)
import { Inter } from "next/font/google";
export const inter = Inter({ subsets: ["latin"], display: "swap" });

next/font removes the network request to Google (privacy + perf) and emits size-adjust/ascent-override so the fallback font occupies the same box → zero CLS on font swap.

Part 4 — Vercel AI SDK and AI-native UIs

4.1 Why this matters in 2026

  • Every product ships an AI feature: chat, summarize, generate, classify.
  • Senior interview asks: streaming, backpressure, cancellation, tool-calling, generative UI, evals.

The senior framing. The AI SDK abstracts provider differences (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) behind one streamText/generateText/streamUI interface, handles the streaming protocol between server and useChat/useCompletion on the client, and standardizes tool-calling. The interview isn't "can you call an LLM" — it's the *systems* concerns: streaming UX without jank, cancellation so you don't bill for abandoned chats, backpressure when the model outpaces render, structured tool outputs, and how you *evaluate* a non-deterministic feature in CI.

4.2 Streaming chat with useChat

// Edge route — app/api/chat/route.ts
import { streamText, convertToCoreMessages } from "ai";
import { openai } from "@ai-sdk/openai";
import { searchDocs } from "@/lib/tools";
import { rateLimit } from "@/lib/ratelimit";

export const runtime = "edge";

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const { ok } = await rateLimit(req);                 // per-user gate BEFORE the model call
  if (!ok) return new Response("Too many requests", { status: 429 });

  const { messages } = await req.json();
  const result = streamText({
    model: openai("gpt-4.1-mini"),
    messages: convertToCoreMessages(messages),
    tools: { searchDocs },
    abortSignal: req.signal,                            // cancel model when client disconnects
    onFinish: ({ usage, finishReason }) => trackTokens(usage, finishReason),
  });
  return result.toDataStreamResponse();
}
// Client
"use client";
import { useChat } from "ai/react";

export function Chat() {
  const { messages, input, handleInputChange, handleSubmit, stop, status } =
    useChat({ api: "/api/chat", experimental_throttle: 50 });

  return (
    <>
      {messages.map((m) => <Message key={m.id} role={m.role} parts={m.parts} />)}
      <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
        <input value={input} onChange={handleInputChange} />
        {status === "streaming"
          ? <button type="button" onClick={stop}>Stop</button>
          : <button type="submit">Send</button>}
      </form>
    </>
  );
}

What's happening. streamText returns immediately with a streaming handle; toDataStreamResponse() serializes tokens, tool calls, and metadata into a protocol useChat understands. useChat manages message state, appends streamed deltas, and exposes status (submitted/streaming/ready/error) and stop(). Passing req.signal as abortSignal means stop() (which aborts the fetch) propagates all the way to cancelling the model generation — so a cancelled chat stops billing tokens.

4.3 Generative UI (streamUI)

  • Model picks which React component to render for the next step (card, chart, confirmation).
  • Define typed tools; each returns a React element.
  • Safety: only stream components safe to render with model-controlled props; no raw HTML or dangerouslySetInnerHTML.

How it works. streamUI (RSC variant) lets each tool's generate function *return a React element* instead of text. The model calls a tool with typed (Zod-validated) arguments; you render a real, vetted component with those args. The model never produces markup — it produces *structured arguments* you map to your own components, which is what keeps it safe.

// server action using streamUI
import { streamUI } from "ai/rsc";
import { openai } from "@ai-sdk/openai";
import { z } from "zod";

export async function submitMessage(prompt: string) {
  const result = await streamUI({
    model: openai("gpt-4.1"),
    prompt,
    text: ({ content }) => <p>{content}</p>,            // plain text path
    tools: {
      showWeather: {
        description: "Display the weather for a city",
        parameters: z.object({ city: z.string(), unit: z.enum(["C", "F"]) }),
        generate: async function* ({ city, unit }) {
          yield <WeatherSkeleton />;                    // stream a loading state
          const data = await getWeather(city);
          return <WeatherCard city={city} unit={unit} data={data} />; // vetted component, typed props
        },
      },
    },
  });
  return result.value;
}

Prompt-injection safety. The model controls *which* tool and *what arguments*, never the rendered HTML. So: validate every tool param with Zod (reject out-of-range values), never pass model output into dangerouslySetInnerHTML or into href/src without an allowlist, treat any action-performing tool (sends email, charges a card) as requiring an explicit human confirmation step, and scope tools to least privilege. A retrieved document can contain "ignore previous instructions" — so retrieved content is *data*, never appended to the system prompt as if it were trusted.

4.4 Streaming UX

  • Token-rate-adjusted typewriter; do not just dump deltas.
  • Render assistant messages in Suspense; avoid relayout per token.
  • experimental_throttle keeps render rate under 60 fps on slow devices.
  • stop() + AbortSignal so cancelled chats do not bill.
  • Per-user rate limit; content policy upstream of model call.

Why throttling matters. A fast model emits many small deltas; naively calling setMessages on each delta triggers a React render *per token*, which on a long conversation re-renders the whole list dozens of times a second → INP spikes and dropped frames. experimental_throttle: 50 coalesces UI updates to ~20fps of state commits (smooth enough for reading, cheap for React). Pair with: virtualize the message list (only render visible messages), memoize each message so finished messages don't re-render while the last one streams, and content-visibility: auto on off-screen messages. The combination is the difference between INP 180ms and 420ms.

const Message = memo(function Message({ parts }: { parts: MessagePart[] }) {
  return <div className="msg">{parts.map(renderPart)}</div>;
});
// only the streaming (last) message re-renders; settled ones are memo-stable by reference

4.5 RAG basics

  • Embed → vector store (Pinecone, pgvector, Turbopuffer, Vercel Vector).
  • Top-k retrieve → pass as context → cite back to UI.
  • Latency budget: 80 ms embed + 60 ms vector + 700 ms first token = ~840 ms TTFB.

End-to-end pipeline. (1) Ingest (offline): chunk documents (~300–800 tokens with overlap, on semantic boundaries), embed each chunk, upsert {embedding, text, metadata} into the vector store. (2) Query (online): embed the user query, similarity-search top-k (cosine), optionally rerank the candidates with a cross-encoder for precision, then build a prompt with the retrieved chunks as context plus instructions to cite sources and say "I don't know" if the context doesn't answer. (3) Generate + cite: stream the answer and surface the source chunks' metadata as clickable citations.

import { embed, generateText } from "ai";
import { openai } from "@ai-sdk/openai";

async function answer(query: string) {
  const { embedding } = await embed({ model: openai.embedding("text-embedding-3-small"), value: query });
  const chunks = await vectorStore.query(embedding, { topK: 5 });         // ~60ms
  const context = chunks.map((c, i) => `[${i + 1}] ${c.text}`).join("\n\n");
  const { text } = await generateText({
    model: openai("gpt-4.1-mini"),
    system: "Answer ONLY from the context. Cite sources like [1]. If unknown, say so.",
    prompt: `Context:\n${context}\n\nQuestion: ${query}`,
  });
  return { text, sources: chunks.map((c) => c.metadata) };
}

Quality levers a senior mentions: chunking strategy and overlap, hybrid search (BM25 + vector) for exact-match terms, reranking, and citation grounding to fight hallucination. Latency levers: cache embeddings of repeated queries, stream first token while retrieval metadata renders.

4.6 Evals + observability

  • Tiny test suite of input/output + LLM-as-judge; run per PR.
  • Log token usage, latency, finish reason, tool call counts.
  • Senior story: "shipped AI feature, INP 180 → 420 ms; fixed via virtualization + per-message memo + token throttle".

Evaluating non-determinism in CI. Build a small golden dataset of representative inputs with either exact expectations (classification/extraction → assert accuracy/F1 deterministically) or rubric-graded outputs (open-ended → LLM-as-judge scoring faithfulness, relevance, and "no hallucination beyond context"). Run on every PR; gate merges on a score threshold rather than exact-string match.

Making the judge non-flaky: set the judge's temperature: 0, give it a precise rubric with examples, ask for a structured score (generateObject with a Zod schema) not prose, average over N runs or use majority vote, and pin the judge model version. Track the *delta* vs. the baseline prompt rather than absolute scores. For RAG specifically, measure retrieval (recall@k, MRR) and generation (faithfulness, relevance) separately so you know which half regressed.

Observability in prod: log token usage, latency (TTFT and total), finishReason (watch for length/content-filter), tool-call counts and failures, and user feedback (thumbs). The onFinish callback is the hook. The performance war story: shipping an AI chat that regressed INP from 180→420ms, root-caused to per-token re-renders of a long unvirtualized list, fixed with list virtualization + per-message memo + experimental_throttle.

Part 5 — State management 2026

5.1 The four buckets

BucketExamplesBest tool 2026
Server statelists from API, paginated dataTanStack Query / SWR / RSC + Server Actions
Global clienttheme, sidebar, current workspaceZustand (or React Context for tiny)
Form / local UIcontrolled inputs, wizardsReact Hook Form + Zod; useReducer
Derived / atomizedcells in spreadsheet, graph nodesJotai or Signals (Preact/Solid)

The one classification that prevents most state mistakes: *server state is not client state.* Server state is a cache of data that lives elsewhere, is shared, and goes stale — it needs fetching, caching, deduping, background refetch, and invalidation (TanStack Query / RSC). Client state is owned by the UI and never stale (theme, which modal is open) — that's Zustand/Context/useState. The classic anti-pattern is storing fetched data in Redux/Zustand and hand-writing loading/error/refetch logic that TanStack Query gives you for free. In the App Router, a lot of "server state" disappears into Server Components + Server Actions entirely — you only reach for TanStack Query on the client when you need polling, infinite scroll, optimistic mutations, or client-side cache sharing.

5.2 Zustand

import { create } from "zustand";

interface UIState {
  sidebarOpen: boolean;
  toggleSidebar: () => void;
}
const useUI = create<UIState>((set) => ({
  sidebarOpen: true,
  toggleSidebar: () => set((s) => ({ sidebarOpen: !s.sidebarOpen })),
}));
// component re-renders only when sidebarOpen changes
const open = useUI((s) => s.sidebarOpen);
  • Single store, no provider, selector-based subscription.
  • Middleware: persist, devtools, immer, subscribeWithSelector.
  • Pattern: keep stores small + feature-scoped; do NOT put server cache here.

Why Zustand is the 2026 default for global client state. No provider (the store is a module singleton with a hook), and selector-based subscriptions: a component subscribing via useUI(s => s.sidebarOpen) only re-renders when *that slice* changes by Object.is, not on every store update. That's the perf property Context lacks (Context re-renders every consumer on any value change).

Selector gotcha: returning a *new object/array* from a selector every call breaks the equality check and re-renders always:

// WRONG — new object each render → always re-renders
const { x, y } = useStore((s) => ({ x: s.x, y: s.y }));
// RIGHT — useShallow for multi-field selection
import { useShallow } from "zustand/react/shallow";
const { x, y } = useStore(useShallow((s) => ({ x: s.x, y: s.y })));

For SSR/Next, create the store *per request* via a context-provided factory to avoid leaking state across users; for client-only globals the module singleton is fine. Keep server cache out of Zustand.

5.3 TanStack Query

  • Stale-while-revalidate cache keyed by queryKey.
  • Background refetch on focus, reconnect, mount.
  • Mutations: onMutate / onError / onSettled for optimism + rollback.
  • useSuspenseQuery pairs cleanly with React 19 Suspense.

Mechanism. Each query is keyed by a serializable queryKey; the cache stores data + status + timestamps. staleTime controls how long data is "fresh" (no refetch); gcTime controls how long unused data lingers before garbage collection. While stale data is shown, a background refetch updates it (SWR). Refetch triggers: window focus, reconnect, remount, key change. Deduping: concurrent components with the same key share one in-flight request.

Optimistic mutation with rollback — the canonical pattern:

const mutation = useMutation({
  mutationFn: (text: string) => api.addTodo(text),
  onMutate: async (text) => {
    await qc.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ["todos"] });          // stop races
    const prev = qc.getQueryData<Todo[]>(["todos"]);
    qc.setQueryData<Todo[]>(["todos"], (old = []) => [...old, { id: "tmp", text }]);
    return { prev };                                          // context for rollback
  },
  onError: (_e, _vars, ctx) => qc.setQueryData(["todos"], ctx?.prev), // rollback
  onSettled: () => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["todos"] }),     // reconcile with server
});

useSuspenseQuery removes the isLoading branch — it suspends, so a parent <Suspense> shows the fallback and an error boundary catches failures, composing with React 19's concurrent model.

5.4 Jotai (atomized state)

  • Shines when many independently subscribable values + derive across them (10K cells, graph nodes).
  • Zustand wins for ~5 global flags — boilerplate-to-feature ratio.

Bottom-up vs top-down. Zustand is one store you select *out of*. Jotai composes state *up* from tiny atoms; components subscribe to exactly the atoms they read, and derived atoms recompute only when their dependencies change. This shines when you have thousands of independently-updating values (spreadsheet cells, canvas nodes, form fields) because updating one atom re-renders only its subscribers — no central store to diff.

import { atom, useAtom } from "jotai";
const cellsAtom = atom<Record<string, number>>({});
const cellAtom = (id: string) => atom(
  (get) => get(cellsAtom)[id] ?? 0,
  (get, set, v: number) => set(cellsAtom, { ...get(cellsAtom), [id]: v }),
);
// A1 updating does not re-render B2 — each cell subscribes to its own derived atom

Use Jotai when the *granularity* of subscription matters; use Zustand when you have a handful of global flags and want minimal ceremony.

5.5 Signals (radar)

  • Preact / Solid / Angular signals — fine-grained reactivity without VDOM diff.
  • TC39 Signals proposal has community momentum.
  • In React: @preact/signals-react, signia, alien-signals — bring up as tradeoff, not production default.

The model. A signal is a reactive value; reading it inside a tracked scope auto-subscribes, and writing it surgically updates exactly the DOM nodes that read it — no VDOM diff, no component re-render. Solid and Preact Signals deliver near-vanilla update performance this way. The TC39 Signals proposal aims to standardize the primitive so frameworks share one core.

In React the fit is awkward: React's model is "re-render the component, then diff," so signals libraries (@preact/signals-react) bolt on fine-grained updates via a Babel transform — useful but not idiomatic, and they fight the React Compiler's assumptions. Senior take: signals are the more efficient reactivity model and worth discussing as a tradeoff, but in React 2026 the Compiler closes most of the perf gap, so signals aren't the production default *in React* — they're the default *in Solid/Preact*.

5.6 Redux Toolkit — still?

  • Yes for legacy migrations + RTK Query codebases.
  • Greenfield 2026: only if org has standardized.

Where RTK still earns its place: large apps with complex, highly-interconnected client state that benefits from a single auditable store, time-travel debugging, and strict action logging (finance, complex editors); teams already invested in RTK Query (a capable server-cache layer comparable to TanStack Query); and any codebase where team standardization value outweighs bundle/boilerplate cost. For greenfield, the 2026 default is RSC + Server Actions for server state, TanStack Query for client server-cache, and Zustand/Jotai for client state — you reach for RTK only when the org has standardized on it or you genuinely need its middleware/devtools rigor.

Part 6 — 30 interview questions on this material

React 19

  • Explain the React Compiler. When does it bail? How do you debug a bailout?

A build-time Babel plugin that auto-memoizes components, hook values, and JSX by inferring each value's dependency set from a control-flow analysis, emitting a hidden memo cache so you stop hand-writing useMemo/useCallback/React.memo. It bails (leaves a component un-optimized, preferring correctness) when it can't prove safety: mutating props/state during render, reading/writing ref.current in render, or any Rules-of-React violation. To debug, check the "Memo ✨" badge in React DevTools to confirm whether a component was optimized, run eslint-plugin-react-compiler which flags un-optimizable code before shipping, and fix the underlying purity violation rather than reaching for manual memo.

  • Server Components vs Client Components, including serialization. How would you pass a Date or Map across?

Server Components run only on the server, ship zero JS, can be async and read DB/secrets, and serialize their output to the RSC Flight payload; Client Components ("use client") ship JS and own interactivity/state but can't be async. The boundary is an *import* boundary — a Client Component can't import a Server Component but can render one passed as children/props. Flight serialization supports primitives, plain objects/arrays, Date, Map, Set, Promise, and Server Action references — so a Date or Map crosses fine as-is; what *doesn't* cross is class instances with methods (a Prisma/Mongoose model) or arbitrary functions, which you convert to plain DTOs first.

  • What does use() do that useContext + Promise + useState cannot?

use can be called conditionally and in loops (no fixed hook slot), and it natively integrates with Suspense — pass it a pending promise and it suspends the nearest boundary, replaying the render when it resolves and throwing to the error boundary on rejection. The useContext + useState + useEffect combination can't read context conditionally, requires an effect-driven state machine for the promise (extra render, manual loading/error), and doesn't suspend. The idiomatic pattern is to create the promise in a Server Component, pass it across the boundary, and unwrap it with use in a Client Component — kicking off the fetch on the server while keeping the promise referentially stable.

  • Implement a Server Action with useOptimistic for adding a comment. Conflict resolution?

Define a "use server" action that re-authenticates, Zod-validates, inserts, and revalidatePaths; on the client wrap the real comments list in useOptimistic(comments, (s, text) => [...s, {id: tmp, text, pending: true}]) and call addOptimistic(text) inside the form's action (which is a transition). The temp item shows immediately with reduced opacity; when the server revalidates, the authoritative list replaces it and the optimistic layer is discarded automatically — no manual rollback. For conflicts, each client only ever optimistically adds its *own* item, so concurrent posts both persist; the revalidated server order is authoritative (last-write-wins on ordering, no lost writes), and if the action throws, the optimistic item simply vanishes on the next commit while you surface the error via useActionState.

  • useTransition vs useDeferredValue vs Suspense — when each?

useTransition when you *own* the state update and want to mark it non-urgent (tab/view/route switches) — it keeps the old UI interactive and gives you isPending. useDeferredValue when you *receive* a value you don't own the setter for and want a lagging copy to drive an expensive render (type-to-filter a huge list). Suspense for *data that isn't loaded yet* — it shows a fallback while a child suspends. They compose: a transition can wrap a navigation that itself suspends. The anti-pattern is wrapping every setState in startTransition, which defers work without making it faster and masks real perf problems.

  • Selective hydration: what if a user clicks before hydration finishes?

React records the event, prioritizes hydrating *that* Suspense boundary first (jumping the queue), then replays the captured event against the now-hydrated tree. So the click isn't lost — it's slightly delayed rather than dropped. This works because React 18+ hydrates boundaries independently and in parallel rather than in one blocking pass, and dispatches replayable events captured at the document level before hydration. The practical implication: wrap interactive regions in their own Suspense boundaries so a heavy unrelated subtree can't block them from hydrating on demand.

  • How does the RSC payload (Flight) work over the wire?

The server renders Server Components into a compact streaming serialization (Flight) that describes the element tree as rows — host elements, props, text, references to Client Component chunks (by module id), and holes where those islands mount. It streams incrementally: the shell first, then suspended subtrees as their data resolves, each chunk referencing earlier rows so the client can progressively reconstruct the tree. The browser parses this into React elements, downloads only the referenced Client Component JS, and hydrates those islands — Server Component code and its imports never ship. On client navigation Next fetches the new route's Flight payload (not HTML) and patches the tree, which is why soft navigation is fast and preserves client state.

Next.js 15

  • Explain PPR. What's prerendered, what streams? How do PPR and middleware interact?

Partial Prerendering moves the static/dynamic decision from per-route to per-component: at build time Next prerenders a static shell and leaves holes wherever a <Suspense> boundary wraps something reading dynamic data (cookies, headers, uncached fetch). The shell serves from the CDN with near-zero TTFB; the dynamic holes render per request on the server and stream into their fallbacks over the same response — so you get static TTFB plus personalization. Anything outside a Suspense boundary that doesn't touch dynamic APIs is prerendered; anything inside one that does becomes a streamed hole (and a dynamic read outside any boundary forces the whole route dynamic). Middleware still runs at the edge in front of the cache on every request, so coarse auth/redirects compose cleanly with the cached shell — you just don't try to personalize the shell itself in middleware.

  • Walk through Next.js 15 fetch caching. Why did the default change to no-store?

Four caches: Request Memoization (dedupes identical fetches within one render), the Data Cache (persistent server cache of fetch results across requests, invalidated by revalidateTag/revalidatePath/time), the Full Route Cache (rendered RSC+HTML for static routes), and the client Router Cache (in-memory prefetched segments). Next 15 flipped the fetch default from cached to no-store — along with uncached GET route handlers and client router cache — because the old cache-by-default silently served stale data and was the top source of "why isn't my update showing" bugs. Now you explicitly opt in with next: { revalidate, tags } or unstable_cache for non-fetch sources, trading a little verbosity for predictable freshness.

  • Edge vs Node runtime — three examples for each.

Edge runs in V8 isolates at every PoP with ~0ms cold start but no Node APIs and limited packages: use it for middleware (auth redirects, A/B/geo), streaming LLM responses (just piping a ReadableStream), and low-latency personalization/redirects. Node has full APIs and slower cold starts: use it for ORM/TCP-database access (Prisma/Drizzle), file and image processing (sharp, uploads), and heavy crypto/PDF generation or any library with native Node deps. The deciding factor is dependencies and compute shape — short, I/O-bound, web-API-only work goes Edge; anything needing Node built-ins or a TCP driver goes Node (though HTTP-based DB drivers like Neon can run on Edge).

  • Design a Next app for e-commerce with 100K SKUs + personalized recs. Mix SSG/ISR/PPR/dynamic.

Product detail pages use ISR (generateStaticParams for the top sellers, on-demand/lazy generation for the long tail with revalidate + revalidateTag('product:'+id) on inventory/price changes) so 100K SKUs aren't all built up front. The PDP itself uses PPR: static shell (images, description, specs from CDN) with the personalized recommendations and live inventory as streamed Suspense holes reading the user's session. Category/search pages are dynamic or cached-with-tags depending on facet cardinality; cart and checkout are dynamic (per-user). Tag the data cache by entity (product, inventory, price) so a price update invalidates surgically rather than rebuilding routes, and run personalization in the streamed hole so the cacheable shell stays shared across users.

  • Auth: cookie-based session + edge middleware + Server Actions. Where do you check authz?

Three layers: edge middleware does *coarse authentication* — verify the signed session cookie (no DB call) and redirect unauthenticated users — but never role/resource checks. Server Components read the verified session to render the right data. Server Actions and Route Handlers re-check authorization on every mutation, against the specific resource (does this user own this project?), because actions are public RPC endpoints anyone can POST to. The cardinal rule: the client user object is a UI hint only; every authorization decision lives on the server at the mutation boundary, re-validating input with Zod too.

  • How do parallel + intercepting routes power Instagram modal-over-page?

A parallel @modal slot renders alongside the page in the layout, and an intercepting route (@modal/(.)photo/[id]) catches soft navigations to /photo/[id] from the feed, rendering the photo as a modal *over* the current feed instead of a full page. The real photo/[id]/page.tsx still exists, so a hard refresh or a shared deep link renders the standalone full page. Same URL, two presentations depending on how you arrived — modal on soft nav, full page on direct load — and it's deep-linkable and shareable for free. The layout renders both {children} and {modal}, with a default.tsx returning null when no modal is active.

  • Bundle is 1.2 MB on initial load. Cut it in half.

First run @next/bundle-analyzer to find the fat client modules. The biggest App Router lever is moving display-only components to Server Components so their code (markdown renderers, date libs, syntax highlighters) never ships; then push "use client" down to interactive leaves so shared utils don't get dragged client-side. next/dynamic with ssr:false for genuinely heavy client-only widgets (charts, editors, maps) so they load on demand, and replace heavy deps (moment→date-fns/Temporal, full lodash→per-method/native). Re-measure after each change — usually moving a few large components server-side plus code-splitting two widgets gets you the 50%.

AI / streaming

  • Implement streaming chat with cancellation + rate limit using Vercel AI SDK.

On an edge route, rate-limit per user *before* the model call (return 429 if exceeded), then call streamText({ model, messages, abortSignal: req.signal, onFinish }) and return result.toDataStreamResponse(). Passing req.signal as abortSignal means when the client aborts, the model generation is cancelled too — so you stop billing for abandoned chats. On the client, useChat({ api, experimental_throttle: 50 }) gives stop() (which aborts the fetch and thus the model) and status to toggle a Stop/Send button. The throttle coalesces token updates to keep render rate sane on slow devices.

  • What is generative UI? How do you keep it safe from prompt injection?

Generative UI lets the model choose *which* vetted React component to render and with *what typed arguments* (via streamUI and Zod-validated tools), rather than producing markup — each tool's generate returns a real component you control. Safety comes from the model never controlling HTML: validate every tool parameter with Zod, never feed model output into dangerouslySetInnerHTML or unguarded href/src, and gate any action-performing tool (send, charge) behind explicit human confirmation. Crucially, treat retrieved/RAG content as untrusted *data*, never appending it to the system prompt as instructions — that's how a document saying "ignore previous instructions" gets neutralized.

  • Add RAG-powered docs search to your product. Design end-to-end.

Offline: chunk docs on semantic boundaries (~300–800 tokens with overlap), embed each chunk, and upsert {embedding, text, metadata} into a vector store (pgvector/Pinecone/Turbopuffer). Online: embed the query, similarity-search top-k, optionally rerank with a cross-encoder for precision, build a prompt with the chunks as context plus "answer only from context, cite sources, say I-don't-know otherwise," then stream the answer and render citations from the chunk metadata. Quality levers: chunking strategy, hybrid BM25+vector for exact terms, reranking, and citation grounding to fight hallucination; latency budget is roughly 80ms embed + 60ms retrieve + 700ms first token ≈ 840ms TTFT, improved by caching repeat-query embeddings and streaming.

  • AI feature regressed INP from 180 to 420 ms. Diagnose + fix.

Profile in the Performance panel during streaming — the regression is almost always per-token re-renders: each streamed delta calls setMessages, re-rendering the entire message list dozens of times a second on a long conversation. Fix with experimental_throttle to coalesce UI updates to ~20fps, memo each message so settled messages stay reference-stable while only the streaming last message re-renders, and virtualize the list so off-screen messages aren't rendered at all (plus content-visibility: auto). That combination — virtualization + per-message memo + token throttle — is what takes INP back under 200ms.

  • How do you evaluate an LLM feature in CI? What if LLM-as-judge is flaky?

Maintain a small golden dataset and run it per PR: for classification/extraction assert accuracy/F1 deterministically; for open-ended outputs use LLM-as-judge scoring faithfulness, relevance, and no-hallucination against a rubric, gating merges on a threshold delta vs. baseline rather than exact strings. To de-flake the judge: set temperature: 0, use a precise rubric with examples, request a structured score via generateObject+Zod (not prose), average over N runs or majority-vote, and pin the judge model version. For RAG, measure retrieval (recall@k, MRR) and generation (faithfulness, relevance) separately so you can tell which half regressed.

  • Backpressure: model emits faster than client renders. Handle without dropping tokens.

The transport is a ReadableStream, so backpressure is handled by the stream's pull mechanism — the server only produces as fast as the consumer pulls, so tokens aren't dropped, they queue. The actual problem is *render* rate, not network: don't re-render per token. Buffer incoming deltas and flush to React state on a throttle (experimental_throttle / requestAnimationFrame-batched), decoupling token arrival from commit frequency. Combined with memoized messages and virtualization, the UI stays at 60fps while every token is still appended in order — coalesced, never lost.

State

  • TanStack Query vs Zustand vs RSC — when each? Can RSC replace TanStack Query?

TanStack Query for client-side *server state* needing caching, dedupe, background refetch, polling, infinite scroll, or optimistic mutations; Zustand for *client* state the UI owns (theme, sidebar, current workspace); RSC + Server Actions for server data you can fetch and mutate on the server without shipping a client cache at all. RSC replaces TanStack Query for the common "fetch on the server, render, mutate via action, revalidate" flow — which is a lot of apps. But it doesn't replace TanStack Query when you need *client-side* interactivity over server data: focus refetch, polling, infinite scroll, cross-component cache sharing, or optimistic UX beyond a single action. So they're complementary — RSC for initial/server-driven data, TanStack Query for rich client-side data interactions.

  • 200 re-renders per keystroke. Diagnose + fix.

Profile with the React DevTools Profiler to see what re-renders on each keystroke — usually a top-level value/setValue lives high in the tree and every child re-renders, or a Context value (or a Zustand selector returning a new object) changes identity every render. Fixes: colocate the input state in the smallest component that needs it; for Context split it or move to Zustand with narrow selectors (and useShallow for multi-field), so only subscribers of the changed slice re-render; use useDeferredValue to keep the expensive filtered list off the typing path; and let the React Compiler (or memo) skip unaffected subtrees. The root cause is almost always state lifted too high plus unstable references — fix locality and equality, not by sprinkling memo blindly.

  • When would you reach for Jotai over Zustand? Concrete example.

When you have many independently-subscribable values and want subscription granularity per value, not a central store you select out of. Concrete example: a spreadsheet with 10K cells where editing A1 must re-render only A1 and the cells deriving from it (B2 = A1+1), not the whole grid. With Jotai each cell is its own atom and derived atoms recompute only when their dependency atoms change, so updates are surgically scoped. Zustand would force one big store and careful selectors to avoid re-rendering 10K cells; for a handful of global flags Zustand's lower ceremony wins, but at high granularity Jotai's atomic model is the right tool.

  • Design state for a Figma-like canvas with 10K nodes.

Split by concern: ephemeral high-frequency state (cursor, drag deltas, hover) lives outside React in refs/an imperative layer updated on requestAnimationFrame so dragging doesn't trigger React renders; committed document state (node positions, properties) is atomized so moving one node re-renders only that node and its dependents — Jotai atoms per node, or a normalized store with fine-grained selectors. Render with a canvas/WebGL layer (or virtualized DOM) so only visible nodes paint, and keep selection/tool state in a small global store (Zustand). Persistence and collaboration go through a CRDT (Yjs/Automerge) syncing the document state, with undo/redo as an immutable command log — never a single monolithic useState re-rendering 10K nodes per interaction.

  • Migrate a Redux Toolkit codebase to Zustand + TanStack Query.

First *classify* the existing store: separate true server state (fetched lists, entities) from client state (UI flags, selections). Move server state to TanStack Query — replace thunks/RTK Query endpoints with useQuery/useMutation, deleting hand-rolled loading/error/refetch logic. Move client state to Zustand stores, feature-scoped, porting reducers to set updaters and keeping selectors narrow. Migrate incrementally slice by slice behind the existing Provider (both coexist during transition), verifying with the DevTools Profiler that re-render counts drop, then remove Redux once the last slice is ported. The win is deleting boilerplate (server-cache logic and action/reducer ceremony); the risk to manage is optimistic-update and cache-invalidation parity, so port those flows carefully with onMutate/rollback.
