docs.search: 03 — React + Modern Stack (Next.js + AI + State) 2026 React 19 · Server Components · Next.js 15 PPR · Vercel AI SDK · Zustand + TanStack Merged from v2/02 (React + state) and v3/08 (React 19 / Next.js 15 / AI SDK). Self-contained. Part 1 — React fundamentals refresher 1.1 Reconciliation + commit Render phase: pure — builds the next fiber tree. May be paused, restarted (concurrent). Commit phase: synchronous — applies DOM mutations + fires effects. Keys identify reorders; never use array index for dynamic lists. Mechanism. React keeps two fiber trees: current (on screen) and workInProgress (being built). Reconciliation diffs the new element tree against current using a heuristic that is O(n) instead of the O(n³) of a general tree diff. The heuristic rests on two assumptions: (1) elements of different *type* produce different trees — so React tears down and rebuilds rather than diffing across a type change; (2) key is a stable identity hint across renders. In concurrent mode the render phase is interruptible: React builds workInProgress in units of work and can yield to the browser between fibers (a scheduler checks shouldYield() against a ~5ms frame budget). Because render can restart, render must be pure — any side effect there can run twice or be thrown away. The commit phase is a single synchronous, uninterruptible pass with three sub-phases: before mutation (run getSnapshotBeforeUpdate , schedule useEffect ), mutation (apply DOM ops, run useLayoutEffect cleanups), and layout (run useLayoutEffect setups, swap current = workInProgress ). Passive effects ( useEffect ) flush asynchronously after paint. Why index keys break. With index keys, reordering or prepending shifts every element's identity, so React reconciles item[0] 's old state into the new item[0] — stale input values, wrong checkbox states, lost focus. // WRONG — index key: deleting the first row keeps the deleted row's DOM state on row 0 {rows.map((row, i) => <EditableRow key={i} row={row} />)} // RIGHT — stable identity survives reorder/insert/delete {rows.map((row) => <EditableRow key={row.id} row={row} />)} A staff-level point: when a list has no naturally stable id (freshly created client rows), generate one at creation ( crypto.randomUUID() ), not at render — generating in render produces a new key every render and remounts the component each time. 1.2 Hooks core Hook Use Gotcha useState Local component state Functional updater for stable updates from async useReducer Complex state transitions Pair with discriminated union actions for TS useEffect Side effects after commit Cleanup runs before next effect + on unmount useLayoutEffect Read DOM before paint Synchronous — blocks paint; rarely needed useMemo / useCallback Memoize expensive values Mostly obsolete in React 19 (Compiler) useRef Mutable box that survives re-render Not reactive; setting it does not trigger render useTransition Non-urgent update flag Use for state-driven view switches useDeferredValue Cheap throttle on expensive renders Best for typing → large filter State is a snapshot, not a variable. Each render closes over the state value it was rendered with. This is why batching multiple setCount(count + 1) calls in one event only increments once — they all read the same snapshot. The functional updater setCount(c => c + 1) reads the *queued* value, so three of them increment by three. The same closure-capture rule is the root cause of stale values inside setTimeout , event listeners, and async callbacks. Effects synchronize, they don't "run on mount." Think of useEffect as: "keep this external system in sync with these reactive values." The dependency array is not an optimization knob — it is the set of values the effect reads. Lying about deps (omitting one to "run once") creates stale closures. If an effect should truly run once with no dependency on render values, it usually shouldn't be an effect at all (move it to a module, an event handler, or a ref -guarded init). function SearchBox({ query }: { query: string }) { const [results, setResults] = useState<string[]>([]); // RIGHT — effect re-syncs whenever `query` changes; cleanup cancels the stale request useEffect(() => { const ctrl = new AbortController(); fetch(`/api/search?q=${query}`, { signal: ctrl.signal }) .then((r) => r.json()) .then(setResults) .catch((e) => { if (e.name !== "AbortError") throw e; }); return () => ctrl.abort(); // cleanup mirrors setup; runs before next effect + unmount }, [query]); return <Results items={results} />; } useRef is your escape hatch for values that must persist without driving renders (timers, previous values, imperative DOM handles). Writing ref.current during render is a Rules-of-React violation (impure); read/write it in effects or handlers. 1.3 Rules of React Components are pure given props + state. Same input → same output. Hooks called in the same order every render. Never mutate props or state; always return new values. Effects describe synchronization; cleanup mirrors setup. Why purity is now load-bearing. Concurrent React may render a component, throw the result away, and render it again (e.g. when a higher-priority update preempts, or under <StrictMode> which intentionally double-invokes render and effects in dev). The React Compiler also depends on purity: it memoizes based on a static read-set analysis and assumes the same inputs produce the same output with no side effects. Break purity and the compiler can serve a stale memoized result. The order rule exists because hooks are stored in a linked list on the fiber indexed by call order, not by name. A conditional hook shifts every subsequent hook's slot, so React reads the wrong state. eslint-plugin-react-hooks enforces rules-of-hooks and honest dependency arrays via exhaustive-deps . // WRONG — conditional hook: slot indices shift between renders function Profile({ id }: { id?: string }) { if (!id) return null; const [user, setUser] = useState(null); // sometimes called → state corruption } // RIGHT — hooks unconditional, branch on the value function Profile({ id }: { id?: string }) { const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null); if (!id) return null; // ... } Mutation rule in practice: state.items.push(x); setState(state) does nothing — same reference, bailout. Always produce a new reference ( setState(s => [...s, x]) ), or use Immer for ergonomic immutable updates. Part 2 — React 19 (the staff-eng mental model) 2.1 React Compiler Babel/SWC plugin that auto-memoizes components and hook values based on read-set analysis at build time. Default in Next.js 15. // Before React 19 const Row = React.memo(function Row({ user, onSelect }) { const full = useMemo(() => `${user.first} ${user.last}`, [user]); const handler = useCallback(() => onSelect(user.id), [onSelect, user.id]); return <li onClick={handler}>{full}</li>; }); // React 19 — write the obvious thing function Row({ user, onSelect }: { user: User; onSelect: (id: string) => void }) { const full = `${user.first} ${user.last}`; return <li onClick={() => onSelect(user.id)}>{full}</li>; } Bailouts: mutate inputs, misuse refs, break Rules of React. Still useMemo when: compiler bails, profile says, value crosses external system. Mechanism. The compiler runs as a Babel plugin during build. It builds a control-flow graph of each component, infers which values derive from which inputs (props, state, hook returns), and emits code backed by a hidden memoization cache (conceptually a useMemoCache(n) array, one slot per memoizable value). At runtime each slot stores [lastDeps, lastValue] ; if deps are referentially equal it reuses the value — exactly what hand-written useMemo / useCallback / React.memo did, but with correct, exhaustive dependencies humans routinely get wrong. It memoizes JSX too, so child elements are skipped when their inputs are unchanged. Enabling and verifying (Next 15). // next.config.ts import type { NextConfig } from "next"; const config: NextConfig = { experimental: { reactCompiler: true } }; export default config; Install eslint-plugin-react-compiler and babel-plugin-react-compiler . The ESLint rule flags code the compiler will skip *before* you ship. In React DevTools, compiler-optimized components show a "Memo ✨" badge — that's how you confirm a component was optimized rather than bailed. Debugging a bailout. The compiler is conservative: if it cannot prove a transformation is safe, it leaves the component un-optimized (correctness over speed). Common causes: mutating props/state during render, reading or writing ref.current during render, calling a function it cannot analyze, or eslint-disable -ing a rules-of-hooks error. To debug: check the DevTools badge, run the compiler's health-check/logger, and fix the underlying purity violation rather than reaching back for manual memo. You still hand-write useMemo for genuinely expensive computations the compiler can't see across a boundary (value passed into a non-React system) or when profiling proves a hot path needs it. 2.2 The use() hook Reads a Promise or a Context. Unlike useContext, callable conditionally. async function ProductPage({ id }: { id: string }) { const product = use(getProduct(id)); // suspends; streams when ready return <ProductCard product={product} />; } function PriceTag({ showTax }: { showTax: boolean }) { const tax = showTax ? use(TaxContext) : null; return <span>{tax ? `${tax}%` : "no tax"}</span>; } Promise must be stable; memoize in parent or hoist to a cache. What use actually does. use is not a hook in the linked-list sense — it can be called inside conditionals and loops because it doesn't allocate a persistent slot. When passed a Promise, it integrates with Suspense: if pending it *throws* the promise (suspending the nearest boundary); when it resolves React replays the render and use returns the value; if it rejects, the nearest error boundary catches it. When passed a Context it reads the value like useContext but is allowed in branches. The stability gotcha. Because a suspended render replays, calling use(fetch(...)) inline in a Client Component creates a *new* promise every render → infinite suspend loop. The promise must be created outside render and be referentially stable. The clean pattern: create it in a Server Component (which doesn't re-render the same way) and pass it down. // Server Component creates the promise once and passes it across the boundary async function Page({ id }: { id: string }) { const userPromise = getUser(id); // not awaited here return ( <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}> <Profile userPromise={userPromise} /> </Suspense> ); } // Client Component unwraps it with use() — promise is stable (came from props) "use client"; function Profile({ userPromise }: { userPromise: Promise<User> }) { const user = use(userPromise); return <h1>{user.name}</h1>; } This is the canonical "start fetching on the server, stream + unwrap on the client" pattern. use over useContext + useState +effect gives you conditional reads, automatic Suspense integration, and no waterfall. 2.3 Server Components vs Client Components Server: never ships JS, can be async, reads DB/fs/env, no hooks/browser APIs. Client ("use client"): ships JS, can use state/effects, cannot be async. Composition: a Client Component can render Server Components only as children/props. Props must be serializable across the boundary (no functions except Server Actions). The mental model. Picture the tree split by a network boundary. Server Components (the default in the App Router — no directive needed) run *only* on the server during request/build. They execute, then *serialize their output* into a compact streaming format, the RSC Payload (Flight) — a description of the rendered tree, including holes where Client Components go and references to their JS chunks. 04 — Modern Web Platform & CSS (2026)

CSS layout · Container queries · :has · View Transitions · Accessibility · Browser APIs

Merged from v2/06. Comprehensive reference for the platform features a senior FE must wield in 2026.

Part 1 — CSS layout in 2026

1.1 Flexbox + Grid mastery

  • Flexbox for one-dimensional layout (rows OR columns).
  • Grid for two-dimensional layout with explicit row/column structure.
  • Subgrid (now widely supported) lets nested grids align to ancestor grid lines.
.grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr 1fr; gap: 16px; }
.nested { display: grid; grid-template-columns: subgrid; grid-column: span 3; }

Depth. The mental model: Flexbox sizes along ONE axis and distributes leftover/overflow space; Grid defines a two-axis coordinate system the children snap into. Reach for Flexbox when content size should drive layout (toolbars, chip rows, anything that wraps), Grid when the layout should drive content placement (page shells, card galleries, forms with aligned label/field columns).

The three properties people get wrong:

  • flex: 1 is shorthand for 1 1 0% (grow, shrink, 0% basis) — items distribute the full container equally regardless of content. flex: 1 1 auto distributes the *leftover* after content. The min-width: auto/min-height: auto default on flex/grid items refuses to shrink below content size — the #1 cause of "my flex child overflows": fix with min-width: 0 on the child (and min-height: 0 for vertical overflow / scroll containers).
  • Grid auto-placement: grid-auto-flow: dense backfills holes (reorders visually, NOT in DOM/tab order — an a11y trap).
  • place-items: center / place-content: center are the modern one-liners for centering. align-content only does something when there's extra space in the cross axis (multi-line flex / grid).

Modern intrinsic sizing keywords are production-ready: min-content, max-content, fit-content(20rem), and minmax(). The canonical responsive-without-media-queries grid:

/* Auto-fit: empty columns collapse to 0 → existing tracks stretch to fill.
   Auto-fill: keeps empty phantom tracks. Use auto-fit for fluid card grids. */
.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 16rem), 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}

Subgrid. Lets a child grid inherit parent track lines so e.g. every card's title/body/footer aligns across cards even with varying content. Baseline since 2023–24 (Chrome 117, Safari 16, Firefox 71).

.card-grid { display: grid; grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto; }
.card { display: grid; grid-template-rows: subgrid; grid-row: span 3; }

Browser support (2026): Flexbox/Grid/subgrid/intrinsic sizing all universal. Gotcha: gap on flexbox shipped later than on grid — fine now, but old margin-based gap hacks in legacy code double up with gap. Avoid: Grid for a single row of buttons (Flexbox is simpler); dense packing where DOM order must equal visual order.

1.2 Container queries (the killer feature)

Style components based on the container width, not the viewport. Composable UI per parent context.

.card { container-type: inline-size; container-name: card; }
@container card (min-width: 480px) {
  .card-body { display: flex; gap: 1rem; }
}
@container card (min-width: 720px) {
  .card-body { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr; }
}
  • Container query units: cqw, cqh, cqi, cqb.
  • Style queries (just stabilizing) allow @container style(--theme: dark).

Depth. This is the feature that finally makes components truly portable: the same <Card> lays out correctly in a 320px sidebar and a 900px main column with zero knowledge of the page. container-type: inline-size establishes a query container on the *inline* (width) axis only. container-type: size queries both axes but requires the element to have an explicit block size (it can't get height from content — that would be circular), which is why inline-size is the 95% case.

Critical gotcha — you query the container, you can't style it. A @container rule matches *descendants* of the container, never the container element itself. So you always need a wrapper: the container is the parent, the queried styles live on children. Shorthand container: card / inline-size sets name and type together.

Container query length units resolve against the nearest query container, not the viewport — perfect for fluid type that respects the component box:

.card { container-type: inline-size; }
.card-title {
  /* clamp floor/ceiling with cqi (1% of container inline size) in the middle */
  font-size: clamp(1rem, 0.8rem + 2cqi, 1.75rem);
}

Style queries (@container style(--variant: compact)) are stable in Chromium and Safari in 2026; Firefox shipping. They query custom-property *values*, not size — useful for theming variants without prop drilling classes. Range syntax for size queries (@container (400px <= width < 800px)) is also stable.

Browser support (2026): size queries universal since 2023. Performance: containment isolates layout/style/paint, so CQs are cheap — but container-type creates a new containing block and a containment boundary, which can re-anchor position: fixed descendants to the container and clip overflow. Avoid: putting container-type on huge wrappers where you didn't intend the containment side effects; querying page-level breakpoints (that's still @media).

1.3 :has() — the parent selector

/* Style the form when it contains an invalid input */
form:has(input:user-invalid) { border-color: red; }
/* Style a card when it has an image */
.card:has(img) { padding-block-start: 0; }
  • Performance: :has() is computed lazily; safe for production in 2026.

Depth. :has() is far more than a parent selector — it's a relational selector enabling previously-impossible patterns: forward sibling styling, quantity queries, and stateful layout driven by descendants. It does NOT add specificity for the :has() keyword itself; its specificity is that of the most specific selector in its argument list (like :is()).

/* "Form has a submitted, still-invalid field" → reveal the error summary */
form:has(:user-invalid) .error-summary { display: block; }

/* Sibling lookahead: dim a label whose checkbox is checked */
label:has(+ input:checked) { opacity: 0.5; }

/* Quantity query: switch grid layout once it has 4+ children */
.gallery:has(> :nth-child(4)) { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr); }

/* Theme the whole page from a descendant state (open modal) → scroll-lock, zero JS */
:root:has(dialog[open]) { overflow: hidden; }

Browser support (2026): universal since late 2023 (Chrome/Edge 105, Safari 15.4, Firefox 121). Gotcha: :has() cannot be nested inside another :has(), and pseudo-elements aren't allowed in its argument. :not(:has(...)) is legal and common. The old performance fear is gone, but extremely broad selectors like body:has(.x) toggled on every keystroke can still cause style recalc — scope the subject element tightly. Avoid: when a JS-toggled state class is clearer and the relationship is event-driven anyway.

1.4 Anchor positioning

  • Position elements relative to other elements (not just parent). Tooltips, popovers without JS.
.button { anchor-name: --btn; }
.tooltip {
  position: absolute;
  position-anchor: --btn;
  top: anchor(bottom);
  left: anchor(center);
  position-area: bottom span-all;
}

Depth. CSS Anchor Positioning decouples a positioned element from its containing block: tether it to any element on the page via a named anchor, even across DOM-distant subtrees, without JS measurement loops (goodbye Popper.js for most cases). The killer companion is position-try-fallbacks — automatic flip/fallback when the anchored element would overflow the viewport.

.btn { anchor-name: --trigger; }

.menu {
  position: fixed;
  position-anchor: --trigger;
  position-area: block-end span-inline-end;   /* below, aligned to start */
  position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline;  /* flip if it would clip */
  width: anchor-size(--trigger width);        /* size to the anchor */
  margin-block-start: 0.5rem;
}

Pair it with the Popover API (§2.2): the menu sits in the top layer (escapes overflow:hidden/stacking-context jail) with light-dismiss for free, while anchor positioning handles placement.

Browser support (2026): Chromium shipped 125 (2024), Safari shipped 18.x (2025), Firefox is the laggard — partial/behind-flag through 2025, broader in 2026 but not yet universal. Gotcha: wrap usage in @supports (anchor-name: --x) and provide a JS/static fallback for Firefox-heavy audiences. Anchor and anchored element must share a common ancestor; the anchored element must be CSS-positioned. When to avoid: production tooltips where Firefox parity is non-negotiable — keep a tested JS fallback until Firefox baseline lands.

1.5 Cascade Layers

  • Group styles into named layers with explicit priority.
@layer reset, base, components, utilities;
@layer base { body { font-family: system-ui; } }
@layer utilities { .hidden { display: none !important; } }

Depth. Cascade layers add a tier *above* specificity: a declaration in a later layer beats one in an earlier layer regardless of selector specificity — solving specificity wars structurally (your utilities layer wins over components even if components uses #id .foo). Order is set once by @layer a, b, c; (first = lowest priority); later @layer blocks slot into that order.

Big gotcha: unlayered styles beat all layered styles in the normal-importance tier. So wrap third-party/legacy CSS in a low layer to subordinate it:

@layer reset, base, tokens, components, utilities;

/* Import a vendor stylesheet directly into a layer to tame it */
@import url("bootstrap.css") layer(vendor);  /* vendor sits below your layers */

@layer components { .btn#primary { background: blue; } }  /* high specificity... */
@layer utilities  { .bg-red { background: red; } }        /* ...still wins (later layer) */

!important inversion: important declarations *reverse* layer order — an !important in your *earliest* layer beats an !important in your latest. Use this to make a reset's !important truly un-overridable.

Browser support (2026): universal since 2022 (all engines). When to use: design systems, taming vendor CSS, eliminating !important escalation. Avoid: over-engineering small apps into 6 layers; mixing layered and unlayered author CSS carelessly (unlayered silently wins).

1.6 @scope (limited support, growing)

@scope (.card) to (.card-body) {
  h2 { color: blue; }   /* applies only to .card h2 not inside .card-body */
}

Depth. @scope gives CSS native scoping with a *donut* model: @scope (root) to (limit) styles from the scoping root down but stops at (and excludes) the lower boundary — solving the classic "style the card but not the nested card" leak. Inside, :scope refers to the root, and proximity matters: when two scoped rules tie on specificity, the one whose root is the nearest ancestor wins (a new cascade tiebreaker).

@scope (.theme-dark) {
  :scope { background: #111; color: #eee; }
  a { color: oklch(0.8 0.15 230); }   /* only links inside .theme-dark */
}

/* Donut: style .media internals but stop before any nested .comments subtree */
@scope (.media) to (.comments) {
  img { border-radius: 0.5rem; }
}

Gotcha — the specificity surprise: the scope root selector does NOT add to inner rules' specificity (a bare img stays 0,0,1), but the *donut limit* selector DOES count. And @scope is still global-cascade, boundary-limited — it does NOT encapsulate like Shadow DOM.

Browser support (2026): Chromium since 118 (2023), Safari 17.4 (2024), Firefox shipped 2025 — so 2026 is effectively baseline but only just; verify your minimum Firefox version. When to use: component CSS without a build step, theme islands. Avoid: relying on it for true encapsulation (use Shadow DOM); audiences pinned to pre-2025 Firefox.

1.7 Color and color spaces

  • oklch() perceptually uniform — use for design tokens.
  • color-mix() blends colors without preprocessor.
  • color-contrast() picks best contrast automatically (2026 stable).
:root {
  --brand: oklch(0.75 0.18 250);
  --brand-hover: color-mix(in oklch, var(--brand), white 15%);
}

Depth. oklch(L C H) = Lightness (0–1), Chroma (0 → ~0.4), Hue (0–360°). Its superpower is *perceptual uniformity*: equal numeric steps look like equal visual steps, so you generate a tint/shade ramp by varying L only while holding C and H — something HSL can't do (HSL lightness is wildly uneven across hues). Wide-gamut: oklch reaches Display-P3 colors sRGB hex can't express; browsers gamut-map for sRGB screens automatically.

:root {
  --h: 250;
  --brand-100: oklch(0.96 0.03 var(--h));
  --brand-500: oklch(0.62 0.16 var(--h));
  --brand-900: oklch(0.30 0.10 var(--h));
}

/* Mix in a perceptual space; name the space or you get muddy sRGB blending */
.btn:hover { background: color-mix(in oklab, var(--brand-500), black 12%); }

/* Relative color syntax (2026 stable): derive from a base color */
.btn:active { background: oklch(from var(--brand-500) calc(l - 0.1) c h); }

Note on the original bullet: the experimental color-contrast() was spec-reworked — the 2026 shipping form is contrast-color(var(--bg)), returning a maximally-contrasting color (typically black or white) for a background. Use for auto-legible text on dynamic backgrounds; newer and less universal than oklch.

Browser support (2026): oklch()/oklab() and color-mix() universal since 2023. Relative color syntax shipped across engines 2024–25. contrast-color() is newest — Chromium/Safari first, treat as progressive enhancement. Gotcha: always name the interpolation space (in oklch) in color-mix/gradients — default sRGB mixing muddies mid-tones, and hue can interpolate "the long way" without shorter hue. Avoid: oklch for hand-tuned brand hex a designer signed off, unless re-verified.

1.8 Custom properties + design tokens

  • Define tokens at :root; override per theme via class or data-* attribute.
  • Use @property to declare types (e.g. number) so they can be animated.

Depth. Custom properties *inherit* and resolve at computed-value time, which is why they cascade through component trees and respond to media/container queries live. The headline 2026 tool is @property, which registers a *typed* custom property with syntax, an inherits flag, and an initial-value. Typing unlocks three things plain --vars can't do: animation/transition of the value (the browser knows how to interpolate <number>/<color>), a guaranteed fallback for invalid values, and meaningful inherits: false.

@property --angle { syntax: "<angle>"; inherits: false; initial-value: 0deg; }

.spinner {
  background: conic-gradient(from var(--angle), #06f, #0cf, #06f);
  transition: --angle 0.6s linear;   /* now animatable because it's typed */
}
.spinner:hover { --angle: 360deg; }

Token architecture: two-tier — *reference* tokens (--blue-500) feed *semantic* tokens (--color-action: var(--blue-500)); components consume only semantic tokens. Theme by overriding semantic tokens on [data-theme="dark"] or via light-dark():

:root { color-scheme: light dark; }
.surface { background: light-dark(white, oklch(0.2 0 0)); }

Browser support (2026): custom properties universal; @property universal since 2024 (Firefox last); light-dark() shipped across engines 2024. Gotcha: an invalid var() falls back to the property's *initial/inherited* value (the "guaranteed-invalid" behavior), NOT the previous value — surprising; @property's initial-value fixes it. Avoid: deep var-of-var chains that hurt debuggability; @property inherits: true for things you don't want cascading.

1.9 Logical properties

  • Use margin-block, padding-inline-start, inset-block-end for i18n / RTL.
  • Avoid top/left/right/bottom in greenfield work.

Depth. Logical properties map to writing-mode-relative axes — inline = text-flow direction (horizontal LTR/RTL, or vertical for vertical-rl), block = line-stacking direction. So margin-inline-start is margin-left in English but margin-right in Arabic *automatically*, with zero RTL-specific CSS — one stylesheet for 100 locales.

.card {
  padding-inline: 1rem;          /* left+right (LTR) / right+left (RTL) */
  padding-block: 0.75rem;        /* top+bottom */
  margin-inline-start: auto;     /* "push to the end" regardless of direction */
  border-inline-start: 3px solid var(--accent);  /* accent on the reading edge */
}
.toast {
  position: fixed;
  inset-block-end: 1rem;         /* bottom in horizontal modes */
  inset-inline-end: 1rem;        /* right in LTR, left in RTL */
  inline-size: min(90vw, 24rem); /* was width */
  max-block-size: 50vh;          /* was max-height */
}

Also text-align: start/end; float: inline-start; the inset shorthand. For truly *physical* effects (a shadow that must always fall bottom-right, an icon that must point physically right) keep physical properties — logical isn't always correct.

Browser support (2026): universal for years. Gotcha: the 2-value margin-block: 1rem 2rem and inset shorthand were spotty in old Safari but fine now; mixing margin-left + margin-inline-start on one box creates confusing overrides. When to avoid physical: almost never in greenfield, except genuinely physical visual effects.

Part 2 — Browser APIs you should know

2.1 View Transitions API

Native page or DOM transitions between states. Smooth, GPU-accelerated, declarative.

// Trigger
document.startViewTransition(() => updateDOM());
/* CSS to customize */
::view-transition-old(root) { animation: fade-out 200ms; }
::view-transition-new(root) { animation: fade-in 200ms; }
  • Next.js + React Router both have View Transitions integrations.

Depth. Mechanically: startViewTransition(cb) (1) snapshots the old DOM as an image, (2) runs your callback to mutate the DOM, (3) snapshots the new state, then (4) cross-fades a pseudo-element tree (::view-transition → ::view-transition-group(name) → ::view-transition-image-pair → -old/-new), which you animate with regular CSS. The DOM is frozen during the callback; it returns a promise with .ready/.finished/.updateCallbackDone for sequencing and .skipTransition() to bail for reduced-motion.

Named transitions are the real power — give an old element and a new element the same view-transition-name and the browser *morphs* one into the other (shared-element transition), e.g. a thumbnail growing into a hero across a route change:

.thumb img  { view-transition-name: hero; }   /* list page */
.detail img { view-transition-name: hero; }   /* detail page → morphs */
::view-transition-group(hero) { animation-duration: 350ms; }
async function navigate(url) {
  if (!document.startViewTransition) return load(url);   // graceful fallback
  const t = document.startViewTransition(async () => { await load(url); });
  await t.finished;
}

Cross-document (MPA) view transitions — the 2024–25 unlock — work with zero JS via @view-transition { navigation: auto; } for same-origin navigations, so server-rendered/multi-page sites get morphing transitions.

Browser support (2026): same-document VT: Chromium 111 (2023), Safari 18 (2024), Firefox shipping 2025–26. Cross-document VT: Chromium + Safari shipped, Firefox later — not yet universal. Gotcha: view-transition-name must be unique per snapshot (duplicates abort the transition); a named element that's display:none/off-DOM at snapshot time breaks the pair. Always feature-detect and honor prefers-reduced-motion. Avoid: wrapping huge un-named subtrees (jank); transitioning on every tiny state change.

2.2 Popover API + Dialog

<button popovertarget="menu">Open</button>
<div id="menu" popover>
  <p>Menu content</p>
</div>
  • Native click-outside-to-close + ESC.
  • No focus trap needed; browser handles it.
  • <dialog> for modal dialogs (with showModal()) — handles focus trap + Esc.

Depth — when to use which. Both popover and <dialog>.showModal() render in the top layer (above everything, escaping overflow:hidden, z-index, stacking contexts — no z-index: 99999 wars). The difference is modality:

Featurepopover (auto)popover="manual"<dialog> modal
Light-dismiss (click outside / Esc)yesEsc onlyEsc only
Closes other popoversyesnon/a
Backdrop / inert pageno (page stays interactive)noyes (::backdrop, rest inert)
Focus trapnonoyes
Use formenus, tooltips, comboboxestoasts, persistent panelsconfirm dialogs, true modals

Rule: non-modal transient UI → popover; blocking interaction that must capture focus → <dialog>.showModal().

<dialog id="confirm">
  <form method="dialog">
    <h2 id="t">Delete file?</h2>
    <p>This cannot be undone.</p>
    <menu>
      <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
      <button value="ok" autofocus>Delete</button>
    </menu>
  </form>
</dialog>
<button id="open">Delete…</button>
const dlg = document.getElementById('confirm');
document.getElementById('open').onclick = () => dlg.showModal();
dlg.addEventListener('close', () => {
  if (dlg.returnValue === 'ok') doDelete();   // method="dialog" sets returnValue
});

A11y: <dialog> gets role="dialog" + aria-modal and focus management free (still add aria-labelledby). popover gives top-layer + light-dismiss but not ARIA semantics — a popover used as a menu still needs role="menu"/menuitem and arrow-key handling.

Browser support (2026): Popover API universal since 2024 (Chromium 114, Safari 17, Firefox 125); <dialog> universal since 2022. Gotcha: invoker pairing via popovertarget is keyboard-accessible without JS; manual .showPopover() means you manage the trigger relationship yourself. Avoid: popover for content that must trap focus (use <dialog>); deeply nested modal dialogs.

2.3 IntersectionObserver

const io = new IntersectionObserver(
  entries => entries.forEach(e => e.isIntersecting && loadMore()),
  { rootMargin: "300px" }
);
io.observe(sentinel);
  • Infinite scroll, lazy-load, viewport tracking.

Depth. IO fires asynchronously off the scroll critical path (no handler jank) when a target's visibility relative to a root crosses a threshold. Options: root (null = viewport), rootMargin (grow/shrink the root box — "300px" preloads early), threshold (number or array of ratios; [0,0.25,0.5,1] to track progressive visibility). Entries expose intersectionRatio, isIntersecting, boundingClientRect, time.

// Scroll-spy: highlight the nav link for the most-visible section
const spy = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
  for (const e of entries) {
    document.querySelector(`nav a[href="#${e.target.id}"]`)
      ?.classList.toggle('active', e.isIntersecting);
  }
}, { rootMargin: '-40% 0px -55% 0px', threshold: 0 });
document.querySelectorAll('section[id]').forEach(s => spy.observe(s));

// One-shot reveal: unobserve after first hit to avoid re-firing
const reveal = new IntersectionObserver((entries, obs) => {
  for (const e of entries) if (e.isIntersecting) {
    e.target.classList.add('in'); obs.unobserve(e.target);
  }
}, { threshold: 0.15 });

Browser support (2026): universal for years. Gotcha: the callback fires once on observe() with the initial state (often isIntersecting: false) — handle it. A custom root must be a scroll ancestor of the target. Always disconnect on cleanup (React useEffect return) or leak. Native loading="lazy" covers most lazy-load needs now — use IO only for custom logic. Avoid: IO as a substitute for loading="lazy"; huge threshold arrays (callback spam).

2.4 ResizeObserver, MutationObserver

  • ResizeObserver: react to element size changes (replaces window.resize per element).
  • MutationObserver: react to DOM mutations (legacy editors, accessibility tooling).

Depth — ResizeObserver. Fires when an *element's* box changes for ANY reason (content, flex, sibling changes — not just window resize), delivering borderBoxSize/contentBoxSize/devicePixelContentBoxSize arrays (prefer these; contentRect is legacy). Container queries cover most "resize → restyle" cases declaratively now, so RO is for JS-needed cases: canvas redraw, virtualization measurement, syncing a chart to its box.

const ro = new ResizeObserver((entries) => {
  for (const entry of entries) {
    const { inlineSize, blockSize } = entry.contentBoxSize[0];
    redrawCanvas(entry.target, inlineSize, blockSize);
  }
});
ro.observe(chartEl, { box: 'content-box' });

Notorious gotcha: *"ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications."* If your callback resizes the observed element (or an ancestor) it can loop; the browser throttles by deferring to the next frame and emits that benign-but-noisy error. Fix: don't cause size changes synchronously in the callback, or guard with a flag / requestAnimationFrame.

MutationObserver watches DOM tree/attribute/character-data changes (childList, attributes, subtree, attributeFilter, characterData). Use for non-framework-controlled DOM (rich-text editors, third-party widgets, jQuery plugins, observing class changes for theming hooks).

const mo = new MutationObserver((records) => {
  for (const r of records) if (r.type === 'childList') hydrateInjectedNodes(r.addedNodes);
});
mo.observe(root, { childList: true, subtree: true, attributeFilter: ['data-state'] });

Browser support (2026): both universal. Avoid: MutationObserver inside a framework that already owns the DOM (fight the framework); broad subtree: true on huge trees (perf). Always disconnect() on teardown.

2.5 Web Workers + Worker pools

  • Move heavy CPU off the main thread.
  • Comlink simplifies the postMessage dance into a typed RPC.
  • SharedArrayBuffer for high-throughput data exchange (requires COOP/COEP headers).

Depth. Workers run in a separate thread with no DOM access; they communicate via postMessage/onmessage (structured-clone serialization, which deep-copies — costly for big objects) or *transferables* (postMessage(buf, [buf]) hands off an ArrayBuffer with zero copy, but the sender loses access). Module workers (new Worker(url, { type: 'module' })) allow import. Use workers for: parsing/CSV, image processing, crypto, diffing, search indexing — anything > ~16ms that would drop frames.

// main.js — Comlink turns postMessage into typed async RPC
import * as Comlink from 'comlink';
const api = Comlink.wrap(new Worker(new URL('./worker.js', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' }));
const result = await api.parseCsv(file);   // looks local, runs off-thread
// worker.js
import * as Comlink from 'comlink';
Comlink.expose({ parseCsv(file) { /* heavy sync work */ return rows; } });

Worker pools amortize spin-up: keep N = navigator.hardwareConcurrency workers, dispatch tasks to the first idle one. SharedArrayBuffer enables true shared memory + Atomics for lock-free coordination, but requires cross-origin isolation headers (COOP: same-origin, COEP: require-corp) — which can break embedding third-party iframes/resources, so it's an opt-in with side effects.

Browser support (2026): workers universal; module workers universal since ~2023 (Firefox last); SAB requires isolation headers. Gotcha: structured clone can't transfer functions/DOM nodes/class instances; large clones briefly block both threads. Avoid: workers for trivial work (message latency > savings); SAB unless you truly need shared memory and can accept cross-origin isolation.

2.6 Service Workers (PWA)

  • Intercept fetch, cache responses, enable offline.
  • Workbox 7 integrates with Vite/webpack/Next.js out of the box.
  • Strategies: cache-first (static), network-first (dynamic), stale-while-revalidate (hybrid).

Depth. A Service Worker is a network proxy between the page and the network, with a lifecycle: install (precache the app shell) → activate (clean old caches, clients.claim()) → running (fetch/message/push/sync). It's HTTPS-only, path-scoped, and runs even with no tab open (enabling push + background sync). The hard part is updates: a new SW installs but waits in "waiting" until all old clients close, unless you skipWaiting().

// sw.js — strategy per request type
self.addEventListener('fetch', (event) => {
  const url = new URL(event.request.url);
  if (url.pathname.startsWith('/api/')) {
    // network-first for dynamic data, fall back to cache offline
    event.respondWith(
      fetch(event.request)
        .then((res) => { caches.open('api').then(c => c.put(event.request, res.clone())); return res; })
        .catch(() => caches.match(event.request))
    );
  } else {
    // cache-first for hashed static assets
    event.respondWith(caches.match(event.request).then(r => r || fetch(event.request)));
  }
});

Strategy cheat-sheet: cache-first (hashed static assets — fast, safe because filename changes bust cache); network-first (user-specific/API data — fresh, offline fallback); stale-while-revalidate (logos, fonts — instant from cache + background refresh). Workbox abstracts all of these (registerRoute + StaleWhileRevalidate, build-time precache manifest).

Browser support (2026): universal (including iOS Safari, with push caveats). Gotcha: caching index.html cache-first is the classic footgun — users stick on a stale app forever; use network-first/SWR for navigations and version your caches. Ship a kill-switch (self.registration.unregister() path) — buggy SWs are sticky. Avoid: SWs for SPAs that don't need offline; aggressive precaching of large bundles.

2.7 Web Components / Custom Elements

  • When you need framework-agnostic components (design system shared across React/Vue/Angular).
  • Lit makes authoring ergonomic.
  • Limitations: a11y is still mostly your problem; SSR support patchy.

Depth. Three primitives: Custom Elements (customElements.define('my-el', class extends HTMLElement) with lifecycle connectedCallback/disconnectedCallback/attributeChangedCallback + observedAttributes), Shadow DOM (attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }) — true style/DOM encapsulation; outside CSS can't leak in except via inherited props, ::part(), and custom properties), and <slot> (project light-DOM children into the shadow tree). Use when a component must outlive any single framework or be embeddable.

class CounterButton extends HTMLElement {
  static observedAttributes = ['count'];
  #shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
  connectedCallback() {
    this.render();
    this.#shadow.querySelector('button').onclick = () =>
      this.setAttribute('count', String((+this.getAttribute('count') || 0) + 1));
  }
  attributeChangedCallback() { this.render(); }
  render() {
    const n = this.getAttribute('count') || 0;
    this.#shadow.innerHTML =
      `<style>button{font:inherit}</style>
       <button aria-label="Increment, current ${n}">Count: ${n}</button>`;
  }
}
customElements.define('counter-button', CounterButton);

2026 ergonomics: *Declarative Shadow DOM* (<template shadowrootmode="open">) enables real SSR of web components across engines. Form-associated custom elements (static formAssociated = true + ElementInternals via attachInternals()) let your component participate in <form> submission and native validation — the fix for the old "web components don't work in forms" pain. Lit cuts the boilerplate.

Browser support (2026): core APIs universal; Declarative Shadow DOM + form-associated/ElementInternals universal as of 2023–24. Gotcha: cross-shadow styling needs intentional API (::part(), custom props); a11y across shadow boundaries (label association, cross-root aria-* referencing) is genuinely hard — cross-root ARIA is still stabilizing. Avoid: web components for app-internal UI where you already have one framework (lose its DX for no portability gain).

2.8 New 2026 APIs to know

  • Speculation Rules API — declarative prerender / prefetch.
  • Long Animation Frames API — observe janky frames > 50 ms.
  • Compute Pressure API — adapt UI on overheating devices.
  • CloseWatcher — unified ESC handling for modals/popovers.
  • Document Picture-in-Picture — popout video / chat.

Depth + examples.

Speculation Rules — declarative pre-render (full render in a hidden tab) or pre-fetch of likely next navigations, with eagerness heuristics (moderate = on hover, conservative = on pointerdown). Big perceived-perf win for same-origin nav:

<script type="speculationrules">
{ "prerender": [{ "where": { "href_matches": "/product/*" }, "eagerness": "moderate" }] }
</script>

Gotcha: prerendered pages run JS — analytics/ads may double-count; gate side effects on document.prerendering / the prerenderingchange event.

Long Animation Frames (LoAF) — supersedes Long Tasks for diagnosing INP; reports slow frames *with attribution* (which script, which container):

new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  for (const e of list.getEntries()) if (e.duration > 50)
    console.warn('Slow frame', e.duration, e.scripts.map(s => s.sourceURL));
}).observe({ type: 'long-animation-frame', buffered: true });

CloseWatcher — one abstraction for "user wants to dismiss" (Esc on desktop, Android back gesture on mobile):

const watcher = new CloseWatcher();
watcher.onclose = () => closeMyCustomDrawer();

Compute Pressure — observe CPU/thermal pressure (nominal→critical) to shed work (lower frame rate, pause animations) on struggling/overheating devices. Document Picture-in-Picture — pop an arbitrary DOM subtree (not just <video>) into an always-on-top window via documentPictureInPicture.requestWindow().

Browser support (2026): Speculation Rules, LoAF, CloseWatcher — Chromium shipped, Safari/Firefox partial/in-progress → progressive enhancement. Compute Pressure & Document PiP — largely Chromium-only in 2026. Avoid: depending on any for core functionality; feature-detect every one and degrade gracefully.

Part 3 — Accessibility (WCAG 2.2 + ARIA)

3.1 The four WCAG principles (POUR)

  • Perceivable: text alt, captions, contrast, resizable text.
  • Operable: keyboard, no traps, enough time, no seizures.
  • Understandable: readable, predictable, input assistance.
  • Robust: semantic HTML, ARIA only where needed.

Depth. POUR is the top of a hierarchy: 4 Principles → 13 Guidelines → testable Success Criteria at levels A / AA / AAA. The legal/contractual target almost everywhere (ADA case law in the US, EN 301 549 / the European Accessibility Act — enforced from June 2025, AODA in Canada) is WCAG 2.1/2.2 Level AA. The EAA in particular makes AA a hard requirement for most consumer-facing digital products sold in the EU as of 2025 — which is why a11y is a launch blocker, not a nice-to-have, in 2026.

The #1 senior insight: the "first rule of ARIA" is don't use ARIA. A native <button>, <a href>, <input>, <select>, <dialog>, or <details> ships with role, keyboard behavior, focus management, and state for free. ARIA only *describes*; it never adds behavior — role="button" on a <div> gives semantics but you still owe the click handler, tabindex="0", and Enter/Space handling. Semantic HTML is the cheapest, most robust accessibility you can ship.

<!-- Robust: zero ARIA, fully accessible, keyboard + SR work automatically -->
<button type="button" aria-pressed="false" class="toggle">Mute</button>
<details><summary>Shipping options</summary><p>…</p></details>

3.2 WCAG 2.2 additions to know

  • Focus appearance — focus indicator must be visible and high contrast.
  • Dragging movements — alternative to dragging (keyboard, single-pointer).
  • Target size — minimum 24×24 CSS px for clickable targets.
  • Consistent help — help mechanism in same place across pages.

Depth — the 2.2 criteria most likely to come up:

  • 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum, AA): a focused element can't be *entirely* hidden by sticky headers/footers/cookie banners. A real gotcha for sticky UIs — set scroll-padding-block so focused items scroll clear.
  • 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (AAA): focus indicator ≥ 2px perimeter and ≥ 3:1 contrast against adjacent colors. Never outline: none without a replacement.
  • 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA): any drag (sliders, kanban, reorder) needs a non-drag alternative (buttons, keyboard).
  • 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum, AA): interactive targets ≥ 24×24 CSS px, or have 24px spacing — smaller than the old 44px AAA guidance but now Level AA.
  • 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (A): don't make users re-enter info already provided in the same process (autofill it).
  • 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (AA): no cognitive-function test to log in — allow password managers / paste; never block paste on password fields.
/* Satisfy focus visibility + 24px target without ugly defaults */
.btn { min-block-size: 24px; min-inline-size: 24px; padding: 0.5rem 0.75rem; }
:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid CanvasText; outline-offset: 2px; }
:root { scroll-padding-block-start: 5rem; }  /* clear the sticky header on focus */

3.3 ARIA patterns reference (Authoring Practices)

ComponentRoleKey ARIA
Tabstablist / tab / tabpanelaria-selected, aria-controls
Comboboxcombobox + listbox + optionaria-expanded, aria-controls, aria-activedescendant
Dialogdialogaria-modal, aria-labelledby
Menumenu / menuitemaria-haspopup, aria-expanded
Tooltiptooltiparia-describedby on target
Treetree / treeitemaria-expanded, aria-level, aria-selected
Alertalertaria-live=assertive
Statusstatusaria-live=polite
Disclosurebuttonaria-expanded, aria-controls
Sliderslideraria-valuemin/max/now, aria-orientation

Depth — full interaction models for the three patterns interviewers grill on (per the WAI-ARIA APG).

Tabs (automatic activation). Keyboard model: Tab enters the tablist and lands on the *active* tab only (roving tabindex — exactly one tab has tabindex="0", the rest -1). ←/→ move between tabs (with automatic activation, also select + show that panel); Home/End jump to first/last; Tab again leaves into the panel. Use automatic activation (select on focus) for cheap panels, manual (Enter/Space) when panels are expensive to load.

<div role="tablist" aria-label="Account settings">
  <button role="tab" id="t1" aria-selected="true"  aria-controls="p1" tabindex="0">Profile</button>
  <button role="tab" id="t2" aria-selected="false" aria-controls="p2" tabindex="-1">Billing</button>
</div>
<div role="tabpanel" id="p1" aria-labelledby="t1" tabindex="0">…profile…</div>
<div role="tabpanel" id="p2" aria-labelledby="t2" tabindex="0" hidden>…billing…</div>
const tabs = [...document.querySelectorAll('[role=tab]')];
function activate(i) {
  tabs.forEach((t, j) => {
    const sel = i === j;
    t.setAttribute('aria-selected', sel); t.tabIndex = sel ? 0 : -1;
    document.getElementById(t.getAttribute('aria-controls')).hidden = !sel;
  });
  tabs[i].focus();
}
document.querySelector('[role=tablist]').addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
  const i = tabs.indexOf(document.activeElement); if (i < 0) return;
  const map = { ArrowRight: i+1, ArrowLeft: i-1, Home: 0, End: tabs.length-1 };
  if (e.key in map) { e.preventDefault(); activate((map[e.key] + tabs.length) % tabs.length); }
});

Combobox (editable, with listbox popup) — aria-activedescendant pattern

The autocomplete pattern. Keyboard model: focus stays in the <input> the whole time; ↓ opens the list and/or moves virtual focus to the next option; ↑ previous; Enter selects the active option and closes; Esc closes (first press clears the list, second can clear the input); Home/End move within the text; typing filters. The highlighted option is pointed to by aria-activedescendant on the input — DOM focus never leaves the input (this distinguishes the activedescendant model from roving tabindex).

<label id="lbl" for="city">City</label>
<div class="combo">
  <input id="city" role="combobox" aria-controls="listbox" aria-expanded="false"
         aria-autocomplete="list" aria-activedescendant="" autocomplete="off">
  <ul id="listbox" role="listbox" aria-labelledby="lbl" hidden>
    <li id="opt-0" role="option">Austin</li>
    <li id="opt-1" role="option" aria-selected="true">Boston</li>
  </ul>
</div>
const input = document.getElementById('city');
const list  = document.getElementById('listbox');
let opts = [...list.querySelectorAll('[role=option]')], active = -1;
function open(o){ list.hidden = !o; input.setAttribute('aria-expanded', o); }
function setActive(i){
  active = (i + opts.length) % opts.length;
  opts.forEach((el, j) => el.classList.toggle('active', j === active));
  input.setAttribute('aria-activedescendant', opts[active].id);
  opts[active].scrollIntoView({ block: 'nearest' });
}
input.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
  switch (e.key) {
    case 'ArrowDown': e.preventDefault(); if (list.hidden) open(true); setActive(active + 1); break;
    case 'ArrowUp':   e.preventDefault(); setActive(active - 1); break;
    case 'Enter':     if (active >= 0){ input.value = opts[active].textContent; open(false); } break;
    case 'Escape':    open(false); input.setAttribute('aria-activedescendant',''); break;
  }
});

Dialog (modal)

Keyboard model: on open, move focus into the dialog (first interactive element or the dialog itself); Tab/Shift+Tab cycle only within the dialog (focus trap); Esc closes; on close, return focus to the trigger. Native <dialog>.showModal() (§2.2) gives the trap, Esc, inert background, and ::backdrop for free — prefer it. If hand-rolling, mark the rest of the page inert.

<div role="dialog" aria-modal="true" aria-labelledby="dtitle" aria-describedby="ddesc">
  <h2 id="dtitle">Confirm purchase</h2>
  <p id="ddesc">Charge $49 to your card?</p>
  <button>Cancel</button><button>Confirm</button>
</div>

Trap essentials: query focusable elements, wrap Tab from last→first and Shift+Tab from first→last (preventDefault at the edges); store document.activeElement before opening and .focus() it back on close.

3.4 Keyboard patterns

  • Tab moves between focusable controls.
  • Arrow keys move within a widget (tabs, menu, listbox).
  • Roving tabindex for widgets with one focusable child.
  • Enter / Space activate buttons; Esc closes overlays.
  • Home / End jump to first / last in a list.

Depth — the two focus-management strategies (interview staple):

  • Roving tabindex: exactly one child has tabindex="0", all others -1; arrow keys move the 0 and call .focus(). The widget is a single Tab stop. Use for tabs, toolbars, radio groups, menus, grids — anywhere real DOM focus should move between items.
  • aria-activedescendant: DOM focus stays on a container/input; a single aria-activedescendant points at the "virtually focused" child id. Use for comboboxes/listboxes where focus must remain in the text field.

Other essentials: never create a keyboard trap (Tab in but not out) — except an *intentional* modal trap that Esc releases. tabindex="0" joins natural order; positive tabindex (1+) is an anti-pattern that breaks order. On SPA route change, move focus to the new <h1>/skip target or SR users are stranded. Provide a "Skip to content" link as the first focusable element.

// Roving tabindex helper for a toolbar
function rove(container, selector = '[role=button]') {
  const items = [...container.querySelectorAll(selector)];
  items.forEach((el, i) => (el.tabIndex = i === 0 ? 0 : -1));
  container.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
    const i = items.indexOf(document.activeElement); if (i < 0) return;
    const next = { ArrowRight: i+1, ArrowLeft: i-1, Home: 0, End: items.length-1 }[e.key];
    if (next == null) return;
    e.preventDefault();
    const t = (next + items.length) % items.length;
    items[i].tabIndex = -1; items[t].tabIndex = 0; items[t].focus();
  });
}

3.5 Screen reader UX

  • Live regions: aria-live=polite for status, assertive for alerts.
  • aria-atomic="true" reads the whole region; default reads only the change.
  • Hide decorative elements with aria-hidden="true".
  • Use proper headings (h1 → h2 → h3 in order; never skip levels).

Depth. A live region announces dynamic changes without moving focus. The element must exist in the DOM before you inject text — SRs only announce *mutations* to an already-present live region, so render an empty <div aria-live="polite"> on load, then set its text. role="status" = implicit aria-live="polite" + aria-atomic="true"; role="alert" = implicit assertive (interrupts the SR immediately — reserve for errors/time-sensitive). aria-relevant controls which mutation types announce (default additions text).

<!-- Present from page load; updated by JS for "Saved", "3 results", etc. -->
<div id="sr-status" role="status" aria-live="polite" class="sr-only"></div>
function announce(msg) {            // toggle text to force re-announce of identical messages
  const el = document.getElementById('sr-status');
  el.textContent = ''; requestAnimationFrame(() => (el.textContent = msg));
}
/* Visually hidden but still read by SRs — NOT display:none (that hides from SR too) */
.sr-only { position:absolute; width:1px; height:1px; padding:0; margin:-1px;
  overflow:hidden; clip-path: inset(50%); white-space:nowrap; border:0; }

Other essentials: one <h1> per page/view; don't skip heading levels (SR users navigate by heading); alt="" (empty) for decorative images (skipped), descriptive alt for meaningful ones; aria-hidden="true" removes from the accessibility tree (but never on a focusable element — you'll create a phantom focus stop with no SR output). Prefer a visible <label for> for accessible names; aria-label/aria-labelledby otherwise.

Gotcha: display:none/visibility:hidden hide from SRs — good for truly hidden, bad if you wanted "visually hidden but announced" (use .sr-only). Over-using assertive makes the app feel like it's shouting.

3.6 Testing

  • axe-core / @axe-core/playwright in CI for automated checks.
  • Manual: keyboard-only walkthrough; screen reader (VoiceOver / NVDA) for critical flows.
  • Contrast: WCAG 2.2 requires 4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text.

Depth. Automated tools (axe-core — the engine behind axe DevTools, Lighthouse a11y, Pa11y) reliably catch only ~30–40% of WCAG issues — missing labels, contrast, ARIA misuse, landmark gaps. They cannot judge whether alt text is *meaningful*, whether focus order makes sense, or whether a custom widget's keyboard model is correct. So CI automation is necessary but not sufficient.

// Playwright + axe-core: fail the build on any serious/critical violation
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';
test('checkout page has no a11y violations', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page })
    .withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag22aa'])
    .analyze();
  const serious = results.violations.filter(v => ['serious','critical'].includes(v.impact));
  expect(serious).toEqual([]);
});

Manual layer: (1) unplug the mouse — Tab through the flow, confirm visible focus, logical order, no traps, Esc closes overlays; (2) real screen readers — VoiceOver+Safari (macOS/iOS), NVDA+Firefox (Windows), TalkBack (Android) are the canonical combos; (3) 200% zoom + 400% reflow with no horizontal scroll; (4) contrast (4.5:1 body, 3:1 large/UI — large = 18.66px bold or 24px regular). For React, lint with eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y and assert roles/names via Testing Library (getByRole('button', { name: /save/i })), which queries the accessibility tree by design.

Gotcha: a "0 violations" axe score is not "accessible." Avoid: treating automated scans as the finish line; testing with only one SR (NVDA/VoiceOver/JAWS behave differently).

Part 4 — Forms 2026

4.1 Native validation

  • required, minlength, maxlength, pattern, type=email/url.
  • Use :user-valid / :user-invalid (pseudo-classes that wait for user interaction).

Depth. The Constraint Validation API gives every control .validity (a ValidityState: valueMissing, typeMismatch, patternMismatch, tooShort, rangeOverflow, …), .validationMessage, .checkValidity(), .reportValidity(), and .setCustomValidity(msg) (non-empty string marks it invalid). The 2026 win is :user-invalid/:user-valid — they match only *after* the user has interacted/blurred, so fields don't scream "invalid" on page load (the long-standing problem with :invalid).

<form novalidate>  <!-- novalidate: suppress native bubbles, drive your own UX -->
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required aria-describedby="email-err">
  <p id="email-err" class="error" aria-live="polite"></p>
  <button>Sign up</button>
</form>
input:user-invalid { border-color: oklch(0.55 0.2 25); }
input:user-valid   { border-color: oklch(0.6 0.15 145); }
const form = document.querySelector('form'), email = form.email;
email.addEventListener('input', () => {
  email.setCustomValidity(email.value.endsWith('@example.com') ? 'Demo domains not allowed' : '');
});
form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
  if (!form.checkValidity()) {
    e.preventDefault();
    const bad = form.querySelector(':invalid');
    document.getElementById('email-err').textContent = bad.validationMessage;
    bad.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true'); bad.focus();
  }
});

Browser support (2026): Constraint Validation universal; :user-invalid/:user-valid universal since 2023 (Chromium 119, Safari 16.5, Firefox 88). Gotcha: type="email" validation is intentionally loose (allows a@b); add pattern for stricter rules. Native bubbles are unstyleable and inconsistent — use novalidate + custom messaging. Avoid: client validation alone — always re-validate server-side.

4.2 React Hook Form + Zod

const Schema = z.object({
  email: z.string().email(),
  age: z.number().int().min(18).max(120),
});
const { register, handleSubmit, formState: { errors } } = useForm({
  resolver: zodResolver(Schema),
});

Depth. RHF is uncontrolled-first: register wires native inputs via refs, so keystrokes don't re-render the whole form (big perf win vs controlled-everything). Zod is the single source of truth — z.infer<typeof Schema> gives the TS type for free, and zodResolver runs the same schema for validation. The *same* Zod schema can validate on the server (Server Action / API route), eliminating client/server drift.

import { useForm } from 'react-hook-form';
import { zodResolver } from '@hookform/resolvers/zod';
import { z } from 'zod';

const Schema = z.object({
  email: z.string().email('Enter a valid email'),
  age: z.coerce.number().int().min(18, 'Must be 18+').max(120),
});
type FormValues = z.infer<typeof Schema>;

function SignupForm() {
  const { register, handleSubmit,
          formState: { errors, isSubmitting } } = useForm<FormValues>({
    resolver: zodResolver(Schema), mode: 'onTouched',
  });
  const onSubmit = async (data: FormValues) => { await api.signup(data); };

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(onSubmit)} noValidate>
      <label htmlFor="email">Email</label>
      <input id="email" {...register('email')}
             aria-invalid={!!errors.email}
             aria-describedby={errors.email ? 'email-err' : undefined} />
      {errors.email && <p id="email-err" role="alert">{errors.email.message}</p>}
      <button disabled={isSubmitting}>Create account</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Ecosystem reality (2026): RHF + Zod is the de-facto React form stack; Zod v3/v4 is mature, and Standard Schema means resolvers also accept Valibot/ArkType. Gotcha: number inputs return strings — use z.coerce.number() or valueAsNumber. mode: 'onTouched'/'onBlur' mirrors :user-invalid UX (don't validate every keystroke from the start). Avoid: wrapping every field in controlled <Controller> when uncontrolled register works (perf); duplicating validation instead of sharing the Zod schema.

4.3 Server Actions for mutations

  • Native form submit triggers Server Action; no client JS required for the submit.
  • Progressive enhancement: form works without JS, gets richer with JS.

Depth. A Server Action ('use server') is an RPC the framework exposes as a form endpoint: pass it to <form action={fn}> and the browser does a native POST that runs the function on the server — works with JS disabled / before hydration, then upgrades to fetch-based submission once hydrated (true progressive enhancement). useActionState (React 19) threads server-returned state (errors/success) back to the UI; useFormStatus exposes pending to child components (submit buttons) without prop drilling.

// actions.ts
'use server';
import { z } from 'zod';
const Schema = z.object({ email: z.string().email() });

export async function subscribe(prevState, formData) {
  const parsed = Schema.safeParse({ email: formData.get('email') });
  if (!parsed.success) return { ok: false, error: parsed.error.flatten().fieldErrors.email?.[0] };
  await db.subscribers.add(parsed.data.email);
  return { ok: true };
}
// form.tsx
'use client';
import { useActionState } from 'react';
import { useFormStatus } from 'react-dom';
import { subscribe } from './actions';

function Submit() {
  const { pending } = useFormStatus();
  return <button disabled={pending}>{pending ? 'Subscribing…' : 'Subscribe'}</button>;
}
export function NewsletterForm() {
  const [state, action] = useActionState(subscribe, { ok: false });
  return (
    <form action={action}>
      <input name="email" type="email" required
             aria-invalid={!!state.error} aria-describedby="err" />
      {state.error && <p id="err" role="alert">{state.error}</p>}
      <Submit />
    </form>
  );
}

Reality (2026): stable in Next.js App Router and React 19; the same Zod schema validates here and on the client (§4.2). Gotcha: Server Actions are exposed POST endpoints — always validate + authorize inside them (never trust the formData); they're not free internal calls. Returning the result through useActionState is the accessible-error path (announce via role="alert"). Avoid: client-only validation assuming the server is safe; long-running work without optimistic UI (useOptimistic).

4.4 Accessible error UX

  • aria-describedby links input to its error message.
  • aria-invalid="true" on the input when error.
  • Focus the first error on submit; announce via aria-live.

Depth — the accessible-error checklist:

1. Associate each error to its input via aria-describedby="<error-id>" so the SR reads it on focus.

2. Mark the field aria-invalid="true" only when actually in error (remove it when fixed) — never preemptively.

3. Move focus to the first invalid field on failed submit (bad.focus()) so keyboard users land on the problem.

4. Announce count/summary via a live region (role="alert" or aria-live="assertive").

5. Error summary at the top with in-page links to each bad field is the gold standard for long forms (GOV.UK pattern).

6. Errors must be text, not color alone (WCAG 1.4.1) — pair the red border with a message and ideally an icon.

function FieldErrorSummary({ errors }) {           // render at top of form on submit
  const entries = Object.entries(errors);
  if (!entries.length) return null;
  return (
    <div role="alert" tabIndex={-1} className="error-summary" ref={el => el?.focus()}>
      <h2>There {entries.length === 1 ? 'is 1 problem' : `are ${entries.length} problems`}</h2>
      <ul>{entries.map(([name, e]) =>
        <li key={name}><a href={`#${name}`}>{e.message}</a></li>)}
      </ul>
    </div>
  );
}

Gotcha: pointing aria-describedby at a node that doesn't exist yet (conditionally rendered) breaks the association — keep the error container in the DOM and toggle its text, or set aria-describedby only when the error renders. Avoid: native validation bubbles in production (inconsistent, unstyleable, vanish on blur); color-only error signaling.

Part 5 — Browser rendering pipeline

5.1 The stages

  • Parse HTML → DOM, parse CSS → CSSOM, combine into render tree.
  • Layout (reflow) — geometry of every box.
  • Paint — fill pixels for each layer.
  • Composite — combine layers into final image (often on GPU).

Depth — the full pixel pipeline: DOM + CSSOM → Style (compute resolved style per element) → Layout (reflow: box geometry of every box; the render tree excludes display:none but includes visibility:hidden) → Layer/Pre-paint (decide compositing layers) → Paint (record draw commands into per-layer display lists) → Composite (raster + the GPU assembles layers; transforms/opacity happen here). Modern engines run much of this off the main thread (compositor thread, raster threads).

Why CSS/JS block differently: CSS is render-blocking (no paint until the CSSOM is ready, to avoid FOUC). A non-async/defer <script> is parser-blocking AND waits for any *preceding* CSS (it might read computed styles). Hence: CSS in <head>, scripts defer/async or at body end, inline critical CSS above the fold.

// Force a synchronous "forced reflow" by reading layout right after a write — DON'T:
el.style.width = '300px';   // invalidates layout
const h = el.offsetHeight;  // forces immediate synchronous layout to answer the read

5.2 What triggers what

ChangeTriggers
width / height / top / left / margin / paddingLayout + Paint + Composite (expensive)
color / backgroundPaint + Composite
transform / opacityComposite only (cheapest, GPU)
filterPaint + Composite (sometimes Layout)
  • Animate transform + opacity. Promote with will-change: transform sparingly.
  • Avoid layout thrash (read → write → read) — batch reads + writes.

Depth. Animate only transform and opacity for 60fps — they run on the compositor and skip Layout *and* Paint entirely (the layer is already rasterized; the GPU just re-composites). Animating width/top/margin reruns Layout every frame (jank); color/box-shadow reruns Paint. will-change: transform (or transform: translateZ(0)) promotes an element to its own layer *ahead of time* so the first frame isn't janky — but each layer costs GPU memory, so promote sparingly and remove will-change after.

Layout thrashing is the classic perf bug: interleaving DOM reads (offsetTop, getBoundingClientRect, getComputedStyle, scrollTop) and writes (style changes) in a loop forces a synchronous reflow on every read. Fix: batch all reads, then all writes (or use requestAnimationFrame / FastDOM).

// BAD: read-write-read-write → N forced reflows
items.forEach(el => { el.style.width = el.previousElementSibling.offsetWidth + 'px'; });

// GOOD: batch reads, then batch writes → 1 reflow
const widths = items.map(el => el.previousElementSibling.offsetWidth); // all reads
items.forEach((el, i) => { el.style.width = widths[i] + 'px'; });       // all writes

content-visibility: auto (universal since ~2024) skips rendering of off-screen subtrees entirely — huge for long pages (pair with contain-intrinsic-size to reserve space and avoid scrollbar jumps). Gotcha: measuring INP/LoAF (§2.8) is how you find these in the wild. Avoid: will-change on many elements (memory blowup); animating layout properties; reading layout inside scroll/resize handlers without rAF batching.

Part 6 — Internationalization

  • Intl.* — DateTimeFormat, NumberFormat, RelativeTimeFormat, ListFormat, PluralRules.
  • next-intl / react-intl for component-level translations.
  • Use logical properties for RTL support without JS hacks.
  • Locale-aware sorting via Intl.Collator.

Next: Doc 05 — Performance + Reliability + Security + Availability.

Depth. The platform Intl namespace replaces almost every i18n library for *formatting*: locale-data-driven, built into the engine, and correct in ways hand-rolled code never is (per-locale plural categories, RTL marks, calendar/numbering systems). Always pass an explicit locale rather than relying on the runtime default.

const loc = 'de-DE';

new Intl.NumberFormat(loc, { style: 'currency', currency: 'EUR' }).format(1234.5);
// "1.234,50 €"  (comma decimal, dot grouping, trailing symbol)

new Intl.DateTimeFormat(loc, { dateStyle: 'full', timeStyle: 'short', timeZone: 'Europe/Berlin' })
  .format(new Date());                                   // tz-correct, localized

new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat(loc, { numeric: 'auto' }).format(-1, 'day');  // "gestern"

new Intl.ListFormat(loc, { type: 'conjunction' }).format(['A','B','C']);  // "A, B und C"

// Plurals: drive message selection by CLDR plural category (en: one/other; pl: 5 categories)
const pr = new Intl.PluralRules('pl-PL');
pr.select(2);   // "few"  — why naive `n === 1 ? 'x' : 'xs'` is wrong outside English

// Locale-aware sort/search — reuse a Collator, never localeCompare in a hot loop
const collator = new Intl.Collator('sv-SE', { sensitivity: 'base', numeric: true });
['Åke','Bo','Ärling'].sort(collator.compare);

// 2026 additions
new Intl.DurationFormat(loc, { style: 'long' }).format({ hours: 1, minutes: 30 }); // "1 Stunde, 30 Minuten"
new Intl.Segmenter(loc, { granularity: 'word' });  // correct word/grapheme boundaries (emoji, CJK)

Other essentials: set document direction (<html dir="rtl" lang="ar">) and rely on logical properties (§1.9) so layout flips automatically; use :dir(rtl) for rare direction-specific overrides. Externalize all strings (ICU MessageFormat via next-intl/react-intl/FormatJS) — never concatenate translated fragments (word order differs per language). Lazy-load locale bundles by route. Test pseudo-localization ([!!! Ţĥîš îš ėхрåñðėð !!!]) to catch hardcoded strings and truncation early.

Browser support (2026): core Intl (Number/DateTime/RelativeTime/List/PluralRules/Collator) universal. Intl.Segmenter and Intl.DurationFormat — Chromium/Safari shipped, Firefox shipped 2024–25 → effectively baseline but verify min versions. Gotcha: formatter construction is *expensive* — memoize/reuse instances, never construct one per render or per array element. Timezone bugs come from omitting timeZone; default-locale bugs from omitting the locale arg. Avoid: shipping moment.js/large date libs when Intl + a tiny wrapper suffices; string concatenation for sentences.
