docs.search: 04 — Modern Web Platform & CSS (2026) CSS layout · Container queries · :has · View Transitions · Accessibility · Browser APIs Merged from v2/06. Comprehensive reference for the platform features a senior FE must wield in 2026. Part 1 — CSS layout in 2026 1.1 Flexbox + Grid mastery Flexbox for one-dimensional layout (rows OR columns). Grid for two-dimensional layout with explicit row/column structure. Subgrid (now widely supported) lets nested grids align to ancestor grid lines. .grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr 1fr; gap: 16px; } .nested { display: grid; grid-template-columns: subgrid; grid-column: span 3; } Depth. The mental model: Flexbox sizes along ONE axis and distributes leftover/overflow space; Grid defines a two-axis coordinate system the children snap into. Reach for Flexbox when content size should drive layout (toolbars, chip rows, anything that wraps), Grid when the layout should drive content placement (page shells, card galleries, forms with aligned label/field columns). The three properties people get wrong: flex: 1 is shorthand for 1 1 0% (grow, shrink, 0% basis ) — items distribute the full container equally regardless of content. flex: 1 1 auto distributes the *leftover* after content. The min-width: auto / min-height: auto default on flex/grid items refuses to shrink below content size — the #1 cause of "my flex child overflows": fix with min-width: 0 on the child (and min-height: 0 for vertical overflow / scroll containers). Grid auto-placement: grid-auto-flow: dense backfills holes (reorders visually, NOT in DOM/tab order — an a11y trap). place-items: center / place-content: center are the modern one-liners for centering. align-content only does something when there's extra space in the cross axis (multi-line flex / grid). Modern intrinsic sizing keywords are production-ready: min-content , max-content , fit-content(20rem) , and minmax() . The canonical responsive-without-media-queries grid: /* Auto-fit: empty columns collapse to 0 → existing tracks stretch to fill. Auto-fill: keeps empty phantom tracks. Use auto-fit for fluid card grids. */ .cards { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 16rem), 1fr)); gap: 1rem; } Subgrid. Lets a child grid inherit parent track lines so e.g. every card's title/body/footer aligns across cards even with varying content. Baseline since 2023–24 (Chrome 117, Safari 16, Firefox 71). .card-grid { display: grid; grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto; } .card { display: grid; grid-template-rows: subgrid; grid-row: span 3; } Browser support (2026): Flexbox/Grid/subgrid/intrinsic sizing all universal. Gotcha: gap on flexbox shipped later than on grid — fine now, but old margin -based gap hacks in legacy code double up with gap . Avoid: Grid for a single row of buttons (Flexbox is simpler); dense packing where DOM order must equal visual order. 1.2 Container queries (the killer feature) Style components based on the container width, not the viewport. Composable UI per parent context. .card { container-type: inline-size; container-name: card; } @container card (min-width: 480px) { .card-body { display: flex; gap: 1rem; } } @container card (min-width: 720px) { .card-body { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr; } } Container query units: cqw, cqh, cqi, cqb. Style queries (just stabilizing) allow @container style(--theme: dark). Depth. This is the feature that finally makes components truly portable: the same <Card> lays out correctly in a 320px sidebar and a 900px main column with zero knowledge of the page. container-type: inline-size establishes a query container on the *inline* (width) axis only. container-type: size queries both axes but requires the element to have an explicit block size (it can't get height from content — that would be circular), which is why inline-size is the 95% case. Critical gotcha — you query the container, you can't style it. A @container rule matches *descendants* of the container, never the container element itself. So you always need a wrapper: the container is the parent, the queried styles live on children. Shorthand container: card / inline-size sets name and type together. Container query length units resolve against the nearest query container, not the viewport — perfect for fluid type that respects the component box: .card { container-type: inline-size; } .card-title { /* clamp floor/ceiling with cqi (1% of container inline size) in the middle */ font-size: clamp(1rem, 0.8rem + 2cqi, 1.75rem); } Style queries ( @container style(--variant: compact) ) are stable in Chromium and Safari in 2026; Firefox shipping. They query custom-property *values*, not size — useful for theming variants without prop drilling classes. Range syntax for size queries ( @container (400px <= width < 800px) ) is also stable. Browser support (2026): size queries universal since 2023. Performance: containment isolates layout/style/paint, so CQs are cheap — but container-type creates a new containing block and a containment boundary, which can re-anchor position: fixed descendants to the container and clip overflow. Avoid: putting container-type on huge wrappers where you didn't intend the containment side effects; querying page-level breakpoints (that's still @media ). 1.3 :has() — the parent selector /* Style the form when it contains an invalid input */ form:has(input:user-invalid) { border-color: red; } /* Style a card when it has an image */ .card:has(img) { padding-block-start: 0; } Performance: :has() is computed lazily; safe for production in 2026. Depth. :has() is far more than a parent selector — it's a relational selector enabling previously-impossible patterns: forward sibling styling, quantity queries, and stateful layout driven by descendants. It does NOT add specificity for the :has() keyword itself; its specificity is that of the most specific selector in its argument list (like :is() ). /* "Form has a submitted, still-invalid field" → reveal the error summary */ form:has(:user-invalid) .error-summary { display: block; } /* Sibling lookahead: dim a label whose checkbox is checked */ label:has(+ input:checked) { opacity: 0.5; } /* Quantity query: switch grid layout once it has 4+ children */ .gallery:has(> :nth-child(4)) { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr); } /* Theme the whole page from a descendant state (open modal) → scroll-lock, zero JS */ :root:has(dialog[open]) { overflow: hidden; } Browser support (2026): universal since late 2023 (Chrome/Edge 105, Safari 15.4, Firefox 121). Gotcha: :has() cannot be nested inside another :has() , and pseudo-elements aren't allowed in its argument. :not(:has(...)) is legal and common. The old performance fear is gone, but extremely broad selectors like body:has(.x) toggled on every keystroke can still cause style recalc — scope the subject element tightly. Avoid: when a JS-toggled state class is clearer and the relationship is event-driven anyway. 1.4 Anchor positioning Position elements relative to other elements (not just parent). Tooltips, popovers without JS. .button { anchor-name: --btn; } .tooltip { position: absolute; position-anchor: --btn; top: anchor(bottom); left: anchor(center); position-area: bottom span-all; } Depth. CSS Anchor Positioning decouples a positioned element from its containing block: tether it to any element on the page via a named anchor, even across DOM-distant subtrees, without JS measurement loops (goodbye Popper.js for most cases). The killer companion is position-try-fallbacks — automatic flip/fallback when the anchored element would overflow the viewport. .btn { anchor-name: --trigger; } .menu { position: fixed; position-anchor: --trigger; position-area: block-end span-inline-end; /* below, aligned to start */ position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline; /* flip if it would clip */ width: anchor-size(--trigger width); /* size to the anchor */ margin-block-start: 0.5rem; } Pair it with the Popover API (§2.2): the menu sits in the top layer (escapes overflow:hidden /stacking-context jail) with light-dismiss for free, while anchor positioning handles placement. Browser support (2026): Chromium shipped 125 (2024), Safari shipped 18.x (2025), Firefox is the laggard — partial/behind-flag through 2025, broader in 2026 but not yet universal . Gotcha: wrap usage in @supports (anchor-name: --x) and provide a JS/static fallback for Firefox-heavy audiences. Anchor and anchored element must share a common ancestor; the anchored element must be CSS- position ed. When to avoid: production tooltips where Firefox parity is non-negotiable — keep a tested JS fallback until Firefox baseline lands. 1.5 Cascade Layers Group styles into named layers with explicit priority. @layer reset, base, components, utilities; @layer base { body { font-family: system-ui; } } @layer utilities { .hidden { display: none !important; } } Depth. Cascade layers add a tier *above* specificity: a declaration in a later layer beats one in an earlier layer regardless of selector specificity — solving specificity wars structurally (your utilities layer wins over components even if components uses #id .foo ). Order is set once by @layer a, b, c; (first = lowest priority); later @layer blocks slot into that order. Big gotcha: unlayered styles beat all layered styles in the normal-importance tier. So wrap third-party/legacy CSS in a low layer to subordinate it: @layer reset, base, tokens, components, utilities; /* Import a vendor stylesheet directly into a layer to tame it */ @import url("bootstrap.css") layer(vendor); /* vendor sits below your layers */ @layer components { .btn#primary { background: blue; } } /* high specificity... */ @layer utilities { .bg-red { background: red; } } /* ...still wins (later layer) */ !important inversion: important declarations *reverse* layer order — an !important in your *earliest* layer beats an !important in your latest. Use this to make a reset's !important truly un-overridable. Browser support (2026): universal since 2022 (all engines). When to use: design systems, taming vendor CSS, eliminating !important escalation. Avoid: over-engineering small apps into 6 layers; mixing layered and unlayered author CSS carelessly (unlayered silently wins). 1.6 @scope (limited support, growing) @scope (.card) to (.card-body) { h2 { color: blue; } /* applies only to .card h2 not inside .card-body */ } Depth. @scope gives CSS native scoping with a *donut* model: @scope (root) to (limit) styles from the scoping root down but stops at (and excludes) the lower boundary — solving the classic "style the card but not the nested card" leak. Inside, :scope refers to the root, and proximity matters: when two scoped rules tie on specificity, the one whose root is the nearest ancestor wins (a new cascade tiebreaker). @scope (.theme-dark) { :scope { background: #111; color: #eee; } a { color: oklch(0.8 0.15 230); } /* only links inside .theme-dark */ } /* Donut: style .media internals but stop before any nested .comments subtree */ @scope (.media) to (.comments) { img { border-radius: 0.5rem; } } Gotcha — the specificity surprise: the scope root selector does NOT add to inner rules' specificity (a bare img stays 0,0,1), but the *donut limit* selector DOES count. And @scope is still global-cascade, boundary-limited — it does NOT encapsulate like Shadow DOM. Browser support (2026): Chromium since 118 (2023), Safari 17.4 (2024), Firefox shipped 2025 — so 2026 is effectively baseline but only just ; verify your minimum Firefox version. When to use: component CSS without a build step, theme islands. Avoid: relying on it for true encapsulation (use Shadow DOM); audiences pinned to pre-2025 Firefox. 1.7 Color and color spaces oklch() perceptually uniform — use for design tokens. color-mix() blends colors without preprocessor. color-contrast() picks best contrast automatically (2026 stable). :root { --brand: oklch(0.75 0.18 250); --brand-hover: color-mix(in oklch, var(--brand), white 15%); }

docs.title: Performance · Reliability · Security · Availability
docs.html:
05 — Performance + Reliability + Security + Availability (2026)

Web Vitals · Bundle · Errors · CSP · CDN · Deployment · 4-sprint plan

Merged from v2/07 (perf/sec/test), v3/13 (FE deployment + reliability toolbelt), v3/14 (FRSA action checklist). The complete senior-FE FRSA playbook in one doc.

> How to use this doc in an interview. FRSA is the "make it production-grade" round. The interviewer wants to see you (a) reach for a *measurement* before a *fix*, (b) name an exact threshold, (c) name the diagnostic step order, and (d) give a concrete config/code snippet with the failure mode it prevents. Every section below follows that shape: original guidance, then depth, then a runnable example with thresholds.

Part 0 — Baseline before you change anything

  • Lighthouse + WebPageTest baseline on top 3 routes.
  • RUM Web Vitals from 7 days of real users.
  • JS error rate from Sentry over 7 days.
  • Bundle size (home route, gzipped) from next build / vite build.
  • Monthly uptime from synthetic monitor.
  • Document these five numbers. They are your before/after.

Why baseline first. Lighthouse is a *lab* number (single cold run, throttled CPU/network) and is great for catching regressions in CI, but it does not represent your users. RUM is the *field* number — it is what Google ranks on (CrUX p75) and what you defend in the interview. The two diverge constantly: a route can score Lighthouse 95 yet fail INP in the field because real users have cheap Android CPUs and click before hydration finishes. Always quote field p75, not lab.

The five numbers, with the exact source command/query:

# 1. Lab perf — top 3 routes, mobile profile, median of 3 runs (don't trust 1 run)
npx lighthouse https://app.example.com/        --preset=perf --form-factor=mobile --throttling-method=simulate --output=json
npx lighthouse https://app.example.com/pricing  --preset=perf
npx lighthouse https://app.example.com/dashboard --preset=perf

# 4. Bundle size, gzipped, per route — the number that actually predicts INP/TBT
next build            # reads the "First Load JS" column
# or
npx vite-bundle-visualizer
-- 2. RUM field p75 from your warehouse (BigQuery CrUX export shown; substitute your RUM table)
SELECT
  ROUND(APPROX_QUANTILES(lcp_ms, 100)[OFFSET(75)]) AS lcp_p75,
  ROUND(APPROX_QUANTILES(inp_ms, 100)[OFFSET(75)]) AS inp_p75,
  ROUND(APPROX_QUANTILES(cls,    100)[OFFSET(75)], 3) AS cls_p75
FROM rum.web_vitals
WHERE event_date >= DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 7 DAY);

Write the five numbers into the PR description / ticket. "Before: LCP p75 3.4s, INP p75 290ms, JS 410KB. After: 1.9s / 160ms / 180KB." That delta is the entire point of the work and the only thing a promo committee or interviewer remembers.

Part 1 — FASTER (Performance)

Targets. p75 LCP < 2.0 s · p75 INP < 200 ms · p75 CLS < 0.1 · TTFB < 800 ms · home JS gz < 200 KB.

2026 threshold table (Google "good" = field p75; these are the numbers to quote):

MetricGood (p75)Needs workPoorWhat it measures
LCP< 2.5 s (aim < 2.0 s)2.5–4.0 s> 4.0 sLargest paint render time
INP< 200 ms200–500 ms> 500 msWorst interaction latency (replaced FID, March 2024)
CLS< 0.10.1–0.25> 0.25Unexpected layout shift
TTFB< 800 ms800–1800 ms> 1800 msServer + network to first byte
FCP< 1.8 s1.8–3.0 s> 3.0 sFirst content paint

INP is the metric most senior candidates fumble. It is the 98th-percentile interaction on the page (not an average), measured as input-delay + processing + presentation-delay, across the *whole page lifetime*. A single 600ms click handler tanks the page's INP. The fix is almost always "break up or yield the long task," which is why scheduler.yield() (1B/1D) matters.

1A — High impact

1A.1 Compress LCP image to AVIF

<img src="/hero.avif"
  srcSet="/hero-640.avif 640w, /hero-1280.avif 1280w, /hero-1920.avif 1920w"
  sizes="100vw" width="1920" height="1080"
  fetchPriority="high" alt="…" />
// or Next.js
<Image src="/hero.png" width={1920} height={1080} priority alt="…" />

Depth. The LCP image has four levers, in priority order: (1) discoverability — the browser must find the URL in the initial HTML, so the LCP image must NOT be lazy-loaded and ideally is preloaded; (2) priority — fetchPriority="high" so it jumps the queue ahead of late scripts; (3) format/size — AVIF beats WebP by ~20–30%, and srcset/sizes ships the right resolution; (4) dimensions — width/height reserve space so the image is also a CLS win.

Common mistake: putting the hero image behind a client component that hydrates late, so the URL only appears after JS runs. The preload scanner never sees it and LCP balloons. Keep the LCP image in server-rendered HTML.

<!-- Belt-and-suspenders: preload the chosen candidate so it starts at HTML parse, before CSS -->
<link rel="preload" as="image"
      href="/hero-1280.avif"
      imagesrcset="/hero-640.avif 640w, /hero-1280.avif 1280w, /hero-1920.avif 1920w"
      imagesizes="100vw"
      fetchpriority="high" />

Never preload more than 1–2 LCP candidates; over-preloading steals bandwidth from the actual LCP element and makes LCP worse.

1A.2 Remove or lazy-load heavy third-party scripts

// Defer non-critical
<script src="/analytics.js" defer />
// Idle-load
requestIdleCallback(() => import("./chat-widget"));
// Off-main-thread
<Partytown forward={["dataLayer.push"]} />
<script type="text/partytown" src="https://gtm.example.com/gtm.js" />

Depth. Third-party JS is the #1 cause of poor field INP because it runs on the main thread during the exact window users try to interact. Triage order: measure each tag's main-thread cost (DevTools Performance → bottom-up, group by URL, or WebPageTest "third party" view) → delete anything with no owner → defer the rest off the critical path → isolate the unavoidable ones (GTM, chat, ads) into a worker via Partytown so they never block the main thread.

// Load chat only after the user shows intent OR the browser is idle — not on page load.
const loadChat = () => import("./chat-widget").then(m => m.mount());
if ("requestIdleCallback" in window) {
  requestIdleCallback(loadChat, { timeout: 5000 });
} else {
  setTimeout(loadChat, 3000);
}
// Even better: load on first scroll / first pointermove, whichever is first.
["pointermove", "scroll", "keydown"].forEach(ev =>
  addEventListener(ev, loadChat, { once: true, passive: true }));

1A.3 Code-split routes + heavy components

const Dashboard = lazy(() => import("./Dashboard"));
<Suspense fallback={<Skeleton />}><Dashboard /></Suspense>
// Next.js dynamic
const Heavy = dynamic(() => import("./Heavy"), { ssr: false, loading: () => <Skeleton /> });

Depth. Route-level splitting is table stakes; the wins after that are: (1) split *interaction-gated* UI (modals, date pickers, rich editors, charts) so it loads on click, not on mount; (2) split *below-the-fold* widgets; (3) avoid ssr: false on anything that contributes to LCP (you'll trade a JS win for an LCP loss). Verify the split actually happened — a stray top-level import of the heavy module pulls it back into the main chunk.

// Interaction-gated: chart code (300KB) ships only when the user opens the panel.
function Analytics() {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
  const Chart = useMemo(() => lazy(() => import("./HeavyChart")), []);
  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={() => setOpen(true)}>Show analytics</button>
      {open && <Suspense fallback={<Skeleton h={320} />}><Chart /></Suspense>}
    </>
  );
}

1A.4 Modern JS only — drop legacy polyfills

"browserslist": [">0.2%", "not dead", "not op_mini all"]

Depth. A 2018-era browserslist forces bundlers/Babel to down-compile async/await, optional chaining, and spread into bloated ES5 with regenerator-runtime — easily 30–50KB of pure waste plus slower runtime. In 2026 every browser in CrUX supports ES2022+. Setting a modern target turns async/?./??/top-level await into themselves. Confirm with the compat output of your bundler and ensure no core-js import remains in the main chunk.

1A.5 Replace heavy libraries

HeavyLighter (2026)Saves (gz)
moment.jsdate-fns / dayjs / Temporal polyfill60 KB
lodash (whole)lodash-es + tree-shake or native70 KB
axiosnative fetch + ofetch / ky14 KB
Material UI fullshadcn/ui + Tailwind, or Radix Primitives100–250 KB
echartsrecharts300 KB
lottie-weblottie-light or Rive90 KB
Draft.jsTiptap or ProseMirror tree-shaken60–120 KB

Depth. The Temporal API is now the right answer for dates — Temporal.PlainDate, Temporal.ZonedDateTime are stable in evergreen browsers in 2026; use the official polyfill only for the long tail. For barrel imports, the cardinal sin is import { debounce } from "lodash" (pulls all of lodash unless your bundler does deep tree-shaking) — write import debounce from "lodash-es/debounce" or just use native. Measure the real delta with source-map-explorer on the built bundle, not the package's advertised size.

// Native replacements that delete a dependency entirely
const sum = arr.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);                 // lodash.sum
const uniq = [...new Set(arr)];                              // lodash.uniq
const groupBy = Object.groupBy(items, (i) => i.category);   // lodash.groupBy (2025 baseline)
const fmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en", { dateStyle: "medium" }).format(d); // moment.format

1A.6 Self-host critical fonts with size-adjust

import { Inter } from "next/font/google";
const inter = Inter({ subsets: ["latin"], display: "swap", preload: true });

Depth. Self-hosting (which next/font does at build time — it downloads the font and serves it from your origin) removes a third-party connection and, critically, eliminates the layout shift from font swap by computing a matched size-adjust/ascent-override fallback. Subset to the glyphs you use, preload only the one or two faces above the fold, and prefer display: swap (text visible immediately with fallback) over optional only if the brand requires the custom face.

/* Hand-rolled fallback metric matching to kill the swap shift (what next/font generates) */
@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("/fonts/inter-var.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-display: swap;
  font-weight: 100 900;
}
@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter-fallback";
  src: local("Arial");
  size-adjust: 107%;      /* tuned so fallback occupies the same box → CLS ≈ 0 */
  ascent-override: 90%;
  descent-override: 22%;
}
:root { --font-sans: "Inter", "Inter-fallback", sans-serif; }

1B — Medium impact

  • CDN for static assets + HTML; Cache-Control immutable for fingerprinted assets.
  • Virtualize long lists (react-window / TanStack Virtual / Virtuoso).
  • Defer / chunk long tasks with scheduler.yield() or setTimeout(0).
  • Prefetch likely next routes (next/link does this; Speculation Rules API).
  • Suspense + streaming SSR; stream the shell to TTFB first.
  • Subset fonts; preload critical face; drop unused variants.
  • Eliminate render-blocking CSS (inline critical, defer non-critical).
  • Reduce hydration cost via Server Components.

Depth — scheduler.yield() (the 2026 INP fix). Long tasks (> 50 ms) block input. The fix is to break work into chunks and *yield to the browser* between them so it can paint and respond to clicks. scheduler.yield() is superior to setTimeout(0) because it yields with continuation priority — your task resumes ahead of other queued tasks instead of going to the back of the line.

// Yield-aware loop: keep the main thread responsive while processing 10k items.
async function processChunked(items, work) {
  const scheduler = globalThis.scheduler;
  let last = performance.now();
  for (const item of items) {
    work(item);
    // Yield if we've held the thread > 50ms (the long-task threshold)
    if (performance.now() - last > 50) {
      if (scheduler?.yield) await scheduler.yield();       // preferred (Baseline 2024+)
      else await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0));        // fallback
      last = performance.now();
    }
  }
}

Cache-Control split — the two-tier strategy:

# Fingerprinted asset (content hash in filename) — cache forever, never revalidate
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# HTML document — always revalidate so deploys go live instantly
Cache-Control: no-cache
# (or, with a CDN: s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=86400)

Speculation Rules — prerender the likely next page so navigation feels instant:

<script type="speculationrules">
{
  "prerender": [{
    "where": { "href_matches": "/product/*" },
    "eagerness": "moderate"
  }]
}
</script>

1C — Polish

  • Inline above-the-fold critical CSS (Critters / Beasties / Next.js auto).
  • Edge runtime / regional rendering for global users.
  • Server Components for content-heavy pages — zero JS on client.
  • Lighthouse CI budget in pipeline.
  • RUM with attribution (web-vitals/attribution).
  • INP-aware UI patterns: optimistic UI, immediate pending state, debounced inputs.

Depth — RUM with attribution. The bare web-vitals library tells you *that* INP is 290ms; the /attribution build tells you *which element and which script* caused it, which is the only thing that makes the data actionable. Ship attribution to your beacon and you can grep production for "the button that's slow."

import { onLCP, onINP, onCLS } from "web-vitals/attribution";

function send(metric) {
  navigator.sendBeacon("/rum", JSON.stringify({
    name: metric.name, value: metric.value, rating: metric.rating, // good|needs-improvement|poor
    target: metric.attribution?.interactionTarget,                  // CSS selector of slow element
    loadState: metric.attribution?.loadState,
    longestScript: metric.attribution?.longAnimationFrameEntries?.[0]?.scripts?.[0]?.sourceURL,
    nav: performance.getEntriesByType("navigation")[0]?.type,
  }));
}
onLCP(send); onINP(send); onCLS(send);  // sendBeacon survives the page unload

Lighthouse CI budget that fails the build on regression:

// lighthouserc.json — assertions block the PR if a budget is blown
{
  "ci": {
    "assert": {
      "assertions": {
        "categories:performance": ["error", { "minScore": 0.9 }],
        "largest-contentful-paint": ["error", { "maxNumericValue": 2000 }],
        "interactive": ["error", { "maxNumericValue": 3500 }],
        "cumulative-layout-shift": ["error", { "maxNumericValue": 0.1 }],
        "total-byte-weight": ["warn", { "maxNumericValue": 1000000 }]
      }
    }
  }
}

1D — INP triage flow

  • Record interaction in DevTools Performance.
  • Identify the bottleneck phase: input delay / processing / presentation.
  • Common fixes: virtualize, debounce, Web Worker, scheduler.yield, defer third-party.
  • Validate with Long Animation Frames API.
  • Add Playwright regression test that fails > 200 ms p95.

Exact diagnostic step order:

1. Reproduce on a throttled profile. DevTools → Performance → CPU 4× slowdown, "Mobile" preset. Field INP is dominated by cheap Android; never debug on an M-series Mac.

2. Record the interaction, then read the Interactions track. It splits the latency into three phases — this tells you the fix:

- Input delay high → main thread was busy when you clicked → defer/yield startup work, split bundles, move third-party off-main-thread.

- Processing duration high → your event handler is the problem → break it up with scheduler.yield(), move CPU work to a Web Worker, debounce.

- Presentation delay high → layout/paint after the handler → virtualize long lists, avoid forced sync layout (read-then-write batching), use content-visibility: auto.

3. Attribute the long script via the Long Animation Frames (LoAF) API.

4. Lock it with a regression test at p95 < 200ms.

// LoAF observer — pinpoints the script + function blocking interactions in production
new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  for (const frame of list.getEntries()) {
    if (frame.duration < 200) continue;
    const worst = frame.scripts.sort((a, b) => b.duration - a.duration)[0];
    navigator.sendBeacon("/loaf", JSON.stringify({
      blockingDuration: frame.blockingDuration,
      sourceURL: worst?.sourceURL,
      sourceFunctionName: worst?.sourceFunctionName,
      duration: worst?.duration,
    }));
  }
}).observe({ type: "long-animation-frame", buffered: true });
// Playwright regression guard — fails CI if interaction p95 > 200ms
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";
test("filter interaction stays under INP budget", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/dashboard");
  const samples: number[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
    const t0 = await page.evaluate(() => performance.now());
    await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Filter" }).click();
    const t1 = await page.evaluate(() => performance.now());
    samples.push(t1 - t0);
  }
  samples.sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const p95 = samples[Math.floor(samples.length * 0.95)];
  expect(p95).toBeLessThan(200);
});

1E — LCP triage flow

  • Find LCP element in DevTools.
  • If image: preload + fetchpriority="high" + AVIF + sizes + aspect-ratio reserved.
  • If text: preload font face; remove blocking CSS above; RSC streaming.
  • Reduce TTFB: cache shell at CDN, PPR, edge runtime.

Exact diagnostic step order:

1. Identify the LCP element. DevTools → Performance → "Timings" track → click the LCP marker; it highlights the node. Or PerformanceObserver for largest-contentful-paint in prod.

2. Decompose LCP into its 4 sub-parts (what WebPageTest's LCP breakdown shows): TTFB → resource load delay → resource load time → element render delay. Fix whichever dominates:

- TTFB dominates → cache the HTML shell at the CDN, use edge/regional rendering, adopt Partial Prerendering (PPR) so the static shell streams instantly.

- Load delay dominates → the browser found the image late → preload it, remove loading="lazy", make sure the URL is in server HTML (not injected by client JS).

- Load time dominates → image too big → AVIF + responsive srcset + compression.

- Render delay dominates → render-blocking CSS/JS or font swap → inline critical CSS, defer the rest, fix font loading.

3. Re-measure in the field, not just lab.

new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  const e = list.getEntries().at(-1); // last LCP candidate is the real one
  console.log("LCP", e.startTime.toFixed(0), e.element, e.url);
}).observe({ type: "largest-contentful-paint", buffered: true });

1F — CLS triage flow

  • Find shifted elements (DevTools Layout Instability).
  • Reserve aspect-ratio / width / height for all media.
  • Avoid late client-injected content; reserve placeholder space.
  • Use next/font or size-adjust to eliminate font swap shift.

Exact diagnostic step order:

1. Find the shifts. DevTools → Performance → "Layout Shift" track (red bars), or Rendering panel → "Layout Shift Regions" highlights them live. Each shift shows the score and the moved nodes.

2. Classify the cause: (a) media without dimensions, (b) ads/embeds/iframes injected late, (c) web-font swap, (d) dynamically inserted content above existing content (banners, cookie bars), (e) animating top/left/height instead of transform.

3. Fix per cause — reserve space with aspect-ratio or explicit width/height, pin late content with min-height, match font metrics (1A.6), and only animate transform/opacity (compositor-only, never shifts layout).

/* Reserve space so async content can't shove the page */
.media        { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; width: 100%; }   /* images, video, embeds */
.ad-slot      { min-height: 250px; }                    /* reserve before the ad arrives */
.skeleton-row { height: 48px; }                         /* match the real row height exactly */
.toast        { transform: translateY(-100%); transition: transform .2s; } /* no layout shift */

Part 2 — RELIABLE

Targets. JS error rate < 0.1% per session · no single crash breaks the page · network failures degrade gracefully.

2A — Granular error boundaries

import { ErrorBoundary } from "react-error-boundary";
function Fallback({ error, resetErrorBoundary }) {
  return <div role="alert"><p>This section failed.</p><button onClick={resetErrorBoundary}>Retry</button></div>;
}
<ErrorBoundary FallbackComponent={Fallback}
  onError={(e, info) => Sentry.captureException(e, { extra: info })}
  onReset={() => refetch()}>
  <CommentsPanel />
</ErrorBoundary>
  • One per independent feature, NOT one global.

Depth. The failure this stops: a render-time exception in *one* widget (a null deref in the comments list) unmounting the *entire* React tree → white screen. A boundary catches the throw, renders a local fallback, and the rest of the page survives. Place boundaries at feature seams — each independently-loaded panel, each route segment, each third-party widget. Pair every lazy import with a boundary so a chunk-load failure (deploy mid-session, flaky network) degrades to a retry button instead of a crash.

Caveat to state out loud: error boundaries catch render/lifecycle errors only. They do not catch errors in event handlers, setTimeout, promises, or SSR. Those need try/catch + manual Sentry.captureException. In 2026, wire React 19's onCaughtError / onUncaughtError root options to your logger so even boundary-handled errors get reported.

// React 19: report every error the boundary swallows, plus the ones it doesn't.
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";
createRoot(document.getElementById("root"), {
  onCaughtError: (error, info) => Sentry.captureException(error, { extra: info, tags: { caught: true } }),
  onUncaughtError: (error, info) => Sentry.captureException(error, { extra: info, level: "fatal" }),
}).render(<App />);

2B — Fetch with timeout + retry

async function fetchRetry(url, { retries = 3, timeoutMs = 8000 } = {}) {
  for (let i = 0; i < retries; i++) {
    const ctrl = new AbortController();
    const t = setTimeout(() => ctrl.abort(), timeoutMs);
    try {
      const res = await fetch(url, { signal: ctrl.signal });
      if (res.status >= 500 && i < retries - 1) throw new Error("5xx");
      return res;
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === retries - 1) throw e;
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, Math.random() * 2 ** i * 200));
    } finally { clearTimeout(t); }
  }
}
  • Only retry idempotent ops. Send Idempotency-Key header for writes.

Depth. Two failure modes this addresses: (1) a request that hangs forever (no client-side timeout) ties up a connection and never resolves — AbortController + a timer fixes it; (2) a transient 5xx / network blip fails a user action that would have succeeded on retry. The retry must use exponential backoff with full jitter — naive fixed-interval retries from thousands of clients create a synchronized "thundering herd" that DDoSes your own recovering server. Only retry idempotent verbs (GET, PUT, DELETE) or POSTs guarded by an Idempotency-Key. Respect Retry-After on 429/503.

// Production-grade: full jitter, retry-only-on-retryable, honor Retry-After, cap total time.
const RETRYABLE = new Set([408, 425, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504]);

async function resilientFetch(url: string, init: RequestInit = {}, opts = { retries: 3, perTryMs: 8000, capMs: 20000 }) {
  const deadline = Date.now() + opts.capMs;
  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
    const ctrl = new AbortController();
    const timer = setTimeout(() => ctrl.abort(new DOMException("timeout", "TimeoutError")), opts.perTryMs);
    try {
      const res = await fetch(url, { ...init, signal: ctrl.signal });
      if (!RETRYABLE.has(res.status) || attempt >= opts.retries) return res;
      const retryAfter = Number(res.headers.get("Retry-After")) * 1000 || 0;
      await sleep(Math.max(retryAfter, backoffJitter(attempt)), deadline);
    } catch (err: any) {
      const retryable = err.name === "TimeoutError" || err.name === "TypeError"; // network down
      if (!retryable || attempt >= opts.retries || Date.now() > deadline) throw err;
      await sleep(backoffJitter(attempt), deadline);
    } finally {
      clearTimeout(timer);
    }
  }
}
const backoffJitter = (n: number) => Math.random() * Math.min(1000 * 2 ** n, 8000); // full jitter, 8s cap
const sleep = (ms: number, deadline: number) =>
  new Promise<void>((r) => setTimeout(r, Math.min(ms, Math.max(0, deadline - Date.now()))));

2C — Race-condition guard (typeahead)

const last = useRef(0);
useEffect(() => {
  const seq = ++last.current;
  const ac = new AbortController();
  fetch(`/search?q=${q}`, { signal: ac.signal })
    .then(r => r.json())
    .then(d => { if (seq === last.current) setResults(d); });
  return () => ac.abort();
}, [q]);

Depth. The bug this prevents: the user types "react", then "redux"; the "react" request is slower and resolves *after* "redux", overwriting the correct results with stale ones (last-write-wins by network timing, not by user intent). Two defenses, used together: (1) the monotonic sequence guard (seq === last.current) drops any response that isn't the latest request even if it arrives; (2) AbortController in the cleanup actually cancels the in-flight request so it never lands and doesn't waste bandwidth. The cleanup runs on every q change because it's in the effect's return — this is the canonical pattern.

// Same guard, encapsulated and cancel-on-unmount safe. Debounce the trigger separately.
function useSearch(query: string, debounceMs = 250) {
  const [results, setResults] = useState<Item[]>([]);
  const reqId = useRef(0);
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = ++reqId.current;
    const ac = new AbortController();
    const t = setTimeout(async () => {
      try {
        const res = await fetch(`/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`, { signal: ac.signal });
        const data = await res.json();
        if (id === reqId.current) setResults(data);   // only the newest wins
      } catch (e: any) {
        if (e.name !== "AbortError") {/* report */}
      }
    }, debounceMs);
    return () => { clearTimeout(t); ac.abort(); };     // cancel both the debounce and the request
  }, [query, debounceMs]);
  return results;
}

> Note: TanStack Query / SWR handle this for you (request dedup + "latest wins" by query key). Reach for the manual guard only when you can't use a data library.

2D — Optimistic UI with rollback

const [opt, addOptimistic] = useOptimistic(todos, (s, t) => [...s, { ...t, pending: true }]);
async function handle(fd) {
  addOptimistic({ id: crypto.randomUUID(), title: fd.get("title") });
  try { await addTodo(fd); } catch { toast.error("Reverted"); }
}

Depth. Optimistic UI applies the mutation to the screen *immediately*, before the server confirms, so the interaction feels instant (a big perceived-perf / INP win). The contract: if the server rejects, you must roll back to the prior state and tell the user. React 19's useOptimistic rolls back automatically — the optimistic value is derived from the real state and is discarded when the action's transition settles, so on a thrown error the UI snaps back to the last committed state for free. You still owe the user a toast and, for important actions, a one-tap retry.

// React 19: optimistic value auto-reverts when the action rejects; we add the user-facing toast.
function Likes({ post }: { post: Post }) {
  const [optimistic, setOptimistic] = useOptimistic(
    post.likes,
    (current, delta: number) => current + delta
  );
  async function like() {
    setOptimistic(1);                          // bump instantly
    try {
      await likePost(post.id);                 // server action
    } catch {
      toast.error("Couldn't save your like");  // optimistic value already reverted by React
    }
  }
  return <button onClick={like}>♥ {optimistic}</button>;
}

With TanStack Query the equivalent is onMutate (snapshot + apply) / onError (restore snapshot) / onSettled (invalidate to reconcile with the server's truth).

2E — Four states per async surface

  • loading, error, empty, success — design + test all four.
  • Skeleton after 200 ms delay (avoid flicker on fast responses).
  • Error fallback offers retry; empty offers next-step CTA.

Depth. The single most common reliability gap in interviews is a candidate who designs only the happy path. Every data surface has four states and you should name all four and what each renders: loading (skeleton, delayed 200ms to avoid flash on fast networks), error (cause + a retry affordance, never a dead-end), empty (distinct from loading — a CTA to create the first item, not a blank box), success (the data). A fifth implicit state — partial/stale — appears once you add background revalidation (2G): show stale data with a subtle refreshing indicator rather than yanking it.

function AsyncSurface<T>({ q }: { q: UseQueryResult<T[]> }) {
  if (q.isPending) return <DelayedSkeleton delayMs={200} />;             // loading
  if (q.isError)   return <ErrorState onRetry={q.refetch} msg={q.error.message} />; // error + retry
  if (!q.data?.length) return <Empty cta="Create your first item" />;    // empty ≠ loading
  return <List items={q.data} stale={q.isFetching} />;                    // success (+ stale flag)
}
// DelayedSkeleton renders null for the first 200ms, then the skeleton — kills flicker on fast responses.

2F — Sentry wired right

Sentry.init({
  dsn: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN,
  release: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_DEPLOY_SHA,
  tracesSampleRate: 0.1,
  replaysOnErrorSampleRate: 1.0,
  ignoreErrors: [/ResizeObserver loop/, /Non-Error promise rejection/],

  • Upload source maps in CI. Tag release SHA. Filter noise.

Depth. Three things separate a useful Sentry setup from a noisy one: (1) source maps uploaded in CI and tied to the release SHA, so a minified a.b is not a function becomes a real file:line — without this the data is useless; (2) release + environment tagging, so you can see "errors spiked on release abc123 in production" and tie a regression to a specific deploy (and trigger auto-rollback); (3) noise control — ignoreErrors, denyUrls for third-party scripts you don't own, and sampling so you don't blow your quota. Set replaysOnErrorSampleRate: 1.0 to always capture a session replay when an error fires — that's the single highest-leverage debugging artifact.

// CI: upload source maps and create the release so stack traces de-minify and deploys are tracked.
// sentry-cli releases new "$DEPLOY_SHA"
// sentry-cli releases files "$DEPLOY_SHA" upload-sourcemaps ./dist --url-prefix '~/assets'
// sentry-cli releases finalize "$DEPLOY_SHA"

Sentry.init({
  dsn: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN,
  release: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_DEPLOY_SHA,    // must match the releases new <sha> above
  environment: process.env.NODE_ENV,

  replaysOnErrorSampleRate: 1.0,                    // always replay on error
  replaysSessionSampleRate: 0.05,
  ignoreErrors: [/ResizeObserver loop/, /Non-Error promise rejection captured/, /Load failed/],
  denyUrls: [/extensions\//, /^chrome:\/\//, /gtm\.js/],
  beforeSend(event) {                               // drop PII before it leaves the browser
    if (event.request?.cookies) delete event.request.cookies;
    return event;
  },
});

2G — Other reliability patterns

  • Background revalidation (TanStack Query refetch on focus + reconnect).
  • Partial-failure tolerance: each widget independently boundary-wrapped.
  • Offline-first via Workbox 7 (only if users need offline).
  • Idempotent mutations: UUID per mutation; server stores result 24h.
  • Graceful degradation when third-party fails (image, analytics, chat, websocket).
  • Top-level error boundary with Reload CTA (no white screen).
  • Synthetic monitoring on critical flows (Checkly / Better Stack).
  • Feature flag kill switches; rehearse the flip.
  • Validate API responses with Zod at the boundary.
  • Crash recovery — preserve user input to localStorage every 5 s.

Depth — validate at the boundary with Zod. The API contract *will* drift; a backend renames a field or sends null where you expected a string, and you get a render crash three components deep with a useless stack. Parsing the response at the network boundary turns a mystery runtime error into a single, clearly-attributed validation failure you can alert on.

import { z } from "zod";
const User = z.object({
  id: z.string().uuid(),
  name: z.string(),
  email: z.string().email(),
  role: z.enum(["admin", "member"]).catch("member"), // tolerate unknown roles instead of crashing
});
async function getUser(id: string) {
  const res = await resilientFetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
  const parsed = User.safeParse(await res.json());
  if (!parsed.success) {
    Sentry.captureException(new Error("User schema drift"), { extra: { issues: parsed.error.issues } });
    throw new Error("Bad response shape");            // one clean failure, not a deep render crash
  }
  return parsed.data;                                  // typed + validated past this line
}

Depth — feature-flag kill switch. Every risky feature ships behind a flag you can flip *off* in seconds without a deploy. Rehearse the flip before you need it. Bootstrap the flag server-side for SSR so the first paint already reflects it (no flicker, no flash of the broken feature).

const flags = await getFlags(userContext);            // edge config / LaunchDarkly bootstrap
return flags.newCheckout ? <NewCheckout /> : <LegacyCheckout />; // flip kills it instantly, no deploy

Part 3 — SECURE

Targets. OWASP Top 10 frontend pass · no third-party JS without SRI · CSP enforcing · no secrets in client · no XSS sinks unprotected.

3A — Content Security Policy (CSP)

Content-Security-Policy:
  default-src 'self';
  script-src 'self' 'nonce-{random}' https://cdn.example.com;
  style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';
  img-src 'self' data: https://images.example.com;
  font-src 'self';
  connect-src 'self' https://api.example.com;
  frame-ancestors 'none';
  base-uri 'self';
  form-action 'self';
  upgrade-insecure-requests;
  report-uri /csp-report;
  • Report-Only first → fix violations → enforce.
  • Use nonces for inline scripts, never unsafe-inline.
  • Test with csp-evaluator (Google).

Attack it stops. Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): if an attacker injects <script> or an inline onerror=, a strict CSP refuses to execute it because it lacks the per-request nonce. CSP is your second line of defense behind output encoding/sanitization — it turns "attacker got a string into the DOM" from account-takeover into a blocked, reported violation.

2026 best practice: strict, nonce + strict-dynamic, not an allowlist. Host allowlists are easily bypassed (open redirects, JSONP endpoints on a trusted CDN). The Google-recommended modern policy uses a per-response nonce plus strict-dynamic, which lets a trusted (nonced) script load further scripts it creates and ignores the host allowlist on supporting browsers.

Content-Security-Policy:
  default-src 'self';
  script-src 'nonce-r4nd0mBase64' 'strict-dynamic' https: 'unsafe-inline';
  object-src 'none';
  base-uri 'none';
  frame-ancestors 'none';
  require-trusted-types-for 'script';
  trusted-types default;
  upgrade-insecure-requests;
  report-to csp-endpoint;
  • 'unsafe-inline'/https: are fallbacks for old browsers — modern browsers ignore them when a nonce + strict-dynamic is present, so the policy is strict where it counts and degrades gracefully.
  • Generate a fresh nonce per response (never reuse, never static) and stamp it on every inline <script nonce>.
  • Roll out: Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only → collect violations via report-to for a week → fix → flip the header name to enforcing.
// Next.js middleware: per-request nonce + enforcing CSP
import { NextResponse } from "next/server";
export function middleware() {
  const nonce = Buffer.from(crypto.randomUUID()).toString("base64");
  const csp = `script-src 'nonce-${nonce}' 'strict-dynamic' https: 'unsafe-inline'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; require-trusted-types-for 'script';`;
  const res = NextResponse.next({ request: { headers: new Headers({ "x-nonce": nonce }) } });
  res.headers.set("Content-Security-Policy", csp);
  return res;
}

3B — Sanitize all user HTML

import DOMPurify from "dompurify";
const clean = DOMPurify.sanitize(userHtml, { USE_PROFILES: { html: true } });
<div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: clean }} />
  • Better: render Markdown via react-markdown with allowed elements.
  • Best: structured editor (Tiptap, ProseMirror) with serialization to known shape.

Attack it stops. Stored/reflected XSS via dangerouslySetInnerHTML (or innerHTML/v-html). Any time you put untrusted HTML in the DOM you have an XSS sink; DOMPurify strips <script>, on* handlers, javascript: URLs, and mXSS vectors. Sanitize on output, in the browser, every render — not once on input (sanitizers improve as new bypasses are found; data sanitized last year may be exploitable today).

// Lock the allowlist to exactly what you render; forbid event handlers + dangerous URI schemes.
const clean = DOMPurify.sanitize(userHtml, {
  ALLOWED_TAGS: ["b", "i", "em", "strong", "a", "p", "ul", "ol", "li", "code", "pre", "br"],
  ALLOWED_ATTR: ["href", "title"],
  ALLOWED_URI_REGEXP: /^(https?:|mailto:)/i,          // blocks javascript:, data: URLs
  FORBID_ATTR: ["style", "onerror", "onload"],
});
// Harden links from sanitized content against tab-nabbing:
DOMPurify.addHook("afterSanitizeAttributes", (node) => {
  if (node.tagName === "A") node.setAttribute("rel", "noopener noreferrer nofollow");
});

3C — Session cookies

Set-Cookie: session=…;
  HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=2592000
  • Never store JWTs in localStorage.
  • CSRF: SameSite=Lax + double-submit token for cross-origin POSTs.

Attack it stops. HttpOnly stops token theft via XSS (script can't read the cookie). Secure stops interception over HTTP. SameSite stops CSRF (the cookie isn't sent on cross-site requests). Storing a JWT in localStorage is the anti-pattern: it's readable by any XSS, has no HttpOnly protection, and persists. Use an HttpOnly cookie for the session and keep the access token in memory only.

Set-Cookie: __Host-session=eyJ...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=2592000
  • The __Host- prefix is enforced by the browser: requires Secure, Path=/, and no Domain — so a subdomain can't overwrite it (subdomain cookie-fixation defense).
  • SameSite=Lax is the right default; use Strict for the most sensitive cookies. For genuinely cross-site flows, add a double-submit CSRF token (a second non-HttpOnly token echoed in a header and compared server-side).

3D — Subresource Integrity (SRI)

<script src="https://cdn.example.com/lib.js"
  integrity="sha384-abc…def" crossorigin="anonymous" />
  • Plugins: vite-plugin-sri / webpack-subresource-integrity.

Attack it stops. Supply-chain / CDN compromise: if the third-party CDN (or a MITM) swaps lib.js for a malicious version, the browser computes its hash, finds it doesn't match integrity, and refuses to execute it. crossorigin="anonymous" is required so the response is readable for hashing. Generate hashes at build time and fail the build if a pinned third-party asset's hash changes unexpectedly.

# Compute the SRI hash for a vendored/CDN file
openssl dgst -sha384 -binary lib.js | openssl base64 -A
# → sha384-oqVuAfXRKap7fdgcCY5uykM6+R9GqQ8K/uxy9rx7HNQlGYl1kP...
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.example.com/app.css"
      integrity="sha384-oqVuAfXRKap7fdgcCY5uykM6..." crossorigin="anonymous" />

3E — No secrets in client bundle

  • gitleaks / TruffleHog in CI.
  • NEXT_PUBLIC_ / VITE_ prefix only for safe public values.
  • Proxy through server endpoint for any call requiring real secret.
  • If leaked: rotate first, audit access, commit fix.

Attack it stops. Credential exfiltration. Anything in the client bundle is public — minification is not secrecy; a grep of your JS finds it. Stripe secret keys, DB strings, signing keys, internal API tokens must live server-side. The bundler prefix (NEXT_PUBLIC_ / VITE_) is the guardrail: only prefixed vars reach the client, so an unprefixed secret can't leak by accident. For any call that needs a real secret, proxy through your own server route that holds the key.

Incident order if a secret leaks: ROTATE → audit access logs → then fix the code. Removing it from git history does nothing — it's already been cloned/scraped. Rotation is the only thing that closes the hole.

# CI gate: block the merge if a secret is detected in the diff (.github/workflows/security.yml)
- run: gitleaks detect --redact --exit-code 1
- run: npx -y @secretlint/cli "**/*"
# Verify nothing secret leaked into the built bundle:
- run: grep -RE "sk_live_|AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|-----BEGIN" ./dist && exit 1 || true

3F — HTTPS + HSTS preload

Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload

Attack it stops. SSL-stripping / protocol-downgrade MITM. HSTS tells the browser to *only* ever connect over HTTPS for max-age seconds — even if the user types http:// or clicks an http link, the browser upgrades before sending anything. preload (after submitting to hstspreload.org) bakes this into the browser so even the *first* visit is protected. Only add preload once you're certain every subdomain serves HTTPS — it's hard to undo.

Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload

3G — Trusted Types

Content-Security-Policy: require-trusted-types-for 'script'; trusted-types default;
const policy = trustedTypes.createPolicy("default", {
  createHTML: (input) => DOMPurify.sanitize(input),
});

Attack it stops. DOM-based XSS at the sink level. Trusted Types makes dangerous sinks (innerHTML, script.src, eval, document.write) throw a TypeError unless they're assigned a value produced by a registered, sanitizing policy. It eliminates an entire bug class: you literally *cannot* assign a raw string to innerHTML anymore, so a missed sanitization becomes a runtime error in dev/CI instead of a vuln in prod. This is the strongest XSS defense available and the 2026 best practice for new apps.

// Single named policy that every sink must go through; report-only first to find violations.
if (window.trustedTypes?.createPolicy) {
  trustedTypes.createPolicy("default", {
    createHTML: (s) => DOMPurify.sanitize(s, { RETURN_TRUSTED_TYPE: true }),
    createScriptURL: (u) => {
      const url = new URL(u, location.origin);
      if (url.origin !== location.origin && url.origin !== "https://cdn.example.com")
        throw new Error("blocked script URL: " + u);     // allowlist script origins
      return u;
    },
  });
}
// Roll out via report-only to catch every existing sink before enforcing:
// Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: require-trusted-types-for 'script'; report-to tt;

3I — Supply chain

  • Dependabot / Renovate weekly bumps.
  • npm audit / pnpm audit in CI; fail on high severity.
  • Lockfile in version control; --frozen-lockfile in CI.
  • Verify package provenance (npm provenance, sigstore) for critical deps.
  • Pin exact versions for security-sensitive packages.

Attack it stops. Malicious-dependency / typosquat / compromised-maintainer attacks (the 2024–2025 wave: event-stream, the xz backdoor, hijacked popular packages publishing crypto-stealers). Defenses, in depth: (1) lockfile committed + --frozen-lockfile so CI installs *exactly* what you reviewed, never a surprise transitive bump; (2) npm audit --audit-level=high failing the build; (3) npm provenance / sigstore attestation verification so you only run packages built from the claimed source by CI; (4) pin exact versions (no ^) for security-critical deps; (5) consider --ignore-scripts on install to neuter postinstall malware, allowlisting the few packages that genuinely need scripts.

// .npmrc — supply-chain hardening
ignore-scripts=true                  // block arbitrary postinstall code by default
audit-level=high
provenance=true                       // require provenance attestations where available
# CI
- run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
- run: pnpm audit --audit-level=high          # fail on high/critical
- run: npx --yes @socketsecurity/cli scan      # behavioral supply-chain scan (install-time risk)

3J — Third-party scripts audit

  • List every <script src> + every npm package that injects DOM scripts.
  • Remove unused; pin versions; load via Partytown where possible.
  • Re-audit monthly.

Attack it stops. Magecart-style skimming and third-party tag compromise: a marketing tag or analytics vendor gets popped and starts exfiltrating form data from *your* checkout. Defenses: inventory every external script (the connect-src/script-src in your CSP *is* your inventory — anything not listed can't run), pin + SRI where the vendor supports it, sandbox what you can (Partytown / iframe), and add a report-to so any new script-src violation alerts you immediately. The CSP connect-src doubles as exfil-prevention: a compromised tag can't POST stolen data to its own server if your CSP only allows your API origin.

3K — Rate limit + CAPTCHA

  • Cloudflare Turnstile / hCaptcha for non-bot signals.
  • Rate limit via Cloudflare WAF / AWS WAF on signup, login, public search.

Attack it stops. Credential stuffing, brute force, scraping, signup spam, and resource-exhaustion DoS on expensive endpoints. The frontend piece is a privacy-friendly CAPTCHA (Turnstile) that yields a token your *server* must verify — never trust the client result. The real enforcement is server/edge-side rate limiting keyed on IP + account, with progressive friction (allow → challenge → block).

// Server: verify the Turnstile token, then apply a sliding-window rate limit per IP+route.
const ok = await fetch("https://challenges.cloudflare.com/turnstile/v0/siteverify", {
  method: "POST",
  body: new URLSearchParams({ secret: process.env.TURNSTILE_SECRET!, response: token, remoteip: ip }),
}).then(r => r.json());
if (!ok.success) return new Response("captcha failed", { status: 403 });

const { success } = await ratelimit.limit(`login:${ip}`); // e.g. Upstash: 5 req / 60s sliding window
if (!success) return new Response("rate limited", { status: 429, headers: { "Retry-After": "60" } });

3L — OAuth / OIDC

  • Use library (Auth.js, Clerk, WorkOS, Kinde), not raw redirects.
  • PKCE for SPAs; refresh tokens in HttpOnly cookies.
  • Strict redirect URI allow-list.
  • Validate id_token signature client-side.

Attack it stops. Authorization-code interception, CSRF on the callback, open-redirect token theft, and token-in-localStorage XSS theft. The non-negotiables in 2026: (1) Authorization Code + PKCE for *all* clients (the implicit flow is dead) — PKCE binds the code to the client that started the flow, so an intercepted code is useless; (2) state parameter to prevent login CSRF; (3) exact-match redirect URI allowlist (no wildcards) to stop open-redirect token leaks; (4) tokens never in localStorage — keep the refresh token in an HttpOnly __Host- cookie and the access token in memory; (5) verify the id_token signature, iss, aud, nonce, and expiry.

// PKCE: generate verifier+challenge, send challenge on /authorize, verifier on /token.
const verifier = base64url(crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32)));
const challenge = base64url(await crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", new TextEncoder().encode(verifier)));
const state = crypto.randomUUID();
sessionStorage.setItem("pkce_verifier", verifier);
sessionStorage.setItem("oauth_state", state);
location.assign(`${issuer}/authorize?` + new URLSearchParams({
  response_type: "code", client_id, redirect_uri, scope: "openid profile email",
  code_challenge: challenge, code_challenge_method: "S256", state,
}));
// On callback: assert returned state === stored state, then exchange code + verifier for tokens
// at a *server* route that sets the refresh token as an HttpOnly __Host- cookie.

Part 4 — AVAILABLE

Targets. 99.95% uptime monthly · no single deploy takes prod down · failures detected within 1 min · region outage invisible.

The uptime math (memorize this). 99.9% = 43 min/month down. 99.95% = 21 min 54s/month. 99.99% = 4 min 23s/month. Each extra nine is ~10× the engineering cost; pick the SLO the product actually needs and budget the rest as an error budget you're allowed to spend on shipping.

4A — High impact

  • Host on global CDN (Vercel / Netlify / Cloudflare Pages) — CDN IS the host.
  • Atomic deploys + one-click rollback (< 60 s). Rehearse it.
  • Preview deploys + smoke tests before merge; Lighthouse CI + visual regression.
  • Synthetic monitoring on critical user journey from 2+ regions every 5 min.
  • Status page + comms templates (Atlassian Statuspage / Better Stack / Cloudflare Page).

Depth — atomic deploy + instant rollback. "Atomic" means a deploy either fully succeeds or doesn't flip the pointer — users never see a half-deployed state with mismatched JS/HTML chunk hashes (which causes mid-session chunk-load errors). Modern platforms achieve this with immutable, content-addressed deploys: each deploy is a complete immutable snapshot at a unique URL, and "going live" is just repointing an alias. Rollback is repointing the alias back — seconds, no rebuild.

# Vercel: every deploy is immutable + addressable; promote/rollback is an alias flip (no rebuild).
vercel deploy --prebuilt --prod        # creates immutable deployment dpl_abc123
vercel promote dpl_abc123              # atomic alias flip to production
vercel rollback                        # instant: re-point alias to the previous good deployment

Rehearse rollback monthly as a game day — a rollback you've never tested is not a rollback.

Depth — synthetic monitoring must test the journey (login → core action), not just GET / → 200. A homepage can return 200 while checkout is broken.

// Checkly / Playwright synthetic check — runs every 5 min from 2+ regions, alerts on failure.
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";
test("critical journey: login → create", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/login");
  await page.getByLabel("Email").fill(process.env.SYNTH_USER!);
  await page.getByLabel("Password").fill(process.env.SYNTH_PASS!);
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Sign in" }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole("heading", { name: "Dashboard" })).toBeVisible({ timeout: 5000 });
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "New item" }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText("Created")).toBeVisible();   // alert if this fails — detect < 1 min
});

4B — Medium impact

  • Multi-region SSR (Vercel Edge / Cloudflare Workers) — app runs in 30+ regions.
  • Stale-while-error fallback at CDN if origin dies.
  • Multi-CDN failover (ioriver.io, NS1, Cedexis) when stakes justify 2× CDN bill.
  • Graceful backend degradation: read-only mode, cached data, error banner with partial actions.
  • Static fallback page on different domain as last resort.
  • Health checks that verify DB + downstream APIs + cache (not just 200 OK).

Depth — stale-while-error / stale-while-revalidate. Configure the CDN to keep serving the last good cached response when the origin returns 5xx or times out. Users see slightly stale content instead of an error page — availability decoupled from origin health.

# Origin response header → CDN serves cached copy for 1 day if origin errors, refreshes in background
Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=600, stale-if-error=86400

Depth — health checks must be deep. A 200 OK from the web tier means nothing if the DB is down. The health endpoint should *actually* probe each critical dependency (with its own short timeout) and return 503 if a hard dependency is down so the load balancer pulls the node.

// /healthz — deep check; degraded vs down distinction drives the LB and the status page.
export async function GET() {
  const checks = await Promise.allSettled([
    pingWithTimeout(() => db.query("SELECT 1"), 500),
    pingWithTimeout(() => cache.ping(), 300),
    pingWithTimeout(() => fetch(`${API}/healthz`), 800),
  ]);
  const dbDown = checks[0].status === "rejected";          // DB is a hard dependency
  const softDown = checks.slice(1).filter(c => c.status === "rejected").length;
  const status = dbDown ? 503 : 200;                       // cache/API soft → degraded, still up
  return Response.json(
    { ok: status === 200, checks: checks.map(c => c.status), degraded: softDown > 0 },
    { status });
}

4C — Polish

  • Quarterly chaos / game day exercises.
  • Error budgets (99.95% = 21 min/month) with burn-rate alerts.
  • k6 / Artillery load testing on perf branch; trend over time.
  • DB resilience: connection pooling (PgBouncer/RDS Proxy), read replicas, PITR backups tested monthly.

Depth — error budget + burn-rate alerts. An SLO of 99.95% gives a monthly budget of ~22 min of downtime. Alert on burn rate, not raw downtime: a *fast burn* (consuming 2% of the budget in 1 hour) pages immediately; a *slow burn* (10% over 3 days) opens a ticket. This is multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting (Google SRE) — it catches real outages fast while ignoring noise.

// k6 smoke/load with SLO thresholds baked in — fails the perf-branch build if budget is blown.
import http from "k6/http"; import { check } from "k6";
export const options = {
  scenarios: { ramp: { executor: "ramping-vus", stages: [
    { duration: "1m", target: 50 }, { duration: "3m", target: 200 }, { duration: "1m", target: 0 } ] } },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.001"],   // < 0.1% errors (the reliability SLO)
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<500", "p(99)<1500"],
  },
};
export default function () {
  const res = http.get("https://staging.example.com/");
  check(res, { "200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

Part 5 — Deployment toolbelt

5.1 Hosting platforms

PlatformSweet spotGotcha
VercelNext.js, RSC, AI streaming, best DXBandwidth $$$ past ~5 TB/mo
NetlifyAstro, Jamstack, simpler pricingNext.js parity lags Vercel
Cloudflare Pages + WorkersEdge-everywhere, unlimited bandwidthV8 isolates only — no Node APIs
Fly.ioLong-running Node + regional PostgresYou operate the machine
Render / RailwayHeroku-style PaaSSmaller community

Selection heuristic. Pick on (1) runtime needs — pure edge (Cloudflare Workers, V8 isolates, no fs/native Node) vs full Node (Fly, Render); (2) framework fit — Next.js RSC/PPR is smoothest on Vercel; (3) data locality — co-locate SSR with your DB region or TTFB suffers from cross-region DB round-trips; (4) egress cost at scale — Cloudflare's free bandwidth wins for high-traffic static/edge, Vercel bandwidth gets expensive past a few TB.

5.2 CI pipeline (FE)

  • Install (frozen lockfile) → lint → typecheck → unit + integration → build → bundle analyze → Lighthouse CI → preview deploy → E2E smoke (Playwright) → visual regression (Chromatic / Percy) → a11y scan (axe).
  • On merge: build immutable artifact → push to production.

Depth — fail fast, gate hard. Order stages cheap-to-expensive so a typo fails in 20s, not after a 5-min E2E run. Each gate should *block* merge, not warn: typecheck error → red; bundle over budget → red; LCP regression → red; new high-sev CVE → red; visual diff → requires approval. The artifact built in CI is the *exact* artifact promoted to prod (build once, deploy the same hash to preview then prod) — never rebuild for prod or you've tested a different artifact than you ship.

# Build-once, promote-same-artifact, with hard quality gates.
jobs:
  ci:
    steps:
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm lint && pnpm typecheck
      - run: pnpm test --coverage
      - run: pnpm build                      # the immutable artifact
      - run: pnpm size-limit                 # bundle budget — fails over threshold
      - run: pnpm audit --audit-level=high
      - run: npx lhci autorun                # Lighthouse budgets (1C)
      - run: pnpm exec playwright test       # E2E smoke on the preview deploy

5.3 Feature flags

ToolWhenFE note
LaunchDarklyEnterprise; ML-driven + auto-rollbackBootstrap server-side for SSR
StatsigFlags + experiments + analyticsStrong React SDK
GrowthBookOSS, SQL-based analysisCheap, transparent
Vercel Flags + Edge ConfigVercel-native, edge-fastSub-ms lookups
Unleash / Flagsmith / ConfigCatOSS or low-costSolid baseline
PostHogOSS analytics + flags + replayGood for startups

Depth — decouple deploy from release. Flags let you ship dark (merge to prod, feature off), then turn on for 1% → 10% → 100% with a kill switch at every step. Bootstrap flags server-side for SSR so the server-rendered HTML already matches the flag state — otherwise you get a hydration mismatch and a flash of the wrong UI. Pair flag rollouts with a metric guardrail: auto-revert the flag if error rate or a key conversion metric regresses.

5.4 Observability

ToolBest at
SentryJS errors + perf + replay; default
Datadog RUMTying FE to backend traces; pricey
HoneycombHigh-cardinality debugging; trace-first
LogRocketSession replay + funnels
SpeedCurvePerf monitoring + competitor benchmarks
web-vitals + sendBeaconVendor-free CWV beacon
OpenTelemetry web SDKStandardize on OTel; avoid vendor lock-in

Depth — the three pillars on the frontend. *Errors* (Sentry, with source maps + release tagging), *RUM/metrics* (web-vitals beacon → your warehouse, p75 field CWV), and *traces* (OTel web SDK propagating traceparent so a slow frontend interaction links to the exact backend span that caused it). Standardize on OpenTelemetry semantics to avoid vendor lock-in; you can swap the backend (Honeycomb, Datadog, Grafana) without re-instrumenting.

Part 6 — Master 4-sprint plan

Sprint 1 — High impact, low effort

  • Compress + optimize LCP image.
  • Lazy-load heavy third-party scripts.
  • Self-host critical fonts.
  • Code-split routes.
  • Wire Sentry with source maps.
  • Granular error boundaries (top 3).
  • Fetch timeout + retry helper.
  • HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite session cookies.
  • HSTS + http→https redirects.
  • Global CDN hosting.
  • Verify atomic deploys + rehearse rollback.

Sprint 1 is the "stop the bleeding" sprint — every item is < 1 day and moves a top-line metric. Exit criteria: LCP p75 improved on top 3 routes, Sentry receiving de-minified errors tagged with release SHA, rollback rehearsed and timed under 60s, security cookie + HSTS headers verified on prod. Quote the before/after deltas from Part 0.

Sprint 2 — High impact, medium effort

  • Lighthouse CI in pipeline.
  • Web Vitals RUM beacon.
  • Replace heavy libraries (moment, axios, MUI full).
  • Virtualize the longest list.
  • Race-condition guard on typeahead.
  • Optimistic UI on most-clicked mutation.
  • CSP Report-Only → fix violations.
  • Sanitize user HTML.
  • SRI on every third-party script.
  • Synthetic monitoring on login → primary action.
  • Status page + comms templates.

Sprint 2 builds the guardrails so Sprint 1's wins don't regress: Lighthouse CI + size-limit budgets in CI catch perf regressions at PR time; RUM beacon makes field data continuous; CSP goes Report-Only to inventory violations before enforcing next sprint.

Sprint 3 — Medium impact

  • Defer + chunk long tasks (scheduler.yield).
  • Prefetch likely routes.
  • Streaming SSR + Suspense.
  • Four states on every async surface.
  • Background revalidation.
  • Idempotent mutations.
  • CSP enforcing mode.
  • Permissions-Policy + X-Frame-Options.
  • Dependabot + npm audit in CI.
  • Multi-region SSR + stale-while-error fallback.
  • Graceful backend degradation.

Sprint 3 is the INP + hardening sprint. Flip CSP from Report-Only to enforcing (violations fixed in Sprint 2), ship scheduler.yield() on the worst long tasks, and add multi-region + stale-if-error so an origin or region blip is invisible.

Sprint 4 — Polish

  • Trusted Types for DOM XSS.
  • Service worker / offline-first if relevant.
  • Synthetic monitor on top 5 journeys.
  • Quarterly chaos / game day.
  • Error budgets + burn-rate alerts.
  • DAST in staging.
  • Annual pen-test.
  • Privacy / GDPR review.

Sprint 4 is defense-in-depth + process. Trusted Types closes the DOM-XSS sink class entirely; chaos/game days and burn-rate alerts turn reliability from reactive to proactive; DAST + pen-test + privacy review satisfy the compliance bar a senior is expected to own.

Scorecard — track monthly

PillarKPITargetTool
Fasterp75 LCP< 2.0 sweb-vitals + RUM
Fasterp75 INP< 200 mssame
Fasterp75 CLS< 0.1same
FasterHome JS gz< 200 KBsize-limit in CI
ReliableJS errors / session< 0.1%Sentry
ReliableMTTR (FE incident)< 15 minPostmortem log
ReliableSynthetic uptime> 99.95%Checkly / Better Stack
SecureCSP enforcementenforcing, 0 high-sevcsp-evaluator
SecureHigh-sev CVEs in prod deps0 open > 7dDependabot
SecureThird-party scripts< 10, 100% SRIManual audit
AvailableMonthly uptime> 99.95%Status + synthetic
AvailableSuccessful canary rollouts> 95%Deploy log
AvailableTime-to-detect< 1 minAlert log

How to run the scorecard. Every metric is a *field/production* number reviewed monthly, with an owner and an alert when it breaches. Faster = CrUX p75, not lab. Reliable = Sentry error rate + MTTR from your postmortem log. Secure = a passing CI gate (CSP enforcing, 0 high-sev CVEs > 7 days, 100% SRI). Available = synthetic uptime + time-to-detect from the alert log. In an interview, walking this table top-to-bottom — naming the target, the tool, and the diagnostic flow behind each row — is the cleanest way to demonstrate senior FRSA ownership.

Next: Doc 06 — System Design Playbook.
