docs.search: 05 — Performance + Reliability + Security + Availability (2026) Web Vitals · Bundle · Errors · CSP · CDN · Deployment · 4-sprint plan Merged from v2/07 (perf/sec/test), v3/13 (FE deployment + reliability toolbelt), v3/14 (FRSA action checklist). The complete senior-FE FRSA playbook in one doc. > How to use this doc in an interview. FRSA is the "make it production-grade" round. The interviewer wants to see you (a) reach for a *measurement* before a *fix*, (b) name an exact threshold, (c) name the diagnostic step order, and (d) give a concrete config/code snippet with the failure mode it prevents. Every section below follows that shape: original guidance, then depth, then a runnable example with thresholds. Part 0 — Baseline before you change anything Lighthouse + WebPageTest baseline on top 3 routes. RUM Web Vitals from 7 days of real users. JS error rate from Sentry over 7 days. Bundle size (home route, gzipped) from next build / vite build. Monthly uptime from synthetic monitor. Document these five numbers. They are your before/after. Why baseline first. Lighthouse is a *lab* number (single cold run, throttled CPU/network) and is great for catching regressions in CI, but it does not represent your users. RUM is the *field* number — it is what Google ranks on (CrUX p75) and what you defend in the interview. The two diverge constantly: a route can score Lighthouse 95 yet fail INP in the field because real users have cheap Android CPUs and click before hydration finishes. Always quote field p75 , not lab. The five numbers, with the exact source command/query: # 1. Lab perf — top 3 routes, mobile profile, median of 3 runs (don't trust 1 run) npx lighthouse https://app.example.com/ --preset=perf --form-factor=mobile --throttling-method=simulate --output=json npx lighthouse https://app.example.com/pricing --preset=perf npx lighthouse https://app.example.com/dashboard --preset=perf # 4. Bundle size, gzipped, per route — the number that actually predicts INP/TBT next build # reads the "First Load JS" column # or npx vite-bundle-visualizer -- 2. RUM field p75 from your warehouse (BigQuery CrUX export shown; substitute your RUM table) SELECT ROUND(APPROX_QUANTILES(lcp_ms, 100)[OFFSET(75)]) AS lcp_p75, ROUND(APPROX_QUANTILES(inp_ms, 100)[OFFSET(75)]) AS inp_p75, ROUND(APPROX_QUANTILES(cls, 100)[OFFSET(75)], 3) AS cls_p75 FROM rum.web_vitals WHERE event_date >= DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 7 DAY); Write the five numbers into the PR description / ticket. "Before: LCP p75 3.4s, INP p75 290ms, JS 410KB. After: 1.9s / 160ms / 180KB." That delta is the entire point of the work and the only thing a promo committee or interviewer remembers. Part 1 — FASTER (Performance) Targets. p75 LCP < 2.0 s · p75 INP < 200 ms · p75 CLS < 0.1 · TTFB < 800 ms · home JS gz < 200 KB. 2026 threshold table (Google "good" = field p75; these are the numbers to quote): Metric Good (p75) Needs work Poor What it measures LCP < 2.5 s (aim < 2.0 s) 2.5–4.0 s > 4.0 s Largest paint render time INP < 200 ms 200–500 ms > 500 ms Worst interaction latency (replaced FID, March 2024) CLS < 0.1 0.1–0.25 > 0.25 Unexpected layout shift TTFB < 800 ms 800–1800 ms > 1800 ms Server + network to first byte FCP < 1.8 s 1.8–3.0 s > 3.0 s First content paint INP is the metric most senior candidates fumble. It is the 98th-percentile interaction on the page (not an average), measured as input-delay + processing + presentation-delay, across the *whole page lifetime*. A single 600ms click handler tanks the page's INP. The fix is almost always "break up or yield the long task," which is why scheduler.yield() (1B/1D) matters. 1A — High impact 1A.1 Compress LCP image to AVIF <img src="/hero.avif" srcSet="/hero-640.avif 640w, /hero-1280.avif 1280w, /hero-1920.avif 1920w" sizes="100vw" width="1920" height="1080" fetchPriority="high" alt="…" /> // or Next.js <Image src="/hero.png" width={1920} height={1080} priority alt="…" /> Depth. The LCP image has four levers, in priority order: (1) discoverability — the browser must find the URL in the initial HTML, so the LCP image must NOT be lazy-loaded and ideally is preloaded; (2) priority — fetchPriority="high" so it jumps the queue ahead of late scripts; (3) format/size — AVIF beats WebP by ~20–30%, and srcset / sizes ships the right resolution; (4) dimensions — width / height reserve space so the image is also a CLS win. Common mistake: putting the hero image behind a client component that hydrates late, so the URL only appears after JS runs. The preload scanner never sees it and LCP balloons. Keep the LCP image in server-rendered HTML. <!-- Belt-and-suspenders: preload the chosen candidate so it starts at HTML parse, before CSS --> <link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero-1280.avif" imagesrcset="/hero-640.avif 640w, /hero-1280.avif 1280w, /hero-1920.avif 1920w" imagesizes="100vw" fetchpriority="high" /> Never preload more than 1–2 LCP candidates; over-preloading steals bandwidth from the actual LCP element and makes LCP worse. 1A.2 Remove or lazy-load heavy third-party scripts // Defer non-critical <script src="/analytics.js" defer /> // Idle-load requestIdleCallback(() => import("./chat-widget")); // Off-main-thread <Partytown forward={["dataLayer.push"]} /> <script type="text/partytown" src="https://gtm.example.com/gtm.js" /> Depth. Third-party JS is the #1 cause of poor field INP because it runs on the main thread during the exact window users try to interact. Triage order: measure each tag's main-thread cost (DevTools Performance → bottom-up, group by URL, or WebPageTest "third party" view) → delete anything with no owner → defer the rest off the critical path → isolate the unavoidable ones (GTM, chat, ads) into a worker via Partytown so they never block the main thread. // Load chat only after the user shows intent OR the browser is idle — not on page load. const loadChat = () => import("./chat-widget").then(m => m.mount()); if ("requestIdleCallback" in window) { requestIdleCallback(loadChat, { timeout: 5000 }); } else { setTimeout(loadChat, 3000); } // Even better: load on first scroll / first pointermove, whichever is first. ["pointermove", "scroll", "keydown"].forEach(ev => addEventListener(ev, loadChat, { once: true, passive: true })); 1A.3 Code-split routes + heavy components const Dashboard = lazy(() => import("./Dashboard")); <Suspense fallback={<Skeleton />}><Dashboard /></Suspense> // Next.js dynamic const Heavy = dynamic(() => import("./Heavy"), { ssr: false, loading: () => <Skeleton /> }); Depth. Route-level splitting is table stakes; the wins after that are: (1) split *interaction-gated* UI (modals, date pickers, rich editors, charts) so it loads on click, not on mount; (2) split *below-the-fold* widgets; (3) avoid ssr: false on anything that contributes to LCP (you'll trade a JS win for an LCP loss). Verify the split actually happened — a stray top-level import of the heavy module pulls it back into the main chunk. // Interaction-gated: chart code (300KB) ships only when the user opens the panel. function Analytics() { const [open, setOpen] = useState(false); const Chart = useMemo(() => lazy(() => import("./HeavyChart")), []); return ( <> <button onClick={() => setOpen(true)}>Show analytics</button> {open && <Suspense fallback={<Skeleton h={320} />}><Chart /></Suspense>} </> ); } 1A.4 Modern JS only — drop legacy polyfills "browserslist": [">0.2%", "not dead", "not op_mini all"] Depth. A 2018-era browserslist forces bundlers/Babel to down-compile async/await, optional chaining, and spread into bloated ES5 with regenerator-runtime — easily 30–50KB of pure waste plus slower runtime. In 2026 every browser in CrUX supports ES2022+. Setting a modern target turns async / ?. / ?? /top-level await into themselves. Confirm with the compat output of your bundler and ensure no core-js import remains in the main chunk. 1A.5 Replace heavy libraries Heavy Lighter (2026) Saves (gz) moment.js date-fns / dayjs / Temporal polyfill 60 KB lodash (whole) lodash-es + tree-shake or native 70 KB axios native fetch + ofetch / ky 14 KB Material UI full shadcn/ui + Tailwind, or Radix Primitives 100–250 KB echarts recharts 300 KB lottie-web lottie-light or Rive 90 KB Draft.js Tiptap or ProseMirror tree-shaken 60–120 KB Depth. The Temporal API is now the right answer for dates — Temporal.PlainDate , Temporal.ZonedDateTime are stable in evergreen browsers in 2026; use the official polyfill only for the long tail. For barrel imports, the cardinal sin is import { debounce } from "lodash" (pulls all of lodash unless your bundler does deep tree-shaking) — write import debounce from "lodash-es/debounce" or just use native. Measure the real delta with source-map-explorer on the built bundle, not the package's advertised size. // Native replacements that delete a dependency entirely const sum = arr.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); // lodash.sum const uniq = [...new Set(arr)]; // lodash.uniq const groupBy = Object.groupBy(items, (i) => i.category); // lodash.groupBy (2025 baseline) const fmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en", { dateStyle: "medium" }).format(d); // moment.format 1A.6 Self-host critical fonts with size-adjust import { Inter } from "next/font/google"; const inter = Inter({ subsets: ["latin"], display: "swap", preload: true }); Depth. Self-hosting (which next/font does at build time — it downloads the font and serves it from your origin) removes a third-party connection and, critically, eliminates the layout shift from font swap by computing a matched size-adjust / ascent-override fallback. Subset to the glyphs you use, preload only the one or two faces above the fold, and prefer display: swap (text visible immediately with fallback) over optional only if the brand requires the custom face. /* Hand-rolled fallback metric matching to kill the swap shift (what next/font generates) */ @font-face { font-family: "Inter"; src: url("/fonts/inter-var.woff2") format("woff2"); font-display: swap; font-weight: 100 900; } @font-face { font-family: "Inter-fallback"; src: local("Arial"); size-adjust: 107%; /* tuned so fallback occupies the same box → CLS ≈ 0 */ ascent-override: 90%; descent-override: 22%; } :root { --font-sans: "Inter", "Inter-fallback", sans-serif; } 1B — Medium impact CDN for static assets + HTML; Cache-Control immutable for fingerprinted assets. Virtualize long lists (react-window / TanStack Virtual / Virtuoso). Defer / chunk long tasks with scheduler.yield() or setTimeout(0). Prefetch likely next routes (next/link does this; Speculation Rules API). Suspense + streaming SSR; stream the shell to TTFB first. Subset fonts; preload critical face; drop unused variants. Eliminate render-blocking CSS (inline critical, defer non-critical). Reduce hydration cost via Server Components. Depth — scheduler.yield() (the 2026 INP fix). Long tasks (> 50 ms) block input. The fix is to break work into chunks and *yield to the browser* between them so it can paint and respond to clicks. scheduler.yield() is superior to setTimeout(0) because it yields with continuation priority — your task resumes ahead of other queued tasks instead of going to the back of the line. // Yield-aware loop: keep the main thread responsive while processing 10k items. async function processChunked(items, work) { const scheduler = globalThis.scheduler; let last = performance.now(); for (const item of items) { work(item); // Yield if we've held the thread > 50ms (the long-task threshold) if (performance.now() - last > 50) { if (scheduler?.yield) await scheduler.yield(); // preferred (Baseline 2024+) else await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0)); // fallback last = performance.now(); } } } Cache-Control split — the two-tier strategy: # Fingerprinted asset (content hash in filename) — cache forever, never revalida

06 — Frontend System Design Playbook + 10 Case Studies (2026)

RADIO framework · Patterns · CRDT vs OT · 10 full case studies

Merged from v1/03, v2/03, v3/09. Per-case structure: requirements, architecture, data model, rendering, state, real-time, perf budget, a11y, edge cases, follow-ups.

> How to read this doc: each case is sized for a real 60-minute FE round. Spend ~5 min on Requirements, ~10 on Architecture + data model, ~20 on the deep-dive the interviewer pulls on (rendering, state, or real-time), ~10 on perf/a11y/edge, ~10 on follow-ups. The senior signal is *naming the trade-off and the number*, not drawing more boxes.

Part 1 — RADIO framework

  • Requirements: clarify scope, prioritize features, surface assumptions, ask about scale.
  • Architecture: high-level boxes — client, BFF/edge, services, cache, CDN.
  • Data model: schema + API endpoints + WebSocket/event payloads.
  • Interface: component tree, key UI states (empty, loading, error, optimistic, conflicted).
  • Optimizations + deep-dives: performance, accessibility, security, offline, i18n.

Running RADIO like a senior (the 60-min budget):

PhaseTimeWhat "good" looks likeFailure mode
Requirements5 min3 functional + 3 non-functional, *quantified* (MAU, p95, payload). Pin scope ("read-path only? collab?").Jumping to boxes before scoping.
Architecture8 minOne diagram: client → edge/BFF → services + the real-time path. Name where state lives.Drawing the backend in depth on a *frontend* round.
Data model7 minTS interfaces for entities + the wire (REST + WS/SSE message shapes). Normalized vs tree.Hand-waving "some JSON".
Interface/Deep-dive25 minComponent tree, the 5 UI states, the *one* hard problem (virtualization math / OT vs CRDT / fan-out).No trade-off named.
Optimize15 minConcrete budgets (LCP/INP/bundle KB), a11y, offline, failure modes."It'll be fast."

Quantify-everything cheat sheet (memorize, drop into Requirements):

  • Core Web Vitals 2026 targets: LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1 (75th percentile, field).
  • A "fast" interaction budget = one frame = 16.6 ms at 60 Hz, 8.3 ms at 120 Hz (ProMotion/high-refresh phones).
  • 3G Fast ≈ 1.6 Mbps / 150 ms RTT; 4G ≈ 9 Mbps / 60 ms. Low-end Android CPU ≈ 4–6× slower than an M-series laptop — *always* state your reference device.
  • JS parse/compile ≈ 1 ms per KB on low-end mobile → a 200 KB bundle costs ~200 ms of main-thread time before it even runs.

Part 2 — Recurring patterns

2.1 Real-time fan-out

  • Per-room actor on a stateful gateway → broadcasts ops to subscribers.
  • Use Redis pubsub or NATS for cross-region; sticky-session on WebSocket gateway.

The core problem: N publishers, M subscribers per room, K rooms. A single doc-actor (single-writer) per room linearizes ops so ordering is trivial; the gateway is horizontally sharded by roomId (consistent hashing) so a room always lands on one node. Cross-node delivery (a subscriber connected to a *different* gateway than the room owner) goes through a pub/sub bus.

Transport decision matrix:

TransportDirectionUse whenCost
WebSocketduplexcollab edits, chat, presencestateful conn, sticky LB, scaling = conn count
SSEserver→clientfeeds, notifications, live counterscheap, auto-reconnect, HTTP/2 multiplexed, no upstream
WebTransport (HTTP/3)duplex, unreliable+reliable2026 low-latency cursors/datagramsnewer, fallback to WS needed
Long-pollserver→clientlegacy/firewalled fallbackhigh overhead, last resort

Rule: SSE for one-way, WS for two-way. Don't reach for WS to push a notification badge.

// Gateway shard: one actor per room, single-writer ordering.
interface RoomActor {
  seq: number;                       // monotonic op sequence
  subscribers: Map<ConnId, Socket>;
  apply(op: Op): { seq: number };    // assigns seq, persists to WAL
  broadcast(op: SeqOp): void;        // to local subs + pub/sub for remote
}
// Client reconnect: send last-seen seq, server replays the gap.
type Resume = { roomId: string; lastSeq: number };

Backpressure & fan-out math: a celebrity room with 50K viewers receiving 10 ops/s = 500K msg/s out of one node — don't. Tier it: hot rooms get a fan-out tree (gateway → regional relays → clients) or collapse to interval snapshots (coalesce ops into a 100–250 ms diff) instead of per-keystroke broadcast. Always cap per-connection send-queue depth and drop-to-snapshot on slow consumers.

2.2 Optimistic mutation

  • Temp ID client-side → apply locally → send to server → reconcile with server ID → revert on error.
  • Idempotency: client-generated request key.
// Optimistic mutation with rollback + idempotency (TanStack Query v5).
function useSendMessage(channelId: string) {
  const qc = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: (text: string) =>
      api.post(`/channels/${channelId}/messages`, {
        text,
        idempotencyKey: crypto.randomUUID(), // dedupe retries server-side
      }),
    onMutate: async (text) => {
      await qc.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ["messages", channelId] });
      const prev = qc.getQueryData(["messages", channelId]);
      const tempId = `tmp_${crypto.randomUUID()}`;
      qc.setQueryData(["messages", channelId], (old: Msg[] = []) => [
        ...old,
        { id: tempId, text, status: "sending", createdAt: Date.now() },
      ]);
      return { prev, tempId };           // context for rollback / reconcile
    },
    onError: (_e, _v, ctx) =>
      qc.setQueryData(["messages", channelId], ctx!.prev), // revert
    onSuccess: (serverMsg, _v, ctx) =>
      qc.setQueryData(["messages", channelId], (old: Msg[] = []) =>
        old.map((m) => (m.id === ctx!.tempId ? serverMsg : m))), // swap tmp→real id
  });
}

Senior nuance: idempotency key is generated once per logical action, not per retry — store it with the optimistic record so a reconnect-replay reuses it. The server keys a dedupe table on it (TTL ~24h) and returns the original result on replay. This is what prevents the classic double-charge / double-post.

2.3 Virtualization

  • Stable item height (measure once / dynamic).
  • Overscan a few rows for smooth scroll.
  • Anchor scroll position on prepend (chat).
  • Restore scroll on back navigation.
// Windowing math + dynamic measurement (TanStack Virtual v3 shape).
function VirtualList({ items }: { items: Row[] }) {
  const parentRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const v = useVirtualizer({
    count: items.length,
    getScrollElement: () => parentRef.current,
    estimateSize: () => 72,        // first-paint guess; real size measured on mount
    overscan: 6,                   // rows rendered beyond viewport each side
    measureElement: (el) => el.getBoundingClientRect().height, // dynamic heights
  });
  return (
    <div ref={parentRef} style={{ height: "100%", overflow: "auto" }}>
      <div style={{ height: v.getTotalSize(), position: "relative" }}>
        {v.getVirtualItems().map((vi) => (
          <div
            key={items[vi.index].id}
            ref={v.measureElement}
            data-index={vi.index}
            style={{ position: "absolute", top: 0, transform: `translateY(${vi.start}px)` }}
          >
            <RowView row={items[vi.index]} />
          </div>
        ))}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

The math to say out loud: visible rows = ceil(viewportHeight / rowHeight). For an 800 px viewport / 72 px rows ≈ 12 visible + 12 overscan = ~24 DOM nodes regardless of a 100K-item list. DOM stays O(viewport), memory stays flat.

Three hard cases interviewers probe:

1. Dynamic heights — estimate, then re-measure on mount; the virtualizer patches getTotalSize() and corrects scroll offset. Cache measured heights by item id so re-renders don't re-thrash.

2. Reverse/chat virtualization (prepend) — when older messages load at the top, the scroll *anchor* must stay on the user's current message. Capture scrollHeight before insert, restore scrollTop += newScrollHeight - oldScrollHeight in a layout effect. Otherwise the viewport jumps.

3. Scroll restoration on back-nav — persist scrollOffset + the top-anchored item id to history state / sessionStorage; on remount, scroll to that item id (offset alone breaks if heights changed).

Alternative for grids: content-visibility: auto + contain-intrinsic-size is a zero-JS win for *uniform offscreen* content (Drive grid, image walls), but it doesn't give you windowed DOM — use it to skip layout/paint, not to bound node count.

2.4 Offline-first toolkit

  • Service Worker: precache shell, runtime cache by route.
  • IndexedDB: user mutations + cached responses.
  • Background Sync API: flush on reconnect.
  • Conflict resolution: LWW, manual merge, CRDT — choose explicitly.
// SW: app-shell precache + per-route runtime strategy.
const SHELL = ["/", "/app.js", "/app.css"];
self.addEventListener("install", (e: any) =>
  e.waitUntil(caches.open("shell-v3").then((c) => c.addAll(SHELL))));

self.addEventListener("fetch", (e: any) => {
  const url = new URL(e.request.url);
  if (url.pathname.startsWith("/api/")) {
    e.respondWith(staleWhileRevalidate(e.request)); // data: SWR
  } else if (SHELL.includes(url.pathname)) {
    e.respondWith(caches.match(e.request));          // shell: cache-first
  } // tiles/images: cache-first w/ LRU eviction
});

// Outbox pattern: queue mutations, flush via Background Sync.
async function enqueueMutation(m: Mutation) {
  const db = await openDB("outbox");
  await db.add("pending", m);                         // durable across tab close
  const reg = await navigator.serviceWorker.ready;
  await reg.sync.register("flush-outbox");            // fires on reconnect
}

Conflict strategy — choose explicitly and justify:

StrategyWhenCost
Last-Write-Wins (LWW)metadata, settings, tree-position opssilent data loss on concurrent edits
Manual mergehigh-value docs, financeUX complexity, needs a merge UI
CRDT (Yjs/Automerge/Loro)text, collaborative treeslarger payload, harder cursor/format anchoring

Decision rule for the room: *text content → CRDT; structural ops (move block, reorder) → LWW with a tombstone + cycle check.* This is exactly how Notion-style editors split it (§Case 4).

2.5 Accessibility checklist

  • Keyboard-only flow walkthrough.
  • Color contrast 4.5:1 (3:1 large text).
  • Focus visible + focus ring tested against WCAG 2.2.
  • aria-live for dynamic updates; do not over-announce.
  • Respect prefers-reduced-motion.

WCAG 2.2 (the senior deltas vs 2.1): 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (sticky headers must not hide the focused element), 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (every drag interaction — Calendar drag-create, Notion reorder, Maps pan — needs a non-drag keyboard/click alternative), 2.5.8 Target Size 24×24 CSS px minimum. Drop these into Calendar/Notion/Maps cases for instant senior signal.

aria-live discipline: polite for result counts and "saved" toasts; assertive only for errors that block the user. Debounce announcements — an autocomplete that fires aria-live on every keystroke is *worse* than silence (screen-reader chatter). Announce the settled count once.

2.6 Senior pitfalls

  • Skipping requirements phase — interviewer wanted you to ask.
  • Designing for 1 user when prompt implies scale — cite numbers.
  • Drawing backend when question is frontend.
  • Not surfacing tradeoffs — name them.
  • Ignoring failure modes, slow networks, low-end devices.

Add to the list, learned from real loops:

  • No measurement story. Stating a budget without *how you'd verify it* (RUM via web-vitals + PerformanceObserver, Lighthouse CI gate in PR, long-task observer) reads junior. Always pair a number with its monitor.
  • Single-region thinking. "WebSocket gateway" with no answer for the user in Sydney hitting a US room. Have a one-liner: regional gateways + global pub/sub bus, or edge-terminated WS.
  • Ignoring the bundle. Drawing a beautiful component tree then shipping 800 KB of JS. Name code-splitting boundaries (route-level + heavy-widget lazy) and a budget.
  • Over-announcing / focus traps in a11y. Saying "I'll add aria-live everywhere" — that's a red flag, not a green one.
  • Hand-waving the failure mode. "On error we revert" — *how*? Show the rollback context (§2.2). Reconnect, partition, slow-3G, and 1% device class need concrete answers.

Case 1 — Collaborative editor (Google Docs / Figma / Notion)

Requirements

  • Multi-user editing with sub-200 ms perceived latency.
  • Cursor presence, comments, history, offline reconciliation.
  • Scale: tens of thousands of concurrent docs, p99 sync < 200 ms in-region.

Pin scope first: *text doc (Docs) vs spatial canvas (Figma) vs block tree (Notion)* — they share a sync core but diverge on data model and rendering. Default to a text/rich-text doc unless told otherwise, and call out the Figma/canvas variant as a deep-dive. Non-functionals to quantify: ≤200 ms remote-op latency in-region, local keystroke ≤16 ms, support ~50 concurrent editors + 10K passive viewers per doc, offline edit then reconcile.

Architecture

 ┌────────┐   WS    ┌──────────────────┐
 │ Client │◀───────▶│  Sync Gateway    │  sharded by docId (consistent hash)
 │ editor │         │  ┌────────────┐  │
 └───┬────┘         │  │ Doc Actor  │  │  single-writer: assigns seq, merges
     │ local model  │  │ (in-mem)   │  │
     │ (Yjs/OT)     │  └─────┬──────┘  │
     ▼              └────────┼─────────┘
 IndexedDB (offline)         │ WAL append + periodic snapshot
                       ┌─────▼──────┐   ┌───────────┐
                       │ Ops log /  │   │ Object     │ snapshots (S3)
                       │ Kafka WAL  │   │ store      │
                       └────────────┘   └───────────┘
   Presence/cursors ── Redis pub/sub (ephemeral, not persisted)
  • Client editor (React + content-editable / canvas) with local model.
  • WebSocket gateway sharded by doc ID; doc-actor in memory per shard.
  • Actor receives ops, transforms/merges, broadcasts to room, periodic snapshots.
  • Object storage for snapshots + WAL for ops log.
  • Presence via Redis pubsub or co-located in actor.

Recovery = latest snapshot + replay WAL ops with seq > snapshot.seq. Snapshot cadence: every N ops (e.g. 500) or T seconds so replay stays bounded.

OT vs CRDT

ApproachProsConsUsed by
OTCompact ops; matureCentral server required; complex for rich structureGoogle Docs, Figma
CRDT (Yjs / Automerge / Loro)P2P-capable, offline-friendlyLarger payloads, tricky cursor formattingNotion (partial), Linear sync
const ydoc = new Y.Doc();
const ytext = ydoc.getText("content");
const provider = new WebsocketProvider("wss://sync/", docId, ydoc);
provider.awareness.setLocalStateField("user", { id, name, color });

The decision, framed for the room: OT needs a central transform server (you always have one here, so that's not a real cost) and is *compact* — an insert is {pos, char}. CRDTs attach a unique, ordered id to every character (e.g. Yjs's YATA), so they merge commutatively without a server and shine offline, but the per-char metadata makes payloads/state larger. 2026 reality: Yjs/Loro have closed most of the size gap (Loro especially with columnar encoding), so the modern default for a *new* collab editor is a CRDT (offline-first for free, simpler reconnection) unless you need OT's tight server-authoritative ordering (e.g. spreadsheet formula recalc, or Figma's binary scene graph). Say: *"CRDT for text, server-authoritative seq for structure — and I'll persist a WAL either way for history/audit."*

Op & message shapes:

// CRDT update (opaque binary on the wire, base64 here for REST fallback)
interface SyncUpdate { type: "update"; docId: string; update: Uint8Array; origin: ConnId; }
// Awareness / presence — ephemeral, debounced ~50ms, never persisted
interface AwarenessMsg {
  type: "awareness";
  clientId: number;
  cursor: { anchor: RelativePosition; head: RelativePosition }; // CRDT relative pos survives concurrent edits
  user: { id: string; name: string; color: string };
}
interface Resume { type: "resume"; docId: string; stateVector: Uint8Array; } // server diffs and replies with missing updates

Cursors use relative positions (anchored to a CRDT id), not absolute offsets — so a remote insert above your selection doesn't visually shift your cursor onto the wrong character.

Rendering / state

  • Initial paint = SSR with latest snapshot.
  • On local op: apply locally first, send to server.
  • Selection rendering as overlays; protect IME composition.

State split: content lives in the CRDT (single source of truth); ephemeral UI (local selection, hover, presence colors) lives in a lightweight store (Zustand/Valtio). Never put per-keystroke content in React state — bind the CRDT to the DOM via a binding layer (y-prosemirror, y-codemirror) and let React render chrome only. Selection/cursors are absolutely-positioned overlays computed from getClientRects(), redrawn on a rAF after DOM settles. IME composition guard: suppress applying remote ops to the active composition range (compositionstart→compositionend) or you corrupt CJK input.

Performance budget

  • Local key → char: < 16 ms.
  • Remote op → on-screen: < 100 ms in-region.
  • Snapshot recovery: < 2 s for 50K op doc.

Add: initial doc load (snapshot fetch + hydrate + first paint) < 1.5 s for a 50-page doc; CRDT memory < 50 MB for a large doc (compact with Y.encodeStateAsUpdate + garbage-collect tombstones); awareness updates throttled to ≤20/s/client to keep a 50-cursor doc under one frame of overlay work.

Edge cases / follow-ups

  • Network partition: buffer local ops, resync diff on reconnect.
  • Conflicting comments on deleted text: anchor by op ID, fallback to nearest neighbor.
  • Cursor positions on remote text inserts.
  • Scale presence to 10K viewers (Redis pub/sub fan-out).
  • How Figma achieves binary-format speed (Wasm, canvas, layer caching).

Q: How do comments survive when the text they anchor to is deleted?

A: Anchor comments to a CRDT *relative position range*, not character offsets. When the underlying text is deleted, the range collapses; we keep the comment but mark it "orphaned" and re-anchor to the nearest surviving sibling position, surfacing it in a margin "resolved/orphaned" tray rather than dropping it.

Q: 10K passive viewers on one doc — how do you not melt the gateway?

A: Viewers don't need per-keystroke ops. Promote them to a snapshot-stream tier: the actor coalesces ops into ~250 ms diffs and fans them out through a relay tree (regional SSE), while only the ≤50 active *editors* hold full-duplex WS. Presence for viewers is aggregated ("+9,950 viewing") not individual cursors.

Q: Figma renders 100K-node files at 60 fps in a browser — how?

A: The scene graph is a Wasm (C++) module with the document in linear memory, rendered to a single <canvas> via WebGL (tiled, with layer/texture caching so only dirty tiles repaint). React only renders the chrome (panels). Multiplayer uses a custom OT-like sync over the binary format, not DOM. The lesson for the room: *for spatial/high-node-count canvases, leave the DOM — use canvas/WebGL/Wasm and treat React as chrome only.*

Q: Offline for an hour, then reconnect — what reconciles?

A: Local edits accumulate in the CRDT in IndexedDB. On reconnect the client sends its state vector; the server replies with exactly the missing updates (and vice versa). CRDT merge is commutative + idempotent, so order doesn't matter and no manual conflict UI is needed for text. Structural ops use LWW with tombstones.

Case 2 — Twitter/X home timeline

Requirements

  • Infinite-scroll feed, mixed media, pull-to-refresh, live "X new posts" pill.
  • 300M MAU; p95 feed latency < 200 ms; 99.99% availability.

Architecture

  • Edge CDN + BFF (timeline service) → returns pre-ranked feed batches.
  • Fan-out hybrid: push for normal users, pull for celebrities.
  • Media CDN with HLS adaptive bitrate.
  • SSE / WebSocket for live notifications.

Fan-out trade-off (the classic): *fan-out-on-write* (push to each follower's materialized timeline) gives O(1) read but explodes for a 100M-follower account (one tweet = 100M writes). *Fan-out-on-read* (pull + merge at read time) is cheap to write but slow to read. Hybrid: push for normal accounts; for celebrities, *don't* fan out — merge their recent posts into followers' timelines at read time. From the FE seat this matters because the BFF response is *already ranked and merged* — the client just renders cursors; we don't re-rank on device. We *do* need to dedupe posts that arrive both via the materialized feed and the live SSE stream (key by post id in a Set).

interface FeedResponse {
  items: FeedItem[];
  cursor: string | null;          // opaque, points after last item
  variantId: string;              // ranking A/B bucket, echoed in analytics
}
type FeedItem =
  | { kind: "post"; post: Post; injectedReason?: "follow" | "recommended" }
  | { kind: "ad"; ad: Ad }
  | { kind: "whoToFollow"; users: User[] };
interface Post {
  id: string; author: UserRef; text: string;
  media?: Media[]; counts: { likes: number; reposts: number; replies: number };
  viewerState: { liked: boolean; reposted: boolean }; createdAt: string;
}
// Live pill: SSE pushes only ids + count, not full posts (cheap, dedupe on prepend)
interface LiveEvent { type: "newPosts"; ids: string[]; count: number }

Rendering / virtualization

  • Server-render first ~5 posts (LCP), then infinite fetch.
  • Virtualized list (react-window / TanStack Virtual) with dynamic height.
  • IntersectionObserver triggers next page ~800 px before bottom.
  • Video: autoplay only when fully in viewport AND not data-saver.

Dynamic height is the crux: posts vary wildly (text vs 4-image grid vs quote-tweet). Reserve space with aspect-ratio on media boxes *before* load (kills CLS), estimate row height, re-measure on mount. The sentinel for next-page is an IntersectionObserver 800 px below the fold so the fetch completes before the user reaches it — perceived-infinite. Respect navigator.connection.saveData and prefers-reduced-data for autoplay/preload.

State

  • TanStack Query infinite query keyed by [feed, cursor].
  • Per-post action state normalized; optimistic.
  • Live pill via SSE; click to prepend.

Normalize posts into a by-id cache so a like in the timeline and the same post in a thread stay consistent (one update, both views reflect it). The infinite query holds *pages of ids*; post bodies live in the normalized cache. Optimistic like flips viewerState.liked + bumps count immediately, reconciles on next fetch.

Budget + edge

  • LCP < 1.8 s cold; INP < 200 ms on like/retweet; total feed JS < 200 KB gz.
  • Scroll restoration on back-nav.
  • aspect-ratio reserved to prevent CLS.
  • Stale optimistic likes reconcile on next fetch.

Verify with field RUM (web-vitals → analytics), not just lab Lighthouse. Bundle gate in CI fails the PR if feed-route JS exceeds 200 KB gz. Scroll restoration persists the top-visible post id + offset to history state.

Follow-ups

  • A/B test ranking via feed-variant ID.
  • Deduplicate posts between fan-out + live-stream feeds.

Q: User scrolls 5,000 posts in one session — memory?

A: Windowed list keeps DOM at O(viewport). But the *data* cache grows unbounded — so cap the in-memory page list (e.g. keep last ~300 items hydrated, evict far-offscreen pages, re-fetch by cursor if they scroll back up). Detach <video>/heavy media for offscreen rows.

Q: How do you keep optimistic likes consistent across the timeline, the post detail, and the profile?

A: Single normalized post-by-id cache; all three views select the same entity. The mutation patches the entity once; React re-renders every subscriber. No per-view duplication, no drift.

Q: Live pill says "12 new posts" — what actually arrives over the wire?

A: Only ids + a count via SSE (bytes, not bodies). On click we prepend, fetch the bodies for those ids if not cached, dedupe against what's already rendered, and anchor scroll so the user's current post doesn't jump.

Q: 99.99% availability — what's the FE failure story?

A: BFF timeout → serve last-cached feed from IndexedDB/HTTP cache with a stale banner; SSE drop → exponential-backoff reconnect with Last-Event-ID to resume; image CDN miss → blurhash placeholder. Never a blank screen.

Case 3 — Netflix-like video streaming UI

Requirements

  • Browse rows, hover trailers, full playback, resume across devices.
  • Massive image asset library, every device class, 190 countries.

Scope/scale to quantify: ~260M subscribers, TV + web + mobile, 190 countries (so i18n + RTL + huge image variant matrix), strict DRM, resume-anywhere via server watch-state. The hard FE problems: memory on long-lived TV sessions, image variant explosion, and adaptive playback without rebuffer.

Architecture

  • Edge-cached SSR shell; row data from recommender BFF.
  • Image CDN with on-the-fly transforms (AVIF / WebP, DPI srcset).
  • HLS adaptive bitrate; trailer as low-bitrate WebM.
  • Watchstate via heartbeat.
interface RowResponse { rowId: string; title: string; titles: TitleCard[]; cursor: string | null; }
interface TitleCard {
  id: string; boxArt: ImageSet;        // multiple aspect ratios + focal point
  trailerId?: string; runtimeMin: number;
  maturity: string; badges: ("new" | "top10" | "leaving")[];
}
interface ImageSet { base: string; widths: number[]; formats: ("avif" | "webp" | "jpg")[]; }
// Resume state synced via heartbeat every ~10s of playback
interface Heartbeat { titleId: string; positionMs: number; durationMs: number; deviceId: string; ts: number; }

Rendering

  • Above-fold row server-rendered with skeleton.
  • Lazy-load below-fold; prefetch row ahead.
  • Hover trailer: 600 ms delay → fetch URL → mount video; cancel on mouseleave.

Each row is a horizontally-virtualized carousel (only render cards near the viewport horizontally); the page vertically lazy-loads rows via IntersectionObserver and *prefetches the next row's data + first card's image* one row ahead. Box art uses <img srcset> with AVIF→WebP→JPG fallback and DPR-aware widths; the CDN does on-the-fly transforms keyed by ?w=&f=&fp= (focal point so cropping never beheads the actor). Hover-trailer is debounced 600 ms (intent), then mounts a muted low-bitrate video, canceled on mouseleave with an AbortController.

Budget / a11y / edge

  • TTI < 3 s on 3G; trailer first frame < 400 ms; memory < 200 MB on TV after 30 min.
  • Captions WebVTT + language picker; aria-live for "now playing".
  • Keyboard nav for row carousel with roving tabindex.
  • Network dip → lower bitrate; never blank for 30 s.
  • DRM (Widevine / FairPlay / PlayReady) via Shaka / hls.js.

Roving tabindex: only one card per row is in the tab order; arrow keys move focus within the row, up/down between rows — exactly the TV remote model. This is the WCAG 2.2 keyboard story for carousels.

Follow-ups

  • Re-rank rows after user preferences.
  • Offline downloads in PWA (SW + IDB).

Q: TV app runs for 6 hours — how do you stay under 200 MB?

A: Aggressively unmount offscreen rows (not just hide), cap the box-art image cache with LRU eviction, reuse a *single* trailer <video> element across cards instead of mounting one per card, and detach the MSE source buffer when leaving playback. Watch for detached-DOM leaks with periodic heap snapshots in soak tests.

Q: ABR — how does the player decide bitrate, and what's the FE's role?

A: hls.js/Shaka runs the ABR algorithm (estimates throughput + buffer health, picks the next segment's variant). FE responsibilities: surface a manual quality override, react to saveData/cellular by capping the ladder, prewarm the manifest on hover, and keep a target buffer (~10–30 s) so a network dip downshifts instead of rebuffering. Target rebuffer ratio < 0.5%.

Q: 190 countries — image and text concerns?

A: One source asset → many CDN-derived variants (locale-specific title art exists too, keyed in ImageSet). Text: full i18n with ICU plurals, RTL mirroring for Arabic/Hebrew (logical CSS properties, not left/right), and per-locale font subsetting to keep payload down.

Q: Offline downloads in a PWA?

A: Store encrypted segments + license in IndexedDB, manifest in Cache Storage; play back via MSE from IDB. DRM persistent licenses (Widevine) with expiry; SW intercepts segment requests and serves from IDB when offline. Enforce per-title storage quota and navigator.storage.estimate() checks.

Case 4 — Notion blocks editor

Requirements + Architecture

  • Block tree (text, headings, lists, toggles, embeds, databases).
  • DnD reorder, slash-command insert, nested blocks, references.
  • Real-time collab + offline + paste/import.
  • Each block = row with parent/order; doc = derived tree.
  • Per-workspace ops log; CRDT inside text; LWW for tree ops.
  • SW caches recent docs; IDB holds pending ops.

**Data model (the senior point): the doc is a *flat list of blocks*, not a nested document.** Each block is a row with parentId + a fractional-index order key. The tree is *derived* by grouping on parentId and sorting by order. This is why Notion can lazy-load, virtualize, and re-parent cheaply.

interface Block {
  id: string;
  parentId: string;        // page or another block
  order: string;           // fractional index (e.g. "a0", "a0V") — insert between without renumbering
  type: "text" | "h1" | "bulleted" | "toggle" | "embed" | "database_view";
  content: Y.XmlText;      // CRDT for rich text inside the block
  props: Record<string, unknown>;  // type-specific (e.g. checked, collapsed, dbViewId)
}
// Tree op (structural) — LWW, idempotent, with cycle guard
interface MoveOp { type: "move"; blockId: string; newParentId: string; newOrder: string; opId: string; ts: number; }

Fractional indexing is the key trick: to insert between blocks "a0" and "a1", generate "a0V" — no neighbor renumbering, no broadcast storm, conflict-tolerant under concurrent inserts. (Use a jitter suffix to avoid interleaving collisions when two users insert at the same gap.)

Rendering / state

  • Virtualize > 200 blocks; each block its own component.
  • Drag handles in portal to avoid layout thrash.
  • Local Yjs doc per page; WebSocket broadcast.
  • Block selection + caret in Zustand; content in CRDT.

Two-tier state again: content per block in a CRDT, selection/caret/drag/hover in Zustand (transient, never synced). Virtualize the flat block list (dynamic heights — a toggle can be 1 line or 500). The drag *ghost* renders in a portal at the body root so dragging doesn't trigger layout in the (virtualized) list. Slash-command opens a popover listbox (same a11y combobox pattern as Case 10).

Edge / follow-ups

  • Drag across nested levels — re-parent with cycle check.
  • Paste from Word / Markdown → sanitize HTML, convert to block tree on worker.
  • Embedded database views with own queries; schedule independently.
  • References survive renaming / moves.
  • Slash-command + mouseless flow.

Q: User drags a parent block into its own child — what happens?

A: A move op runs a cycle check: walk up the newParentId ancestry; if blockId appears, reject the drop (visual "can't drop here" cue). Without this you create a detached cycle that breaks tree derivation. The check is O(depth), trivial.

Q: Paste 50 pages from Google Docs — how do you not freeze the tab?

A: Parse + sanitize the HTML and convert to the block tree in a Web Worker (DOMPurify + a mapping pass), streaming blocks back in chunks so the main thread inserts incrementally. Never parse a megabyte of HTML on the main thread — it'll blow the INP budget badly.

Q: A block references another page by id; the target gets renamed/moved — does the link break?

A: No — references store the stable block/page id, never the title or path. The displayed title is resolved at render from the current entity, so renames update everywhere and moves don't orphan the link. Deletion → tombstone, link renders as "deleted" rather than 404.

Q: An embedded database view inside a doc — how does it not stall page load?

A: Each database_view block owns its query and a *separate* TanStack Query/cache entry, fetched lazily when it scrolls into view (it's in the virtualized list). The page renders with a skeleton for the view; the doc's CRDT load doesn't wait on it. They invalidate independently.

Case 5 — Google Drive file browser

Requirements + Architecture

  • Folder tree, list/grid, search, resumable upload, preview, share.
  • Millions of files per user; deep nested folders.
  • Folder list paginated by cursor; search via Algolia/Elastic.
  • Upload via tus.io or resumable PUT (Range, chunked).
  • Server thumbnail service → CDN → in-line viewer (PDF/Office).
interface DirPage { entries: Entry[]; cursor: string | null; }
interface Entry {
  id: string; name: string; kind: "folder" | "file";
  mime?: string; size?: number; modifiedAt: string;
  thumb?: string; sharedWithMe: boolean; permission: "view" | "comment" | "edit" | "owner";
}
// Resumable upload (tus): client persists state so a tab close resumes
interface UploadState {
  fileId: string; uploadUrl: string;        // tus location
  offset: number; total: number; chunkSize: number;  // resume from offset
  fileKey: string;                          // local IDB handle for the blob
}

Rendering / budget

  • Tree virtualizes per branch; folders fetch children lazily.
  • Grid with content-visibility: auto for offscreen.
  • 5K-item folder under 1 s to first row paint.
  • Search results stream; first result < 300 ms.

The tree is a virtualized *flattened* view of expanded nodes (expansion lazily fetches children by cursor). The grid uses content-visibility: auto + contain-intrinsic-size so offscreen thumbnails skip layout/paint with zero JS — perfect because grid cells are uniform. Thumbnails lazy-load with loading="lazy" + IntersectionObserver priority for the visible band.

Edge / follow-ups

  • Resumable upload across tab close — persist state to IDB.
  • Stale share permissions — re-check on every preview; banner if lost.
  • Very deep folders — limit breadcrumb to N with "…" expansion.
  • Sync tree across tabs (BroadcastChannel).
  • 100K-file folder without freezing the browser.

Q: 100K files in one folder — how does the UI not die?

A: Server paginates by cursor; client *virtualizes* (never hold 100K DOM nodes). Fetch ahead one page via an IntersectionObserver sentinel. Sorting/filtering happens server-side (can't sort 100K client-side responsively) — the cursor encodes the sort key. Selection state is a Set<id>, not per-row booleans, so "select all" is O(1) conceptually with a "select-all-matching" server flag.

Q: Upload 4 GB, user closes the tab at 60% — resume?

A: tus resumable protocol: chunked PUT with a server-tracked offset. We persist UploadState (upload URL + offset + a File System Access handle or IDB blob ref) to IndexedDB. On relaunch, HEAD the upload URL to get the server offset and resume from there. Parallelize a few chunks, checksum each, retry failed chunks with backoff.

Q: A file was shared with the user, then un-shared while they had it open — what do they see?

A: Permissions are re-checked on every privileged action (open preview, download). If revoked, the preview request 403s → show a "you no longer have access" banner and evict the cached entry. We don't trust the cached permission field for authorization — it's a UI hint only; the server is authoritative.

Q: Two tabs open, user creates a folder in one — does the other update?

A: BroadcastChannel posts a lightweight invalidation {type:"dirChanged", parentId}; the other tab invalidates that query key and refetches the affected page (not the whole tree). Avoids polling and keeps tabs consistent.

Case 6 — Slack-like chat

Requirements + Architecture

  • Channels, DMs, threads, reactions, typing indicators, search, file uploads, unfurled links.
  • 1M concurrent WebSocket connections per region.
  • WebSocket gateway with channel fan-out; channel state cached client-side.
  • Threads as parent message + child sub-channel.
interface Message {
  id: string; channelId: string; authorId: string;
  text: string; ts: string;            // server timestamp = ordering key
  clientMsgId: string;                 // optimistic dedupe key
  threadId?: string; replyCount?: number;
  reactions: { emoji: string; count: number; me: boolean }[];
  attachments?: Attachment[];
}
// WS frames (Slack-style typed envelope)
type WsFrame =
  | { type: "message"; msg: Message }
  | { type: "typing"; channelId: string; userId: string }   // ephemeral, ~3s TTL
  | { type: "reaction"; messageId: string; emoji: string; userId: string; op: "add" | "remove" }
  | { type: "presence"; userId: string; status: "active" | "away" }
  | { type: "ack"; clientMsgId: string; serverId: string };  // optimistic reconcile

Rendering / state / budget

  • Reverse-chronological list with reverse virtualization.
  • Day separators + sticky channel header.
  • Inline media with reserved aspect-ratio.
  • Normalized message store; channel cursor in URL.
  • Optimistic send (tmp ID → server ID).
  • Typing indicators in-memory (Redis pubsub).
  • Send → echo < 200 ms; switch channel < 100 ms (hover prefetch); shell < 2 s.

Reverse virtualization is the hard part: newest at bottom, scrolling *up* loads older (prepend), which must anchor scroll (§2.3 case 2). Day separators are derived, not stored. Normalized message store keyed by id; the channel view holds an ordered id list. Switching channels feels instant because hovering a channel in the sidebar prefetches its last page.

Edge / follow-ups

  • Out-of-order delivery: order by server timestamp; fetch missed window.
  • Massive scroll-back: anchor to msg ID, fetch around, virtualize.
  • Background tab disconnect → polling → reconnect on focus.
  • Read receipts + unread counts efficiently.
  • Real-time search-as-you-type without thundering.

Q: Messages can arrive out of order over WS — how do you render correctly?

A: WS delivery isn't a total order across reconnects. Order by server ts (or a per-channel server seq), not arrival. On reconnect, send last-seen seq/ts; server replays the gap. If a message arrives with a seq that skips ahead, we know there's a hole and fetch the missing window before rendering past it — otherwise the user sees a gap that silently fills wrong.

Q: 1M connections per region — how does the client side stay cheap?

A: One WS per *tab*, multiplexing all channels (don't open a socket per channel). A SharedWorker can hold a single socket shared across tabs of the same workspace. Background tabs downgrade: on visibilitychange hidden, close the WS and fall back to periodic catch-up fetch; reconnect + replay on focus. Server uses sticky-session LB + channel pub/sub fan-out.

Q: Unread counts and read receipts for a user in 500 channels — efficiently?

A: Don't track per-message read state client-side. Server stores a per-(user,channel) lastReadTs; unread = messages with ts > lastReadTs, and the badge count comes from the server (or is derived cheaply from the channel's latest seq minus lastRead seq). Mark-as-read is debounced and sent as a single lastReadTs update when the bottom is visible, not per message.

Q: Search-as-you-type across a huge workspace without hammering the backend?

A: Debounce (~150 ms) + cancel in-flight (AbortController), require a min query length, SWR-cache by query, and stream results. Recent/local matches show instantly from an IDB cache while the server query is in flight, then merge. Same combobox a11y as Case 10.

Case 7 — Stripe-style checkout

Requirements + Architecture

  • Card collection, 3DS, Apple Pay / Google Pay / Klarna, saved cards, multi-step.
  • PCI: never let card data hit your server.
  • Iframe-isolated card fields on Stripe domain; postMessage to/from parent.
  • Server creates PaymentIntent; client confirms; 3DS popup if required.

The whole architecture exists to keep card data out of PCI scope. Card inputs are cross-origin iframes served from Stripe's domain (Stripe Elements) — your JS *never* touches the PAN, so you stay in the lowest PCI tier (SAQ A). The parent page communicates with the iframes only via postMessage (validation state, focus, errors), never raw values.

 Your page (your origin)            Stripe origin (iframe)
 ┌───────────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────┐
 │ checkout shell (SSR)   │◀──msg──▶│ card number field    │  PAN never leaves here
 │ pay button, summary    │         │ expiry / cvc fields  │
 └─────────┬─────────────┘         └──────────────────────┘
           │ 1. POST /create-intent (amount, currency, idempotencyKey)
           ▼
   Your server ──▶ Stripe API: PaymentIntent → returns client_secret
           │ 2. stripe.confirmPayment(client_secret)  (tokenization in iframe)
           ▼
   3DS challenge? ──▶ modal/redirect ──▶ webhook confirms ──▶ your server fulfills
interface CreateIntentReq { amount: number; currency: string; idempotencyKey: string; }
interface CreateIntentRes { clientSecret: string; intentId: string; }
// Field-level errors mapped for aria-describedby
interface FieldError { field: "number" | "expiry" | "cvc" | "postal"; code: string; message: string; }

Rendering / state / a11y / edge

  • SSR shell; payment iframe lazy on intent to checkout.
  • Buttons disabled until iframe ready; shimmer.
  • Apple Pay native-style with canMakePayment feature detect.
  • Wizard state in URL search params (back/forward survives).
  • Errors structured by field for aria-describedby.
  • All fields labeled; aria-live error messages.
  • Keyboard-only flow scripted in CI.
  • 3DS popup blocked → redirect flow fallback.
  • Network failure mid-confirm → idempotency key prevents double-charge.

Wizard state in URL params (?step=shipping) so browser back/forward and refresh survive — critical because users *do* hit back mid-checkout. Apple/Google Pay buttons render only after canMakePayment() feature-detects support (don't show a wallet button that 404s). Pay button is disabled until all iframes report ready and valid.

Follow-ups

  • EU SCA (Strong Customer Authentication).
  • Offline-capable checkout in brick-and-mortar POS.

Q: Network drops right after the user hits Pay — how do you guarantee no double-charge?

A: The idempotencyKey is generated once when the user enters checkout and reused on every retry of /create-intent and confirm. Stripe (and your server) dedupe on it, returning the *original* PaymentIntent rather than creating a second. The client, on reconnect, re-queries the intent status by intentId instead of blindly re-confirming. Also disable the Pay button on first click + show a spinner to prevent double-submit.

Q: 3DS challenge — popup is blocked by the browser. Fallback?

A: Detect the blocked popup (the window.open returns null) and fall back to a full-page redirect 3DS flow (return_url brings them back to a status page that polls the intent). Mobile Safari especially blocks popups, so redirect is the safer default; we feature-detect and prefer the inline iframe challenge when allowed.

Q: How is this accessible for a screen-reader / keyboard-only user?

A: Every Stripe Element is labeled (<label for> paired with the iframe), errors are mapped to aria-describedby per field and announced via a polite aria-live region (not per keystroke — on blur/submit). Focus moves to the first invalid field on submit. The entire flow is scripted keyboard-only in CI (Playwright), since you can't manually QA an iframe-based form every release.

Q: EU SCA — what changes?

A: SCA mandates two-factor (3DS2) for most EU card payments, so the 3DS path is the *norm*, not the exception. We design the confirm step assuming a challenge will happen (no surprise modal jank), support exemptions (low-value, recurring) signaled by the server, and keep the redirect fallback first-class since 3DS2 challenge UIs vary by issuer.

Case 8 — Maps app

Requirements + Architecture

  • Pan/zoom, vector tiles, markers, routes, traffic, search, directions.
  • Smooth on low-end Android; offline PWA mode.
  • Vector tile server (Mapbox GL / MapLibre) → MVT, WebGL render.
  • Geocoding + routing as REST; cached results.
  • Marker layer separate from base (different z + cadences).

The defining constraint: 60 fps pan/zoom on a 2018 mid-range Android. That forces the map render *out of React entirely* — MapLibre GL renders MVT vector tiles to WebGL on its own rAF loop; React owns only the chrome (search box, sidebar, info card). During a pan/zoom gesture, no React state updates — driving React re-renders off pointermove would tank the frame rate.

// Tile request key + viewport
interface TileKey { z: number; x: number; y: number; }   // slippy-map coords
// Routing/geocoding are REST, cached by normalized query
interface RouteReq { from: LngLat; to: LngLat; mode: "drive" | "walk" | "transit"; avoid?: string[]; }
interface RouteRes { geometry: GeoJSON.LineString; durationS: number; distanceM: number; steps: Step[]; }

Rendering / budget

  • Canvas/WebGL main render; React only for chrome (sidebar, search, info card).
  • rAF for pan/zoom; avoid React state during interaction.
  • Markers clustered server-side at low zoom; client-side at high.
  • 60 fps on 2018 mid-range Android.
  • Tile fetch < 300 ms p95; pre-fetch ring outside viewport.

Markers are a separate layer (different z-index and update cadence than the base map) so a traffic-overlay refresh doesn't repaint every pin. Clustering is server-side at low zoom (can't ship 1M points to a phone) and client-side at high zoom where counts are small. Prefetch a ring of tiles just outside the viewport so a pan never shows blank.

Edge / follow-ups

  • Slow tile → last-cached until new arrives; never blank.
  • Routing input swap (A↔B) — recompute optimistic, cancel previous.
  • Geolocation denied → soft-prompt + IP fallback.
  • Cache map tiles offline (SW + stale-while-revalidate by tile URL).
  • Reconcile traffic overlay without re-rendering markers.

Q: Why is React the wrong tool for the map surface, and where does it still belong?

A: React's reconciliation + state batching can't keep up with 60 fps continuous gestures touching thousands of features. The map is imperative WebGL with its own render loop. React stays for *discrete* UI — search results, the directions panel, the selected-place card — where its declarative model is a win and updates are infrequent.

Q: 50,000 markers in the viewport — how do you render them?

A: Never as DOM nodes. Render them as a WebGL symbol layer (GPU-drawn) or cluster them: server-side clustering at low zoom returns ~hundreds of cluster bubbles with counts; expand to individual pins only at high zoom where the count is small. Hit-testing is done against the GL feature buffer, not DOM.

Q: User goes into a tunnel / offline — what still works?

A: SW caches tiles cache-first with stale-while-revalidate keyed by tile URL; recently-viewed areas and the active route's tiles are pre-cached. Offline, we render last-cached tiles (never blank), show an "offline" indicator, and queue geocoding/routing requests if they came online recently. Full offline regions = explicit "download this area" → bulk tile + routing-graph cache in IDB.

Q: User swaps start/end of a route while a request is in flight?

A: Cancel the in-flight request (AbortController), optimistically swap the A/B markers and reverse the displayed line as a placeholder, then render the authoritative geometry when the new route returns. Debounce rapid edits so we don't fire a request per keystroke in the address fields.

Case 9 — Calendar app

Requirements + Architecture

  • Day/week/month, drag-to-create, drag-to-resize, recurring, time-zone aware, invitees, conflicts.
  • Sub-second view switching; offline draft creation.
  • Server returns event windows; recurring expanded server-side or client RRULE.
  • Conflict detection client-side; invitee status via separate channel.
interface CalEvent {
  id: string; title: string;
  startUtc: string; endUtc: string;     // ALWAYS store UTC
  tz: string;                            // originating tz (for "floating" + DST correctness)
  rrule?: string;                        // RFC 5545 recurrence, e.g. "FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=MO,WE"
  exdates?: string[];                    // exceptions (deleted/moved instances)
  attendees: { email: string; status: "accepted" | "declined" | "tentative" | "needsAction" }[];
}
// Query is window-keyed; server returns expanded instances OR rules to expand client-side
interface WindowReq { startUtc: string; endUtc: string; }

Rendering / state / edge

  • Week view = CSS Grid with rows by 15-min slot; events via row-start/span.
  • Drag-create with pointer events; preview follows mouse with rAF.
  • TanStack Query window-keyed (start..end).
  • Optimistic create/move/resize; revert on server reject.
  • Time zone changes (DST) — store UTC, render in user TZ.
  • Overlapping events — auto-shrink to columns with width 1/N.
  • Long event spanning days — horizontal bar.

Week view is a CSS Grid: 96 rows (15-min slots) × 7 day columns; an event is grid-row: start / span duration. Drag-create/resize uses Pointer Events; the preview rectangle follows the cursor via rAF (snap to 15-min). All mutations are optimistic with revert. Overlap layout is the classic algorithm: group events that intersect in time, assign each a column, width = 1 / columns of the group, offset by column index — runs on the visible window only.

Follow-ups

  • Sync two tabs (BroadcastChannel + cache invalidation).
  • 1000-event week without dropping frames.

Q: Daylight Saving Time — how do you not show events an hour off?

A: Store every event in UTC plus its originating IANA tz. Render by converting UTC → the user's current tz with a proper library (Temporal API in 2026, or Luxon). DST is handled by the tz database: a 9 AM weekly recurring meeting stays at 9 AM local across the DST boundary because we expand the RRULE in local time, *then* convert to UTC per instance — not by adding fixed 24h offsets (which would drift an hour).

Q: Recurring events — expand on server or client?

A: Trade-off. Client-side RRULE expansion (e.g. rrule.js) is bandwidth-light (send the rule once) and great offline, but heavy rules over long windows can be CPU-costly. Server-side expansion returns concrete instances (simple client) but is chatty for "next 2 years." Hybrid: server expands the *visible window* it's asked for; client expands locally when scrolling offline. Exceptions (exdates, single-instance edits) are overlaid on top of the expansion.

Q: 1,000 events in one week view without dropping frames?

A: Only compute layout + render for the *visible window* (and only the visible day columns). The overlap algorithm runs on that subset, not the whole calendar. Use transform/translate for drag previews (compositor-only, no layout), keep drag updates on rAF, and avoid re-running overlap layout on every pointermove — recompute on drop.

Q: An invitee accepts while you're looking at the event — how does status update live?

A: Attendee status comes over a separate real-time channel (SSE/WS) keyed by event id, patching just that event's attendees in the normalized cache — no full re-fetch, no re-layout of the grid. Two tabs stay consistent via BroadcastChannel invalidation.

Case 10 — Production-grade autocomplete

Requirements + Architecture

  • As-you-type, keyboard + mouse, async backend, ranking, recents, sectioned results.
  • p99 first suggestion < 150 ms; fully accessible WAI-ARIA Combobox.
  • Edge function returns top-N; cached per query with SWR.
  • Recents in IDB merged with server results.
interface SuggestResponse {
  sections: { title: string; items: Suggestion[] }[];   // "Recent", "People", "Files"
  query: string;                                        // echo to discard stale responses
}
interface Suggestion { id: string; label: string; type: string; score: number; }

Rendering / state

  • Popup listbox in portal anchored to input.
  • Virtualize > 50 results.
  • Show "Searching…" only > 200 ms.
function useAutocomplete(query) {
  const [results, setResults] = useState([]);
  const last = useRef(0);
  const debounced = useDeferredValue(query);
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = ++last.current;
    const ac = new AbortController();
    fetch(`/api/search?q=${debounced}`, { signal: ac.signal })
      .then(r => r.json())
      .then(d => { if (id === last.current) setResults(d.items); });
    return () => ac.abort();
  }, [debounced]);
  return results;
}

The four production concerns this hook gets right: (1) cancel stale requests (AbortController), (2) discard out-of-order responses (id === last.current race guard — even canceled requests can resolve), (3) keep the input responsive (useDeferredValue so typing never blocks on render), (4) debounce/min-length upstream. Add SWR caching by query string so backspacing to a prior query is instant. Show the "Searching…" affordance *only* after 200 ms so fast responses don't flash a spinner.

Accessibility (WAI-ARIA Combobox 1.2)

  • Input role="combobox", aria-expanded, aria-controls, aria-activedescendant.
  • Listbox role="listbox"; items role="option" + aria-selected.
  • Keyboard: ↑↓ navigate, Enter selects, Esc closes, Home/End jump.
  • aria-live region announces result count.
// Combobox wiring — note aria-activedescendant (focus stays in the input).
<input
  role="combobox" aria-expanded={open} aria-controls="ac-list"
  aria-autocomplete="list"
  aria-activedescendant={active ? `opt-${active}` : undefined}
  onKeyDown={onKey} value={query} onChange={onChange}
/>
<ul id="ac-list" role="listbox">
  {items.map((it, i) => (
    <li id={`opt-${it.id}`} key={it.id} role="option"
        aria-selected={i === activeIndex}>{it.label}</li>
  ))}
</ul>
<div aria-live="polite" className="sr-only">{items.length} results</div>

The senior detail: focus never leaves the input — keyboard navigation moves a *virtual* highlight via aria-activedescendant, not real DOM focus. This keeps typing live while arrowing through options. The aria-live count is announced once on settle (debounced), not per keystroke (§2.5).

Follow-ups

  • Re-rank from user clicks over time.
  • Multi-select with chips + search inside selected.
  • IntelliSense-style typeahead in a code editor.

Q: How do you keep a 10K-result dropdown smooth?

A: Don't render 10K options — cap server top-N (~50) and virtualize the listbox; aria-activedescendant works with windowing if you keep the active option mounted (scroll it into view on navigation). Past ~50 the user should refine, not scroll, so we section + cap rather than infinite-scroll a combobox.

Q: Race conditions — explain how a slow earlier request can corrupt results.

A: User types "re" then "react". The "re" request is slower and resolves *after* "react", overwriting the correct results with stale ones. Two defenses: (1) the monotonic id guard drops any response that isn't the latest, (2) AbortController cancels the older fetch. We use both because abort isn't guaranteed to fire before the older promise resolves.

Q: Recents from IDB + live server results — how do you merge without flicker?

A: Show cached recents *immediately* (synchronous from IDB/memory) in a "Recent" section so the dropdown is never empty, then merge server sections in when they arrive, deduping by id and keeping recents pinned to the top section. SWR semantics: stale-then-revalidate, and the layout doesn't jump because sections are stable slots.

Q: This in a code editor (IntelliSense)?

A: Same combobox a11y, but suggestions are computed from a language server (LSP) — debounce on the document position, cancel on cursor move, and rank by scope/relevance. Render in a portal anchored to the caret rect (getBoundingClientRect of the cursor), and the "results" are virtualized since a member list can be large. Latency budget is tighter (feels laggy past ~50 ms) so we cache per-prefix aggressively.

Appendix — Senior interview "how to ship a risky change"

  • Behind a feature flag, default off.
  • Deploy via rolling / canary.
  • Enable for internal → 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% gated on SLO health.
  • Watch latency, errors, business KPIs at each step.
  • Rollback runbook ready — flag off + revert deployment if needed.
  • Postmortem the rollout regardless of outcome.

Frontend-specific rollout notes (the details that earn senior signal):

  • Flag evaluation must be fast and offline-safe. Bootstrap flags in the SSR/HTML payload (no render-blocking client fetch, no flash of the old UI). Cache the last-known flag set so a flag-service outage doesn't break the app.
  • Decouple deploy from release. Ship dark code behind the flag; "release" is flipping the flag, instantly reversible without a redeploy. This is the whole point — a revert that needs a build+deploy is too slow during an incident.
  • Guard the metrics that matter for FE: Core Web Vitals (INP regressions are the silent killer of a "harmless" UI change), JS error rate (Sentry), bundle size delta (CI gate), and the business KPI the change targets. Watch them *per cohort* at each ramp step.
  • Bake time + automatic rollback. Hold each ramp step long enough to see real traffic across device classes and timezones; wire an automated rollback (flag off) if error rate or INP crosses a threshold, rather than relying on a human watching a dashboard at 2 AM.
  • Clean up flags. A stale flag is tech debt and a config-explosion risk; remove it once the change is 100% and stable. Track flag age and fail CI on flags older than N days.

Next: Doc 07 — DSA + Machine Coding.

Pin scope ("read-path only? collab?"). Jumping to boxes before scoping. Architecture 8 min One diagram: client → edge/BFF → services + the real-time path. Name where state lives. Quantify-everything cheat sheet (memorize, drop into Requirements): Core Web Vitals 2026 targets: LCP ≤ 2.5 s , INP ≤ 200 ms , CLS ≤ 0.1 (75th percentile, field). A "fast" interaction budget = one frame = 16.6 ms at 60 Hz, 8.3 ms at 120 Hz (ProMotion/high-refresh phones). 3G Fast ≈ 1.6 Mbps / 150 ms RTT; 4G ≈ 9 Mbps / 60 ms. Low-end Android CPU ≈ 4–6× slower than an M-series laptop — *always* state your reference device. JS parse/compile ≈ 1 ms per KB on low-end mobile → a 200 KB bundle costs ~200 ms of main-thread time before it even runs. Part 2 — Recurring patterns 2.1 Real-time fan-out Per-room actor on a stateful gateway → broadcasts ops to subscribers. Use Redis pubsub or NATS for cross-region; sticky-session on WebSocket gateway. The core problem: N publishers, M subscribers per room, K rooms. A single doc-actor (single-writer) per room linearizes ops so ordering is trivial; the gateway is horizontally sharded by roomId (consistent hashing) so a room always lands on one node. Cross-node delivery (a subscriber connected to a *different* gateway than the room owner) goes through a pub/sub bus. Transport decision matrix: Transport Direction Use when Cost WebSocket duplex collab edits, chat, presence stateful conn, sticky LB, scaling = conn count SSE server→client feeds, notifications, live counters cheap, auto-reconnect, HTTP/2 multiplexed, no upstream WebTransport (HTTP/3) duplex, unreliable+reliable 2026 low-latency cursors/datagrams newer, fallback to WS needed Long-poll server→client legacy/firewalled fallback high overhead, last resort Rule: SSE for one-way, WS for two-way. Don't reach for WS to push a notification badge. // Gateway shard: one actor per room, single-writer ordering. interface RoomActor { seq: number; // monotonic op sequence subscribers: Map<ConnId, Socket>; apply(op: Op): { seq: number }; // assigns seq, persists to WAL broadcast(op: SeqOp): void; // to local subs + pub/sub for remote } // Client reconnect: send last-seen seq, server replays the gap. type Resume = { roomId: string; lastSeq: number }; Backpressure & fan-out math: a celebrity room with 50K viewers receiving 10 ops/s = 500K msg/s out of one node — don't. Tier it: hot rooms get a fan-out tree (gateway → regional relays → clients) or collapse to interval snapshots (coalesce ops into a 100–250 ms diff) instead of per-keystroke broadcast. Always cap per-connection send-queue depth and drop-to-snapshot on slow consumers. 2.2 Optimistic mutation Temp ID client-side → apply locally → send to server → reconcile with server ID → revert on error. Idempotency: client-generated request key. // Optimistic mutation with rollback + idempotency (TanStack Query v5). function useSendMessage(channelId: string) { const qc = useQueryClient(); return useMutation({ mutationFn: (text: string) => api.post(`/channels/${channelId}/messages`, { text, idempotencyKey: crypto.randomUUID(), // dedupe retries server-side }), onMutate: async (text) => { await qc.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ["messages", channelId] }); const prev = qc.getQueryData(["messages", channelId]); const tempId = `tmp_${crypto.randomUUID()}`; qc.setQueryData(["messages", channelId], (old: Msg[] = []) => [ ...old, { id: tempId, text, status: "sending", createdAt: Date.now() }, ]); return { prev, tempId }; // context for rollback / reconcile }, onError: (_e, _v, ctx) => qc.setQueryData(["messages", channelId], ctx!.prev), // revert onSuccess: (serverMsg, _v, ctx) => qc.setQueryData(["messages", channelId], (old: Msg[] = []) => old.map((m) => (m.id === ctx!.tempId ? serverMsg : m))), // swap tmp→real id }); } Senior nuance: idempotency key is generated once per logical action, not per retry — store it with the optimistic record so a reconnect-replay reuses it. The server keys a dedupe table on it (TTL ~24h) and returns the original result on replay. This is what prevents the classic double-charge / double-post. 2.3 Virtualization Stable item height (measure once / dynamic). Overscan a few rows for smooth scroll. Anchor scroll position on prepend (chat). Restore scroll on back navigation. // Windowing math + dynamic measurement (TanStack Virtual v3 shape). function VirtualList({ items }: { items: Row[] }) { const parentRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null); const v = useVirtualizer({ count: items.length, getScrollElement: () => parentRef.current, estimateSize: () => 72, // first-paint guess; real size measured on mount overscan: 6, // rows rendered beyond viewport each side measureElement: (el) => el.getBoundingClientRect().height, // dynamic heights }); return ( <div ref={parentRef} style={{ height: "100%", overflow: "auto" }}> <div style={{ height: v.getTotalSize(), position: "relative" }}> {v.getVirtualItems().map((vi) => ( <div key={items[vi.index].id} ref={v.measureElement} data-index={vi.index} style={{ position: "absolute", top: 0, transform: `translateY(${vi.start}px)` }} > <RowView row={items[vi.index]} /> </div> ))} </div> </div> ); } The math to say out loud: visible rows = ceil(viewportHeight / rowHeight) . For an 800 px viewport / 72 px rows ≈ 12 visible + 12 overscan = ~24 DOM nodes regardless of a 100K-item list. DOM stays O(viewport), memory stays flat. Three hard cases interviewers probe: 1. Dynamic heights — estimate, then re-measure on mount; the virtualizer patches getTotalSize() and corrects scroll offset. Cache measured heights by item id so re-renders don't re-thrash. 2. Reverse/chat virtualization (prepend) — when older messages load at the top, the scroll *anchor* must stay on the user's current message. Capture scrollHeight before insert, restore scrollTop += newScrollHeight - oldScrollHeight in a layout effect. Otherwise the viewport jumps. 3. Scroll restoration on back-nav — persist scrollOffset + the top-anchored item id to history state / sessionStorage; on remount, scroll to that item id (offset alone breaks if heights changed). Alternative for grids: content-visibility: auto + contain-intrinsic-size is a zero-JS win for *uniform offscreen* content (Drive grid, image walls), but it doesn't give you windowed DOM — use it to skip layout/paint, not to bound node count. 2.4 Offline-first toolkit Service Worker: precache shell, runtime cache by route. IndexedDB: user mutations + cached responses. Background Sync API: flush on reconnect. Conflict resolution: LWW, manual merge, CRDT — choose explicitly. // SW: app-shell precache + per-route runtime strategy. const SHELL = ["/", "/app.js", "/app.css"]; self.addEventListener("install", (e: any) => e.waitUntil(caches.open("shell-v3").then((c) => c.addAll(SHELL)))); self.addEventListener("fetch", (e: any) => { const url = new URL(e.request.url); if (url.pathname.startsWith("/api/")) { e.respondWith(staleWhileRevalidate(e.request)); // data: SWR } else if (SHELL.includes(url.pathname)) { e.respondWith(caches.match(e.request)); // shell: cache-first } // tiles/images: cache-first w/ LRU eviction }); // Outbox pattern: queue mutations, flush via Background Sync. async function enqueueMutation(m: Mutation) { const db = await openDB("outbox"); await db.add("pending", m); // durable across tab close const reg = await navigator.serviceWorker.ready; await reg.sync.register("flush-outbox"); // fires on reconnect } Conflict strategy — choose explicitly and justify: Strategy When Cost Last-Write-Wins (LWW) metadata, settings, tree-position ops silent data loss on concurrent edits Manual merge high-value docs, finance UX complexity, needs a merge UI CRDT (Yjs/Automerge/Loro) text, collaborative trees larger payload, harder cursor/format anchoring Decision rule for the room: *text content → CRDT; structural ops (move block, reorder) → LWW with a tombstone + cycle check.* This is exactly how Notion-style editors split it (§Case 4). 2.5 Accessibility checklist Keyboard-only flow walkthrough. Color contrast 4.5:1 (3:1 large text). Focus visible + focus ring tested against WCAG 2.2. aria-live for dynamic updates; do not over-announce. Respect prefers-reduced-motion. WCAG 2.2 (the senior deltas vs 2.1): 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (sticky headers must not hide the focused element), 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (every drag interaction — Calendar drag-create, Notion reorder, Maps pan — needs a non-drag keyboard/click alternative), 2.5.8 Target Size 24×24 CSS px minimum. Drop these into Calendar/Notion/Maps cases for instant senior signal. aria-live discipline: polite for result counts and "saved" toasts; assertive only for errors that block the user. Debounce announcements — an autocomplete that fires aria-live on every keystroke is *worse* than silence (screen-reader chatter). Announce the settled count once. 2.6 Senior pitfalls Skipping requirements phase — interviewer wanted you to ask. Designing for 1 user when prompt implies scale — cite numbers. Drawing backend when question is frontend. Not surfacing tradeoffs — name them. Ignoring failure modes, slow networks, low-end devices. Add to the list, learned from real loops: No measurement story. Stating a budget without *how you'd verify it* (RUM via web-vitals + PerformanceObserver , Lighthouse CI gate in PR, long-task observer) reads junior. Always pair a number with its monitor. Single-region thinking. "WebSocket gateway" with no answer for the user in Sydney hitting a US room. Have a one-liner: regional gateways + global pub/sub bus, or edge-terminated WS. Ignoring the bundle. Drawing a beautiful component tree then shipping 800 KB of JS. Name code-splitting boundaries (route-level + heavy-widget lazy) and a budget. Over-announcing / focus traps in a11y. Saying "I'll add aria-live everywhere" — that's a red flag, not a green one. Hand-waving the failure mode. "On error we revert" — *how*? Show the rollback context (§2.2). Reconnect, partition, slow-3G, and 1% device class need concrete answers. Case 1 — Collaborative editor (Google Docs / Figma / Notion) Requirements Multi-user editing with sub-200 ms perceived latency. Cursor presence, comments, history, offline reconciliation. Scale: tens of thousands of concurrent docs, p99 sync &lt
