08 — Behavioral · Companies · Negotiation · Take-Home (2026)

STAR stories · Company-specific themes · Salary playbook · Take-home blueprint

Merged from v1/05 (behavioral + company playbook) and v3/11 (QA + negotiation + take-home). The closing volume.

Part 1 — STAR framework + 12 universal stories

1.1 STAR format

  • Situation — context in 1–2 sentences.
  • Task — your specific responsibility.
  • Action — what YOU (not the team) did, with concrete steps.
  • Result — outcome with NUMBERS and reflection on what you learned.

How interviewers actually score it. At senior+ they listen for the ratio of "I" to "we", the presence of a real decision under constraint, and whether the result has a number you can defend. A story with no number reads as a hypothetical; a story that is all "we" reads as someone who rode along. Budget your 90 seconds roughly: Situation 10s, Task 10s, Action 50s, Result 20s. The Action is where signal lives — spend most words there.

Senior-specific tells the panel grades:

  • Did you change the *direction* of the work, or just execute someone else's plan?
  • Did you weigh a tradeoff explicitly (named the option you rejected and why)?
  • Did you bring others along — review, mentoring, alignment — vs heroics?
  • Did you measure impact *after* shipping, not just claim it?

Common anti-patterns that tank scores:

  • The "we" story (no individual contribution visible).
  • The conflict with no resolution ("…and they were just wrong").
  • The result with no metric ("it went really well").
  • The 4-minute ramble (you never reached the Result).

1.2 The 12 universal stories to prepare

  • Tell me about a project you led end-to-end.
  • Tell me about a time you disagreed with a manager / senior engineer / PM.
  • Tell me about a time you made a mistake that mattered.
  • Tell me about a time you raised the bar on a team's quality.
  • Tell me about a difficult performance / production problem you solved.
  • Tell me about a time you mentored someone (junior or peer).
  • Tell me about a feature you shipped that users loved.
  • Tell me about a time you removed something (code, dependency, scope, headcount).
  • Tell me about a time you delivered under ambiguity.
  • Tell me about a time you championed accessibility / security / DX.
  • Tell me about a tradeoff you made between speed and quality.
  • Tell me about a time you influenced without authority.

Below: one fleshed-out, senior-FE STAR example per story. Swap in your own project names and numbers — keep the structure, the named tradeoff, and the closing metric.

Story 1 — Led a project end-to-end

> S: Our checkout was a 9,000-line React class-component monolith; conversion had plateaued and any change took two engineers a full sprint to ship safely.

> T: I owned rebuilding checkout to a typed, server-driven flow without a conversion regression and without freezing the roadmap.

> A: I wrote a one-page RFC, split the work into a strangler migration behind a flag, defined a typed step-machine (Zod-validated payloads), and shipped step-by-step behind a 5% → 25% → 100% rollout. I ran weekly demos and paired with the two least-confident engineers so the knowledge spread.

> R: Shipped in 7 weeks; checkout p75 INP dropped 410ms → 180ms, conversion +2.3% (≈$1.4M annualized), time-to-ship a checkout change went from 2 weeks to 2 days. Learned: the flag-gated strangler bought the confidence to ship Fridays.

Story 2 — Disagreed with a manager / senior / PM

> S: My PM wanted to ship a redesigned settings page in one big-bang release for a launch date.

> T: I believed big-bang would regress power users and wanted a staged rollout, but I didn't own the timeline.

> A: Instead of arguing in standup, I pulled the funnel data, prototyped both, and brought a one-pager showing a staged rollout hit the *same* launch date for 90% of users while de-risking the long tail. I said the date was non-negotiable for me too — I was solving for it, not against it.

> R: We staged it; caught a save-race bug at 10% that would've hit 100% of users on launch day. Hit the date, zero rollback. Learned: disagreement lands when you adopt the other person's constraint as your own and bring data.

Story 3 — A mistake that mattered

> S: I shipped a "harmless" date-library bump to our scheduling UI on a Thursday.

> T: It was my change, my review I'd rushed.

> A: Within an hour support flagged appointments showing the wrong day for users in half-hour-offset timezones. I rolled back immediately, posted in the incident channel owning it by name before anyone asked, then wrote a blameless postmortem. The root fix: a timezone test matrix (UTC, IST, NPT, Chatham) in CI so the class of bug couldn't recur.

> R: Customer-impact window was 52 minutes; zero data loss. The matrix later caught two more regressions before release. Learned: "harmless" bumps need the same test gate as features.

Story 4 — Raised the bar on quality

> S: Our team's PRs routinely shipped with no tests and flaky CI everyone ignored ("just re-run it").

> T: As the senior IC I wasn't asked to fix this, but velocity was bleeding to rework.

> A: I quantified it — 30% of weekly bugs traced to three untested modules. I added Vitest + RTL to those modules first (led by example, not mandate), set a *non-blocking* coverage report on PRs, fixed the top 5 flaky tests, and wrote a 1-page testing guide. Once the team saw green CI again, I proposed a soft coverage floor and they agreed.

> R: Escaped-bug rate dropped ~40% over the quarter; CI flake rate went 15% → under 2%. Learned: lead quality bars with evidence and example before policy.

Story 5 — Hard performance / production problem

> S: Our dashboard's main route had p95 INP of 600ms; users reported "laggy typing" in a filter box.

> T: I owned the perf workstream that quarter.

> A: I profiled in DevTools Performance + measured INP in the field via web-vitals/RUM. Root cause: every keystroke synchronously re-rendered a 4,000-row table. I debounced input, moved filtering into useDeferredValue, virtualized the table (TanStack Virtual), and memoized row components — verifying each change against RUM, not just my fast laptop.

> R: p95 INP 600ms → 150ms; "laggy" tickets to zero in 3 weeks; the busy route passed Core Web Vitals "good" for 96% of sessions. Learned: measure in the field — my M-series laptop hid the problem entirely.

Story 6 — Mentored someone

> S: A mid-level engineer joined strong on React but shaky on async and testing, and was stalling on a real-time feature.

> T: I was their informal mentor and reviewer.

> A: Rather than rewriting their PR, I pair-debugged a race condition with them, walked through the microtask queue on a whiteboard, and set up a weekly 30-min "async clinic." I reviewed for teaching — comments explained the *why* and pointed at docs, not just "change this."

> R: They shipped the real-time presence feature solo two sprints later and now run the clinic themselves; promoted within the year. Learned: reviewing to teach scales better than reviewing to fix.

Story 7 — Feature users loved

> S: Power users kept asking for keyboard navigation; mouse-only flows were slow for them.

> T: I pitched and led a Cmd-K command palette.

> A: I prototyped on a Friday, validated with 6 power users, then built it properly: fuzzy search, recent-actions ranking, full a11y (focus trap, ARIA, screen-reader labels), and a registry so any team could register commands. I instrumented usage from day one.

> R: Within a month 38% of weekly-active power users used it daily; median task time for the top 3 workflows dropped ~45%. Most-upvoted item in our changelog. Learned: ship instrumentation with the feature so "loved" is a number.

Story 8 — Removed something

> S: We carried a 90KB-gzip charting library used on exactly two screens, dragging bundle and LCP.

> T: I owned bundle health.

> A: I audited usage, found we used ~4 chart types, replaced it with ~6KB of hand-rolled SVG plus lazy-loading the one complex screen, and deleted the dependency, its wrapper abstraction, and 1,200 lines of dead config.

> R: Main bundle −82KB gzip; dashboard LCP 2.9s → 2.1s; one fewer CVE to track. Learned: the best perf win is often deletion, not optimization.

Story 9 — Delivered under ambiguity

> S: Leadership wanted "an analytics view" for a new product with no spec, no designs, and a 3-week window before a customer demo.

> T: I had to define *and* build it.

> A: I interviewed 3 target customers in two days, wrote my own one-page spec with explicit non-goals, got a 15-minute sign-off, and shipped the smallest version that answered the top 3 questions customers asked — behind a flag so we could iterate post-demo without a release.

> R: Demo landed the deal; v1 shipped in 2.5 weeks and iterated to GA from real usage. Learned: under ambiguity, writing the spec yourself *is* the leadership.

Story 10 — Championed a11y / security / DX

> S: Our app had never been a11y-audited and we were about to sign an enterprise customer with a VPAT requirement.

> T: No one owned a11y; I volunteered.

> A: I ran axe + manual screen-reader (VoiceOver/NVDA) passes, triaged ~120 issues by severity, fixed the WCAG-A blockers myself (focus management, labels, contrast), added jest-axe to CI to prevent regressions, and ran a lunch-and-learn so the team could maintain it.

> R: Passed the VPAT review, unblocked a 6-figure contract, and a11y CI now catches ~3 regressions/month before merge. Learned: a11y is cheapest as a CI gate, not a pre-signature scramble.

Story 11 — Speed vs quality tradeoff

> S: A competitor shipped a feature and sales wanted ours in two weeks; doing it "right" was a month.

> T: I had to decide what to cut without creating a mess we'd regret.

> A: I split it: a deliberately scoped v1 in two weeks (one happy path, feature-flagged, with a tracked tech-debt ticket and a written "what we knowingly skipped" note), but refused to cut tests on the payment path or skip the error states. I made the cut *explicit and reversible* rather than silent.

> R: Hit the two-week date; v1 converted well enough to justify the proper v2, shipped a month later with zero rework on the core. Learned: speed/quality is fine when the debt is named, tracked, and the non-negotiables (money, data, a11y) are protected.

Story 12 — Influenced without authority

> S: Three teams each hand-rolled their own data-fetching, causing inconsistent caching and duplicated bugs; I owned none of them.

> T: I wanted a shared TanStack Query layer but couldn't mandate it.

> A: I built it for my own team first, measured the win (fewer bugs, less code), then wrote it up and offered to do the first migration *for* each team in a pairing session. I made adoption lower-effort than the status quo and let the data argue.

> R: All three teams adopted within a quarter; duplicated fetching bugs dropped to near-zero and we deleted ~2K lines. Learned: influence without authority = make the better path the easier path, then prove it with one team's numbers.

1.3 Story-writing checklist

  • Specific dates / project names / numbers (3 engineers, 2-week sprint, 200K MAU).
  • Show your decision-making, not just outcome.
  • Include one disagreement or constraint you navigated.
  • End with a measured result + what you would do differently.
  • Keep each story to 90 seconds verbal — practice with a timer.

Build a reusable story bank. Most of the 12 prompts can be answered from 5–6 real projects. Map each project to the prompts it can serve, so in the room you pick the strongest angle on the fly rather than memorizing 12 scripts. Keep a one-line "headline metric" per project committed to memory — it anchors the whole story.

The follow-up drill. Senior interviewers always probe: "What would you do differently?", "How did the other person react?", "What was the hardest part?", "How did you measure that?". Pre-write a one-sentence answer to each of those four for every story. The follow-ups are where weak candidates fall apart.

Part 2 — Company-by-company (2026 cycles)

2.1 Google (L4 → L6 frontend)

Format

  • Phone screen: 1 DSA + 1 frontend (JS-focused).
  • Onsite: 2 coding (DSA + JS/React), 1 frontend system design, 1 behavioral (Googleyness), 1 deep dive (L5+).

2026 reality. Google still runs a genuine DSA bar even for frontend specialists — expect one round that is pure algorithms (no React). The frontend coding round runs in a shared editor (often CoderPad) building real DOM/JS without a framework, or React if you ask. System design is *frontend* system design (rendering, state, data fetching, perf), not distributed-backend. The L5+ "deep dive" is a 45-min interrogation of one resume project — depth, your specific contribution, tradeoffs.

What they actually probe: correctness under edge cases, clean abstraction, platform reasoning (event loop, layout, network), and *structured* communication. Googleyness = collaboration, intellectual humility, comfort with ambiguity, doing the right thing without being told.

Recent themes

  • Build a typeahead from scratch (cancel, debounce, race-guard, a11y).
  • Polyfill Promise.all and defend rejection design.
  • Design YouTube comments / Google Docs cursors.
  • Convert janky list to virtualized; INP impact.
  • Bundle-tripling feature — how do you intervene without blocking?
  • Disagree with a tech lead (Googleyness).

Value mapping (Googleyness): structured thinking, intellectual humility, "disagree respectfully then commit", user-first. In behavioral, narrate your *reasoning process* out loud — Google rewards visible structured thinking as much as the conclusion.

Example Q1 — "Build a typeahead, then make it production-grade."

> Arc: naive version, then layer (1) input debounce, (2) AbortController to cancel in-flight requests, (3) a request-sequence guard so a slow earlier response can't overwrite a newer one, (4) keyboard a11y (aria-activedescendant, arrows, Escape), (5) recent-query cache. Call out the race-guard explicitly — "the subtle bug is out-of-order responses; I key results to the latest query id." That sentence is the senior signal.

Example Q2 (behavioral) — "Disagreeing with a tech lead."

> Use Story 2. Land the Googleyness beat: "I understood *their* constraint first, brought data instead of opinion, and once we made the call I committed fully — including the parts I'd argued against." Humility + data + commit is exactly the rubric.

2.2 Meta (E4 → E6)

Format

  • 1 coding (DSA + product), 1 product architecture, 1 behavioral.
  • E5+: career deep dive.

2026 reality. Meta's FE loop is famously product-flavored. The coding round mixes a DSA-ish problem with a "build this UI behavior" task. The signature round is product architecture (their FE system design): given a product ("design Stories"), you drive the whole thing — data model, component tree, state/caching, network strategy, pagination, real-time, perf, edge cases — while the interviewer pokes at tradeoffs. You are expected to *drive*; silence kills the round.

What they actually probe: ownership and impact (E5+ must show scope beyond their own tasks), execution speed, and fast, defensible pragmatic tradeoffs. The career deep dive (E5+) maps your real scope to the level rubric.

Recent themes

  • Design Facebook News Feed with ranking + ads.
  • Real-time presence + typing on Messenger.
  • Implement event delegation; why React uses synthetic events.
  • Instagram Stories pre-fetch on slow networks.
  • Feature flag infrastructure isolated from network latency.

Value mapping: "Move Fast", "Focus on Impact", "Be Bold", "Be Open". Lead behavioral answers with *impact and your role in it*; quantify scope (users, revenue, eng-time saved). E6 answers must show you shaped *team/org* direction, not just delivered a feature.

Example Q1 — "Design the News Feed (frontend)."

> Drive it: data model (feed items in a normalized cache, cursor pagination), component architecture (virtualized feed list, per-type item renderers), fetching (infinite scroll with prefetch-ahead + stale-while-revalidate), client-side dedup + ad insertion at intervals, optimistic like/comment with reconciliation, perf (virtualization, image lazy-load, code-split item types). End on the hardest tradeoff: "prefetch aggressiveness vs mobile data — I'd tune by connection type via the Network Information API."

Example Q2 (behavioral) — "Biggest impact in the last 6 months."

> Use Story 1 or 7. Lead with the number: "I drove a checkout rebuild that lifted conversion 2.3%, ≈$1.4M annualized." Then *move fast* (flag-gated strangler in 7 weeks, no 6-month freeze) and *ownership* (you wrote the RFC, drove rollout). Impact-first, not chronology-first.

2.3 Amazon (SDE Frontend Engineer L5 → L6)

Format

  • OA: 2 coding + debug round.
  • Onsite: 2 coding, 1 frontend system design, 2 behavioral (Leadership Principles).

2026 reality. Amazon is the most *behaviorally* weighted FAANG loop. Roughly half the onsite is Leadership Principles, and a dedicated Bar Raiser (outside-team interviewer with veto power) drills your LP stories with relentless follow-ups: "What was *your* specific contribution? What data did you have? What did you do *differently* next time?" Coding is solid-not-elite LeetCode (medium); the FE system design is real (design a product UI). Vague "we" stories fail here harder than anywhere.

What they actually probe: evidence-backed LP stories with crisp "I" ownership, customer obsession, willingness to disagree then commit. They literally map answers to specific LPs.

Recent themes

  • Image gallery with zoom + lazy + reduced-motion.
  • Shopping cart survives refresh; reconciles on login.
  • LCP diagnostics in DevTools + WebPageTest.
  • Raised the bar (Insist on Highest Standards).
  • Disagreed and committed.

LP cheat-sheet (FE loops hit these most): Customer Obsession, Ownership, Invent and Simplify, Are Right A Lot, Insist on the Highest Standards, Bias for Action, Dive Deep, Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit, Deliver Results. Prep at least two stories per top LP — the Bar Raiser may ask the same LP twice and you can't reuse.

Example Q1 (behavioral) — "Insisted on the highest standards."

> Use Story 4. Hit Dive Deep ("30% of weekly bugs traced to three untested modules") and Deliver Results (escaped-bug −40%, flake 15%→2%). Have the "what would you do differently" ready: "I'd have made the coverage report a soft gate from day one instead of waiting for buy-in."

Example Q2 — "Cart that survives refresh and reconciles on login."

> Optimistic local cart in localStorage (or IndexedDB), keyed and versioned; on auth, send local cart to server and merge (union by SKU, sum quantities, server is source of truth for price/availability), handle conflicts (out-of-stock → flag, don't drop silently), reconcile across tabs via the storage event / BroadcastChannel. Name the edge: "two tabs, one logs in — I broadcast the reconciled cart so the other tab doesn't clobber it."

Comp note

  • L5/L6 frontend: $200K – $420K TC. Stock 5/15/40/40 over 4 yrs — front-load via signing bonus.

Negotiation implication: the 5/15/40/40 RSU vest makes years 1–2 cash-light. Amazon pays two signing bonuses (year 1 and year 2) precisely to bridge this. Negotiate both up — that's where the give is, since base is band-capped and RSU grants are constrained by the back-load.

2.4 Apple (Web / Internet Services)

Format

  • Team-by-team variation. Common: 1 phone (JS + DSA), 4–5 onsite rounds on fundamentals.

2026 reality. Apple is decentralized — each team (Web Apps, Internet Services, Media, Maps web) runs its own loop, so calibrate with your recruiter. The throughline is fundamentals and craft: deep JS (event loop, closures, prototypes), CSS mastery (cascade, specificity, layout, paint), browser internals, and a strong accessibility bias (VoiceOver is first-class). Less framework trivia, more "do you understand the platform." Expect one round that goes pixel-precise.

What they actually probe: depth of fundamentals, attention to detail/craft, collaboration, and whether you sweat the UX details Apple is known for.

Recent themes

  • Event loop + microtasks + rAF interaction.
  • Undo/redo for rich-text editor.
  • CSS specificity + cascade given a tangle.
  • Media controller with VoiceOver a11y.
  • Measuring rendering perf on 60 Hz vs 120 Hz (ProMotion).

Value mapping: craft, collaboration, taste, accessibility-as-default. In behavioral, tell a story where a *detail* mattered — Apple respects the engineer who noticed the 1px jank.

Example Q1 — "Undo/redo for a rich-text editor."

> Command pattern with two stacks (undo/redo), each action a reversible command (apply/invert); coalesce rapid keystrokes into one undo unit (debounce by time/word boundary); clear the redo stack on a new action; persist as a bounded ring buffer to cap memory. The hard part: "selection state must be part of the snapshot, or undo restores text but loses the caret — that feels broken." That UX detail is the Apple signal.

Example Q2 (behavioral) — "Made a product visibly better through a detail."

> Use Story 5 or a focused craft story: a 16ms animation jank you traced to a layout thrash, fixed with transform/will-change, validated on a 120Hz ProMotion display *and* a 60Hz one. Land the taste beat: "users don't file a bug for 'feels slightly off,' they just trust the app less — so I treat perceived smoothness as a real requirement."

2.5 Netflix (Senior UI Engineer)

Format

  • Hiring-for-judgment. Coding bar high; 3–4 rounds.
  • Less LeetCode; more "explain a perf/a11y problem you led".

2026 reality. Netflix hires senior+ only and screens hard for judgment and seniority of thought, not LeetCode trivia. Rounds lean toward "walk me through a hard problem you owned" and real-world FE (TV-app constraints, streaming, low-end-device perf). The culture round is serious — they genuinely assess fit with "Freedom & Responsibility" and the "team, not family" ethos. Expect to defend decisions like a staff engineer; weak judgment fails fast even with strong code.

What they actually probe: the quality of your *decisions*, your sense of when to stop, your comfort with high autonomy/high accountability, ability to operate without process.

Recent themes

  • TV-app row carousel with D-pad focus management.
  • Streaming video buffer + bitrate adaptation.
  • Removed a tool / framework — impact.

Value mapping: Judgment, Selflessness, Courage, Curiosity, Freedom & Responsibility. Behavioral answers should show you exercising judgment *with autonomy* — no one told you, you saw it, you owned it, you knew when to stop.

Example Q1 — "TV-app carousel with D-pad focus."

> Spatial navigation: maintain a focus model independent of DOM order; on D-pad input compute the nearest focusable in that direction (geometry or precomputed grid), scroll the row to keep focus centered, virtualize off-screen tiles (TVs have tiny memory/CPU budgets), prefetch metadata/art for the next few tiles. Name the constraint: "on a 5-year-old smart TV you have ~60ms of JS budget per frame, so I avoid layout in the hot path and use transforms only."

Example Q2 (behavioral) — "A project you would not do today."

> Use Story 8 or 11 framed as judgment: "We adopted a heavy framework for a small surface; I over-indexed on future flexibility we never used. Today I'd ship the smaller, deletable thing and earn the complexity. I later removed it — bundle −82KB." Netflix loves the engineer who can crisply critique their own past decision.

Comp note

  • No equity. Base-heavy ($500K – $700K). Negotiation = base only. Bring competing offers.

Negotiation implication: there is exactly one number — base salary (Netflix historically lets you choose a cash/stock-option split, but model it as all-cash). No vesting cliff means no golden handcuffs, but also no upside lever to trade. Your *only* leverage is a competing offer's TC and market data. Name your best-supported base and hold it with data; there's nowhere else to move.

2.6 Figma (Senior Web Engineer)

Format

  • 1 coding (machine coding ~75 min), 2 system design, 1 behavioral, 1 project deep dive.

2026 reality. Figma's bar is machine coding — build a working, interactive component in ~75 minutes (real DOM, real state, often canvas/SVG), graded on working software + code quality + UX, not algorithm cleverness. The two design rounds skew toward hard FE problems Figma faces: rendering thousands of nodes, real-time collaboration/multiplayer, and performance. Product-mindedness is explicitly valued — they want engineers who care how it *feels*.

What they actually probe: can you build a real, polished interactive thing fast and cleanly; do you reason about rendering/perf at scale; do you have product taste.

Recent themes

  • Build a real-time cursor + selection sync mini-Figma.
  • How Figma renders multi-thousand layers in canvas.
  • Feature flag rollout for risky UX experiment.
  • Hard cross-stack perf debug.

Value mapping: "Play" (craft/delight), "Grow as you go", "Ship", product-mindedness. Behavioral: a feature users loved and *why it delighted* them.

Example Q1 — "Render thousands of layers in canvas."

> Not the DOM — a single canvas (or WebGL) scene graph; cull off-viewport nodes; spatial index (quadtree/R-tree) for hit-testing and viewport queries; dirty-rect rendering so you only repaint what changed; batch draw calls; requestAnimationFrame decoupling input from render; offload heavy work (image decode, geometry) to workers/OffscreenCanvas. Name the cliff: "at 10k+ nodes, per-node DOM is dead on arrival from layout cost alone — that's why it's a canvas."

Example Q2 — machine coding: "Build a multiplayer cursor sync."

> Build the real thing: a cursor store keyed by userId, a mock WebSocket abstraction you can swap, throttle outbound cursor updates (~30–60Hz), interpolate remote cursors between updates so they glide instead of teleport, render with transform (no layout), clean up on disconnect. Even mocked, show the throttle + interpolation — that's the senior signal you've thought about bandwidth and feel.

2.7 Vercel (Senior)

Format

  • Async take-home OR live coding, 1–2 system design, behavioral, leadership panel.

2026 reality. Unsurprisingly Next.js-/RSC-centric. Expect deep questions on App Router, Server Components, streaming, caching, edge runtime. The take-home (if chosen) is judged on real-world quality and a clean deploy; the live round may have you build streaming UI with the AI SDK. The leadership panel probes how you operate in a fast, opinionated, remote-first org.

What they actually probe: deep modern-React/Next mental model, performance and DX instincts, ability to ship polished work autonomously, culture fit for a fast remote team.

Recent themes

  • Next.js cache invalidation across regions.
  • Streaming chat with AI SDK in the live round.
  • Scaling FE with RSC adoption story.

Value mapping: customer obsession (DX is the product), bias for shipping, ownership, openness. Behavioral: an autonomous-shipping story and a "drove adoption of a new paradigm" story.

Example Q1 — "Next.js cache invalidation across regions."

> Distinguish the layers (Data Cache, Full Route Cache, Router Cache, CDN). Use revalidateTag/revalidatePath for on-demand purges tied to mutations (Server Actions), revalidate for time-based ISR, cache: 'no-store' for always-fresh. Multi-region: tag-based invalidation propagates through Vercel's edge network; the gotcha is client-side Router Cache staleness — you may need router.refresh() after a mutation. Name it: "the bug users hit is the *client* router cache, not the server — that's the one people forget."

Example Q2 (behavioral) — "Drove an RSC adoption."

> Use Story 12 reshaped: migrated one route to RSC first, measured the TTFB/bundle win, wrote it up, and migrated other teams' routes *for* them in pairing sessions. Land: "I made the new paradigm the easier path with a working example and real numbers, rather than mandating it."

2.8 Linear (Senior)

Format

  • Take-home → onsite (3 rounds). Heavily product-coded.

2026 reality. Linear is the most product/craft-obsessed loop on this list. The take-home and onsite reward keyboard-first UX, speed, polish, and an almost designer-level feel for interaction. They care that your UI is *fast* (optimistic, instant) and *delightful*. Code quality matters but taste matters as much — a technically correct but clunky submission won't pass.

What they actually probe: product taste, interaction craft, performance/instant-feel, and whether you sweat keyboard/details like they do.

Recent themes

  • Keyboard-first command bar (Cmd-K).
  • Real-time sync engine — CRDTs, offline patches.

Value mapping: craft, quality, speed, opinionated product sense. Behavioral: "a feature users loved" and "raised the bar on UX quality."

Example Q1 — "Build a Cmd-K command bar."

> A command registry (id, title, keywords, action, optional context predicate); fuzzy matching ranked by recency + frequency + match quality; full keyboard control (Cmd-K open, arrows, Enter, Escape, focus trap); instant open (no async on the hot path — preload commands); a11y (role="combobox", aria-activedescendant). Land the craft beat: "it has to open in <1 frame and feel weightless — any spinner on open and it's failed."

Example Q2 — "Real-time sync with offline support."

> Local-first store as the UI's source of truth (optimistic), a mutation log of changes, sync to the server with last-write-wins or CRDT merge for conflict-free fields, reconcile on reconnect by replaying unsynced patches, dedupe via change IDs. Name the hard part: "ordering and conflict resolution when two clients edit offline — CRDTs for collaborative fields, LWW for scalar fields where a CRDT is overkill."

2.9 Stripe (Senior)

Format

  • 1 take-home OR 90-min build, 2 design (system + integration), 1 debug, 1 leadership.

2026 reality. Stripe is rigorous and correctness/reliability-obsessed — they handle money, and it shows. The debug round is signature: you're dropped into an unfamiliar codebase with a bug and must reproduce, isolate, and fix it under time pressure (graded on method, not luck). Integration design probes API/SDK boundaries (iframes, cross-origin comms, idempotency). The leadership round values integrity and rigorous thinking ("Operating Principles").

What they actually probe: correctness, careful handling of edge cases and failure, systematic debugging method, integrity/rigor in reasoning.

Recent themes

  • Checkout iframe + parent page comms layer.
  • Diagnose flaky payment confirmation.
  • Regrettable code — what you learned.

Value mapping (Operating Principles): "Users first", rigor, "trust and amplify", integrity, "think big, start small". Behavioral: a "mistake that mattered" told with total ownership and a systemic fix.

Example Q1 — "Checkout iframe + parent page comms."

> Embed checkout in an iframe for PCI isolation; communicate via postMessage with strict origin allow-listing on *both* sides (never *); a typed, versioned message protocol with a load handshake; never trust message contents without validation; resize via posted height; handle 3DS by opening a modal/redirect and posting the result back. Name the security beat: "the classic bug is accepting postMessage without checking event.origin — that's an XSS/clickjacking vector with money attached."

Example Q2 — debug round method.

> Narrate the method before you find the bug: reproduce reliably first (the flake is the symptom), form a hypothesis, bisect (git/log/binary-search the surface), add targeted logging/assertions, confirm root cause, write a failing test, then fix, then verify the test passes. For "flaky payment confirmation," lead toward a race: "confirmation arrives via webhook *and* client poll; without idempotency they race and the UI double-confirms — I'd key on a server-side idempotency token."

2.10 Airbnb (Senior)

Format

  • 1 coding (JS + algo), 1 React/UI build, 1 system design, 1 behavioral (core values).

2026 reality. Airbnb runs a balanced FE loop: one algo-flavored coding round, one React UI build (build a real interactive component — search/filters, gallery — graded on component design, state, a11y, polish), one FE system design, and a behavioral round explicitly mapped to core values. Airbnb visibly cares about accessibility and inclusive design.

What they actually probe: component/state design, real UI polish and a11y, and strong values alignment (belonging, host/guest empathy).

Recent themes

  • Search with filters; debounce, sticky filter, URL sync.
  • Listing detail page with image gallery + map + booking.
  • Championed a11y on a project.

Value mapping (core values): "Champion the Mission", "Be a Host" (empathy/hospitality), "Embrace the Adventure", "Be a Cereal Entrepreneur" (resourcefulness). Behavioral: an a11y/inclusion story and a resourcefulness-under-constraint story.

Example Q1 — "Search with filters."

> Filters as the single source of truth synced to the URL (shareable, back-button-correct) via searchParams; debounce text input but apply discrete filters immediately; cancelable result fetching (AbortController + race guard); sticky filter bar with proper focus management; loading/empty/error states on every result region. Land it: "URL as state means a shared link reproduces the exact search — a hospitality detail, not just an engineering one."

Example Q2 (behavioral) — "Championed accessibility."

> Use Story 10. Tie it to "Be a Host": "accessibility is hospitality — a guest using a screen reader should book as smoothly as anyone. I ran the audit, fixed the WCAG-A blockers, and added jest-axe to CI so it stays fixed." Values + a real CI mechanism = the Airbnb combo.

2.11 Quick fire (Shopify, Square, Uber)

  • Shopify — Hydrogen/Remix; storefront with caching tiers.
  • Square — TS-heavy machine coding; payment flows.
  • Uber — large org coordination + driver/rider real-time map.

Shopify (2026): Life Story interview (deep, values-led behavioral covering your whole arc and motivations) + technical (Hydrogen/Remix, web fundamentals, storefront-scale perf). Probes: ownership mindset, impact, fit with their "crafter" remote culture, edge-rendering/caching. Example Q: "Design a fast product page on 3G in an emerging market" → SSR/streaming, image optimization, cache tiers (CDN + data), minimal JS hydration.

Square/Block (2026): TS-heavy machine coding, often a payment or forms flow; strong typing and correctness expected. Probes: clean typed code, money/validation edge cases, reliability. Example Q: "Build a typed multi-step payment form with validation and idempotent submit" → Zod schemas, discriminated-union step state, idempotency key on submit, error recovery.

Uber (2026): Coding + FE system design with a real-time bent (driver/rider map, live ETA), plus behavioral on operating in a large cross-team org. Probes: real-time data handling, map/perf at scale, cross-team coordination. Example Q: "Design the rider map with live driver positions" → WebSocket/stream of positions, interpolation/throttling, viewport-bounded subscriptions, marker virtualization, reconnect/backoff.

Part 3 — Salary negotiation playbook

3.1 The mental model

  • Recruiters do not set comp; they argue for it. Your counters must be things a recruiter can paste into an email — market data, competing offers, qualifications.
  • There is almost always more room than the first offer.
  • Multiple offers > one offer > no offer.
  • Levels matter more than dollars: E4 → E5 changes trajectory more than +$30K TC.

Reframe: the recruiter is your advocate, not your adversary. Their job is to close you at a number their comp committee approves. Give them ammunition (data, competing offers, your level case) and they fight internally for you. Be warm and collaborative, never adversarial — "help me make this work" beats "match this or I walk."

Leverage is the whole game. Your BATNA (best alternative — current job or another offer) sets the floor. Everything else is theater on top of leverage. No leverage → small wins (signing bonus). Real competing offer → big wins (base, level, equity). Build leverage *before* you need it by clustering interviews.

Comp committees, not recruiters, set bands. At big companies the recruiter takes your case to a committee. This is why "what's possible?" framing works — you're asking them to go ask, not asking them to personally bend.

3.2 The five-step script

  • Receive offer warmly. Never accept or reject on the call.
  • Ask for full breakdown in writing: base, signing, target RSU value, refresher policy, performance bonus, on-target equity, vesting, start date flex.
  • Take 24–72 hours; gather competing offers + Levels.fyi data + internal promo timelines.
  • Respond with structured ask: "I'm excited about the role. Based on [data], my target is $X base / $Y stock / $Z signing. Can your team see what is possible?"
  • Iterate. After second offer, push politely once more. Then accept warmly.

Word-for-word: the offer call (step 1).

> "This is fantastic news — thank you, I'm genuinely excited about the team. I want to give this the consideration it deserves rather than react on the spot. Could you send the full breakdown in writing, and I'll come back within a few days with any questions?"

Then stop talking. Don't reveal a number. Don't say yes. Don't say "that's a bit low." Just get it in writing.

Email template: requesting the written breakdown (step 2).

Subject: Re: Offer — [Your Name]

Hi [Recruiter],

Thank you again — I'm really excited about [Team/Role]. So I can evaluate
this properly, could you send the full details in writing:

- Base salary
- Signing bonus (and whether it's split across years)
- Equity: grant value, vesting schedule, and refresher policy
- Target annual bonus (% and how it's assessed)
- Level / title
- Start-date flexibility
- Relocation / remote arrangement, if any

I'll review and come back with any questions by [date].

Best,
[Your Name]

Email template: the structured counter (step 4).

Subject: Re: Offer — [Your Name]

Hi [Recruiter],

I've reviewed the offer and I'm excited about the role and team. Based on
the level of the work and current market data, I was hoping we could get
closer to:

- Base: $X
- Equity: $Y/yr
- Signing: $Z

For context: I have a competing offer at [Company] at $[TC] total, and
Levels.fyi medians for this level land around $[median]. I'd much rather
be here — if we can close the gap, I'm ready to sign.

What's possible on your end?

Thanks,
[Your Name]

Word-for-word: the second push (step 5), after they improve once.

> "I really appreciate you moving on this — it means a lot. This is close. If we could get the base to $X (or add $Z to the signing to bridge year one), I'd be ready to sign today. Is there any room there?"

"I'd be ready to sign today" is the unlock — it tells the recruiter the deal closes if they spend the chip. Use it only when it's true.

3.3 What each lever moves

LeverNegotiable?Typical moveNotes
BaseNarrow+5–10%Constrained by band per level/location
Signing bonusWide+$25K–$150KRecruiter discretion; ask first if base is capped
Equity (RSU)Modest+10–25%Easier at hiring than later; ask for refresh targets
LevelSometimesHugeBring evidence; ask early in the loop
Start dateYesN/ASometimes secures a competing offer or vesting cliff payout
Remote / reloOftenVariablePost-2024 hybrid normalization

Order of operations: push level first and earliest (during/just after the loop, not at offer — it changes the whole band and is nearly impossible to fix later). Then equity (biggest TC lever once level is set). Then base (small % but it compounds and anchors refreshers and bonus). Then signing (easiest yes, but one-time — use it to bridge gaps the band can't close). Don't lead with signing; it caps your upside on the durable levers.

Sign-on clawbacks: signing bonuses usually carry a 12-month clawback (leave early, repay pro-rata). Fine if you intend to stay, but factor it if you're hedging.

3.4 Lines you can actually use

  • "I'm thrilled about the role. I have another offer at $X TC; would your team be able to match?"
  • "My current TC is $Y after refresh; to move I need $Y + 25% to justify the risk."
  • "The signing bonus is great. Can we shift some into base, since base anchors my refresher value?"
  • "Your RSU is 25/25/25/25; my current is 5/15/40/40 so year 2 worries me. Could we close that gap with signing?"

More field-tested lines:

  • (Anchoring without a competing offer) "Based on Levels.fyi medians for this level and the scope we discussed, I was expecting closer to $X — can we get there?"
  • (When they ask your current comp) "I'd rather focus on the value of this role and market for the level — what range did you have in mind for this position?"
  • (When they ask your expectations first) "I'm sure your offer will be competitive — I'm more interested in the right level and team. What's the band for this role?"
  • (Pushing level) "The work you've described is squarely L5 scope — I'm already operating at that level. Can we calibrate the level to the responsibilities?"
  • (Closing warmly) "Thank you for working with me on this — I'm genuinely excited to join. Send the updated letter and I'll sign."
  • (Exploding offer pushback) "I'm very interested, but I have an active loop wrapping up next week. Could we extend the deadline to [date] so I can give you a real yes?"

3.5 Mistakes that cost real money

  • Telling recruiter your current comp before they name theirs.
  • Accepting verbally on the call.
  • Showing desperation.
  • Negotiating once and stopping — there is almost always a second round.
  • Forgetting refreshers + on-target bonus.

More expensive mistakes:

  • Negotiating against yourself. Naming a number, then lowering it before they respond ("…but I'm flexible"). State your ask once and go quiet.
  • Only comparing year-1 TC. Sign-on-heavy offers look big in year 1 then cliff in year 2. Compare *steady-state* (years 2–4) and model refreshers.
  • Ignoring the vesting schedule. $600K TC on 5/15/40/40 is not the same as on 25/25/25/25 — front-loaded vests are worth materially more.
  • Treating "best and final" as literally final. It often isn't, especially with a competing offer in hand. Test it once, politely.
  • Burning goodwill. Aggressive, adversarial, or dishonest tactics can get an offer rescinded. Stay warm.
  • Resigning on a verbal offer. Never quit until the signed letter is in hand.

3.6 2026 senior FE comp benchmarks (USD, US-based)

CompanyLevelMedian TCRange
GoogleL5$420K$340K – $560K
GoogleL6$600K$480K – $820K
MetaE5$430K$340K – $570K
MetaE6$640K$500K – $880K
AmazonSDE III$300K$240K – $440K
AmazonPrincipal$540K$400K – $760K
AppleICT4$380K$300K – $510K
NetflixSenior$650K$500K – $850K
StripeL3$430K$340K – $560K
FigmaSenior$420K$340K – $540K
VercelSenior$370K$300K – $470K

Source: aggregated public Levels.fyi medians 2026. Always check Levels.fyi day-of for current data.

Reading the table correctly:

  • TC = base + annualized equity + target bonus. Equity is valued at *grant-time* price; actual value moves with the stock — a strong public-company offer can over- or under-deliver vs the number.
  • Level mapping (rough): Google L5 ≈ Meta E5 ≈ Amazon SDE III ≈ Apple ICT4 ≈ "Senior". Google L6 ≈ Meta E6 ≈ Amazon Principal(-ish) ≈ "Staff".
  • Private companies (Figma, Linear, Stripe): equity is illiquid; value the offer on cash + your probability-weighted view of the equity, not the headline. Ask about last 409A, preferred price, and liquidity/secondary programs.
  • Location matters in 2026: SF/NYC bands sit at the top of these ranges; many companies still geo-adjust fully-remote roles. Negotiate the *band*, not just the offer.

3.7 Competing offer workflow

  • Interview at 2–4 companies in parallel; cluster onsites within ~2 weeks.
  • When first offer arrives, ask others: "I have an offer expiring on [date]; can you accelerate?"
  • Companies will compress 2–3 weeks into 1 to compete.
  • Never lie about an offer; have a real second option.

The acceleration email (to companies still in-loop once you have an offer):

Subject: Timeline update — [Your Name]

Hi [Recruiter],

Quick update: I've received an offer with a decision deadline of [date].
[Company] remains my top choice and I'd hate to decide without your team
in the picture. Is there any way to accelerate the remaining steps so I
can consider both fairly?

Thanks,
[Your Name]

Sequencing tips:

  • Aim for offers that *overlap in time* — an expired offer is zero leverage. Push to align deadlines.
  • Use the deadline of your *least*-preferred offer to pressure your *most*-preferred company's timeline.
  • If your top choice can't accelerate, ask your in-hand offer for an extension ("I want to give you a confident yes") — most grant a week.
  • Keep numbers honest. Recruiters talk; a fabricated offer that gets verified ends the process. You can decline to share the letter while stating the TC.

3.8 Special cases

  • Netflix — cash-only; name your best base, defend with market data.
  • Amazon — front-load signing because RSU back-loaded; year-1 cash matters.
  • Startups — preference, dilution history, last 409A, exercise window. RSUs vs ISOs vs NSOs differ.

Startup equity — what to actually ask for:

  • % ownership, not just share count (shares are meaningless without total outstanding).
  • Strike price + last 409A valuation (sets your tax exposure and break-even).
  • Preferred price / last round valuation (your common shares sit below preferred in a liquidation).
  • Vesting + cliff (standard 4yr/1yr; watch for back-loaded or longer schedules).
  • Exercise window after leaving (90 days is brutal; ask for extended/10-year exercise — increasingly common in 2026).
  • ISO vs NSO (ISOs can get favorable tax treatment but watch AMT; NSOs taxed as income at exercise).
  • Dilution history and runway (how many rounds left before you're diluted; how much cash, what burn).

Big-tech special cases:

  • Netflix: truly cash-only mental model — one base number, defend with the strongest market data and any competing TC. No equity lever exists.
  • Amazon: base is band-capped and RSUs back-load (5/15/40/40), so push *both* year-1 and year-2 signing bonuses — that's where year-1/2 cash gets bridged.
  • Google/Meta: equity is the biggest lever and refreshers matter enormously — always ask the refresher policy, since the initial grant is only ~4 years of a much longer relationship.
  • Pre-IPO (Stripe/Figma/Linear-tier): ask about secondary/tender programs and double-trigger RSUs (vest on time *and* a liquidity event) — these determine when paper becomes cash.

Part 4 — Take-home project guide

4.1 What companies actually grade

  • Does the app work end-to-end?
  • Is the code clean, modular, testable?
  • Edge cases (loading, error, empty, offline, network race)?
  • Is the README a window into how you think?
  • Did you go above the minimum without exceeding the time budget?

The grading rubric reviewers actually use (reconstruct it for yourself):

| Dimension              | Weight | What earns top marks                                   |
|------------------------|--------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| Correctness / works    | 25%    | Runs from a clean clone; all stated features work      |
| Code quality           | 20%    | Clear naming, small modules, no dead code, typed       |
| Edge cases & states    | 15%    | Loading / empty / error / offline / race all handled   |
| Testing                | 15%    | Meaningful tests on critical paths, not coverage theater|
| README / communication | 15%    | Tradeoffs, "with more time", how-to-run, why-choices   |
| Polish / craft         | 10%    | A11y, responsive, perceived performance, small delight |

Reviewers spend ~20–30 minutes. They clone, read the README, run it, skim the code, run the tests. If it doesn't run from a clean clone, you fail before they read a line — test the clean-clone path yourself.

4.2 Time budget

  • Spend exactly the specified hours. Over = poor scoping; under = low effort.
  • 60–90 min plan before coding: read spec twice, draw architecture, write TODO list, identify stretch items.

A worked 6-hour budget:

0:00–0:45  Read spec twice. Write down explicit requirements + assumptions.
           Sketch architecture + component tree. List must-haves vs stretch.
0:45–1:15  Scaffold: stack, lint/TS/test config, CI stub, deploy target.
1:15–4:00  Build the happy path end-to-end. Commit in small, labeled steps.
4:00–4:45  Edge cases: loading / empty / error / race / a11y basics.
4:45–5:30  Tests on critical paths. Fix what they surface.
5:30–6:00  README, clean-clone test, deploy, final commit. STOP.

Reserve the last 30 minutes for the README and the clean-clone test — these disproportionately move the score and are what tired candidates skip. If you're running over, *cut scope* (drop a stretch feature) rather than ship something half-built; write what you cut under "With more time."

4.3 Default 2026 stack

  • FE: Next.js 15 (App Router + RSC) OR Vite + React 19 (SPA-only).
  • TS strict; no any, no implicit any.
  • State: TanStack Query + Zustand (or useState for trivial).
  • Validation: Zod + React Hook Form.
  • Style: Tailwind v4 or CSS Modules; avoid heavy UI kits.
  • Testing: Vitest + RTL; Playwright for E2E happy path.
  • CI: tiny GitHub Action for lint + typecheck + tests.
  • Host: Vercel preview deploy — link in README.

Choosing Next vs Vite: if the brief involves data fetching, SSR, SEO, or a server boundary → Next.js 15. If it's a pure client widget (editor, visualization, game) with no server needs → Vite + React 19 scaffolds faster and is easier to run. Don't reach for Next just to look modern; an unnecessary server is complexity a reviewer will note.

Restraint is a graded signal. The fastest way to fail a 4-screen take-home is Redux + Saga + GraphQL + a custom design system. Match tooling to scope: useState for trivial local state, TanStack Query only if there's real server state, Zustand only if there's real cross-tree client state. Justify every dependency in the README.

4.4 Project structure

app/                  # routes (or pages/)
components/
  ui/                 # design primitives
  features/           # feature-folded
lib/                  # cross-cutting utils
hooks/                # custom hooks
schemas/              # Zod schemas
tests/
  unit/               # vitest
  e2e/                # playwright
README.md
.github/workflows/ci.yml

A concrete, fleshed-out layout for a typical "kanban board" brief:

.
├── app/
│   ├── layout.tsx
│   ├── page.tsx                 # board route
│   └── api/
│       └── cards/route.ts       # mock persistence endpoint
├── components/
│   ├── ui/                      # Button, Card, Spinner, Dialog
│   └── features/
│       └── board/
│           ├── Board.tsx        # column layout + DnD context
│           ├── Column.tsx

├── hooks/

Feature-folding (everything for "board" in one folder) reads far better than type-folding (all components in one giant folder) once the app has more than a couple of screens.

Minimal CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml):

name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4

A green CI badge in the README signals "I work the way a senior engineer works" for almost no effort.

4.5 README template (steal this)

A complete, copy-paste README in one block (what reviewers love to open):

# Kanban — take-home for [Company]

> A keyboard-accessible kanban board with drag-and-drop, optimistic
> updates, and persistence to a mock API.

## Live demo
https://kanban-takehome.vercel.app

## Run locally
pnpm install
pnpm dev          # http://localhost:3000
pnpm test         # unit + component
pnpm test:e2e     # playwright

## Tech choices and why
- Next.js 15 (App Router) — route handler gives a realistic mock
  persistence layer without a separate server.
- TanStack Query — server cache + optimistic move/create with rollback
  on error; saved hand-rolling cache invalidation.
- @dnd-kit — accessible DnD (keyboard + pointer) out of the box, hard to
  get right by hand in the time budget.
- Zod — one schema validates API payloads and types the client.
- Tailwind v4 — fast styling, no runtime cost.

## Architecture (~150 words)
Board state lives in TanStack Query keyed by board id. Mutations (create,
move) are optimistic: the cache updates immediately, the request fires,
and on error we roll back and toast. The route handler persists to an
in-memory store (swap for a DB in prod). DnD is decoupled from
persistence — drop computes the new column+index, then dispatches a move
mutation. Tradeoff: optimistic-first for instant feel over strict
consistency; on conflict the server response reconciles position.

## Beyond the spec
- Full keyboard DnD (Tab to card, Space to lift, arrows to move).
- Loading / empty / error / offline states on every async surface.
- Optimistic updates with rollback + toast on failure.
- INP ~120ms on the board route (web-vitals in console).

## With more time
- Real-time multi-user sync (WebSocket + per-card version for conflicts).
- Offline-first with a mutation queue replayed on reconnect.
- Visual regression tests (Playwright snapshots).

## Testing
- Unit/component (Vitest + RTL): move logic, optimistic rollback,
  empty/error rendering. ~85% on lib + hooks.
- E2E (Playwright): create card → drag to next column → reload →
  position persists.

## Known limitations
- Single board only; no auth (out of scope per brief).
- In-memory persistence resets on server restart.

4.6 Bar-raising touches

  • Storybook page for 1–2 key components.
  • Lighthouse / WebPageTest screenshot in README.
  • Accessibility audit (axe report or manual checklist).
  • Dark mode + prefers-reduced-motion + prefers-contrast.
  • Keyboard demo GIF (VHS or screen recorder).
  • 5-min Loom walkthrough explaining decisions.

Highest-ROI touches (do these first if time is short):

1. A clean-clone-tested README + live deploy. Single biggest score-per-minute.

2. Real edge-case states (empty/error/loading/offline) — most submissions skip these, so they're cheap differentiation.

3. Keyboard accessibility on the core interaction — instantly reads as senior.

4. One thoughtful "with more time" + a named tradeoff in the README — shows judgment.

5. A 3–5 min Loom walking the reviewer through your decisions — humanizes you and surfaces reasoning the code can't.

Skip the gold-plating (Storybook, exhaustive tests, animation polish) until the fundamentals above are done. A reviewer trusts an honest, tight 80% far more than a sprawling, half-working 120%.

4.7 Common pitfalls

  • Over-engineering: no Redux + Saga + GraphQL for 4-screen app.
  • Under-testing: at least the critical paths.
  • Skipping error/empty states.
  • Ignoring a11y.
  • No README story.
  • Going way over budget.

Pitfalls that quietly fail you:

  • Doesn't run from a clean clone (committed node_modules, missing env example, hard-coded local path, lockfile mismatch). Always git clone to a fresh dir and run the README steps verbatim before submitting.
  • Committed secrets / API keys — instant negative signal. Use .env.example and document required vars.
  • A single 4,000-line commit — small, labeled commits tell the story of how you work; reviewers read your git history.
  • Console errors/warnings on load — open DevTools and clear them; an unhandled React key warning undercuts a "I sweat the details" claim.
  • Lying in the README ("87% coverage" with two trivial tests) — reviewers check. Underclaim and overdeliver.
  • No assumptions section — when the spec is ambiguous, *state your assumption and move on*; reviewers grade judgment, not mind-reading.

4.8 Common briefs to be ready for

  • Trello-like kanban with DnD + persistence.
  • GitHub repo browser via API (search, paginate, view, star).
  • Weather dashboard with multi-city + charts + offline fallback.
  • TODO app with optimistic + undo + sync to mock backend.
  • Notion-lite block editor (text + heading + bullet + slash).
  • Stripe-like multi-step checkout + 3DS-style modal.
  • Music player UI: album list → tracks → playing bar with rAF.
  • Typeahead over JSON dataset; explain ranking tradeoffs.

The "senior move" for each brief — what separates a pass from a strong pass:

  • Kanban: keyboard-accessible DnD + optimistic move with rollback + persistence that survives reload.
  • GitHub browser: debounced search with request cancellation + a race guard, rate-limit handling, proper empty/error states for the API.
  • Weather dashboard: offline fallback via cached last-good data + Service Worker, and graceful degradation when one city's data fails (not a whole-page crash).
  • TODO + sync: optimistic create/toggle with undo (the undo tests whether you modeled state well), and reconciliation with the mock backend on conflict.
  • Block editor: clean content model (array of typed blocks), slash-menu, full keyboard navigation, and contenteditable handled deliberately (not naively).
  • Checkout: typed multi-step state machine, validation per step (Zod), idempotent submit, and a focus-trapped accessible modal for the 3DS step.
  • Music player: requestAnimationFrame-driven progress bar (not setInterval), Media Session API, keyboard controls.
  • Typeahead: debounce + cancel + race guard + ranking you can *explain* (prefix vs fuzzy, recency weighting) + full a11y combobox semantics.

In every case the differentiators are the same four: handle the network race, handle the empty/error states, make it keyboard-accessible, and explain one real tradeoff in the README.

Part 5 — Negotiation + interview cadence checklist

  • Block 2-week onsite cluster on calendar.
  • Pre-rehearse 6 STAR stories with timer.
  • Levels.fyi data printed for 5 target companies.
  • Resume tuned with measurable outcomes (numbers in every bullet).
  • LinkedIn matches resume; recent activity (posts / comments).
  • Refresh referrals at target companies 4 weeks before applying.
  • Practice 5 system design walkthroughs out loud.
  • First 24 hours after any offer: gather counter-data; no decision yet.
  • Have one trusted friend rehearse the negotiation call with you.
  • After every interview round: write down 3 questions you saw + 1 you bombed; iterate.

A week-by-week cadence that builds leverage:

Week -6   Refresh resume (numbers in every bullet) + LinkedIn. Line up referrals.
Week -4   Apply / activate referrals in a batch so loops cluster, not stagger.
Week -3   Rehearse 6 STAR stories (timer) + 5 FE-system-design walkthroughs aloud.
Week -2   Phone screens. After each: log 3 questions seen + 1 you bombed; iterate.
Week -1   Cluster onsites within ~2 weeks so offers overlap in time.
Week  0   Offers arrive. First 24h: gather counter-data, no decision. Then negotiate.
Week +1   Counter, iterate once or twice, accept warmly, get it in writing, resign.

The day-of-offer discipline (re-read this when an offer lands):

1. Be warm, get it in writing, commit to nothing on the call.

2. Pull Levels.fyi for the exact level *today* and line up any competing offers.

3. Send one structured counter with data and a real "what's possible?".

4. Iterate once, maybe twice — then close warmly with "I'd sign today."

5. Compare offers on steady-state TC (years 2–4), not year-1, and account for vesting shape.

6. Never resign your current job until the new offer letter is signed and in hand.

End of consolidated corpus. You now have a category-organized, version-preserving knowledge base. Doc 00 (Learning Path) is your hub; this doc closes the loop on the human side of the loop.

4.8 Common briefs to be ready for

docs.search: 08 — Behavioral · Companies · Negotiation · Take-Home (2026) STAR stories · Company-specific themes · Salary playbook · Take-home blueprint Merged from v1/05 (behavioral + company playbook) and v3/11 (QA + negotiation + take-home). The closing volume. Part 1 — STAR framework + 12 universal stories 1.1 STAR format Situation — context in 1–2 sentences. Task — your specific responsibility. Action — what YOU (not the team) did, with concrete steps. Result — outcome with NUMBERS and reflection on what you learned. How interviewers actually score it. At senior+ they listen for the ratio of "I" to "we", the presence of a real decision under constraint, and whether the result has a number you can defend. A story with no number reads as a hypothetical; a story that is all "we" reads as someone who rode along. Budget your 90 seconds roughly: Situation 10s, Task 10s, Action 50s, Result 20s. The Action is where signal lives — spend most words there. Senior-specific tells the panel grades: Did you change the *direction* of the work, or just execute someone else's plan? Did you weigh a tradeoff explicitly (named the option you rejected and why)? Did you bring others along — review, mentoring, alignment — vs heroics? Did you measure impact *after* shipping, not just claim it? Common anti-patterns that tank scores: The "we" story (no individual contribution visible). The conflict with no resolution ("…and they were just wrong"). The result with no metric ("it went really well"). The 4-minute ramble (you never reached the Result). 1.2 The 12 universal stories to prepare Tell me about a project you led end-to-end. Tell me about a time you disagreed with a manager / senior engineer / PM. Tell me about a time you made a mistake that mattered. Tell me about a time you raised the bar on a team's quality. Tell me about a difficult performance / production problem you solved. Tell me about a time you mentored someone (junior or peer). Tell me about a feature you shipped that users loved. Tell me about a time you removed something (code, dependency, scope, headcount). Tell me about a time you delivered under ambiguity. Tell me about a time you championed accessibility / security / DX. Tell me about a tradeoff you made between speed and quality. Tell me about a time you influenced without authority. Below: one fleshed-out, senior-FE STAR example per story. Swap in your own project names and numbers — keep the structure, the named tradeoff, and the closing metric. Story 1 — Led a project end-to-end > S: Our checkout was a 9,000-line React class-component monolith; conversion had plateaued and any change took two engineers a full sprint to ship safely. > T: I owned rebuilding checkout to a typed, server-driven flow without a conversion regression and without freezing the roadmap. > A: I wrote a one-page RFC, split the work into a strangler migration behind a flag, defined a typed step-machine (Zod-validated payloads), and shipped step-by-step behind a 5% → 25% → 100% rollout. I ran weekly demos and paired with the two least-confident engineers so the knowledge spread. > R: Shipped in 7 weeks; checkout p75 INP dropped 410ms → 180ms, conversion +2.3% (≈$1.4M annualized), time-to-ship a checkout change went from 2 weeks to 2 days. Learned: the flag-gated strangler bought the confidence to ship Fridays. Story 2 — Disagreed with a manager / senior / PM > S: My PM wanted to ship a redesigned settings page in one big-bang release for a launch date. > T: I believed big-bang would regress power users and wanted a staged rollout, but I didn't own the timeline. > A: Instead of arguing in standup, I pulled the funnel data, prototyped both, and brought a one-pager showing a staged rollout hit the *same* launch date for 90% of users while de-risking the long tail. I said the date was non-negotiable for me too — I was solving for it, not against it. > R: We staged it; caught a save-race bug at 10% that would've hit 100% of users on launch day. Hit the date, zero rollback. Learned: disagreement lands when you adopt the other person's constraint as your own and bring data. Story 3 — A mistake that mattered > S: I shipped a "harmless" date-library bump to our scheduling UI on a Thursday. > T: It was my change, my review I'd rushed. > A: Within an hour support flagged appointments showing the wrong day for users in half-hour-offset timezones. I rolled back immediately, posted in the incident channel owning it by name before anyone asked, then wrote a blameless postmortem. The root fix: a timezone test matrix (UTC, IST, NPT, Chatham) in CI so the class of bug couldn't recur. > R: Customer-impact window was 52 minutes; zero data loss. The matrix later caught two more regressions before release. Learned: "harmless" bumps need the same test gate as features. Story 4 — Raised the bar on quality > S: Our team's PRs routinely shipped with no tests and flaky CI everyone ignored ("just re-run it"). > T: As the senior IC I wasn't asked to fix this, but velocity was bleeding to rework. > A: I quantified it — 30% of weekly bugs traced to three untested modules. I added Vitest + RTL to those modules first (led by example, not mandate), set a *non-blocking* coverage report on PRs, fixed the top 5 flaky tests, and wrote a 1-page testing guide. Once the team saw green CI again, I proposed a soft coverage floor and they agreed. > R: Escaped-bug rate dropped ~40% over the quarter; CI flake rate went 15% → under 2%. Learned: lead quality bars with evidence and example before policy. Story 5 — Hard performance / production problem > S: Our dashboard's main route had p95 INP of 600ms; users reported "laggy typing" in a filter box. > T: I owned the perf workstream that quarter. > A: I profiled in DevTools Performance + measured INP in the field via web-vitals/RUM. Root cause: every keystroke synchronously re-rendered a 4,000-row table. I debounced input, moved filtering into useDeferredValue , virtualized the table (TanStack Virtual), and memoized row components — verifying each change against RUM, not just my fast laptop. > R: p95 INP 600ms → 150ms; "laggy" tickets to zero in 3 weeks; the busy route passed Core Web Vitals "good" for 96% of sessions. Learned: measure in the field — my M-series laptop hid the problem entirely. Story 6 — Mentored someone > S: A mid-level engineer joined strong on React but shaky on async and testing, and was stalling on a real-time feature. > T: I was their informal mentor and reviewer. > A: Rather than rewriting their PR, I pair-debugged a race condition with them, walked through the microtask queue on a whiteboard, and set up a weekly 30-min "async clinic." I reviewed for teaching — comments explained the *why* and pointed at docs, not just "change this." > R: They shipped the real-time presence feature solo two sprints later and now run the clinic themselves; promoted within the year. Learned: reviewing to teach scales better than reviewing to fix. Story 7 — Feature users loved > S: Power users kept asking for keyboard navigation; mouse-only flows were slow for them. > T: I pitched and led a Cmd-K command palette. > A: I prototyped on a Friday, validated with 6 power users, then built it properly: fuzzy search, recent-actions ranking, full a11y (focus trap, ARIA, screen-reader labels), and a registry so any team could register commands. I instrumented usage from day one. > R: Within a month 38% of weekly-active power users used it daily; median task time for the top 3 workflows dropped ~45%. Most-upvoted item in our changelog. Learned: ship instrumentation with the feature so "loved" is a number. Story 8 — Removed something > S: We carried a 90KB-gzip charting library used on exactly two screens, dragging bundle and LCP. > T: I owned bundle health. > A: I audited usage, found we used ~4 chart types, replaced it with ~6KB of hand-rolled SVG plus lazy-loading the one complex screen, and deleted the dependency, its wrapper abstraction, and 1,200 lines of dead config. > R: Main bundle −82KB gzip; dashboard LCP 2.9s → 2.1s; one fewer CVE to track. Learned: the best perf win is often deletion, not optimization. Story 9 — Delivered under ambiguity > S: Leadership wanted "an analytics view" for a new product with no spec, no designs, and a 3-week window before a customer demo. > T: I had to define *and* build it. > A: I interviewed 3 target customers in two days, wrote my own one-page spec with explicit non-goals, got a 15-minute sign-off, and shipped the smallest version that answered the top 3 questions customers asked — behind a flag so we could iterate post-demo without a release. > R: Demo landed the deal; v1 shipped in 2.5 weeks and iterated to GA from real usage. Learned: under ambiguity, writing the spec yourself *is* the leadership. Story 10 — Championed a11y / security / DX > S: Our app had never been a11y-audited and we were about to sign an enterprise customer with a VPAT requirement. > T: No one owned a11y; I volunteered. > A: I ran axe + manual screen-reader (VoiceOver/NVDA) passes, triaged ~120 issues by severity, fixed the WCAG-A blockers myself (focus management, labels, contrast), added jest-axe to CI to prevent regressions, and ran a lunch-and-learn so the team could maintain it. > R: Passed the VPAT review, unblocked a 6-figure contract, and a11y CI now catches ~3 regressions/month before merge. Learned: a11y is cheapest as a CI gate, not a pre-signature scramble. Story 11 — Speed vs quality tradeoff > S: A competitor shipped a feature and sales wanted ours in two weeks; doing it "right" was a month. > T: I had to decide what to cut without creating a mess we'd regret. > A: I split it: a deliberately scoped v1 in two weeks (one happy path, feature-flagged, with a tracked tech-debt ticket and a written "what we knowingly skipped" note), but refused to cut tests on the payment path or skip the error states. I made the cut *explicit and reversible* rather than silent. > R: Hit the two-week date; v1 converted well enough to justify the proper v2, shipped a month later with zero rework on the core. Learned: speed/quality is fine when the debt is named, tracked, and the non-negotiables (money, data, a11y) are protected. Story 12 — Influenced without authority > S: Three teams each hand-rolled their own data-fetching, causing inconsistent caching and duplicated bugs; I owned none of them. > T: I wanted a shared TanStack Query layer but couldn't mandate it. > A: I built it for my own team first, measured the win (fewer bugs, less code), then wrote it up and offered to do the first migration *for* each team in a pairing session. I made adoption lower-effort than the status quo and let the data argue. > R: All three teams adopted within a quarter; duplicated fetching bugs dropped to near-zero and we deleted ~2K lines. Learned: influence without authority = make the better path the easier path, then prove it with one team's numbers. 1.3 Story-writing checklist Specific dates / project names / numbers (3 engineers, 2-week sprint, 200K MAU). Show your decision-making, not just outcome. Include one disagreement or constraint you navigated. End with a measured result + what you would do differently. Keep each story to 90 seconds verbal — practice with a timer. Build a reusable story bank. Most of the 12 prompts can be answered from 5–6 real projects. Map each project to the prompts it can serve, so in the room you pick the strongest angle on the fly rather than memorizing 12 scripts. Keep a one-line "headline metric" per project committed to memory — it anchors the whole story. The follow-up drill. Senior interviewers always probe: "What would you do differently?", "How did the other person react?", "What was the hardest part?", "How did you measure that?". Pre-write a one-sentence answer to each of those four for every story. The follow-ups are where weak candidat

docs.html:
09 — Advanced Production FE Techniques (2026)

20 parts of real prod patterns: React internals · rendering · network · state · real-time · large data · a11y · auth · AI · telemetry · testing · debug

Techniques senior FE engineers actually reach for in production. Not theory — the patterns Figma, Linear, Stripe, Vercel, Notion, Netflix actually ship. Pair with Doc 03 (modern stack), Doc 05 (FRSA), Doc 06 (system design).

Part 1 — React internals + advanced patterns

1.1 Fiber + reconciliation

  • Fiber = a linked-list of work units; React can pause + resume + abort work.
  • Two phases: render (pure, can pause) → commit (DOM mutations, synchronous).
  • Concurrent renderer can prepare multiple versions of UI; only commits one.
  • Senior tell: explain why state updates outside startTransition feel sluggish under load.

A fiber node holds type, pendingProps, memoizedState (the hook chain), and child/sibling/return pointers so React walks the tree as a list, yielding to the browser every ~5ms via the scheduler. Updates outside startTransition are synchronous-priority: they block paint until the whole tree reconciles. Marking the expensive update as a transition lets React interrupt it to keep typing responsive.

const [tab, setTab] = useState("all");
const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();
function select(next: string) {

Scale gotcha: a single non-transition setState that triggers a huge subtree (e.g. a 5k-row list filter) starves input handlers — wrap the heavy update, keep the controlled input value as urgent state.

1.2 StrictMode double-rendering

  • React intentionally invokes function components + effects twice in dev to surface impure render and missing cleanup.
  • Cleanup must be idempotent — useEffect cleanup runs between the double mount.
  • Treat your useEffect "setup → cleanup → setup" as a contract.

StrictMode mounts, unmounts, then remounts each component in dev (effects run setup → cleanup → setup). It is the cheapest way to catch subscriptions that leak, refs that double-register, or one-time side effects fired in render. It is dev-only — production runs once.

useEffect(() => {
  const sub = stream.subscribe(onMsg);
  return () => sub.unsubscribe(); // must fully undo setup

Scale gotcha: code that "works" because it accidentally relied on a single mount (e.g. incrementing a server counter in an effect) double-fires in StrictMode and again under React 19's offscreen prerendering — make effects idempotent, not order-dependent.

1.3 Batching (automatic in React 18+)

  • All setState calls in any event handler, promise, setTimeout, or native event are batched into a single re-render.
  • flushSync(() => setState(...)) opts out of batching — synchronous, useful for measuring DOM after change.

Automatic batching means multiple setStates across awaits collapse to one render, cutting wasted commits. flushSync forces a synchronous commit so you can read post-render layout (e.g. scroll a freshly inserted node into view) before the next line runs.

flushSync(() => setItems(next));
listRef.current?.lastElementChild?.scrollIntoView();

Scale gotcha: flushSync defeats concurrency and triggers a synchronous reflow — calling it in a loop or on every keystroke reintroduces the jank batching removed. Use it once, after the mutation, never inside a render or effect body.

1.4 Compound components

// Tabs.Tab + Tabs.Panel pattern — shares state via Context
<Tabs defaultValue="overview">
  <Tabs.List>

Compound components share implicit state through Context so consumers compose freely without prop-drilling activeTab everywhere. The parent owns state; children read it via a private context hook that throws if used outside the provider.

Scale gotcha: Context re-renders every consumer on any value change — for large tab sets memoize the context value and split selection state from heavy panel content so switching a tab doesn't re-render unrelated panels.

1.5 Polymorphic components (as prop)

type Props<C extends React.ElementType> = { as?: C } & React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<C>;
function Button<C extends React.ElementType = "button">({ as, ...rest }: Props<C>) {
  const Comp = as || "button";

Polymorphic components let one styled component render any element/component while keeping prop types correct for the chosen tag (href valid only when as="a"). Add ref forwarding with ComponentPropsWithRef and a generic forwardRef wrapper for full correctness.

Scale gotcha: the as prop explodes TypeScript inference time in large design systems — prefer the Radix asChild/Slot pattern (1.6) over deep polymorphic generics once you have hundreds of components, or compile times and editor hovers degrade badly.

1.6 Slot pattern (Radix style)

  • Use @radix-ui/react-slot — Slot forwards refs + props to a single child instead of rendering a wrapper element.
  • Powers asChild={true} composition: <Button asChild><Link href="…">Go</Link></Button>.

Slot merges the parent's props, event handlers, refs, and className onto its single child element so you avoid an extra DOM wrapper and inherit the child's semantics. asChild is the ergonomic switch that picks Slot vs the default element.

import { Slot } from "@radix-ui/react-slot";
function Button({ asChild, ...props }: { asChild?: boolean } & React.ComponentProps<"button">) {
  const Comp = asChild ? Slot : "button";

Scale gotcha: Slot merges event handlers by calling both — if the child also defines onClick, both fire; and only a single child is allowed, so a fragment or multiple children throws at runtime, easy to hit when content is conditionally rendered.

1.7 Render props + headless components

  • Headless: provide behavior, no markup. Examples: React Aria, Radix Primitives, Headless UI, TanStack Table.
  • You own the look + a11y; the library owns the state machine + keyboard.

Headless libraries return state + prop-getters; you spread them onto your own markup, keeping full control of styling while inheriting correct ARIA and keyboard behavior. This is why design systems standardize on TanStack Table / React Aria rather than styled black-box widgets.

const table = useReactTable({ data, columns, getCoreRowModel: getCoreRowModel() });
return table.getRowModel().rows.map(r => (
  <tr key={r.id}>{r.getVisibleCells().map(c =>

Scale gotcha: headless gives you the rope to omit a11y — prop-getters supply roles/aria, but if you don't spread them (or override role), you ship an inaccessible widget that automated axe tests may still pass. Treat the getter spread as mandatory.

1.8 State machines (XState)

  • Use for wizards, async retry, payment flows, video player, anything with > 4 states + guards.
const machine = createMachine({
  initial: "idle",
  states: {
  • Replaces tangled useEffect chains for complex async.
  • Visualize at stately.ai — designers can validate flows.

A statechart makes illegal transitions unrepresentable: you only reach loading via SUBMIT, so double-submits and "retry while already saving" bugs vanish. XState v5 uses setup() for typed actors/guards and useMachine to bind in React.

Scale gotcha: teams over-model trivial UI as machines and pay the boilerplate tax. Reserve XState for genuinely stateful flows (>4 states, guards, parallel regions); for simple async, useReducer or TanStack Query mutation states are lighter.

1.9 useSyncExternalStore

  • Subscribe to non-React state (window size, localStorage, Zustand, observers) tear-free in concurrent mode.
function useWindowWidth() {
  return useSyncExternalStore(
    cb => { window.addEventListener("resize", cb); return () => window.removeEventListener("resize", cb); },

This hook is the official way to read mutable external sources without tearing (different parts of one render seeing different values) under concurrent rendering. The three args are subscribe, client snapshot, and server snapshot — the last prevents hydration mismatch.
