Scale gotcha: the snapshot getter must return a referentially stable value — returning a fresh object/array each call causes an infinite render loop. Memoize or use useSyncExternalStoreWithSelector to compare derived slices.

1.10 useImperativeHandle (escape hatch, use sparingly)

  • Expose an imperative API from a child to a parent ref — e.g. <Modal ref={r}> with r.current.open().
  • Senior tell: prefer declarative props; reach for this only when the prop model doesn't fit (focus(), scrollIntoView(), play()).

useImperativeHandle customizes what a parent ref sees, exposing methods instead of the raw DOM node. Legitimate when the action is truly imperative and momentary — focus, play, scroll — where modeling it as state would be awkward.

const Video = forwardRef<{ play(): void }, { src: string }>((p, ref) => {
  const el = useRef<HTMLVideoElement>(null);
  useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({ play: () => el.current?.play() }), []);

Scale gotcha: imperative handles bypass React's data flow, so parent/child can desync — calling .open() while the parent also controls open via prop creates two sources of truth. Pick one model per component; React 19 lets you take ref as a normal prop, reducing forwardRef boilerplate.

Part 2 — Rendering + hydration optimization

2.1 The rendering spectrum

ModeWhen the HTML is builtJS sent to client
SSGAt build timeHydration JS
ISRBuild + on-demand revalidateHydration JS
SSRPer request on serverHydration JS
Streaming SSRPer request, streamed in chunksHydration JS, selective
CSRIn the browser after JS loadsEverything
RSCPer request on serverZero for Server Components; islands hydrate
PPRStatic shell at build + dynamic streamsHydration JS for dynamic islands

The axis that matters is *when HTML is produced* vs *how much JS ships to make it interactive*. RSC and PPR win in 2026 because they push the static shell to the CDN edge instantly and stream only the dynamic, per-request parts, while Server Components ship zero client JS.

// Next.js PPR: static shell, dynamic island streamed in
export const experimental_ppr = true;
export default function Page() {

Scale gotcha: mixing modes per route is the real skill — a single cookies()/headers() call or uncached fetch opts a whole route out of static rendering, silently turning fast SSG into per-request SSR. Audit with the build's static/dynamic markers.

2.2 Streaming SSR (React 18+)

  • renderToReadableStream / renderToPipeableStream emit HTML chunk-by-chunk.
  • Suspense boundaries flush as ready (out-of-order).
  • Selective hydration: React prioritizes hydrating the part the user is interacting with.
  • Result: TTFB drops to network-only; LCP drops if shell is small.

Streaming sends the shell immediately and flushes each Suspense boundary's HTML as its data resolves, using inline <script> to slot late chunks into place. The browser paints the shell before slow data is ready, so TTFB and LCP decouple from your slowest query.

const stream = await renderToReadableStream(<App />, {
  bootstrapScripts: ["/main.js"],
  onError(e) { logServerError(e); },

Scale gotcha: once the shell flushes you've already sent a 200 and committed headers — you can no longer redirect or change status for errors found mid-stream. Resolve auth/redirects *before* the first byte, and design error UI to render inline within boundaries.

2.3 Islands architecture

  • Static HTML by default; "islands" of interactivity hydrate independently.
  • Astro / Fresh / Qwik are island-first frameworks.
  • Best for content-heavy sites (blog, docs, marketing) — Server Components in Next.js give similar results.

Islands ship mostly static HTML and hydrate only flagged interactive components, each with its own tiny JS bundle and its own hydration trigger. For content sites this cuts client JS by an order of magnitude versus a full SPA.

---
import Counter from "../Counter.tsx";
---

Scale gotcha: islands can't share live client state easily — two islands that must coordinate go through a shared store (nanostores) or events, and over-using client:load everywhere reconstitutes a slow SPA. Keep interactive islands few and coarse.

2.4 Resumability (Qwik)

  • Qwik serializes all closures into HTML; "resumes" instead of hydrating.
  • Zero JS until user interacts; download only the handler needed.
  • Tradeoff: large HTML payload; production maturity vs React ecosystem.

Resumability skips hydration entirely: Qwik serializes app state and event-handler references into the HTML, so the page is interactive on load and the matching handler chunk is fetched lazily only when an event fires. Time-to-interactive is constant regardless of app size.

export const Counter = component$(() => {
  const c = useSignal(0);
  return <button onClick$={() => c.value++}>{c.value}</button>; // $ = lazy boundary

Scale gotcha: the serialized state bloats HTML and the on-first-interaction fetch adds latency to the very first click — pre-warm critical handlers, and weigh the smaller ecosystem (fewer libs, fewer hires who know it) against the TTI win before betting a large app on it.

2.5 Selective hydration tricks

  • Wrap heavy interactive trees in <Suspense> so React de-prioritizes their hydration.
  • Lazy hydration libraries (react-lazy-hydration) defer non-critical islands until idle / visible / interaction.

Wrapping a subtree in Suspense tells React it may hydrate later and out of order; React also re-prioritizes to hydrate whatever the user clicks first. You can go further and gate hydration on idle/visible/interaction for non-critical widgets.

function WhenVisible({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const [show, set] = useState(false); const ref = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  useEffect(() => { const o = new IntersectionObserver(([e]) => e.isIntersecting && set(true));

Scale gotcha: deferring hydration on something the user might touch immediately (sticky header, search box) produces "dead" UI that swallows the first click. Reserve lazy hydration for genuinely below-the-fold widgets, and always hydrate on first pointer/focus as a fallback.

2.6 Speculation Rules API

<script type="speculationrules">
{
  "prerender": [
  • Browser-native pre-render of likely next pages.
  • Outperforms next/link prefetch on full navigation.

Speculation Rules let the browser fully prerender a next page in a hidden tab (running its JS) or just prefetch the document, keyed off URL patterns and an eagerness hint tied to hover/pointerdown heuristics. Activation on click is near-instant because the page is already rendered.

Scale gotcha: prerender *executes* the target page, firing analytics, A/B exposure, and fetches before navigation — gate side effects behind document.prerendering / the prerenderingchange event, and use conservative eagerness to avoid wasting bandwidth and skewing metrics.

2.7 Early Hints (HTTP 103)

  • Server sends 103 with Link headers BEFORE the final response — browser can start preconnect / preload while server thinks.
  • Cuts TTFB-to-LCP latency on slow backend by 100–300 ms.
  • Supported on Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge, Fastly.

A 103 Early Hints response carries Link: rel=preload/preconnect headers the browser acts on while the origin is still composing the final 200, overlapping server think-time with asset fetching. Biggest wins are on slow/database-bound backends.

HTTP/1.1 103 Early Hints
Link: </css/app.css>; rel=preload; as=style
Link: <https://cdn.img.example>; rel=preconnect

Scale gotcha: hint the wrong assets (e.g. a hashed bundle name that changed) and you waste bandwidth and connections; also many intermediary proxies still strip 103. Verify end-to-end via the CDN, and only hint truly render-blocking, stable resources.

Part 3 — Bundle + build optimization

3.1 Modern build tools

ToolStrengthWhen to pick
Viteesbuild dev + Rollup prod; ergonomicNew SPAs, libraries, Vue/Svelte, anything not Next
Next.js (Turbopack)Tight integration with RSC + Server ActionsProduction React apps with full-stack needs
RspackWebpack-API compatible + Rust speedWebpack migration without rewriting config
BunBundler + runtime; fastest installGreenfield TS apps that want speed
esbuildRaw speed; minimal plugin APILibraries with simple build needs
SWCRust transpiler — replaces BabelAlready in Next, Vite plugins

In 2026 the dividing line is RSC: if you need Server Components/Actions, Next.js + Turbopack is the integrated path; otherwise Vite (now on Rolldown, its Rust Rollup) is the default for SPAs and libraries. Rspack/Rsbuild is the escape hatch for legacy Webpack configs that can't be rewritten.

// vite.config.ts — split heavy vendors deterministically
export default defineConfig({
  build: { rollupOptions: { output: { manualChunks: { editor: ["monaco-editor"] } } } },

Scale gotcha: dev (esbuild/Rolldown) and prod (Rollup) bundlers differ, so a build can pass locally and bloat in CI — always test the production build, not just vite dev, and pin the toolchain to avoid silent transform differences across the team.

3.2 Tree-shaking checklist

  • Use ESM imports; never default-import a big object then destructure.
  • Set "sideEffects": false in package.json for pure libraries.
  • Verify with Bundle Analyzer / statoscope; look for unexpected transitives.
  • Replace named-import-from-deep-path with index-export only if the lib supports tree-shaking.

Tree-shaking only works on static ESM with honest sideEffects metadata; one CommonJS dependency or a barrel file with side effects can drag in an entire library. Verify, never assume — analyzers reveal the transitive deps that re-bundled a "removed" module.

// package.json — let bundlers drop unused exports but keep CSS
{ "sideEffects": ["*.css", "./src/polyfills.ts"] }

Scale gotcha: barrel files (index.ts re-exporting everything) defeat tree-shaking in many bundlers because importing one symbol pulls the whole barrel's side-effect graph — import from the deep path, or have the lib ship "sideEffects": false, and watch for __esModule interop wrappers that block elimination.

3.3 Module Federation

  • Multiple independently deployed micro-frontends share a single runtime.
  • Best for: large orgs with team-per-domain (Figma plugins, Walmart, Microsoft 365).
  • 2026 evolution: Native ESM Federation via Import Maps; Server-Side Module Federation for RSC.
  • Don't reach for it under 100 engineers.

Module Federation lets independently built/deployed apps consume each other's modules at runtime and share singletons (one React copy) via a negotiated shared scope. It buys org-scale independent deploys at the cost of runtime coupling.

new ModuleFederationPlugin({
  name: "host",
  remotes: { cart: "cart@https://cart.app/remoteEntry.js" },

Scale gotcha: version skew is the killer — if host and remote disagree on a singleton major (two Reacts), you get hook-dispatcher crashes at runtime, not build time. Enforce a shared-deps contract and runtime version checks; below ~100 engineers a monorepo is simpler and faster.

3.4 Code splitting strategies

  • Route-level: default for SPAs and Next.js.
  • Component-level: lazy() for heavy widgets (charts, editor, video).
  • Vendor-level: manual chunks for large deps (react-pdf, monaco-editor).
  • Conditional: admin code only loaded if user.isAdmin.

Split along the axes of *who needs what when*: routes by default, then carve out heavy or rarely-used widgets and admin-only code so the common path stays lean. Pair each lazy() boundary with a Suspense fallback and a preload-on-intent.

const Editor = lazy(() => import("./Editor"));
const preloadEditor = () => import("./Editor"); // call on hover/focus
<button onMouseEnter={preloadEditor} onClick={open}>Edit</button>

Scale gotcha: over-splitting creates a waterfall of tiny chunks that's *slower* than one bundle on high-latency networks; and a lazy() chunk that fails to load (deploy rotated the hash) throws — add an error boundary with retry and preload critical routes.

3.5 Monorepo orchestration

  • Turborepo / Nx / pnpm workspaces.
  • Remote build cache — Turborepo Remote Cache, Nx Cloud — slashes CI 50–80%.
  • Task graph: lint+test+build run only on affected packages.
  • Shared TS config + ESLint config as packages.

Monorepo tooling builds a task graph from package dependencies and a content hash of inputs, so unchanged packages restore from cache (local or remote) instead of rebuilding. Affected-only execution keeps CI time proportional to the change, not the repo.

// turbo.json
{ "tasks": { "build": { "dependsOn": ["^build"], "outputs": ["dist/**"] },
             "test": { "dependsOn": ["build"], "cache": true } } }

Scale gotcha: caches are only correct if every input is declared — an undeclared env var or generated file produces a false cache hit that ships stale output. Pin inputs/globalDependencies explicitly, and beware remote-cache poisoning from one bad CI run propagating to everyone.

3.6 Bundle size budget enforcement

// .size-limit.json
[
  { "name": "Home", "path": ".next/static/chunks/pages/index*.js", "limit": "180 KB" },
  • Fails PR on regression — performance becomes a contract.

Budgets turn bundle size into a CI gate so regressions fail the PR instead of slowly rotting performance over quarters. Track gzipped (or brotli) size on the critical entry chunks, and post the delta as a PR comment for visibility.

Scale gotcha: a single shared chunk's growth can blow many route budgets at once and block unrelated PRs — budget the *delta* per PR and the absolute on key routes, exempt vendor chunks you can't fix quickly, and review limits quarterly so they ratchet down rather than drift up.

Part 4 — Network optimization

4.1 Resource hints reference

HintWhat it doesWhen
dns-prefetchDNS lookup earlyCross-origin domain you will fetch from
preconnectDNS + TCP + TLS earlyCritical cross-origin (fonts, image CDN)
preloadFetch the resource at high priorityCritical fonts, LCP image, hero CSS
prefetchFetch at low priority for next navLikely next route
modulepreloadPreload ESM module + its importsCritical JS chunks
fetchpriorityHint priority on <img>, <link>, fetch()LCP image gets "high"; below-fold "low"

Hints let you front-run the browser's preload scanner for resources it can't discover early (fonts referenced in CSS, the LCP image set via JS, the next route). Use the strongest hint matching your certainty: preconnect for origins you'll definitely use, preload for this-page-critical bytes, prefetch for maybe-next.

<link rel="preconnect" href="https://cdn.img" crossorigin>
<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.avif" fetchpriority="high">

Scale gotcha: preloading too much *demotes* truly critical bytes (every preload competes for bandwidth) and triggers "preloaded but not used" console warnings; preconnecting to many origins wastes sockets. Hint only 2–4 critical resources and measure LCP before/after.

4.2 HTTP/2 + HTTP/3

  • HTTP/2: multiplexing, header compression, server push (deprecated in favor of Early Hints).
  • HTTP/3 (QUIC): UDP-based, eliminates head-of-line blocking, faster handshake.
  • Enable at CDN; clients negotiate automatically.

HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection but still suffers TCP-level head-of-line blocking on packet loss; HTTP/3 moves to QUIC over UDP with per-stream loss recovery and a 0-1 RTT handshake, which shines on lossy mobile networks. Both negotiate via ALPN automatically.

listen 443 quic reuseport;     # HTTP/3
listen 443 ssl;                # HTTP/2 fallback
add_header Alt-Svc 'h3=":443"; ma=86400';  # advertise h3

Scale gotcha: with multiplexing, old "domain sharding" and "concat everything" tricks become anti-patterns (they hurt caching and priority), but splitting into hundreds of requests still costs per-request overhead and can overflow the server's stream/flow-control limits. Measure; don't cargo-cult either era.

4.3 Compression

  • Brotli for text > gzip — ~20% better compression at same CPU.
  • Pre-compress static assets in build (.br + .gz) for zero CPU at request time.
  • Dynamic responses: enable Brotli at the CDN edge.

Brotli at max quality beats gzip ~15–25% on text, and pre-compressing static assets at build time means zero per-request CPU. For dynamic responses use a moderate Brotli level (4–6) at the edge to balance ratio vs latency. Zstd is emerging for dynamic content.

// Vite: emit .br and .gz alongside assets
import compression from "vite-plugin-compression";
export default { plugins: [compression({ algorithm: "brotliCompress" }), compression()] };

Scale gotcha: compressing already-compressed payloads (images, video, WOFF2 fonts) wastes CPU for no gain and can add bytes — scope compression to text MIME types, and never compress responses that mix secrets with attacker-influenced reflected input over the same context (BREACH).

4.4 Connection optimization

  • Keep-Alive + multiplexed HTTP/2 — many requests on one connection.
  • Coalesce small requests into batches (DataLoader pattern on FE).
  • Avoid CORS preflights via simple headers (Content-Type: text/plain or use credentials: omit).

Coalescing many small reads into one batched request cuts per-request overhead and round-trips; a frontend DataLoader collects calls within a tick and fires one fetch. Keeping requests "simple" (allowed methods/headers) avoids the extra OPTIONS preflight round-trip.

const loader = new DataLoader<string, User>(async (ids) =>
  (await fetch(`/api/users?ids=${ids.join(",")}`).then(r => r.json())).map(Object));
const [a, b] = await Promise.all([loader.load("1"), loader.load("2")]); // one network call

Scale gotcha: over-coalescing increases latency for the first caller (it waits for the batch window) and creates a single point of failure — one batch error fails N logical reads. Cap batch size, set a short debounce, and map batch errors back to per-key rejections.

Part 5 — Asset pipeline (the place where most wins hide)

5.1 Images — the full menu

  • Formats: AVIF (best), WebP (broad fallback), JPEG XL (rising), JPEG (legacy).
  • Responsive: srcset + sizes for DPR + viewport variants.
  • Art direction: <picture> with different crops per viewport.
  • LCP image: fetchpriority="high", preload, no lazy.
  • Below fold: loading="lazy", decoding="async".
  • Placeholder: BlurHash (compressed blur), LQIP (low-quality JPEG), or dominant color.
  • CDNs: Cloudflare Images, Cloudinary, Imgix, Vercel Image Optimization — transform on the fly.
<picture>
  <source srcSet="/h-960.avif 1x, /h-1920.avif 2x" type="image/avif" media="(max-width: 768px)" />
  <source srcSet="/h-2400.avif" type="image/avif" />

Images are usually the LCP element, so wins compound: serve AVIF/WebP, ship only the resolution the viewport needs via srcset/sizes, reserve space with width/height to kill CLS, and prioritize the hero while lazy-loading the rest. A blurhash/LQIP placeholder hides decode latency.

Scale gotcha: lazy-loading the LCP image (a global loading="lazy" default, or a framework <Image> without priority) delays LCP by a full round-trip — explicitly opt the hero into fetchpriority="high". Always set explicit dimensions; intrinsic-only sizing reintroduces layout shift.

5.2 Video

  • HLS / DASH for adaptive bitrate; players: hls.js, Shaka Player, video.js, MUX Player.
  • Autoplay rules — muted, playsinline, user gesture for sound.
  • Hover trailer: low-bitrate WebM; pre-fetch on hover with 600 ms grace.
  • Reserved aspect-ratio prevents CLS.

Adaptive streaming (HLS/DASH) ships a manifest of bitrate variants so the player switches quality to match bandwidth; for short autoplay loops a single muted, playsinline MP4/WebM is lighter than a full ABR stack. Reserve aspect-ratio so the player doesn't shift layout on load.

import Hls from "hls.js";
useEffect(() => { const v = ref.current!;
  if (Hls.isSupported()) { const h = new Hls(); h.loadSource(src); h.attachMedia(v); return () => h.destroy(); }

Scale gotcha: autoplay is blocked unless muted + playsinline, and even then iOS Low Power Mode and Data Saver can refuse — always provide a poster and tap-to-play fallback, and don't preload full video on hover for every card (debounce with a grace period or you saturate the network on a grid).

5.3 Fonts

  • Variable fonts — one file, infinite weights/widths.
  • Subset to glyphs actually used (glyphhanger, fonttools).
  • font-display: swap (or optional for stricter LCP).
  • size-adjust to eliminate font-swap CLS.
  • next/font / @fontsource auto-subset + self-host.

One variable WOFF2, subset to the glyphs you render and self-hosted, removes a third-party connection and dozens of static weights. font-display: swap avoids invisible text; size-adjust/ascent-override on a fallback metric-matches the web font so the swap doesn't shift layout.

@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter"; src: url("/inter.woff2") format("woff2-variations");
  font-weight: 100 900; font-display: swap;

Scale gotcha: font-display: swap trades CLS for a flash of fallback text, and skipping metric-matching makes the swap reflow your LCP text. For strictest LCP use optional (no swap after the block period) on body text, and preload only the one weight used above the fold.

5.4 Critical CSS extraction

  • Inline above-the-fold CSS in <head>; defer rest.
  • Tools: Critters (Vue), Beasties (Astro), Next.js built-in critical CSS.
  • Tradeoff: larger HTML; but one less round-trip.

Inlining the CSS needed for the initial viewport removes a render-blocking round-trip, letting first paint happen from the HTML alone; the full stylesheet then loads non-blocking. Tools compute the critical set per page automatically.

<style>/* inlined above-the-fold rules */ .hero{...}</style>
<link rel="preload" href="/app.css" as="style" onload="this.rel='stylesheet'">
<noscript><link rel="stylesheet" href="/app.css"></noscript>

Scale gotcha: inlined critical CSS isn't cached across navigations (it lives in the HTML), so repeat visits re-download it; and a stale "critical" set after a design change ships a flash of wrong styling. Regenerate every build and keep the inlined set small (<14KB to fit the first congestion window).

5.5 Icons

  • SVG sprite OR per-icon component (tree-shaken).
  • lucide-react / react-icons; never bundle the whole pack.

Import icons individually so the bundler tree-shakes the rest of the pack, or use one cached SVG sprite referenced by <use> to avoid duplicating path data per instance. Either beats shipping a 2MB icon font or the whole library object.

import { Search } from "lucide-react"; // single icon, tree-shaken
// or sprite:
<svg width={20} height={20}><use href="/icons.svg#search" /></svg>

Scale gotcha: barrel imports like import * as Icons from "react-icons" defeat tree-shaking and pull megabytes; some icon libs re-export through a barrel that breaks shaking even on named imports — verify the icon chunk size in the analyzer and prefer per-icon deep imports or a sprite at design-system scale.

Part 6 — State management at production scale

6.1 TanStack Query advanced

  • queryKey is your cache identity — design it stable + serializable.
  • staleTime vs gcTime: staleTime = how long fresh; gcTime = how long unused stays in memory.
  • Infinite queries: useInfiniteQuery + getNextPageParam for cursor pagination.
  • Suspense mode (useSuspenseQuery) — throws Promises; React Suspense catches.
  • Optimistic via onMutate: snapshot prev → cancel queries → set optimistic → return rollback ctx.
  • Mutation defaults: retry: 0 for non-idempotent.

The query key *is* the cache identity, so structure it as a serializable hierarchy (["todos", filters]) to scope invalidation. The canonical optimistic flow cancels in-flight refetches, snapshots, applies the optimistic value, rolls back in onError, then reconciles in onSettled.

useMutation({
  mutationFn: rename,
  async onMutate(next) { await qc.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ["todo", next.id] });

Scale gotcha: forgetting cancelQueries lets an in-flight GET resolve *after* your optimistic write and clobber it; and staleTime: 0 refetches on every mount/focus, hammering the API on busy dashboards. Set deliberate staleTime, and never auto-retry non-idempotent mutations.

6.2 Zustand at scale

  • Split into feature slices via combine middleware.
  • persist middleware with versioned migrations.
  • subscribeWithSelector for non-React listeners.
  • immer middleware for clean nested updates.
  • Don't put server data here — that's TanStack's job.

At scale, compose Zustand from typed slices, select narrowly so components re-render only on what they read, and persist with versioned migrations so old localStorage shapes upgrade safely. Keep it for *client* state — UI, drafts, selection — not server cache.

const useStore = create<Store>()(persist(immer((set) => ({
  count: 0, inc: () => set((s) => { s.count++; }),
})), { name: "app", version: 2, migrate: (s, v) => v < 2 ? upgrade(s) : s }));

Scale gotcha: selecting the whole store (useStore()) or returning a new object/array from the selector re-renders on every change — use useShallow for object selectors. Mixing server data into Zustand reintroduces the cache-invalidation problems TanStack Query already solves.

6.3 Multi-tab state sync

  • BroadcastChannel — broadcast within same origin across tabs.
  • Storage events fire when localStorage changes in another tab.
  • Web Locks API — coordinate single-leader work (e.g. one tab does the WebSocket).
// Lock pattern
await navigator.locks.request("primary-tab", async (lock) => {
  // I am the only tab doing this

Use BroadcastChannel for live cross-tab messaging (logout, cache bust), storage events as a fallback, and the Web Locks API to elect a single "leader" tab that owns the shared WebSocket/refresh loop while others consume its results.

Scale gotcha: a leader tab can die without releasing app-level state — the Web Lock auto-releases on close so a new leader is elected, but any in-memory work is lost. Make leader work resumable (persist progress to IDB), and debounce broadcast storms when many tabs react to one event.

6.4 Optimistic concurrency

  • Version number per resource; PUT includes If-Match: <etag>.
  • Server rejects on stale version → UI surfaces conflict + merge UX.
  • CRDTs auto-merge; OT requires server-side transform.

Optimistic concurrency sends the version/ETag you read with your write; the server rejects with 412 if someone else wrote first, so you never silently overwrite. The UI then surfaces a conflict/merge flow instead of last-write-wins data loss.

const res = await fetch(`/doc/${id}`, {
  method: "PUT", headers: { "If-Match": etag }, body: JSON.stringify(next),
});

Scale gotcha: under high contention (hot document, many editors) 412s become frequent and a naive "reload and retry" loop livelocks — for truly collaborative docs move to CRDTs/OT (Part 7) where edits merge automatically; reserve ETag concurrency for low-contention single-owner resources.

6.5 Undo/redo with command pattern

  • Every user action = a Command with do() + undo().
  • Stack of commands; cap at N (memory).
  • Persist to IDB for crash recovery.

Model each mutation as a reversible command with do/undo; an undo stack and redo stack give linear history, and capping the stack bounds memory. Persisting the stack to IndexedDB survives reloads/crashes.

type Cmd = { do(): void; undo(): void };
const undoStack: Cmd[] = [], redoStack: Cmd[] = [];
function run(c: Cmd) { c.do(); undoStack.push(c); redoStack.length = 0; }

Scale gotcha: commands that close over stale references or large data break (undo restores a value that no longer matches reality) or blow memory — store minimal diffs/patches (immer produceWithPatches) not full snapshots, and in collaborative apps use *selective* undo (undo only your own ops via the CRDT undo manager), since a global stack would revert other users' work.

Part 7 — Real-time + collaboration

7.1 WebSocket production checklist

  • Heartbeat ping every 25 s; close + reconnect if no pong in 60 s.
  • Exponential backoff on reconnect with jitter; cap at 30 s.
  • Message framing: JSON with version + type + id + payload.
  • Binary frames for high-throughput (MessagePack, Protobuf).
  • Sticky session at the load balancer; reconnect resumes via session ID.
  • Heartbeat after tab returns from background (visibilitychange).

A production socket needs application-level heartbeats (proxies silently drop idle connections), jittered exponential backoff so a server restart doesn't trigger a synchronized reconnect stampede, and a resumable session ID so a reconnect replays missed messages rather than refetching everything.

let delay = 1000;
function connect() {
  const ws = new WebSocket(url);

Scale gotcha: thousands of clients reconnecting at once after a deploy is a self-inflicted DDoS — backoff *with jitter* is mandatory. Also a backgrounded tab's timers throttle so heartbeats stop; re-sync and verify the socket on visibilitychange rather than trusting it survived.

7.2 SSE vs WebSocket vs Polling

ProtocolDirectionUse
PollingClient → serverLast-resort or low-frequency
Long pollingServer can hold requestLegacy compatibility
SSEServer → client only, text onlyNotifications, live feed, AI streaming
WebSocketBidirectional, text + binaryChat, collab editing, multiplayer

Pick the least powerful tool that fits: SSE for one-way server pushes (notifications, token streaming) since it's plain HTTP, auto-reconnects with Last-Event-ID, and traverses proxies cleanly; WebSocket only when you need low-latency *bidirectional* or binary traffic (collab, multiplayer).

const es = new EventSource("/stream");
es.onmessage = (e) => append(JSON.parse(e.data));
es.onerror = () => {/* browser auto-reconnects, resending Last-Event-ID */};

Scale gotcha: over HTTP/1.1 the browser caps ~6 SSE connections per origin, so multiple tabs/streams starve — multiplex over HTTP/2 or share one EventSource across tabs via a leader (6.3). For AI streaming, SSE beats WebSocket because it reconnects and resumes by event id for free.

7.3 CRDTs

  • Conflict-free Replicated Data Types — local writes merge without coordination.
  • Libraries: Yjs (most popular), Automerge, Loro (Rust + WASM), Liveblocks (managed).
  • Network: WebSocket / WebRTC; awareness protocol for presence.
  • Pair with IndexedDB for offline persistence; flush on reconnect.
import * as Y from "yjs";
import { WebsocketProvider } from "y-websocket";
import { IndexeddbPersistence } from "y-indexeddb";
const ydoc = new Y.Doc();
new IndexeddbPersistence("doc-id", ydoc);     // offline cache
new WebsocketProvider("wss://sync/", "doc-id", ydoc);
const ytext = ydoc.getText("content");
ytext.observe(event => { /* re-render */ });

CRDTs let every client apply edits locally and merge deterministically without a central transform server — concurrent inserts converge to the same state. Yjs syncs compact binary updates over any provider, persists to IndexedDB for offline-first, and replays on reconnect.

Scale gotcha: CRDT documents accumulate tombstone/history metadata, so a long-lived doc's update log grows unbounded and slows load — periodically snapshot and garbage-collect. CRDTs guarantee *convergence*, not *intent*: two valid merges can still produce semantically odd results (interleaved characters), so add app-level constraints where it matters.

7.4 Presence + awareness

  • Awareness state lives outside the doc — ephemeral, not persisted.
  • Per-user: { cursor, selection, color, name, avatar }.
  • Broadcast over WebSocket; render overlays in screen coords.
  • Throttle to 30 fps to avoid flooding.

Presence (cursors, selections, "who's here") is ephemeral and lives *outside* the persisted CRDT doc, broadcast as transient state keyed by client id and cleared on disconnect. Render remote cursors as absolutely-positioned overlays mapped from document positions to screen coords.

provider.awareness.setLocalStateField("cursor", { anchor, head });
provider.awareness.on("change", () => render([...provider.awareness.getStates()]));

Scale gotcha: cursor/selection updates fire on every mousemove and flood the wire and every peer's render loop in a busy room — throttle to ~30fps and coalesce, and clean up stale states (awareness has a timeout, but a hard tab-kill can leave ghost cursors until it elapses).

7.5 WebRTC for P2P (rare but powerful)

  • Data channels for chat / cursors without a central server.
  • Signaling still needed (offer/answer/ICE) — usually over WebSocket.
  • STUN + TURN servers handle NAT traversal.
  • Use cases: video conferencing, screen sharing, file transfer.

WebRTC opens an encrypted P2P data/media channel after a signaling exchange (offer/answer/ICE candidates) over your own transport; STUN discovers public addresses and TURN relays when NAT traversal fails. Data channels give sub-50ms peer cursors/file transfer without server bandwidth.

const pc = new RTCPeerConnection({ iceServers: [{ urls: "stun:stun.l.google.com:19302" }] });
const ch = pc.createDataChannel("cursors");
ch.onmessage = (e) => render(JSON.parse(e.data));

Scale gotcha: P2P doesn't scale past small meshes — N peers means N² connections, so beyond ~4–6 participants you need an SFU (selective forwarding unit) server. A meaningful fraction of networks block P2P entirely, so a TURN relay (which costs bandwidth and undoes the "serverless" benefit) is mandatory.

Part 8 — Forms + input at scale

8.1 RHF + Zod canonical setup

const Schema = z.object({
  email: z.string().email(),
  age: z.coerce.number().int().min(18),
const { register, handleSubmit, formState: { errors, isSubmitting } } = useForm<FormValues>({
  resolver: zodResolver(Schema),
  defaultValues: { age: 18 },

React Hook Form keeps inputs uncontrolled (refs) so keystrokes don't re-render the whole form, and zodResolver runs one schema as the single source of truth for validation *and* the inferred TypeScript type. The same Zod schema can validate the payload server-side.

Scale gotcha: z.coerce.number() turns empty string into 0 and NaN into surprises, masking "field left blank" as valid — prefer explicit z.string().min(1).pipe(z.coerce.number()), and remember RHF won't re-render on a field you don't register/watch, so derived UI needs an explicit watch/useWatch.

8.2 Async validation

  • z.string().refine(async v => await api.checkUnique(v), "Already taken").
  • Debounce server checks (300 ms).
  • Show pending state inline; don't block submit.

Async refinements (username availability, coupon validity) run a server check inside validation; debounce so you don't hit the API per keystroke, show an inline pending indicator, and treat the final answer as authoritative on submit. Always re-check server-side — the client check is UX, not security.

const checkEmail = useMemo(() => debounce(async (v: string, cb: (ok: boolean) => void) =>
  cb(await api.isEmailFree(v)), 300), []);
// in resolver: z.string().email().refine(v => new Promise(r => checkEmail(v, r)), "Taken")

Scale gotcha: async validators race — a slow response for an old value can resolve after a newer one and show a stale error; key results to the current value (or use an AbortController/request id) and ignore out-of-date responses. Never let an in-flight check silently block submit forever if the network hangs.

8.3 Dynamic / schema-driven forms

  • Schema-driven UI: schema → form renderer (JSON Schema, Zod-to-form).
  • Conditional fields via watch().
  • useFieldArray for dynamic lists (line items, tags).

For forms whose shape comes from config/data, render fields from a schema so adding a field is a data change, not a code change; useFieldArray manages dynamic row lists with stable keys, and watch drives conditional visibility. Discriminated unions model "type X reveals fields Y".

const { fields, append, remove } = useFieldArray({ control, name: "items" });
fields.map((f, i) => (
  <div key={f.id}><input {...register(`items.${i}.qty`)} />

Scale gotcha: use the field array's generated f.id as the React key, never the array index — indexing breaks RHF's internal mapping when you remove/reorder rows, causing values to "jump" between inputs. Conditional fields also keep stale values when hidden; unregister or strip them before submit.

8.4 File uploads (production-grade)

  • Resumable via tus.io or chunked PUT with Range.
  • Pre-signed S3 / R2 URLs — upload directly from browser, no server proxy.
  • Progress UI from XHR.upload.onprogress (fetch doesn't expose progress; use XHR for now).
  • Persist upload state to IDB; resume on reopen.
  • Validate MIME + magic-bytes server-side; never trust client.

Production uploads go browser→storage directly via a short-lived pre-signed URL (no server proxy bandwidth), chunked + resumable (tus) so a dropped connection resumes mid-file, with progress from XHR's upload.onprogress. Validate type by magic bytes server-side after upload.

const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();
xhr.upload.onprogress = (e) => setPct(Math.round((e.loaded / e.total) * 100));
xhr.open("PUT", presignedUrl); xhr.setRequestHeader("Content-Type", file.type); xhr.send(file);

Scale gotcha: fetch still can't report upload progress reliably across browsers, so XHR remains the pragmatic choice. Never trust the client Content-Type/extension — an attacker renames evil.html to .png; verify magic bytes and re-encode/scan server-side, and scope pre-signed URLs tightly (size, type, short TTL).

8.5 Drag-and-drop + clipboard + paste

  • Drag-drop: drop event + e.dataTransfer.files.
  • Paste files: paste event + e.clipboardData.items.
  • Clipboard API: navigator.clipboard.write([new ClipboardItem({ "image/png": blob })]).
  • File System Access API: window.showOpenFilePicker / showSaveFilePicker (Chromium only).

Support all the ways users supply files: drag-drop (dataTransfer.files), paste (clipboardData.items, great for screenshots), and the async Clipboard API for programmatic copy of rich content. The File System Access API enables true open/save with a persistent handle (Chromium only; feature-detect).

el.addEventListener("paste", (e) => {
  for (const item of e.clipboardData!.items)
    if (item.type.startsWith("image/")) upload(item.getAsFile()!);

Scale gotcha: you must preventDefault on dragover or the browser navigates to the dropped file; clipboard write requires a user gesture and secure context or it silently rejects; and File System Access is Chromium-only, so always provide an <input type="file"> fallback and handle the permission prompt being denied.

8.6 Pointer events + gestures

  • PointerEvent unifies mouse + touch + pen.
  • Use-gesture / Hammer.js for swipe / pinch / rotate.
  • PointerCapture for drag that survives leaving the element.

Pointer Events unify mouse/touch/pen so one handler covers all inputs; setPointerCapture routes all subsequent events for that pointer to your element so a drag survives the cursor leaving the node. touch-action CSS prevents the browser from stealing the gesture for scroll.

el.onpointerdown = (e) => { el.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId); startDrag(e); };
el.onpointermove = (e) => e.buttons && drag(e);
// CSS: el { touch-action: none; }  ← required so the browser doesn't scroll instead

Scale gotcha: forgetting touch-action: none means on mobile the browser scrolls instead of dragging; and you must release capture and handle pointercancel (OS gesture interrupts) or the element gets stuck mid-drag. Use a battle-tested lib (@use-gesture/react) for pinch/rotate rather than hand-rolling multi-pointer math.

Part 9 — Large data + visualization

9.1 Virtualization libraries

  • react-window — fast, fixed/variable height.
  • @tanstack/virtual — headless, framework-agnostic.
  • react-virtuoso — feature-rich (chat, grid, table, sticky headers).
  • AG Grid — enterprise virtualized table with frozen / pinned / pivot.

Virtualization renders only the rows in (and just around) the viewport, so a 100k-row list mounts ~20 DOM nodes instead of 100k. @tanstack/virtual is headless (you own markup), Virtuoso handles hard cases (reverse/chat, variable height) out of the box, AG Grid is the enterprise full-feature table.

const v = useVirtualizer({ count: rows.length, getScrollElement: () => parentRef.current,
  estimateSize: () => 40, overscan: 8 });
<div style={{ height: v.getTotalSize() }}>{v.getVirtualItems().map(i =>

Scale gotcha: variable-height rows with a wrong estimateSize cause scroll-position jumps as real heights measure in; use measureElement for dynamic content. Browsers cap element height around ~16–33M px, so beyond hundreds of thousands of rows you must page/window the data itself, not just the DOM.

9.2 Virtualized table tricks

  • Column virtualization for wide tables (50+ columns).
  • Frozen / sticky columns + headers — manual transform: translate3d on scroll.
  • Expandable rows — re-measure on expand, anchor scroll.
  • Selection across virtualized rows — store IDs in Set, not indexes.

Wide tables need *column* virtualization too (render only visible columns), frozen columns/headers via sticky positioning or synced transforms, and selection stored as a Set of stable IDs — not row indexes, which are meaningless when only a window is mounted. Re-measure on row expand and anchor scroll so content doesn't jump.

const selected = useRef(new Set<string>());
const toggle = (id: string) => selected.current.has(id)
  ? selected.current.delete(id) : selected.current.add(id);

Scale gotcha: "select all" across a virtualized/paged dataset can't enumerate every id (they aren't loaded) — model it as { mode: "all", excluded: Set } and resolve server-side, or you silently select only the rendered window. Frozen-column transforms also fight the virtualizer's transforms; keep one element responsible for each axis.

9.3 Charts at scale

  • < 1K points: SVG (Recharts, Victory) — interactive, easy a11y.
  • 1K–100K: Canvas (Chart.js, uPlot) — fast, less interactive.
  • 100K+: WebGL (regl, Deck.gl, Plotly WebGL).
  • Decimation algorithms: LTTB (Largest Triangle Three Buckets) preserves shape with 10× fewer points.

Match the renderer to point count: SVG for small interactive charts (each point is a DOM node, easy hover/a11y), Canvas (uPlot) once SVG nodes choke the DOM, WebGL for hundreds of thousands of points. Decimate with LTTB to draw the visual shape with a fraction of the points.

const sampled = lttb(series, Math.min(series.length, containerWidthPx * dpr));
chart.setData(sampled); // never plot more points than physical pixels

Scale gotcha: plotting more data points than horizontal pixels is wasted work and invisible — always decimate to ~pixel resolution and re-decimate on zoom (the visible range changes which points matter). SVG with thousands of nodes kills hover/INP, so cross to Canvas before it tanks interaction latency.

9.4 WebGL / WebGPU on the web

  • Three.js + React Three Fiber — 3D scenes, product configurators, viz.
  • PixiJS — 2D canvas at 60 fps for games / heavy interactive.
  • WebGPU (Chrome stable, Safari shipping) — compute shaders + lower overhead than WebGL.
  • Use for: real-time filters, ML inference, particle systems, dataviz at scale.

R3F lets you express Three.js scenes declaratively as React components while keeping the render loop off React's reconciler; PixiJS is the 2D equivalent for sprite-heavy 60fps work. WebGPU adds compute shaders and lower CPU overhead, making in-browser ML/particle work practical.

import { Canvas } from "@react-three/fiber";
<Canvas><mesh rotation={[0.4, 0.2, 0]}><boxGeometry /><meshStandardMaterial /></mesh></Canvas>

Scale gotcha: never drive per-frame animation through React state — setState every frame triggers reconciliation and tanks FPS; mutate refs/uniforms inside useFrame. WebGL/WebGPU contexts are limited and lost on GPU pressure/tab-switch; handle webglcontextlost and dispose geometries/textures or you leak GPU memory until the tab crashes.

9.5 WebAssembly

  • Use cases: image / video codecs (Squoosh), crypto (libsodium), database (SQLite WASM), CV / ML (TensorFlow.js wasm backend), parsers (PEG.js).
  • Author: Rust → wasm-bindgen, AssemblyScript, Emscripten C/C++.
  • Performance: 1.5–3× JS for hot loops; near-zero startup with streaming compile.

WASM shines for CPU-bound hot loops — codecs, crypto, SQLite, parsers — where predictable numeric performance beats the JIT. Compile streaming (instantiateStreaming) so it parses as it downloads, and run it in a Worker so the main thread stays responsive. SharedArrayBuffer enables threads with COOP/COEP headers.

const { instance } = await WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming(fetch("/codec.wasm"), imports);
const out = instance.exports.encode(ptr, len); // run inside a Web Worker

Scale gotcha: crossing the JS↔WASM boundary and copying data in/out of linear memory has real overhead, so chatty fine-grained calls erase the speedup — batch work per call and pass large buffers. Threads need SharedArrayBuffer, which requires cross-origin isolation (COOP+COEP) headers that can break third-party embeds; plan the isolation tradeoff early.

Part 10 — Animation + motion

10.1 Animation tier list

ToolStrengthWhen
CSS transitionsGPU-accelerated, simpleHover, focus, simple state changes
CSS animations + keyframesDeclarative, loopingLoaders, attention-grabbers
Web Animations APIJS-driven, GPU-acceleratedComplex sequences, runtime params
Framer MotionDeclarative React, layout animationsReact UI work — drag, gestures, page transitions
GSAPMost powerful, broad browser supportMarketing sites, complex orchestration
LottieAfter Effects → JSONDesigner-handed micro-illustrations
RiveLottie alternative, state machinesInteractive, lighter file

Reach for the cheapest tier that does the job: CSS transitions/keyframes for state and loops (the compositor handles them off-main-thread), WAAPI for JS-controlled sequences, Motion (Framer) for React layout/gesture work, GSAP for heavy orchestration. Lottie/Rive carry designer-authored vector animations.

el.animate([{ transform: "translateY(8px)", opacity: 0 }, { transform: "none", opacity: 1 }],
  { duration: 200, easing: "ease-out", fill: "both" }); // WAAPI, runs on compositor

Scale gotcha: Lottie JSON can be huge and its renderer burns main-thread CPU during scroll — prefer Rive (state machines, smaller files) or dotLottie, and lazy-load animation libs (Motion/GSAP are 30–100KB) so they don't bloat the initial bundle for a single hover effect.

10.2 FLIP technique

  • First, Last, Invert, Play — measure first + last position, apply inverse transform, animate to identity.
  • Used by Framer Motion layout animations, react-flip-toolkit.

FLIP animates expensive layout changes cheaply: measure the element's First and Last rects, apply an Inverting transform so it *looks* unmoved, then Play by transitioning the transform to identity — animating only transform (compositor-only) instead of top/width (layout-thrashing).

const first = el.getBoundingClientRect();
reorderDOM();                              // triggers the layout change
const last = el.getBoundingClientRect();

Scale gotcha: measuring many elements (getBoundingClientRect in a loop) forces synchronous layout (reflow) per call — batch all reads before any writes to avoid layout thrash, and cap FLIP to the on-screen items in a virtualized list or you measure thousands of detached nodes.

10.3 View Transitions API (native)

document.startViewTransition(() => updateDOM());
/* Customize per element */
main { view-transition-name: main; }
::view-transition-old(main) { animation: fade-out 200ms; }
  • Native, GPU-accelerated, integrated with Next.js + React Router.

The View Transitions API snapshots the old DOM, runs your update callback, snapshots the new DOM, and crossfades/morphs between them — giving native shared-element transitions with CSS-controlled animations. Cross-document transitions enable MPA page animations with zero JS via @view-transition.

Scale gotcha: every shared view-transition-name must be unique per snapshot — two visible elements with the same name throw and abort the transition, which bites in lists where you template the name. Generate names from stable ids, and always feature-detect since the callback blocks rendering and isn't supported everywhere yet.

10.4 Performance rules

  • Animate transform + opacity — both composite-only.
  • will-change: transform sparingly; promotes to layer, costs memory.
  • Honor prefers-reduced-motion always.
  • 60 fps target = 16.7 ms per frame; 120 fps target = 8.3 ms.

Only transform and opacity animate on the compositor without layout/paint, so they hold 60–120fps; everything else (width, top, box-shadow, filter) risks main-thread jank. will-change promotes an element to its own layer for smoothness but each layer costs GPU memory. Honor reduced-motion unconditionally.

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { * { animation: none !important; transition: none !important; } }
.card { will-change: transform; } /* add just before animating, remove after */

Scale gotcha: leaving will-change on many elements permanently explodes GPU memory and can *slow* rendering (too many layers to composite) — apply it right before the animation and remove it after. Animating box-shadow/filter for hover on a long list silently drops frames; animate a pseudo-element's opacity instead.

Part 11 — Accessibility at production scale

11.1 Headless component libraries

  • Radix Primitives — unstyled accessible primitives (dialog, popover, dropdown).
  • React Aria (Adobe) — composable hooks for a11y behavior.
  • shadcn/ui — Radix + Tailwind, copy-paste components.
  • Headless UI (Tailwind Labs) — fewer primitives, deep React integration.

Headless a11y libraries encapsulate the hard parts — focus trapping, ARIA wiring, keyboard patterns, collision-aware positioning — while leaving styling to you, so you ship correct semantics without reinventing them per component. React Aria goes lowest-level (hooks), Radix mid-level (primitives), shadcn ships Radix + Tailwind you own.

import * as Dialog from "@radix-ui/react-dialog";
<Dialog.Root><Dialog.Trigger>Open</Dialog.Trigger>
  <Dialog.Portal><Dialog.Overlay /><Dialog.Content>{/* focus-trapped, labelled */}

Scale gotcha: copy-paste (shadcn) means *you* own the a11y over time — a refactor that drops Dialog.Title or overrides aria-* silently breaks screen readers, and there's no library update to fix it for you. Keep the required parts (title/description) and run axe in CI so design tweaks don't regress semantics.

11.2 Focus management

  • Trap focus in modals (radix / focus-trap-react).
  • Restore focus to trigger on close.
  • Roving tabindex for composite widgets (tabs, menus, listbox).
  • Skip link to main content (Tab + Enter on first tab stop).

Focus is the keyboard user's cursor: trap it inside open modals, restore it to the trigger on close, and use a roving tabindex (one tabbable item, arrow keys move within) for composite widgets so Tab doesn't walk every menu item. A skip link lets users jump past nav.

const trigger = useRef<HTMLElement | null>(null);
function open() { trigger.current = document.activeElement as HTMLElement; setOpen(true); }
function close() { setOpen(false); trigger.current?.focus(); } // restore focus

Scale gotcha: portals/modals rendered at the document root escape DOM order, so focus restoration and "click outside" break if you don't track the trigger explicitly; and async-rendered content can move focus while the screen reader is mid-sentence. Don't autoFocus deep inputs that scroll the modal on open, and never trap focus without an Escape route.

11.3 Screen reader testing

  • Manual: NVDA + Firefox (Windows), VoiceOver + Safari (Mac/iOS), TalkBack (Android).
  • Automated: axe-core / @axe-core/playwright catches ~70% of WCAG failures.
  • Don't over-announce; use aria-live=polite for status, assertive only for alerts.

Automated tools (axe) catch a meaningful slice fast and in CI — contrast, missing labels, bad roles — but the rest (focus order, announcement quality, logical reading) needs a real screen reader. Test the actual SR+browser pairings users use, since behavior differs across NVDA/VoiceOver/TalkBack.

import { injectAxe, checkA11y } from "axe-playwright";
test("dialog a11y", async ({ page }) => { await page.goto("/settings");
  await injectAxe(page); await checkA11y(page); });

Scale gotcha: a green axe run is not "accessible" — it can't tell if focus order makes sense or if a live region announces too much/too little. Teams that ship on automated coverage alone pass audits and still fail real users; budget periodic manual SR passes on critical flows (checkout, signup, settings).

11.4 Live regions

  • aria-live=polite reads after current speech; assertive interrupts.
  • aria-atomic=true reads the whole region; default reads only the change.
  • aria-relevant=additions text removals (rarely needed; default works).

Live regions announce dynamic changes without moving focus: polite queues after current speech (status, toasts), assertive interrupts (errors). The region must exist in the DOM *before* you write to it, and aria-atomic controls whether the whole region or just the diff is read.

const [msg, setMsg] = useState("");
<div aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true" className="sr-only">{msg}</div>
// later: setMsg("3 results loaded"); ← announced politely

Scale gotcha: injecting the aria-live element and its text in the same render often fails to announce — the region must be present first, then mutated. Overusing assertive (or putting whole chat logs in a live region) floods users with interruptions; reserve assertive for genuine alerts and throttle rapid updates.

11.5 Color + motion

  • Contrast 4.5:1 normal text; 3:1 large text.
  • Test in forced-colors mode (Windows High Contrast).
  • prefers-reduced-motion: skip non-essential motion.
  • prefers-contrast: more, more pronounced borders / states.

Meet WCAG contrast (4.5:1 body, 3:1 large/UI), and don't convey state by color alone (add icons/text). Respect forced-colors (Windows High Contrast strips your colors), prefers-reduced-motion, and prefers-contrast so OS-level accessibility prefs actually take effect in your UI.

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .btn { border: 1px solid ButtonText; } /* system colors; don't fight the override */
}

Scale gotcha: in forced-colors mode the browser replaces your colors with the user's system palette, so a button styled only with background-color becomes invisible — rely on system color keywords and visible borders, and never disable the override with forced-color-adjust: none on interactive elements just to keep your brand color.

11.6 Accessible virtualization

  • Virtualized lists break tabbing — implement keyboard nav within the virtual viewport.
  • Announce row count via aria-rowcount; current row via aria-rowindex.
  • Test with screen reader; auto-checks miss this.

Virtualization removes off-screen rows from the DOM, which breaks Tab order and screen-reader counting (the SR thinks there are 20 rows, not 20,000). Expose the true totals with aria-rowcount/aria-rowindex/aria-setsize, and drive navigation with arrow keys (roving tabindex) so focus scrolls the window into view.

<div role="grid" aria-rowcount={total}>
  {virtualRows.map(v => <div role="row" aria-rowindex={v.index + 1} key={v.key}>…</div>)}
</div>

Scale gotcha: if the focused row scrolls out of the virtual window it gets unmounted, dropping focus to <body> and stranding keyboard users — keep the focused row rendered (pin it) or move focus before it unmounts. Automated checks can't catch this; only a real SR + keyboard pass on the long list will.

Part 12 — Internationalization + localization

12.1 ICU MessageFormat

  • Pluralization, gender, select, number / date formatting.
  • Tools: FormatJS / react-intl, lingui, i18next.
{count, plural, =0 {No items} one {# item} other {# items}}
{gender, select, female {She} male {He} other {They}} purchased {item}

ICU MessageFormat encodes plural/gender/select logic *in the translation string* so translators control grammar per language (Polish has 4 plural forms, Arabic 6) instead of you concatenating fragments in code. The runtime picks the right branch from CLDR plural rules.

Scale gotcha: never build sentences by concatenation (count + " items") — word order, pluralization, and gender vary per locale and you'll produce broken grammar translators can't fix. Keep the *whole* sentence as one ICU message with placeholders, and watch that interpolated numbers/dates get locale-formatted, not stringified raw.

12.2 Lazy loading translations

  • Split by locale + by route; load on demand.
  • SSR: detect locale via Accept-Language header; serve only that locale.
  • Fallback locale (en) for missing keys.

Ship only the active locale's messages, split further per route, so a French user never downloads English+Spanish+German catalogs. On SSR, detect locale from Accept-Language/cookie and inline just that catalog; fall back to a default locale for missing keys rather than rendering raw ids.

const messages = await import(`../locales/${locale}.json`).then(m => m.default);
<IntlProvider locale={locale} defaultLocale="en" messages={messages}>{children}</IntlProvider>

Scale gotcha: a missing key shouldn't render the raw id to users — configure a fallback chain and an onError that logs (not throws) so untranslated strings degrade to the default locale. Dynamic message ids (formatMessage({ id: key })) also defeat static extraction, leaving keys unextracted; keep ids static.

12.3 RTL (right-to-left)

  • Use logical CSS properties (margin-inline-start, padding-block).
  • dir="rtl" on <html>.
  • Mirror icons that imply direction (arrows, breadcrumbs).
  • Test in Arabic, Hebrew with real text — line-height + descenders surprise.

Author layout with logical properties (margin-inline-start, inset-inline, text-align: start) so a single dir="rtl" on <html> flips the whole UI without per-component overrides. Mirror only directional icons (back arrows, breadcrumbs); leave logos and clocks alone.

.panel { margin-inline-start: 1rem; padding-inline: 1.5rem; } /* auto-flips in RTL */
[dir="rtl"] .chevron { transform: scaleX(-1); } /* mirror directional glyphs */

Scale gotcha: physical properties (margin-left, left: 0) and hard-coded translateX don't flip and break RTL; an audit usually finds dozens. Bidi text (an Arabic name in an English sentence, or a phone number) needs Unicode isolation (<bdi>/dir="auto") or numbers/punctuation render in the wrong order.

12.4 Locale-aware APIs

  • Intl.NumberFormat, DateTimeFormat, RelativeTimeFormat, ListFormat, PluralRules.
  • Intl.Collator for locale-aware sorting.
  • Intl.Segmenter for word / sentence boundaries (CJK, Thai).

The native Intl namespace formats numbers, currencies, dates, relative times, and lists per locale with zero dependencies, and Intl.Collator sorts correctly (ä near a in German). Intl.Segmenter finds word/sentence boundaries in languages without spaces (Thai, Japanese).

new Intl.NumberFormat("de-DE", { style: "currency", currency: "EUR" }).format(1234.5); // "1.234,50 €"
[...].sort(new Intl.Collator("sv").compare); // locale-correct, not byte order

Scale gotcha: Intl constructors are expensive to create — instantiating a NumberFormat inside a render or a sort comparator (per element!) tanks performance on large lists. Memoize formatters per locale, and never sort strings with the default < comparator, which gives wrong, locale-blind ordering.

Part 13 — Multi-tenant + theming

13.1 Tenant data isolation

  • All queries scoped by tenant ID; server enforces via session or JWT claim.
  • URL pattern: workspaceSlug.example.com OR /w/[slug]/...
  • Workspace switcher with prefetch on hover.
  • Cache invalidation on switch — TanStack Query queryClient.clear() per switch.

Every request must be scoped to the tenant the *server* derives from session/JWT — never a client-supplied tenant id, which is trivially forged. Put the tenant in the URL (subdomain or /w/[slug]), and clear/namespace client caches on switch so tenant A's data can't bleed into tenant B.

function switchWorkspace(slug: string) {
  queryClient.clear();                 // drop prior tenant's cached data
  router.push(`/w/${slug}`);           // server re-derives tenant from route + session

Scale gotcha: the cross-tenant data leak is the catastrophic bug — a cached query keyed without tenant id, or a server query that trusts a header, can show one customer another's records. Always include tenant id in the query key *and* enforce row-level scoping server-side; client clearing is hygiene, not the security boundary.

13.2 Theming with design tokens

  • Tokens at :root via CSS custom properties.
  • Multiple themes: data-theme="dark" / data-theme="brand-x".
  • color-scheme: light dark — browser-native scrollbars + form controls.
  • Tools: Style Dictionary, Tokens Studio (Figma), Open Props.
:root { --brand: oklch(0.7 0.18 250); --bg: white; --fg: #111; }
[data-theme="dark"] { --bg: #111; --fg: white; }
[data-tenant="acme"] { --brand: oklch(0.6 0.2 30); }

CSS custom properties make themes runtime-switchable with zero rebuild: components read var(--brand), and a data-theme/data-tenant attribute on <html> swaps the values. color-scheme opts native UI (scrollbars, controls) into dark mode; OKLCH keeps perceptual lightness consistent across hues.

Scale gotcha: deep nesting of var() references (token → semantic → component) can produce invalid values that silently fall back to initial/unset, breaking layout subtly. Keep a flat-ish token graph, set a fallback (var(--x, #000)), and generate tokens from one source (Style Dictionary) so CSS, JS, and Figma never drift.

13.3 Per-tenant assets

  • Logo, favicon via CDN with tenant ID in path.
  • Custom CSS injected at edge from tenant config.
  • Edge config (Vercel Edge Config / Cloudflare KV) for sub-ms tenant lookups.

Resolve tenant branding (logo, favicon, accent, custom CSS) at the edge from a key-value config keyed by tenant, so the lookup is sub-millisecond and onboarding a customer needs no redeploy. Inject the resolved theme attributes/CSS into the HTML before the app boots.

const tenant = await edgeConfig.get(hostname);          // sub-ms KV lookup
res.headers.set("x-tenant-theme", tenant.theme);        // app reads + applies pre-paint

Scale gotcha: tenant-supplied custom CSS is an injection surface — unsanitized, it can exfiltrate data via background: url() or break layout globally. Scope it (shadow DOM or a wrapped class), allow-list properties, and never inject tenant-controlled <style>/HTML into a context where it can read other tenants' DOM or tokens.

13.4 Anti-flicker dark mode

  • Apply theme in a tiny inline <script> in <head> before paint.
  • Server reads cookie; sets data-theme on <html>; client never flickers.

To avoid a flash of the wrong theme, the theme must be set on <html> *before first paint* — either the server reads a cookie and renders data-theme directly, or a tiny render-blocking inline script in <head> sets it from localStorage/prefers-color-scheme synchronously, before React hydrates.

<script>
  document.documentElement.dataset.theme =
    localStorage.theme ?? (matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches ? "dark" : "light");

Scale gotcha: setting the theme in a useEffect guarantees a flash because effects run after paint; and in SSR/RSC, reading localStorage on the server is impossible, so you get a hydration mismatch if server and client disagree. Persist the choice in a *cookie* the server can read, or accept the tiny inline blocking script — there is no flicker-free option that defers to React.

Part 14 — Authentication + authorization

14.1 Session vs JWT

ApproachProCon
Session in HttpOnly cookieServer can revoke instantly; XSS-safeServer keeps state (Redis)
JWT in HttpOnly cookieStateless validationRevocation requires blacklist or short TTL
JWT in localStorage—XSS-vulnerable; do NOT use

The token *storage* decides your XSS exposure: HttpOnly cookies are unreadable by JS, so a script injection can't steal them, whereas anything in localStorage is one XSS away from full account takeover. Sessions revoke instantly (server state); JWTs are stateless but can't be un-issued without a denylist or short TTL.

res.setHeader("Set-Cookie",
  `session=${id}; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=3600`);

Scale gotcha: "stateless JWT" sounds scalable until you need instant logout/ban — a stolen long-lived JWT stays valid until expiry. Keep access tokens short (5–15 min) with a revocable refresh token (14.2), and never put tokens in localStorage "for convenience"; the convenience is also the attacker's.

14.2 Refresh token rotation

  • Short-lived access token (5–15 min) + long-lived refresh token.
  • Each refresh issues a new refresh token; old one is invalidated.
  • Detect refresh-token theft: if the same token is used twice, kill the session.
  • Refresh token in HttpOnly cookie; access token in memory.

Rotation issues a new refresh token on every use and invalidates the old one, so a stolen token can be used at most once. If the *same* refresh token is presented twice, you know it was replayed (theft) and revoke the entire token family — a strong automatic breach response.

async function refresh(oldRt: string) {
  const fam = await db.findRT(oldRt);
  if (!fam || fam.used) { await db.revokeFamily(fam.familyId); throw new Error("reuse detected"); }

Scale gotcha: rotation + multi-tab racing means two tabs can both present the same refresh token within milliseconds and trigger false "reuse" revocation, logging the user out. Serialize refresh through a single leader tab (Web Locks, 14.3) or a grace window keyed by the new token, or rotation fights itself under normal use.

14.3 Silent renewal

  • Background fetch refreshes token before expiry — user doesn't notice.
  • Pause fetch on tab hidden; resume on visible.
  • Web Locks API to ensure only one tab refreshes at a time.

Renew the access token in the background just before it expires so requests never 401 mid-flow; pause the timer when the tab is hidden (battery, pointless refreshes), and elect a single tab to perform the refresh so N tabs don't all rotate the refresh token simultaneously.

navigator.locks.request("token-refresh", async () => {
  if (Date.now() > expiry - 60_000) await refresh(); // only the lock holder refreshes
});

Scale gotcha: without the lock, every open tab fires a refresh at once → with rotation (14.2) that's instant "reuse detected" lockout. Combine the Web Lock with a BroadcastChannel that distributes the new access token to follower tabs, and handle the lock-holder tab closing mid-refresh (another must take over).

14.4 Multi-tab session sync

  • User logs out in tab A → tab B reflects within 1 s.
  • BroadcastChannel for "logged-out" event.
  • Storage events on a "logout-at" timestamp key.

When a user logs out (or is logged out remotely) in one tab, every other tab must drop to a logged-out state fast, or a stale tab keeps showing protected data. Broadcast a logout event across tabs and have each clear caches and redirect; a storage timestamp key is the fallback for browsers without BroadcastChannel.

const ch = new BroadcastChannel("session");
function logout() { ch.postMessage("logout"); location.assign("/login"); }
ch.onmessage = (e) => { if (e.data === "logout") { queryClient.clear(); location.assign("/login"); } };

Scale gotcha: clearing the *cache* in other tabs isn't enough — in-flight requests with the now-revoked cookie may still resolve and render protected data for a moment; gate render on a loggedOut flag and abort pending requests. Confirm the server cookie is actually cleared, since a client-only logout leaves a valid session behind.

14.5 Fine-grained authorization (CASL / Cedar / OPA)

import { defineAbility } from "@casl/ability";
const ability = defineAbility((can) => {
  if (user.role === "admin") can("manage", "all");
{ability.can("update", post) && <EditButton />}
  • Centralize rules; never re-check in scattered if statements.
  • Server re-verifies on every mutation — client checks are UX only.

Centralizing authorization rules (CASL, Cedar, OPA) gives one source of truth that both UI gating and server enforcement consume, so a permission change happens in one place instead of dozens of scattered if (role === …) checks that drift out of sync.

Scale gotcha: client-side ability.can() only hides buttons — it is *not* security; an attacker calls the API directly. Every mutation/query must re-evaluate authorization server-side, ideally with the identical rule definition shared between client and server so what the UI shows and what the API allows never diverge.

14.6 SSO / OAuth / OIDC

  • Use library: Auth.js, Clerk, WorkOS, Kinde, Keycloak.
  • PKCE for SPAs.
  • Strict redirect URI allow-list.
  • Validate id_token signature; don't trust unverified claims.

Don't hand-roll OAuth/OIDC — use a vetted library, run Authorization Code + PKCE (no client secret in the browser), strictly allow-list redirect URIs, and validate the id_token signature, iss, aud, exp, and nonce before trusting any claim. The state param defends against CSRF on the callback.

// PKCE: send code_challenge on auth, code_verifier on token exchange
const verifier = randomString();
const challenge = base64url(await sha256(verifier));

Scale gotcha: trusting an unverified id_token (or skipping aud/nonce checks) lets a token minted for another app be replayed against yours — always verify the signature against the provider's JWKS and that the audience matches your client id. A permissive redirect-URI allow-list (wildcards, http://) is the classic account-takeover hole; pin exact HTTPS URIs.

Part 15 — AI integration in production

15.1 Streaming chat (Vercel AI SDK)

// Edge route
export const runtime = "edge";
export async function POST(req) {
// Client
const { messages, input, handleInputChange, handleSubmit, stop } = useChat({
  api: "/api/chat", experimental_throttle: 50,

The AI SDK streams model output token-by-token over a data stream protocol, with useChat managing message state, tool-call rendering, and abort on the client. Running on the edge minimizes TTFB to first token; onFinish is where you record usage/cost server-side (the client value can't be trusted for billing).

Scale gotcha: serverless/edge functions have an execution time limit, so a long generation can be cut off mid-stream — stream incrementally and persist the assembled message server-side in onFinish, not only client-side, since a dropped connection loses client state. Rate-limit per user *before* calling the model, or one tab can rack up huge spend.

15.2 Generative UI (streamUI)

  • Model picks which React component to render for next step.
  • Define typed tools; each returns a React element.
  • Safety: only stream components safe to render with model-controlled props; no raw HTML or dangerouslySetInnerHTML.

Generative UI lets the model invoke typed tools that each return a *React component* instead of text, so the LLM drives which widget renders (a weather card, a chart, a form) with validated props. The component allow-list and prop schema are your safety boundary.

const ui = await streamUI({
  model, messages,
  tools: { showWeather: { parameters: z.object({ city: z.string() }),

Scale gotcha: treat model-chosen component props as untrusted input — never pass them to dangerouslySetInnerHTML, href/src without validation (prompt-injected javascript: URLs), or eval. Allow-list which components the model may render and Zod-validate every prop, since a jailbroken model will try to render whatever it can.

15.3 RAG

  • Embed query → vector store top-k → pass as context → cite chunks in UI.
  • Stores: Pinecone, pgvector, Turbopuffer, Vercel Vector, Qdrant, Weaviate.
  • Latency budget: 80 ms embed + 60 ms vector + 700 ms first token.

RAG grounds answers in your data: embed the query, retrieve top-k similar chunks from a vector store, inject them as context, and render citations so users can verify. Hybrid (vector + keyword/BM25) retrieval plus a rerank step beats pure vector similarity for precision.

const emb = await embed({ model, value: query });
const chunks = await store.query({ vector: emb.embedding, topK: 8 });
const answer = await streamText({ model, system: buildContext(chunks), messages });

Scale gotcha: retrieval quality, not the model, is usually why RAG answers are wrong — bad chunking (splitting mid-sentence), stale embeddings after content edits, or dumping too many low-relevance chunks that bury the answer and blow the context budget. Re-embed on content change, rerank, and always show citations so unsupported claims are visible.

15.4 Token throttling + backpressure

  • Use experimental_throttle to limit re-renders to 50 ms.
  • Render messages in Suspense; avoid relayout per token.
  • Per-message memo; virtualize long chat lists.

Streaming emits tokens faster than the UI should re-render; throttling coalesces updates to ~50ms frames so React doesn't reconcile per token. Memoize each settled message so only the streaming one re-renders, and virtualize long transcripts so the DOM stays bounded.

const Message = memo(({ m }: { m: Msg }) => <Markdown>{m.content}</Markdown>);
// useChat({ experimental_throttle: 50 }) → batches token updates into 20fps frames

Scale gotcha: re-rendering a growing markdown message on every token causes O(n²) work (re-parse the whole string each token) and visible jank on long answers — throttle, and parse markdown incrementally or only re-render the changed tail. A 500-message chat without virtualization also locks up scroll; window it.

15.5 Cancellation + cost control

  • stop() propagates AbortSignal to server; cancelled chats don't bill.
  • Per-user rate limit at edge (Cloudflare Rate Limiting, Upstash).
  • Content moderation upstream of model call (OpenAI moderation, llamaguard).

stop() aborts the fetch, and the AI SDK forwards the AbortSignal so the server cancels the upstream model call — you stop paying for tokens nobody will read. Rate-limit per user/IP at the edge *before* the model call, and run cheap moderation upstream to reject abusive prompts without spending model budget.

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const { success } = await ratelimit.limit(userId); // before any model call
  if (!success) return new Response("Too many requests", { status: 429 });

Scale gotcha: forgetting to thread req.signal/abortSignal into the model call means a user who closes the tab still incurs the full generation cost — the connection drops but the upstream request runs to completion. Always propagate the abort, and put the rate-limit/moderation gate *before* the expensive call.

15.6 Evals

  • Test suite of input/output pairs with LLM-as-judge.
  • Run on every PR + nightly.
  • Tools: Braintrust, Langsmith, OpenAI Evals, Helicone, Promptfoo.

Evals are the test suite for non-deterministic systems: a dataset of inputs with graders (exact-match, regex, or LLM-as-judge for open-ended quality) that score prompt/model changes so you catch regressions before shipping. Run on every PR that touches prompts and nightly against production samples.

// promptfoo config (yaml-equivalent)
const eval = { prompts: ["./prompt.txt"], providers: ["openai:gpt-4.1-mini"],
  tests: [{ vars: { q: "refund policy" }, assert: [{ type: "llm-rubric", value: "cites policy doc" }] }] };

Scale gotcha: LLM-as-judge is itself non-deterministic and biased (favors verbose answers, can be gamed) — pin the judge model/version, calibrate against human labels periodically, and combine with deterministic assertions where possible. Evals on a stale dataset give false confidence; refresh from real production failures continuously.

Part 16 — Telemetry + observability deep dive

16.1 OpenTelemetry browser SDK

  • Vendor-neutral; ship to any backend (Datadog, Honeycomb, Grafana, SigNoz).
  • Auto-instruments fetch, XHR, document load, history changes.
  • Custom spans around feature flows.
const tracer = trace.getTracer("checkout");
tracer.startActiveSpan("submit-order", async span => {
  span.setAttribute("order.value", total);

OpenTelemetry gives vendor-neutral instrumentation: auto-spans for fetch/XHR/page-load plus custom spans around business flows, all exportable to any OTLP backend so you're not locked to one APM. The browser span's traceparent propagates into backend traces for one end-to-end view (16/20.7).

Scale gotcha: tracing every event from every browser is a firehose that blows your observability bill and the beacon adds bytes/CPU on the client — sample (head or tail), batch exports via sendBeacon, and never put PII in span attributes (they're stored and queryable). Auto-instrumentation can also double-count spans if combined with framework instrumentation.

16.2 Sentry deep features

  • Performance: tracesSampleRate; tag transactions by route.
  • Replay sampling: replaysOnErrorSampleRate=1.0 keeps replays only for errors.
  • Privacy masking: replaysSession.maskAllText / blockAllMedia.
  • Breadcrumbs: user navigations, fetch, console.log captured leading up to error.
  • Custom context: Sentry.setContext("user", { tenantId }).

Sentry correlates an error with the breadcrumb trail (clicks, fetches, navigations) and an optional session replay that reconstructs the exact DOM leading up to it, collapsing repro time from days to minutes. Sample replays on error (not all sessions) to control cost, and mask PII by default.

Sentry.init({ dsn, tracesSampleRate: 0.1,
  replaysOnErrorSampleRate: 1.0, replaysSessionSampleRate: 0.0,
  integrations: [Sentry.replayIntegration({ maskAllText: true, blockAllMedia: true })] });

Scale gotcha: replay with default masking off captures passwords, tokens, and PII into a third party — a compliance incident waiting to happen; mask aggressively and block media. Also tracesSampleRate: 1.0 in production floods quota and adds overhead; sample, and add ignoreErrors/denyUrls to filter browser-extension noise that drowns real issues.

16.3 Web Vitals with attribution

  • web-vitals/attribution exposes WHICH element caused slow LCP / shifted CLS / janky INP.
  • Beacon includes: element selector, longest task, connection type, device memory.
  • Tag with deploy SHA to correlate regressions.

The attribution build of web-vitals reports not just the metric value but the *cause* — which element was the LCP, which node shifted for CLS, which interaction drove a slow INP — so you fix the specific offender instead of guessing. Tag beacons with the deploy SHA to pin regressions to a release.

import { onINP } from "web-vitals/attribution";
onINP((m) => beacon({ value: m.value, target: m.attribution.interactionTarget,
  delay: m.attribution.inputDelay, sha: BUILD_SHA }));

Scale gotcha: lab metrics (Lighthouse) and field metrics (RUM) diverge — your fast dev machine never reproduces the p75 INP a low-end Android user sees. Trust *field* data weighted at p75+, and send the beacon on visibilitychange/pagehide (not unload, which is unreliable) or you lose the final INP for the session.

16.4 Long Animation Frames API

const obs = new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  for (const entry of list.getEntries()) {
    if (entry.duration > 50) {
  • Replaces the older Long Task API; gives per-script attribution + interaction details.

LoAF reports frames that took too long to render along with per-script attribution (source URL, function, invoker) and timing breakdown, so you can see *which* code blocked the main thread and caused poor INP — a big upgrade over Long Tasks, which only said "something was slow."
