Scale gotcha: script attribution is coarsened across origins for privacy — third-party (analytics, ads) blocking scripts may show as anonymous, so you can see *that* a third party janks but not always *where*. Pair LoAF beacons with deploy SHA and route, and remember collecting these from all users adds observer overhead; sample.

16.5 Heatmaps / session funnels

  • PostHog (OSS), FullStory, Hotjar, Mixpanel.
  • Track key conversion events; surface funnel drop-offs.
  • Cohort analysis — by signup date, by plan, by feature exposure.

Product analytics (PostHog, Mixpanel) instrument named events and assemble funnels so you see *where* users drop in a flow, plus heatmaps for click/scroll behavior and cohort retention. Track a small set of meaningful events with stable names rather than auto-capturing everything.

posthog.capture("checkout_step_completed", { step: 3, plan, experiment: variant });

Scale gotcha: auto-capture and session recording grab PII (typed card numbers, emails) and balloon event volume/cost — mask sensitive inputs, define a deliberate event taxonomy, and beware that ad-blockers drop a meaningful share of these beacons, biasing your funnel toward less privacy-conscious users. Proxy through your own domain to recover coverage.

Part 17 — Testing at production scale

17.1 MSW (Mock Service Worker)

  • Intercepts fetch / XHR via Service Worker — tests + Storybook + dev use same mocks.
  • Handlers as code, not fixtures.
import { http, HttpResponse } from "msw";
export const handlers = [
  http.get("/api/users/:id", ({ params }) =>

MSW intercepts at the network layer (Service Worker in browser, request interceptor in Node), so the same handlers power unit tests, Storybook, and local dev — your app makes real fetch calls and never knows it's mocked. Handlers are code, so they can model state, errors, and latency.

Scale gotcha: an unhandled request silently passes through (or errors) depending on onUnhandledRequest — set it to "error" in tests so a forgotten mock fails loudly instead of hitting a real (or nonexistent) endpoint. Drifting mocks that no longer match the real API give false-green tests; pair MSW with contract tests (17.5) to keep them honest.

17.2 Playwright sharding + parallelism

  • Shard across CI runners: playwright test --shard=1/4.
  • Trace viewer: --trace on captures DOM + console + network for failed tests.
  • Auth state cached via storageState — one login per worker, not per test.

Playwright parallelizes within a machine (workers) and across machines (--shard), cutting wall-clock E2E time near-linearly; cache authenticated storageState once in global setup so tests start logged in instead of re-running login each time. Traces on failure capture DOM+network+console for instant repro.

// global-setup: log in once, reuse everywhere
await page.context().storageState({ path: "auth.json" });
// project: use: { storageState: "auth.json", trace: "on-first-retry" }

Scale gotcha: flaky E2E tests destroy trust in the suite — most flake is timing (asserting before the app settles); use web-first auto-retrying assertions (expect(locator).toBeVisible()), never waitForTimeout. Shared auth state can leak data between tests if they mutate the same account; isolate per-worker data for mutating flows.

17.3 Visual regression

  • Chromatic (Storybook-native), Percy, Applitools, Lost Pixel.
  • Run on PR; review diffs in Chromatic UI.
  • Useful for design system changes that affect 100s of components.

Visual regression snapshots rendered components/pages and diffs pixels on each PR, catching unintended visual changes (a token tweak that shifts 200 components) that assertion-based tests miss entirely. Storybook stories double as the snapshot inventory, so coverage grows with your component library.

// Story renders the state; the VRT tool snapshots + diffs it across commits
export const Loading = { args: { status: "loading" } };

Scale gotcha: rendering nondeterminism (animations, timestamps, random data, font loading, antialiasing) produces false diffs that train reviewers to rubber-stamp — freeze time, disable animations, mock data, and wait for fonts before snapshotting. Diffing whole pages is brittle; snapshot components in isolation so one layout change doesn't redline every page.

17.4 Component testing

  • Storybook + Vitest browser mode — test components in a real browser.
  • Stories double as test cases (play() function).
  • Faster than E2E, more realistic than jsdom unit tests.

Component tests render a single component in a real browser (Vitest browser mode / Playwright CT) — more faithful than jsdom (real layout, real events) yet far faster than full E2E. A Storybook play() function drives interactions and assertions, so one story is both documentation and test.

export const SubmitsForm = {
  play: async ({ canvasElement }) => { const c = within(canvasElement);
    await userEvent.type(c.getByLabelText("Email"), "a@b.co");

Scale gotcha: jsdom lies about layout (no real box model, no getBoundingClientRect), so tests for focus order, scroll, or virtualization pass in jsdom and fail in real browsers — run those in browser mode. But browser-mode tests are heavier; keep pure-logic units in jsdom and reserve real-browser runs for DOM/interaction-sensitive components.

17.5 Contract testing

  • Pact / Schemathesis verify API contracts between FE + BE.
  • Cuts integration bugs from "deployed and broken" to "PR fails fast".

Contract testing pins the shape of the FE↔BE interface: the consumer (FE) declares expected requests/responses, and the provider (BE) verifies it still satisfies them in CI — so a breaking API change fails the provider's PR instead of breaking production after both deploy. It's how you keep MSW mocks honest against the real API.

// consumer expectation (Pact-style)
provider.given("user 1 exists").uponReceiving("get user")
  .withRequest({ method: "GET", path: "/api/users/1" })

Scale gotcha: contract tests only cover the interfaces you write contracts for — undeclared endpoints and optional fields slip through, giving false safety. They add a broker/coordination step between FE and BE pipelines; without ownership and a shared broker, contracts go stale and teams disable them. Treat the contract as a co-owned artifact.

17.6 Test impact analysis

  • Run only tests affected by changed files.
  • Vitest + nx affected, Turborepo --filter, Jest --findRelatedTests.
  • Critical when test suite grows past 10K tests.

Test impact analysis maps the dependency graph from changed files to the tests that exercise them, so a one-line change runs 30 tests instead of 30,000 — keeping CI feedback fast as the suite grows past 10k tests. Monorepo tools (nx affected, Turborepo filters) compute this from the project graph.

nx affected -t test --base=origin/main   # only projects touched by this PR

Scale gotcha: impact analysis is only as correct as its dependency graph — dynamic imports, runtime config, shared fixtures, and global setup create implicit dependencies the graph misses, so a "safe" change can skip a test that would have caught the bug. Run the *full* suite on main/nightly and before release as a backstop, and use affected-only for PR speed.

Part 18 — Feature flags + experimentation at scale

18.1 Anti-flicker SSR flag eval

  • Evaluate flags on the server in the layout/page; never let client default-render the off state.
  • Vercel Edge Config / Cloudflare KV for sub-ms lookups.
  • Bootstrap initial flag values into the HTML; client SDK hydrates from them.

Evaluate flags on the server (edge) and render the correct variant in the initial HTML, then bootstrap those values to the client SDK so hydration matches — otherwise the client renders the control, then flips to the variant after the SDK loads, producing a visible flicker and a hydration mismatch.

const flags = await getFlags(userId);          // edge KV, sub-ms
return <html data-flags={JSON.stringify(flags)}>{flags.newNav ? <NewNav /> : <Nav />}</html>;

Scale gotcha: client-only flag eval guarantees flicker on every flagged surface and skews experiment metrics (the control flashes before the variant), and async client eval makes the page CLS-unstable. Pin flag values server-side for the request, pass them through once, and avoid re-evaluating mid-session, which can flip a user's variant and corrupt their assignment.

18.2 Bucketing + exposure

  • Stable hash(userId + experimentId) → 0–10000 → bucket.
  • Log exposure ONLY when user actually sees / interacts with the variant.
  • Avoid "exposed but never reached" pollution of metrics.

Deterministic bucketing — hash(userId + experimentId) into a 0–10000 range — assigns a stable variant without server state, so the same user always sees the same arm. Log an *exposure* event only when the user actually reaches/sees the treatment, so users who never hit the surface don't dilute the analysis.

const bucket = murmur3(`${userId}:${expId}`) % 10000;
const variant = bucket < 5000 ? "control" : "treatment";
if (rendered) track("exposure", { expId, variant }); // log on actual exposure only

Scale gotcha: logging exposure at *assignment* instead of at *render* inflates the denominator with users who never saw the variant, biasing the result toward null and hiding real effects. Salt the hash per experiment (raw userId lets a popular user's bucket correlate across experiments), and keep bucketing identical client/server or assignment flips between renders.

18.3 Holdouts

  • Permanent 5% holdout that never sees new features — gives clean baseline for long-term metrics.
  • Critical for measuring cumulative impact of many small experiments.

A global holdout keeps a small fraction of users on the old experience across *all* experiments, giving a clean long-term baseline to measure the cumulative impact of dozens of individually-tiny wins — which otherwise vanish into noise when measured one at a time.

const inHoldout = murmur3(`${userId}:global-holdout`) % 10000 < 500; // permanent 5%
if (inHoldout) return baselineExperience();

Scale gotcha: a permanent holdout means 5% of users deliberately get a worse, aging product, with real revenue/UX cost and support confusion ("why is my account different?") — rotate or cap holdout duration, exclude it from other experiments' assignment (or you double-count), and make sure critical fixes (security, not features) still reach holdout users.

18.4 Sequential testing + auto-stop

  • Stop early when statistical significance reached (mSPRT, Bayesian).
  • Auto-rollback if guardrail metric breaches (latency, errors, crash rate).

Sequential/always-valid tests (mSPRT, Bayesian) let you peek at results continuously and stop as soon as significance is reached without inflating false positives — unlike fixed-horizon t-tests where peeking invalidates the p-value. Pair with automatic rollback when a guardrail (errors, latency, crash rate) regresses.

if (alwaysValidPValue(data) < 0.05) ship();          // safe to peek continuously
if (guardrail.errorRate > baseline * 1.2) rollback(); // auto-revert on harm

Scale gotcha: peeking at a *fixed-horizon* experiment and stopping the moment it looks significant is the classic p-hacking trap that ships false wins — use a sequential method designed for continuous monitoring, or pre-commit to a sample size. Auto-rollback on a noisy guardrail can flap (roll out, roll back, repeat); require sustained breach over a window before reverting.

18.5 Flag debt

  • Every flag has owner + expiry + Linear ticket.
  • Quarterly cleanup: drop flags at 100% for > 90 days.
  • Linter rule that flags expired flags as warnings.

Every flag is temporary debt: tag it with an owner, an expiry date, and a tracking ticket at creation, then sweep flags that have been at 100% (or 0%) for >90 days. A lint rule that warns on expired/stale flag references keeps cleanup from being purely manual.

// codegen'd flag registry with metadata enables the lint rule + dashboard
export const FLAGS = { newNav: { owner: "growth", expires: "2026-03-01", ticket: "GRO-412" } } as const;

Scale gotcha: unremoved flags compound into combinatorial test/QA explosion (N flags = 2^N states nobody verifies) and a permanent if future engineers fear to delete because they don't know if it's load-bearing. Removing a flag is a two-step ship (set to 100%, then delete the branch a release later) so you can revert without code if the rollout regresses.

Part 19 — Deploy + edge patterns

19.1 Edge runtime tradeoffs

  • Vercel Edge / Cloudflare Workers / Deno Deploy = V8 isolates; no Node APIs.
  • Cold start ~0 ms; runs in 300+ PoPs globally.
  • Use for: middleware (auth, A/B), streaming AI, geo redirects, image optimization.
  • Don't use for: ORM, file system, heavy crypto.

Edge runtimes are V8 isolates (not containers) so they start in ~0ms and run in hundreds of PoPs near users, ideal for latency-sensitive, lightweight work — auth/redirect middleware, A/B routing, streaming. They lack Node APIs, native modules, and have CPU/memory limits, so heavy or stateful work stays in regional functions.

export const config = { runtime: "edge" };
export function middleware(req: Request) {
  const country = req.headers.get("x-vercel-ip-country");

Scale gotcha: edge code far from your database can be *slower* than a regional function — every query is a cross-continent round-trip — so a chatty ORM at the edge tanks latency despite the "0ms cold start." Keep edge work close to data (read replicas / edge KV) or compute-only; put data-heavy logic in a region next to the DB.

19.2 Stale-while-revalidate at the CDN

Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300, stale-if-error=86400
  • max-age: how long fresh.
  • stale-while-revalidate: how long stale can be served while async refresh.
  • stale-if-error: how long stale can be served if origin errors.

SWR serves a cached response instantly even after max-age expires, returning the stale copy while asynchronously revalidating in the background, so users almost never wait on the origin. stale-if-error keeps serving stale content when the origin is down — free resilience.

Scale gotcha: SWR means users can see stale data for the whole revalidate window, which is wrong for anything that must be current (pricing, inventory, auth state) — scope SWR to tolerant content and use explicit invalidation/purge or short TTLs for the rest. Also Vary/cookie-bearing responses often bypass shared caches entirely; verify what's actually cacheable at the CDN.

19.3 Edge config (runtime config without redeploy)

  • Vercel Edge Config / Cloudflare KV / Upstash Redis.
  • Use for: feature flags, A/B rules, kill switches, banner messages.
  • Sub-ms lookups at the edge; no cold start.

Edge config stores are read-optimized KV replicated to every PoP for sub-ms reads, so you can change feature flags, A/B rules, kill switches, and banners *without a deploy* — critical for incident response (flip a kill switch in seconds) and ops who shouldn't need a CI pipeline to change a message.

import { get } from "@vercel/edge-config";
const killed = await get<boolean>("checkout_disabled"); // sub-ms, no redeploy needed
if (killed) return new Response("Maintenance", { status: 503 });

Scale gotcha: edge config is eventually consistent across PoPs and write-throttled — a flip can take seconds to propagate globally and isn't for high-frequency writes (use a real database for that). Don't read it on a hot path without caching per request either; thousands of reads per render add up even at sub-ms each.

19.4 Multi-region active-active

  • App runs in 30+ regions; each region has its own DB read replica.
  • Writes go to primary region; reads stay local.
  • Tools: Cloudflare D1, Vercel Storage, Turso, PlanetScale, CockroachDB, Spanner.

Active-active runs the app in many regions reading from a local replica (low read latency everywhere) while writes route to a primary (or a globally-consistent DB like Spanner/CockroachDB). Most apps are read-heavy, so local reads + occasional cross-region writes is the pragmatic 90% pattern.

// route reads local, writes to primary region
const db = req.method === "GET" ? localReplica() : primaryRegion();

Scale gotcha: replica lag means read-your-own-writes breaks — a user updates their profile (write to primary) then reads a stale local replica and sees the old value. Pin a user to the primary (or read-after-write consistency) for a short window after a write, and design UI to tolerate eventual consistency or you ship "my change didn't save" bugs.

19.5 Atomic deploys

  • Each deploy is immutable; old version stays live until new is verified.
  • Rollback = one click, re-promote previous artifact.
  • Per-PR preview deploys for safe experimentation.

Atomic, immutable deploys mean each release is a self-contained artifact promoted instantly; the old version keeps serving until the new one is healthy, so rollback is re-promoting the previous artifact (one click, seconds) rather than rebuilding. Per-PR preview URLs let you test in a production-like env before merge.

vercel deploy --prebuilt    # immutable artifact
vercel promote <previous-deployment-url>  # instant rollback to known-good

Scale gotcha: the frontend is atomic but the *database/API* is not — a deploy requiring a schema change can break the moment new assets load against an old API (or vice versa). Use expand/contract migrations (additive first, deploy, then remove) and keep the API backward-compatible for the overlap window, since clients on the old bundle keep calling for minutes after you ship.

19.6 Static fallback for worst case

  • Cloudflare Always Online / CloudFront origin failover — serves last good HTML if origin dies.
  • Simple "we're experiencing issues" page on different domain as last resort.

Layered fallback keeps *something* up when the origin dies: the CDN serves the last successfully cached HTML (Always Online / origin failover), and a fully static status page on an independent domain/provider is the last resort if even the CDN config is the problem. Defense in depth for availability.

Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60, stale-if-error=604800  # serve stale up to a week on outage

Scale gotcha: a cached "last good" page can serve stale or personalized content to the wrong user (a logged-in shell with someone's name) during an outage — only fall back to *non-personalized* HTML, and host the ultimate status page on a different DNS provider/registrar, since a DNS or account-level failure takes a "fallback" that shares infrastructure down with the main site.

Part 20 — Profiling + debugging in production

20.1 Performance panel (Chrome DevTools)

  • Record interaction → identify long tasks (yellow blocks > 50 ms).
  • Bottom-Up view groups by function — find the actual hot spots.
  • Flame chart shows call stack; look for wide blocks at the top.
  • "Performance insights" panel auto-detects INP / LCP / CLS issues.

Record a real interaction, then read the flame chart top-down for wide blocks (long-running functions) and the Bottom-Up view to find which functions cost the most aggregate time. Long tasks (>50ms, flagged) are your INP/responsiveness culprits; the insights panel auto-attributes LCP/CLS/INP.

// bracket the suspect interaction for a clean trace
performance.mark("a"); doExpensiveWork(); performance.mark("b");
performance.measure("work", "a", "b"); // shows as a labeled track in the panel

Scale gotcha: profiling on your fast dev machine with an unthrottled CPU hides the jank low-end users feel — always enable 4–6× CPU throttling and "Slow 4G" to reproduce field conditions. Dev builds (unminified, extra checks) have different perf characteristics than prod; profile a production build for representative numbers.

20.2 React DevTools Profiler

  • Record interaction → see which components rendered + why (props changed, state changed, parent re-rendered).
  • "Highlight updates when rendering" overlays paint indicators.
  • React 19.2: Performance Tracks integrate React scheduler into Chrome timeline.

The Profiler records commits and shows which components rendered, how long each took, and *why* (props/state/parent), so you can pinpoint wasteful re-renders. "Highlight updates" flashes re-rendering components live; React 19.2's Performance Tracks put React's scheduler work directly into the Chrome timeline alongside browser events.

const Row = memo(function Row({ data }: { data: Item }) { return <li>{data.name}</li>; });
// Profiler "why did this render?" reveals an unstable prop (new object/fn each parent render)

Scale gotcha: the most common finding is a parent passing a fresh object/array/function literal each render, breaking memo on every child — but don't blindly memo/useCallback everything; the wrapping has its own cost and React Compiler (19+) auto-memoizes, so measure first and let the compiler handle the rest rather than hand-memoizing the whole tree.

20.3 Memory leaks

  • Common patterns: timers not cleared, event listeners not removed, refs held to detached DOM, closures over large data.
  • DevTools Memory panel → heap snapshots → diff before/after action.
  • Allocation Timeline shows retained objects over time.
  • Use WeakRef for caches; WeakMap for metadata.

Leaks come from retained references the GC can't collect: uncleared intervals, un-removed listeners, detached DOM held by a ref/closure, or an ever-growing cache. Diff heap snapshots before/after repeating an action — a steadily climbing retained size with detached nodes is the signature.

useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(tick, 1000);
  window.addEventListener("resize", onResize);
  return () => { clearInterval(id); window.removeEventListener("resize", onResize); }; }, []);

Scale gotcha: closures silently retain everything in scope — a single event listener capturing a large array (or a parent component instance) pins megabytes, and setInterval/observers not cleaned up keep firing on unmounted components. Use WeakMap/WeakRef for caches keyed by objects so entries collect automatically, and always pair every subscribe with an unsubscribe.

20.4 Source map upload (mandatory)

  • Sentry CLI / Datadog CI uploads source maps on release.
  • Without it, stack traces are obfuscated and useless.
  • Tag with release SHA; production builds reference correct map.

Production bundles are minified, so stack traces are gibberish unless you upload source maps to your error tracker at release time, keyed by the release/SHA so the symbolicated trace points at real files and lines. Upload maps privately; don't serve them publicly.

sentry-cli sourcemaps upload --release "$GIT_SHA" ./dist
# build injects the same release id so events resolve against the right map

Scale gotcha: serving source maps publicly (leaving them in the deployed dist) exposes your unminified source and logic to anyone — upload them to the error tracker and use hidden-source-map to strip the reference from the public bundle. A release/SHA mismatch between the uploaded map and the running bundle silently produces wrong line numbers, so wire the same id into both build and upload.

20.5 Replay-driven debugging

  • Sentry Replay / LogRocket / FullStory captures real session DOM + console + network.
  • Reproduce a bug from a user's exact session — minutes, not days.
  • Privacy: mask PII (replaysSession.maskAllText, blockAllMedia).

Session replay reconstructs the user's exact DOM mutations, console, and network timeline leading to an error, so you watch the bug happen instead of guessing from a stack trace — turning "can't reproduce" into a 5-minute fix. Capture replays only on error (cost) and mask sensitive content by default.

Sentry.replayIntegration({ maskAllText: true, blockAllMedia: true,
  mask: [".sensitive"], networkDetailAllowUrls: ["/api/public"] });

Scale gotcha: replay is a privacy and compliance minefield — default-on text/media capture records PII, passwords, and PHI into a third party, and GDPR/HIPAA may forbid it entirely; mask by default and allow-list what's safe, never the reverse. Replays add client payload/CPU, so sample and capture-on-error rather than recording every session.

20.6 Production debug toggles

  • ?debug=1 query param enables verbose console + dev-only overlays.
  • Internal-only feature flag gates a debug panel for engineers.
  • Always strip in production; never ship to all users.

A gated debug mode — query param or internal-only flag — surfaces verbose logs, render overlays, and state inspectors *in production* for engineers diagnosing a live issue, without shipping that overhead/exposure to all users. Gate it behind an authenticated internal check, not just an obscure URL.

const debug = new URLSearchParams(location.search).has("debug") && user.isInternal;
debug && console.debug("state", store.getState()); // never leak internal state to real users

Scale gotcha: a debug toggle reachable by *anyone* (just a query param, no auth check) leaks internal state, API shapes, and sometimes secrets to attackers, and verbose logging in the hot path tanks performance for whoever flips it — gate on an authenticated internal-user/flag check, and ensure debug-only code is tree-shaken or no-op'd for the public bundle.

20.7 Distributed tracing

  • Pass W3C traceparent header from FE fetch → BE → DB.
  • See one trace span the entire user request across services.
  • Honeycomb / Tempo / Jaeger / Datadog APM.

Propagating the W3C traceparent header from the browser fetch through every backend service and DB call stitches one distributed trace, so you see the full waterfall of a slow user request across services and find *which* hop is slow — not just that the page was slow. The frontend span is the root of that trace.

fetch("/api/order", { headers: { traceparent: `00-${traceId}-${spanId}-01` } });
// each downstream service reads traceparent, creates a child span, re-propagates

Scale gotcha: a single broken hop that doesn't forward traceparent (a legacy service, a proxy that strips headers, a queue) severs the trace, leaving an orphaned span you can't correlate — audit every service for propagation. Tracing 100% of requests is unaffordable at scale; use tail-based sampling so you keep the slow/error traces and drop the boring fast ones.

20.8 Live error triage workflow

  • Sentry alarm fires → engineer paged.
  • Open Sentry issue → see stack trace + breadcrumbs + replay.
  • Reproduce with replay video or breadcrumb sequence.
  • Check correlated deploys (Sentry shows release associated with each event).
  • If correlated → rollback the deploy (Vercel revert button).
  • If not → write a fix + a regression test before closing.

The triage loop: alert fires → open the issue (symbolicated trace + breadcrumbs + replay) → check the release it correlates with → if a recent deploy caused it, roll back *first* (mitigate, then diagnose), else write a fix plus a regression test that reproduces it before closing. Rollback over hotfix when a deploy is the obvious cause.

// every event carries the release so Sentry can show "first seen in <SHA>"
Sentry.init({ release: GIT_SHA, environment: "production" });

Scale gotcha: the instinct to debug-then-fix under a live incident wastes the mitigation window — if the issue correlates with a deploy, roll back immediately (seconds via atomic deploys, 19.5) and investigate from the safe state, since every minute of a live error costs users. Always land a regression test with the fix, or the same bug returns; closing on a "should be fixed" hunch without a repro is how incidents recur.

The browser's preload scanner finds <img>/<link> in HTML but *not* JS-injected or CSS-referenced resources — hint those explicitly.

<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.avif" fetchpriority="high">
<script src="/analytics.js" defer></script> <!-- never blocks interactivity -->

Scale gotcha: hinting too aggressively inverts the table — every preload competes for the same bandwidth, so over-preloading actively *delays* your true LCP element. Keep high-priority hints to the 2–3 genuinely render-critical resources and let everything else load at default/low priority.

B. Storage tier

StorageWhenMax sizePersistence
Memory (variables)Hot pathRAMPage lifetime
sessionStoragePer-tab state~5 MBTab lifetime
localStoragePersisted simple kv~5 MBUntil cleared
IndexedDBStructured data, large blobsGBsUntil cleared
Cache API (Service Worker)Network responsesGBsUntil purged
Origin Private File SystemSandboxed file I/OGBsUntil cleared

Match data to the right tier: ephemeral hot state in memory, small per-tab/persisted KV in session/localStorage, structured/large data in IndexedDB, network responses in the Cache API, high-throughput file I/O in OPFS. localStorage is *synchronous* — reading it blocks the main thread — so anything sizable belongs in async IndexedDB.

const db = await openDB("app", 2, { upgrade(d) { d.createObjectStore("docs"); } });
await db.put("docs", largeBlob, "doc-1"); // async, GB-scale, off the main thread

Scale gotcha: localStorage's ~5MB sync API blocks rendering and throws QuotaExceededError silently mid-write, corrupting state; never store large or hot data there. Browser storage is also evictable under pressure (especially on iOS) unless you call navigator.storage.persist(), so treat it as a cache, not a database, and handle eviction gracefully.

C. Performance budgets by app type

App typeLCPINPJS gzNotes
Landing / marketing< 1.5 s< 100 ms< 100 KBMostly static; aggressively trim
Content / blog< 2.0 s< 200 ms< 200 KBSSG/ISR; image-heavy
Dashboard SaaS< 2.5 s< 200 ms< 400 KBBehind auth; lazy-load below fold
Editor / IDE< 3.0 s< 200 ms< 600 KBWorker + canvas; lazy-load features
Game / 3D< 5.0 s< 16 ms (60 fps)< 2 MBWebGL / WASM dominates

Budgets scale with app complexity but the *Core Web Vitals* thresholds (LCP <2.5s, INP <200ms, CLS <0.1 at p75) are fixed by Google and affect ranking — the JS budget is what you trade against features. Marketing pages must be ruthless (every KB hurts conversion); editors get more headroom because users accept a load for a heavyweight tool.

// enforce per app type in CI (Lighthouse CI assertions)
{ "assertions": { "largest-contentful-paint": ["error", { "maxNumericValue": 2500 }] } }

Scale gotcha: budgets are p75-of-real-users targets, not lab numbers — a build that hits LCP 1.5s in Lighthouse on a fast machine can be 4s at p75 on real mobile devices. Enforce against *field* data (CrUX/RUM) and gate CI on the lab proxy; INP (which replaced FID) is the hardest to hold as JS grows, so budget main-thread work, not just bytes.

D. Frameworks senior FE should be familiar with

  • React + Next.js, React + Vite, React + Remix / TanStack Start
  • Vue + Nuxt
  • Svelte + SvelteKit
  • Astro (islands / content sites)
  • Qwik (resumability)
  • SolidJS (signal-first)
  • Lit (web components)
  • htmx (server-rendered interactivity)

A staff FE should reason about the *model* each framework embodies, not just syntax: React/Next (RSC + concurrent), Svelte/Solid (fine-grained signals, no VDOM), Astro (islands), Qwik (resumability), htmx (server-driven HTML). The 2026 convergence is signals + server-first rendering — even React added compiler-based reactivity, narrowing the gap.

// SolidJS: the signal updates only the exact DOM node, no component re-render
const [count, setCount] = createSignal(0);
return <button onClick={() => setCount(count() + 1)}>{count()}</button>;

Scale gotcha: framework choice is a multi-year hiring and ecosystem bet, not a benchmark — picking SolidJS/Qwik for a raw-perf win can starve you of libraries, integrations, and engineers who know it. Match the model to the problem (content site → Astro, app → Next/TanStack), and weigh team familiarity and library maturity above micro-benchmark deltas.

E. Things to drop in 2026

  • moment.js — use date-fns / dayjs / Temporal polyfill.
  • axios for new code — use native fetch + ofetch / ky.
  • redux + sagas for greenfield — use TanStack Query + Zustand.
  • CSS-in-JS that ships runtime CSS (styled-components) — use Tailwind / CSS Modules / vanilla-extract / Panda CSS.
  • class component patterns for new code — function components + hooks.
  • jQuery in any new code.
  • localStorage for session tokens — HttpOnly cookies.
  • moment-timezone — use Intl + Temporal.
  • Webpack 4 — migrate to Vite / Rspack / Turbopack.

The through-line of 2026 deprecations: drop runtime cost and security footguns for platform-native or zero-runtime alternatives. Runtime CSS-in-JS (styled-components) breaks RSC and ships a runtime tax — use zero-runtime (vanilla-extract, Panda) or utility CSS; moment is huge and mutable — use Temporal (now shipping) or date-fns; tokens belong in HttpOnly cookies, never JS-readable storage.

// Temporal: immutable, timezone-correct, no mega-dependency
const dt = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from("2026-06-05T10:00[America/New_York]");
dt.add({ hours: 5 }).toLocaleString("en-US"); // DST-safe, no moment-timezone

Scale gotcha: ripping these out wholesale across a large codebase is risky — do it incrementally behind the build (a lint rule banning new moment/axios/styled-components imports while legacy usages migrate), since a big-bang replacement of a date or styling library introduces subtle timezone/visual regressions at scale. Ban the *new* usage first, then burn down the old.

End of document. 20 parts. Reference often; pair with Doc 03 (modern stack), Doc 05 (FRSA), Doc 06 (system design). When you can defend any 3 techniques here with a real production story, you are operating at staff level.

docs.search: 09 — Advanced Production FE Techniques (2026) 20 parts of real prod patterns: React internals · rendering · network · state · real-time · large data · a11y · auth · AI · telemetry · testing · debug Techniques senior FE engineers actually reach for in production. Not theory — the patterns Figma, Linear, Stripe, Vercel, Notion, Netflix actually ship. Pair with Doc 03 (modern stack), Doc 05 (FRSA), Doc 06 (system design). Part 1 — React internals + advanced patterns 1.1 Fiber + reconciliation Fiber = a linked-list of work units; React can pause + resume + abort work. Two phases: render (pure, can pause) → commit (DOM mutations, synchronous). Concurrent renderer can prepare multiple versions of UI; only commits one. Senior tell: explain why state updates outside startTransition feel sluggish under load. A fiber node holds type , pendingProps , memoizedState (the hook chain), and child / sibling / return pointers so React walks the tree as a list, yielding to the browser every ~5ms via the scheduler. Updates outside startTransition are synchronous-priority: they block paint until the whole tree reconciles. Marking the expensive update as a transition lets React interrupt it to keep typing responsive. const [tab, setTab] = useState("all"); const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition(); function select(next: string) { Scale gotcha: a single non-transition setState that triggers a huge subtree (e.g. a 5k-row list filter) starves input handlers — wrap the heavy update, keep the controlled input value as urgent state. 1.2 StrictMode double-rendering React intentionally invokes function components + effects twice in dev to surface impure render and missing cleanup. Cleanup must be idempotent — useEffect cleanup runs between the double mount. Treat your useEffect "setup → cleanup → setup" as a contract. StrictMode mounts, unmounts, then remounts each component in dev (effects run setup → cleanup → setup). It is the cheapest way to catch subscriptions that leak, refs that double-register, or one-time side effects fired in render. It is dev-only — production runs once. useEffect(() => { const sub = stream.subscribe(onMsg); return () => sub.unsubscribe(); // must fully undo setup Scale gotcha: code that "works" because it accidentally relied on a single mount (e.g. incrementing a server counter in an effect) double-fires in StrictMode and again under React 19's offscreen prerendering — make effects idempotent, not order-dependent. 1.3 Batching (automatic in React 18+) All setState calls in any event handler, promise, setTimeout, or native event are batched into a single re-render. flushSync(() => setState(...)) opts out of batching — synchronous, useful for measuring DOM after change. Automatic batching means multiple setState s across awaits collapse to one render, cutting wasted commits. flushSync forces a synchronous commit so you can read post-render layout (e.g. scroll a freshly inserted node into view) before the next line runs. flushSync(() => setItems(next)); listRef.current?.lastElementChild?.scrollIntoView(); Scale gotcha: flushSync defeats concurrency and triggers a synchronous reflow — calling it in a loop or on every keystroke reintroduces the jank batching removed. Use it once, after the mutation, never inside a render or effect body. 1.4 Compound components // Tabs.Tab + Tabs.Panel pattern — shares state via Context <Tabs defaultValue="overview"> <Tabs.List> Compound components share implicit state through Context so consumers compose freely without prop-drilling activeTab everywhere. The parent owns state; children read it via a private context hook that throws if used outside the provider. Scale gotcha: Context re-renders every consumer on any value change — for large tab sets memoize the context value and split selection state from heavy panel content so switching a tab doesn't re-render unrelated panels. 1.5 Polymorphic components (as prop) type Props<C extends React.ElementType> = { as?: C } & React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<C>; function Button<C extends React.ElementType = "button">({ as, ...rest }: Props<C>) { const Comp = as || "button"; Polymorphic components let one styled component render any element/component while keeping prop types correct for the chosen tag ( href valid only when as="a" ). Add ref forwarding with ComponentPropsWithRef and a generic forwardRef wrapper for full correctness. Scale gotcha: the as prop explodes TypeScript inference time in large design systems — prefer the Radix asChild /Slot pattern (1.6) over deep polymorphic generics once you have hundreds of components, or compile times and editor hovers degrade badly. 1.6 Slot pattern (Radix style) Use @radix-ui/react-slot — Slot forwards refs + props to a single child instead of rendering a wrapper element. Powers asChild={true} composition: <Button asChild><Link href="…">Go</Link></Button>. Slot merges the parent's props, event handlers, refs, and className onto its single child element so you avoid an extra DOM wrapper and inherit the child's semantics. asChild is the ergonomic switch that picks Slot vs the default element. import { Slot } from "@radix-ui/react-slot"; function Button({ asChild, ...props }: { asChild?: boolean } & React.ComponentProps<"button">) { const Comp = asChild ? Slot : "button"; Scale gotcha: Slot merges event handlers by calling both — if the child also defines onClick , both fire; and only a single child is allowed, so a fragment or multiple children throws at runtime, easy to hit when content is conditionally rendered. 1.7 Render props + headless components Headless: provide behavior, no markup. Examples: React Aria, Radix Primitives, Headless UI, TanStack Table. You own the look + a11y; the library owns the state machine + keyboard. Headless libraries return state + prop-getters; you spread them onto your own markup, keeping full control of styling while inheriting correct ARIA and keyboard behavior. This is why design systems standardize on TanStack Table / React Aria rather than styled black-box widgets. const table = useReactTable({ data, columns, getCoreRowModel: getCoreRowModel() }); return table.getRowModel().rows.map(r => ( <tr key={r.id}>{r.getVisibleCells().map(c => Scale gotcha: headless gives you the rope to omit a11y — prop-getters supply roles/aria, but if you don't spread them (or override role ), you ship an inaccessible widget that automated axe tests may still pass. Treat the getter spread as mandatory. 1.8 State machines (XState) Use for wizards, async retry, payment flows, video player, anything with > 4 states + guards. const machine = createMachine({ initial: "idle", states: { Replaces tangled useEffect chains for complex async. Visualize at stately.ai — designers can validate flows. A statechart makes illegal transitions unrepresentable: you only reach loading via SUBMIT , so double-submits and "retry while already saving" bugs vanish. XState v5 uses setup() for typed actors/guards and useMachine to bind in React. Scale gotcha: teams over-model trivial UI as machines and pay the boilerplate tax. Reserve XState for genuinely stateful flows (>4 states, guards, parallel regions); for simple async, useReducer or TanStack Query mutation states are lighter. 1.9 useSyncExternalStore Subscribe to non-React state (window size, localStorage, Zustand, observers) tear-free in concurrent mode. function useWindowWidth() { return useSyncExternalStore( cb => { window.addEventListener("resize", cb); return () => window.removeEventListener("resize", cb); }, This hook is the official way to read mutable external sources without tearing (different parts of one render seeing different values) under concurrent rendering. The three args are subscribe, client snapshot, and server snapshot — the last prevents hydration mismatch. Scale gotcha: the snapshot getter must return a referentially stable value — returning a fresh object/array each call causes an infinite render loop. Memoize or use useSyncExternalStoreWithSelector to compare derived slices. 1.10 useImperativeHandle (escape hatch, use sparingly) Expose an imperative API from a child to a parent ref — e.g. <Modal ref={r}> with r.current.open(). Senior tell: prefer declarative props; reach for this only when the prop model doesn't fit (focus(), scrollIntoView(), play()). useImperativeHandle customizes what a parent ref sees, exposing methods instead of the raw DOM node. Legitimate when the action is truly imperative and momentary — focus, play, scroll — where modeling it as state would be awkward. const Video = forwardRef<{ play(): void }, { src: string }>((p, ref) => { const el = useRef<HTMLVideoElement>(null); useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({ play: () => el.current?.play() }), []); Scale gotcha: imperative handles bypass React's data flow, so parent/child can desync — calling .open() while the parent also controls open via prop creates two sources of truth. Pick one model per component; React 19 lets you take ref as a normal prop, reducing forwardRef boilerplate. Part 2 — Rendering + hydration optimization 2.1 The rendering spectrum Mode When the HTML is built JS sent to client SSG At build time Hydration JS ISR Build + on-demand revalidate Hydration JS SSR Per request on server Hydration JS Streaming SSR Per request, streamed in chunks Hydration JS, selective CSR In the browser after JS loads Everything RSC Per request on server Zero for Server Components; islands hydrate PPR Static shell at build + dynamic streams Hydration JS for dynamic islands The axis that matters is *when HTML is produced* vs *how much JS ships to make it interactive*. RSC and PPR win in 2026 because they push the static shell to the CDN edge instantly and stream only the dynamic, per-request parts, while Server Components ship zero client JS. // Next.js PPR: static shell, dynamic island streamed in export const experimental_ppr = true; export default function Page() { Scale gotcha: mixing modes per route is the real skill — a single cookies() / headers() call or uncached fetch opts a whole route out of static rendering, silently turning fast SSG into per-request SSR. Audit with the build's static/dynamic markers. 2.2 Streaming SSR (React 18+) renderToReadableStream / renderToPipeableStream emit HTML chunk-by-chunk. Suspense boundaries flush as ready (out-of-order). Selective hydration: React prioritizes hydrating the part the user is interacting with. Result: TTFB drops to network-only; LCP drops if shell is small. Streaming sends the shell immediately and flushes each Suspense boundary's HTML as its data resolves, using inline <script> to slot late chunks into place. The browser paints the shell before slow data is ready, so TTFB and LCP decouple from your slowest query. const stream = await renderToReadableStream(<App />, { bootstrapScripts: ["/main.js"], onError(e) { logServerError(e); }, Scale gotcha: once the shell flushes you've already sent a 200 and committed headers — you can no longer redirect or change status for errors found mid-stream. Resolve auth/redirects *before* the first byte, and design error UI to render inline within boundaries. 2.3 Islands architecture Static HTML by default; "islands" of interactivity hydrate independently. Astro / Fresh / Qwik are island-first frameworks. Best for content-heavy sites (blog, docs, marketing) — Server Components in Next.js give similar results. Islands ship mostly static HTML and hydrate only flagged interactive components, each with its own tiny JS bundle and its own hydration trigger. For content sites this cuts client JS by an order of magnitude versus a full SPA. --- import Counter from "../Counter.tsx"; --- Scale gotcha: islands can't share live client state easily — two islands that must coordinate go through a shared store (nanostores) or events, and over-using client:load everywhere reconstitutes a slow SPA. docs.html:
10 — More Advanced Production FE Techniques (Volume II, 2026)

V8 + GC · RSC internals · Scroll-driven CSS · Temporal · OPFS · WebTransport · OT internals · Durable Objects · WebAuthn · Mobile · DevX

Continuation of Doc 09 with 20 more parts. Everything here is real production patterns that senior engineers at Figma, Linear, Notion, Stripe, Vercel use. Pair with Doc 09.

Part 1 — V8 internals + memory management

1.1 Hidden classes + inline caches

  • V8 builds a hidden class per object shape; constant property layout = fast property access.
  • Adding properties after construction creates a new hidden class — slow.
  • Senior pattern: initialize all properties in the constructor, even to null.
  • Inline caches memoize property lookup per call site; polymorphic call sites are slower.

Mechanism. V8 represents every object with a Map (internally called a "hidden class" or "Shape") that records the property names, their order, and their storage offsets. When you read obj.x, V8 doesn't do a hash lookup — it checks the object's Map, and if the Map matches the one it cached at this call site, it reads directly from a fixed byte offset. That cache lives at the call site (an *inline cache*, IC). The IC has four states:

  • uninitialized → first run, no info yet.
  • monomorphic → exactly one Map seen; fastest, can be inlined by TurboFan.
  • polymorphic → 2–4 Maps seen; V8 keeps a small list and linear-scans it.
  • megamorphic → >4 Maps; V8 gives up on the per-site cache and falls back to a slow global lookup. This is the silent killer in generic code (loggers, serializers, virtual-DOM differs).

Transition chains. Adding properties in a *consistent order* lets many objects share the same transition chain ({} → {x} → {x,y}). Adding them in different orders forks the tree and produces distinct Maps that all hit the same call sites → polymorphic/megamorphic.

// BAD: shape diverges → two hidden classes, polymorphic ICs downstream
function makePointBad(a, b, flag) {
  const p = {};
  if (flag) { p.x = a; p.y = b; }     // shape A: x then y
  else      { p.y = b; p.x = a; }     // shape B: y then x  (DIFFERENT Map!)
  return p;
}

// GOOD: one shape, monomorphic. Initialize every field, same order, no conditionals.
class Point {
  constructor(x = 0, y = 0) {
    this.x = x;        // always present
    this.y = y;        // always present, always after x
    this.label = null; // declare even when unused → no later transition
  }
}
const pts = Array.from({ length: 1e6 }, (_, i) => new Point(i, i));
// dist() below sees ONE Map forever → monomorphic IC → TurboFan inlines the field loads.
function dist(p) { return Math.hypot(p.x, p.y); }

Gotcha: delete p.x demotes the object to *dictionary mode* (slow hash-map backing store) and the whole transition chain is abandoned. To "remove" a field on a hot object, set it to null/undefined, never delete.

Diagnose IC state in Node: node --allow-natives-syntax then %HaveSameMap(a, b) and %DebugPrint(obj) (look for map = 0x... — same address = same hidden class).

1.2 Deoptimization patterns

  • Mixing types in a hot loop (sometimes number, sometimes string) → deopt.
  • Arguments object access (use rest parameters).
  • try/catch around hot loops (V8 historically refused to inline; less true now).
  • with statement, delete operator on objects → deopt.
  • Diagnose: --trace-opt --trace-deopt in Node flags (or DevTools "Optimize for Performance").

Mechanism. V8 runs your code in Ignition (bytecode interpreter), collects type feedback, and once a function is "hot" hands it to TurboFan, which compiles *speculative* optimized machine code: "I assume x is always a Smi (small int), so I'll emit integer add." If that assumption is later violated (you pass a string), V8 must *bail out* — discard the optimized code, restore interpreter state mid-frame (a "deopt"), and resume in Ignition. If it re-optimizes and deopts repeatedly, V8 marks the function deoptimized too many times and stops optimizing it entirely — the worst state: permanently slow.

Key deopt triggers in 2026 V8:

  • Type instability of fields and arguments (Smi → HeapNumber → String at the same site).
  • arguments aliasing in sloppy mode — use rest (...args).
  • Holey vs packed arrays. new Array(n) or assigning past length creates a *holey* elements kind (HOLEY_SMI_ELEMENTS); V8 must check each slot for holes. Push from empty to stay *packed*.
  • -0, NaN, and reading out of bounds silently switch elements kinds (Smi → Double).
// Observe a deopt. Run: node --trace-deopt --trace-opt deopt.js
function sum(arr) {
  let s = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) s += arr[i]; // TurboFan assumes Smi elements
  return s;
}
const ints = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
for (let i = 0; i < 1e6; i++) sum(ints);   // optimizes to integer add

sum([1, 2, "3"]);  // ← string forces PACKED_SMI → PACKED_ELEMENTS, prints:
//  [deoptimizing (DEOPT eager): ... reason: wrong map / not a Smi]

Gotcha: a try/catch no longer blocks optimization in modern V8, but a try/finally that throws across an inlined frame still can. The bigger real-world trap is keeping *one polymorphic helper* (e.g. clone(x)) that every type flows through — it goes megamorphic and never optimizes. Specialize hot paths or monomorphize with a type tag.

1.3 Generational GC

  • Young generation (small, scavenge often). Most objects die young.
  • Old generation (mark-sweep + compaction). Promoted after surviving two scavenges.
  • Major GC pauses are the INP killer — minimize allocations in hot loops.

Mechanism (Orinoco, V8's GC). The heap is split:

  • Young generation (new space), a few MB, managed by a semi-space Scavenger (Cheney's algorithm): two equal halves, from and to. Allocation is a pointer bump in from. On scavenge, live objects are copied to to, the spaces flip, and dead objects are reclaimed *for free* (you never touch them). Objects surviving two scavenges are promoted to old space.
  • Old generation (old space), managed by a Mark-Compact collector: tri-color marking (white/grey/black) traces from roots, then sweeps free space and occasionally compacts to defragment.

Modern V8 hides most of this from your frame budget with concurrent marking (marking on a background thread while JS runs) and incremental steps, plus parallel scavenging. But the final "atomic pause" of a major GC still stops the main thread, and that's what shows up as a long task / bad INP. Allocation rate drives GC frequency: the faster you allocate, the more often the scavenger runs and the sooner objects get promoted into the expensive old space.

// Measure GC pressure from the page (Chrome). Run with: chrome://flags → enable
// "Experimental Web Platform features" for measureUserAgentSpecificMemory.
performance.mark('hot-start');
// ...hot path...
performance.measure('hot', 'hot-start');

// Node: surface GC pauses on the event loop
const { PerformanceObserver } = require('node:perf_hooks');
new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  for (const e of list.getEntries())
    if (e.entryType === 'gc')
      console.log(`GC ${e.detail.kind} took ${e.duration.toFixed(2)}ms`);
}).observe({ entryTypes: ['gc'] });

Gotcha: a giant long-lived array of small objects forces every minor GC to scan it via the remembered set (old→young pointers). Prefer a Float64Array/struct-of-arrays layout for million-element hot data so the GC has *zero* pointers to trace.

1.4 Reducing allocations in hot paths

  • Reuse arrays/objects via object pools.
  • Prefer typed arrays (Float32Array) for numerical hot loops.
  • Avoid creating closures per render in animation/scroll loops.
  • Use Map for dynamic dictionaries; object literal for static shape.

Mechanism. Every object literal, array, closure, bound function, and even {...spread} is a heap allocation that the scavenger must later process. In a 60fps loop (16.6ms budget) or a scroll handler firing at 120Hz, per-frame garbage is what creates the sawtooth memory graph and intermittent GC jank. The fix is structural: hoist allocations out of the loop, reuse buffers, and prefer flat typed-array storage so there are no per-element objects to collect.

// Object pool for a particle system — zero allocations per frame.
class Vec2Pool {
  #buf; #n = 0;
  constructor(cap) { this.#buf = new Float32Array(cap * 2); }
  acquire(x, y) { const i = this.#n++ * 2; this.#buf[i] = x; this.#buf[i + 1] = y; return i; }
  reset() { this.#n = 0; }                    // "free everything" = pointer reset, no GC
  x(i) { return this.#buf[i]; } y(i) { return this.#buf[i + 1]; }
}

const pool = new Vec2Pool(10_000);
function frame(particles) {
  pool.reset();                               // reuse the same Float32Array forever
  for (let i = 0; i < particles.length; i++) {
    pool.acquire(particles[i].x, particles[i].y);
  }
  // ...draw from the pool's buffer in one tight loop...
}

Gotcha: arrow functions you pass to arr.forEach/.map inside a render allocate a fresh closure every call. In hot loops, switch to a plain for loop and call a *hoisted* named function. Also: Map is the right tool for dynamic string keys (no hidden-class churn, no prototype-pollution risk), while a frozen object literal is best for a fixed-shape config the JIT can inline.

1.5 Heap snapshot triage

  • Take baseline snapshot.
  • Reproduce the suspected leak (open + close modal 5×).
  • Take second snapshot.
  • Diff: "Comparison" view, sort by Delta Size.
  • Click retainer chain — find what is holding the object.
  • Common: closure scope, detached DOM, event listeners on window.

Mechanism + workflow. A heap snapshot is a graph: nodes (objects) and edges (references). The two metrics that matter:

  • Shallow size — bytes the object itself occupies.
  • Retained size — bytes that would be freed if this object were deleted (it + everything only it keeps alive). A small object with a huge retained size is your leak root.

The three-snapshot technique beats two: snapshot → do the action 7× → snapshot → do it 7× more → snapshot. Use the "Objects allocated between snapshot 1 and 2, still alive at 3" filter. Anything that grows linearly with the repetition count is leaking. Then follow Retainers (bottom panel) up the chain to the GC root. The classic culprits:

  • Detached DOM: filter the Summary view by Detached — a removed node still referenced by a JS variable keeps its entire subtree alive.
  • Closures: a long-lived callback (event listener, setInterval, observer) closes over a big object.
  • Forgotten listeners on window/document that were never removeEventListener'd.
// A real leak: each modal open registers a window listener closing over `bigData`.
function openModal(bigData /* 5MB */) {
  const onResize = () => layout(bigData);     // closure retains bigData
  window.addEventListener('resize', onResize);
  // BUG: no cleanup — bigData survives every close forever.
}

// Fixed with AbortController (one signal cleans up N listeners atomically):
function openModalFixed(bigData) {
  const ac = new AbortController();
  window.addEventListener('resize', () => layout(bigData), { signal: ac.signal });
  return () => ac.abort();   // call on modal close → listener + closure GC'd
}

Gotcha: snapshots themselves pin objects — take them in an Incognito window with extensions disabled, and force a GC (the trash-can icon) before each snapshot so you're not counting collectible garbage.

1.6 WeakRef + FinalizationRegistry

  • WeakRef holds a reference that does not prevent GC.
  • Use for caches where the consumer may keep the object alive elsewhere.
const cache = new Map();
function getOrLoad(key) {
  const ref = cache.get(key);
  const cached = ref?.deref();
  if (cached) return cached;
  const obj = load(key);
  cache.set(key, new WeakRef(obj));
  return obj;
}

Mechanism + the gotchas the snippet hides. WeakRef.deref() returns the target *or* undefined if it's been collected. FinalizationRegistry lets you run a cleanup callback *after* an object is collected — but with no timing guarantee and no guarantee it runs at all (e.g. on tab close). The naïve Map<key, WeakRef> above leaks the WeakRef wrapper and the Map entry even after the target dies — the map grows unbounded with dead refs. You need a registry to evict the stale key:

class WeakCache<K, V extends object> {
  #map = new Map<K, WeakRef<V>>();
  // When a value is GC'd, the registry fires with the held key → delete the dead entry.
  #reg = new FinalizationRegistry<K>((key) => {
    const ref = this.#map.get(key);
    if (ref && ref.deref() === undefined) this.#map.delete(key); // re-check: may be replaced
  });

  get(key: K, load: () => V): V {
    const hit = this.#map.get(key)?.deref();
    if (hit) return hit;
    const val = load();
    this.#map.set(key, new WeakRef(val));
    this.#reg.register(val, key, val); // 3rd arg = unregister token
    return val;
  }
}

Gotcha: never use WeakRef/FinalizationRegistry for application logic (closing files, releasing locks) — use using/Symbol.dispose (§4.6) which is deterministic. WeakRef is *only* for caches and observability. Also: a value reachable from the same turn you deref() it stays alive for that whole turn, so don't assume promptness.

1.7 Long-running tab memory budget

  • Mobile target: < 200 MB after 30 min usage.
  • Desktop target: < 500 MB for editor-class apps.
  • Tools: performance.memory (Chrome only), Memory tab heap snapshots.
  • Crash detector: Sentry can track tab-was-killed events via Crash Reporting API.

Mechanism. performance.memory is deprecated and coarse. The 2026 tool is performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory(), which returns a per-context, per-type breakdown (JS, DOM, shared) — but it *requires cross-origin isolation* (COOP+COEP, see §13.1) and only resolves at a GC-safe point. Pair it with the crash/oom Reporting API and document.wasDiscarded to detect when the browser killed your tab under memory pressure.

async function sampleMemory() {
  if (!('measureUserAgentSpecificMemory' in performance)) return;
  try {
    const { bytes, breakdown } = await (performance as any)
      .measureUserAgentSpecificMemory();
    beacon('mem', { mb: (bytes / 1048576).toFixed(1), breakdown });
  } catch (e) {
    // SecurityError => page is not crossOriginIsolated. Check this flag first:
    if (!crossOriginIsolated) console.warn('Set COOP+COEP to enable memory API');
  }
}
setInterval(sampleMemory, 60_000);

// Detect a tab the browser discarded/OOM-killed, on next load:
if (document.wasDiscarded) beacon('tab-discarded', { url: location.href });

Gotcha: budgets are *steady-state* numbers — what matters for a 30-min editor session is the slope, not the absolute. Plot RSS over time in RUM; a flat-but-high line is fine, a rising line means a leak. The mobile 200MB ceiling is where iOS Safari's Jetsam starts discarding tabs, so treat it as a hard wall, not a guideline.

Part 2 — React 19 internals (deeper)

2.1 RSC + Flight protocol

  • Server Components serialize their output as "Flight" — a streaming format React understands.
  • Client receives a chunk stream; React parses and reconciles into the tree.
  • Allows server to push updates: client subscribes once, server streams chunks as they resolve.
  • Bundle decoupling: server-only code never reaches the client bundle.
  • Debug: React DevTools shows server vs client component badges.

Mechanism. Flight is a line-delimited wire format where each row is id:payload. React serializes the *rendered output* of Server Components (not their source) into a tree of references. Three row types you'll see in the network tab:

  • M/module rows → a Client Component reference: { id: "./Button.js", name: "default", chunks: [...] }. The server sends only a *pointer*; the client lazy-loads the actual JS chunk.
  • J/value rows → the serialized element tree, with $L1 placeholders pointing at not-yet-resolved chunks.
  • S/Suspense rows → boundaries; later rows *back-fill* the placeholder as the server resolves async data, which is how streaming + out-of-order resolution works.
// Conceptual: what one Flight stream looks like over the wire (newline-delimited).
// 1:I["./Chart.client.js",["chunk-abc.js"],"default"]   <- client component ref
// 0:["$","main",null,{"children":["$","$L1",null,{}]}]   <- tree, $L1 = pending
// 2:"Resolved server data string"
// 1:["$","$L2",null,{"data":"$2"}]                       <- back-fills the boundary

// You rarely write Flight by hand; you produce it by rendering RSC to a stream:
import { renderToReadableStream } from 'react-server-dom-webpack/server';
const stream = renderToReadableStream(<App />, clientManifest);
// Client side, this reads the same stream and reconciles incrementally:
import { createFromReadableStream } from 'react-server-dom-webpack/client';
const root = createFromReadableStream(stream); // returns a thenable React renders

Gotcha: only serializable props cross the boundary — no functions (except Server Actions, which serialize as a special reference), no class instances, no Symbol. Passing an event handler from a Server to a Client Component throws at render time. The fix is to make the consuming component a Client Component and define the handler there, or pass a Server Action.

2.2 React Compiler internals

  • Performs read-set analysis at build time per function.
  • Auto-inserts memoization hooks into IR; preserves original semantics.
  • Bailouts on: mutation, ref misuse, breaking Rules of React, dynamic property access.
  • CLI: react-compiler-healthcheck reports % of files compiled.
  • Inspect: __REACT_DEVTOOLS_COMPONENT_FILTERS shows compiler-optimized components.

Mechanism. The compiler (Babel plugin) lowers each component into its own SSA-based IR (HIR), runs alias/mutation analysis to compute, for every value, *which props/state it depends on*, then emits a hidden useMemoCache slot array ($ = useMemoCache(n)). Each computed value gets a guarded cache slot: recompute only when its tracked dependencies change by Object.is. It's useMemo/useCallback/memo applied *exhaustively and correctly*, at sub-component granularity — including memoizing JSX subtrees so unchanged children skip reconciliation.

// You write:
function Profile({ user, theme }) {
  const greeting = `Hi ${user.name}`;        // depends only on user.name
  return <Banner color={theme.bg}>{greeting}</Banner>;
}

// Compiler emits (simplified):
function Profile({ user, theme }) {
  const $ = useMemoCache(4);
  let greeting;
  if ($[0] !== user.name) { greeting = `Hi ${user.name}`; $[0] = user.name; $[1] = greeting; }
  else greeting = $[1];
  let banner;
  if ($[2] !== theme.bg || $[1] !== greeting) { banner = <Banner color={theme.bg}>{greeting}</Banner>; /* ...store... */ }
  else banner = $[3];
  return banner;
}

Gotcha: the compiler silently bails out (no error, just no optimization) when you break the Rules of React — mutating props, reading refs during render, conditional hooks, or accessing values it can't prove are immutable. Run npx react-compiler-healthcheck and add eslint-plugin-react-hooks's compiler rules; a file that "isn't getting faster" is usually a silent bailout. Use the "use no memo" directive to opt a single function out while you fix it.

2.3 ref as a prop (React 19)

  • No more forwardRef — pass ref directly as a prop.
// React 19
function MyInput({ ref, ...rest }: { ref?: React.Ref<HTMLInputElement> }) {
  return <input ref={ref} {...rest} />;
}
// caller
const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);
<MyInput ref={inputRef} />

Mechanism. In React 19, ref is a normal prop on function components — forwardRef is deprecated (still works, but lint will nudge you off it). The JSX transform no longer strips ref into a special arg; it's part of props. This composes far better because you can spread it, default it, and forward it conditionally.

import { useRef, useImperativeHandle } from 'react';

type Handle = { focus: () => void; clear: () => void };

// ref-as-prop + imperative handle, no forwardRef needed:
function SearchBox({ ref, onSearch }: { ref?: React.Ref<Handle>; onSearch: (q: string) => void }) {
  const input = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);
  useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({
    focus: () => input.current?.focus(),
    clear: () => { if (input.current) input.current.value = ''; },
  }), []);
  return <input ref={input} onChange={(e) => onSearch(e.target.value)} />;
}

Gotcha: ref cleanup changed too — a ref callback may now return a cleanup function (like an effect), and React calls it on unmount instead of calling the callback again with null. If you wrote ref={el => { if (el) setup(el); else teardown(); }}, migrate to ref={el => { setup(el); return () => teardown(); }}. The old null call still happens for callbacks that don't return a cleanup, for back-compat.

2.4 mergeRefs pattern

function mergeRefs<T>(...refs: (React.Ref<T> | undefined)[]) {
  return (value: T) => {
    refs.forEach(ref => {
      if (typeof ref === "function") ref(value);
      else if (ref) (ref as any).current = value;
    });
  };
}
// usage
<input ref={mergeRefs(localRef, props.ref)} />

Mechanism + the cleanup-aware version. You need mergeRefs whenever a component has its *own* ref to a node AND must forward the consumer's ref to the same node (every design-system primitive does this). The naïve version above leaks: callback refs aren't cleaned up and object refs are never reset to null. The React-19-correct version returns a cleanup and handles both ref shapes:

function mergeRefs<T>(...refs: (React.Ref<T> | undefined)[]): React.RefCallback<T> {
  return (value: T | null) => {
    const cleanups: Array<() => void> = [];
    for (const ref of refs) {
      if (typeof ref === 'function') {
        const ret = ref(value);
        if (typeof ret === 'function') cleanups.push(ret); // React 19 cleanup-returning callback
      } else if (ref) {
        (ref as React.RefObject<T | null>).current = value;
      }
    }
    // Returned cleanup runs on unmount → resets object refs, invokes callback cleanups.
    return () => {
      for (const c of cleanups) c();
      for (const ref of refs)
        if (ref && typeof ref !== 'function') (ref as React.RefObject<T | null>).current = null;
    };
  };
}

Gotcha: prefer the react-merge-refs package or Radix's internal useComposedRefs in production — they memoize the merged callback so it's stable across renders. An inline mergeRefs(...) creates a new callback every render, which fires ref(null) then ref(node) on *every* commit, thrashing any setup/teardown in the callback. Memoize with useCallback keyed on the input refs.

2.5 Context performance — selector pattern

  • Default Context re-renders ALL consumers when value changes.
  • use-context-selector library subscribes to a slice; only re-renders if slice changed.
  • Alternative: Zustand store + Context wrapper (best of both).

Mechanism. React Context has no selector primitive: any consumer of useContext(C) re-renders whenever the provider's value identity changes, regardless of which field it reads. use-context-selector works by storing the value in a mutable ref + a versioned subscription list; consumers register a selector and are notified imperatively, bailing out via Object.is on the selected slice — bypassing React's "context changed → re-render all" path. Zustand does the same thing but as a standalone store you can also use outside React.

import { createStore, useStore } from 'zustand';
import { createContext, useContext, useRef } from 'react';

type CartState = { items: Item[]; total: number; addItem: (i: Item) => void };
const StoreCtx = createContext<ReturnType<typeof makeStore> | null>(null);
const makeStore = () => createStore<CartState>((set) => ({
  items: [], total: 0,
  addItem: (i) => set((s) => ({ items: [...s.items, i], total: s.total + i.price })),
}));

export function CartProvider({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const store = useRef(makeStore()).current; // one store per provider instance
  return <StoreCtx.Provider value={store}>{children}</StoreCtx.Provider>;
}

// Selector: this component re-renders ONLY when `total` changes, not when items mutate.
export function CartTotal() {
  const store = useContext(StoreCtx)!;
  const total = useStore(store, (s) => s.total); // sliced subscription
  return <span>${total.toFixed(2)}</span>;
}

Gotcha: with the React Compiler enabled you still need this — the compiler memoizes *renders*, but it can't change Context's all-or-nothing *subscription* semantics. Also avoid returning a fresh object/array from a selector (s => ({a: s.a})) without useShallow, or you'll re-render every time because the new object fails Object.is.

2.6 Suspense list (revealOrder)

  • SuspenseList coordinates reveal of multiple siblings.
  • revealOrder="forwards" / "backwards" / "together" controls reveal sequence.
  • Useful for chat / feed where you want top-down reveal even if items resolve out of order.

Mechanism. SuspenseList orchestrates the *display order* of sibling Suspense boundaries independent of their *resolution order*. With revealOrder="forwards", even if item 3's data arrives first, React holds it hidden (showing its fallback) until items 1 and 2 reveal — preventing the "content pops in randomly" jank. tail="collapsed" shows only the next pending fallback rather than all of them at once.

import { SuspenseList, Suspense } from 'react';

function Feed({ ids }: { ids: string[] }) {
  return (
    // forwards = strictly top-down reveal; collapsed = one spinner at a time
    <SuspenseList revealOrder="forwards" tail="collapsed">
      {ids.map((id) => (
        <Suspense key={id} fallback={<PostSkeleton />}>
          <Post id={id} />          {/* each Post reads a promise (use(fetchPost(id))) */}
        </Suspense>
      ))}
    </SuspenseList>
  );
}

Gotcha: as of React 19.x, SuspenseList is not yet in the stable public API for some build targets — it ships in experimental/canary and is gated. Confirm it's exported from your React version before relying on it; in stable apps the common fallback is to order reveals manually with a state machine or staggered CSS. Also: revealOrder only affects the *initial* reveal, not subsequent updates.

2.7 React 19.2 Activity component

  • Hides part of the tree but keeps state + DOM alive ("activity off").
  • Use for tabs / wizards where you want to preserve mounted state without re-rendering.
  • Replaces the older "keepalive" patterns hacked via display:none.

Mechanism. <Activity mode="hidden"> unmounts *effects* (so timers, subscriptions, intersection observers pause) but preserves component state and DOM, and de-prioritizes any rendering inside it to the lowest scheduler lane. When you flip back to mode="visible", effects re-mount and state is exactly as you left it — scroll position, form input, expanded rows. This is structurally different from display:none, which keeps effects running (wasting CPU) and from unmounting, which destroys state.

import { Activity, useState } from 'react';

function Tabs() {
  const [active, setActive] = useState<'search' | 'profile'>('search');
  return (
    <>
      <nav>
        <button onClick={() => setActive('search')}>Search</button>
        <button onClick={() => setActive('profile')}>Profile</button>
      </nav>
      {/* Both stay mounted; the hidden one's effects pause, its state persists. */}
      <Activity mode={active === 'search' ? 'visible' : 'hidden'}>
        <SearchPanel />   {/* keeps query, results, scroll when you tab away */}
      </Activity>
      <Activity mode={active === 'profile' ? 'visible' : 'hidden'}>
        <ProfilePanel />
      </Activity>
    </>
  );
}

Gotcha: because effects *unmount* when hidden, any effect with external side effects (analytics "view" pings, websocket subscriptions) will fire its cleanup on hide and re-run on show — design those to be idempotent. Don't store huge component trees in hidden Activity blocks indefinitely; the DOM is retained and counts against your memory budget (§1.7).

2.8 React 19.2 Performance Tracks

  • Adds a "React" track to Chrome Performance panel.
  • Shows scheduler events, commits, and effects on the timeline.
  • Pair with Long Animation Frames to attribute jank.

Mechanism. React 19.2 emits entries via the User Timing / performance.measure API tagged with a custom track name, so the Chrome Performance panel renders dedicated "⚛ Scheduler" and "⚛ Components" swim-lanes. You see render lanes (their priority), individual commits, and which component's effects ran — lined up against the main-thread flame chart and the Long Animation Frames (LoAF) track, so you can attribute a 200ms long task to a specific over-rendering component.

// You don't enable anything in code (dev builds auto-instrument), but you can add
// your own marks into the same timeline to correlate app events with React work:
performance.mark('route:dashboard:start');
// ...navigation + data load...
performance.measure('route:dashboard', { start: 'route:dashboard:start' });

// Read LoAF from RUM to know WHEN to open the profiler:
new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  for (const e of list.getEntries() as PerformanceLongAnimationFrameTiming[])
    if (e.duration > 200) beacon('loaf', { dur: e.duration, scripts: e.scripts?.map(s => s.sourceURL) });
}).observe({ type: 'long-animation-frame', buffered: true });

Gotcha: the React track only appears in development/profiling builds — production bundles strip the instrumentation for performance. Profile a representative dev build (with NODE_ENV tuned to keep it realistic), not a clean prod build, when chasing render jank.

2.9 Suspense + transition coordination

  • startTransition wraps state updates → React tries to keep current UI rendered while preparing next.
  • useTransition gives isPending — show inline spinner without unmounting current view.
  • Combine with Suspense: transition lets old data show until new data resolves.

Mechanism. A normal state update that hits a suspending component shows the Suspense *fallback* (unmounts current content). Wrapping that update in startTransition marks it non-urgent: React renders the next tree *in the background* and keeps the current committed UI on screen until the new tree is ready — no fallback flash. isPending lets you show a subtle inline indicator meanwhile. This is the mechanism behind "type in a filter, old results stay visible, dimmed, until new ones arrive."

import { useState, useTransition, Suspense, use } from 'react';

function Results({ query }: { query: string }) {
  const data = use(searchCache(query)); // suspends on cache miss
  return <ul>{data.map((r) => <li key={r.id}>{r.title}</li>)}</ul>;
}

export function Search() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();
  return (
    <>
      <input onChange={(e) => {
        const q = e.target.value;
        startTransition(() => setQuery(q)); // non-urgent → keep old results visible
      }} />
      <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>
        <div style={{ opacity: isPending ? 0.6 : 1 }}>
          <Results query={query} />  {/* on a transition, old list stays during fetch */}
        </div>
      </Suspense>
    </>
  );
}

Gotcha: the input value itself must be an urgent update or typing feels laggy — keep setQuery for the *committed* query inside the transition, but drive the controlled input from a *separate* urgent state (or an uncontrolled input). Also, a transition only suppresses the fallback if the boundary was *already revealed*; the very first mount still shows the fallback.

2.10 Owner vs Parent in DevTools

  • Owner = component that created the JSX element.
  • Parent = component in the rendered tree above it.
  • Owner stack tells you where a bug propagated FROM, not just where it lives.
  • useDebugValue exposes custom values in the inspector.

Mechanism. *Parent* is the structural tree relationship (who renders inside whom at runtime). *Owner* is who wrote the JSX that produced the element — which determines what props/closures it captured. They differ whenever you pass elements as props/children: <Layout>{<Widget />}</Layout> — Layout is Widget's *parent*, but whatever component wrote that JSX is its *owner*. React 19 exposes captureOwnerStack() so error overlays can show the *owner* chain, which is usually where a bad prop actually originated.

import { captureOwnerStack } from 'react';

function useDebuggableValue<T>(label: string, value: T): T {
  // Surfaces a labeled value in the DevTools hook inspector.
  React.useDebugValue(`${label}: ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
  return value;
}

function RiskyChild({ data }: { data: unknown }) {
  if (data == null) {
    // Owner stack tells you WHICH component passed the bad `data`, not just the parent.
    console.error('null data', captureOwnerStack());
  }
  return <div>{String(data)}</div>;
}

Gotcha: captureOwnerStack() returns a meaningful stack only in development (returns null in prod). The owner relationship is also why a context value can be "missing" even though the parent provides it — if the element was *created* (owned) outside the provider's subtree and merely passed down as a child, it reads context from where it was rendered (parent), not where it was written. Knowing the difference resolves most "why is my context undefined" bugs.

Part 3 — Modern CSS (deeper)

3.1 Scroll-driven animations (native)

@keyframes reveal {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(40px); }
  to   { opacity: 1; transform: none; }
}
.card {
  animation: reveal linear;
  animation-timeline: view();      /* progress = element's position in viewport */
  animation-range: entry 0% cover 30%;
}
/* Scroll-linked progress bar */
.progress {
  animation: grow linear;
  animation-timeline: scroll(root);
}
  • No JS, no rAF, GPU-accelerated.
  • view() timeline ties to element position in viewport; scroll() timeline ties to container scroll.
  • Progressive enhancement — falls back gracefully where unsupported.

Mechanism. A scroll-driven animation replaces *time* with *scroll progress* as the animation's "clock." Two timeline types: scroll(<scroller> <axis>) maps the scroll position of a scroll container to 0–100%, and view(<axis> <inset>) maps a *subject element's* progress through the scrollport.
