Crucially these run off the main thread in the compositor, so they don't jank even when JS is busy — unlike requestAnimationFrame-driven scroll effects. Named timelines (scroll-timeline-name/view-timeline-name) let a timeline declared on one element drive an animation on another.

/* Named timeline: a parent declares it; a distant child consumes it. */
.gallery {
  scroll-timeline-name: --gallery;
  scroll-timeline-axis: x;
  overflow-x: auto;
}
.indicator {
  animation: fill linear;
  animation-timeline: --gallery;     /* driven by the gallery's horizontal scroll */
}
@keyframes fill { to { width: 100%; } }

/* Always guard so non-supporting browsers don't run a timeline-less animation: */
@supports (animation-timeline: scroll()) {
  .card { animation: reveal linear both; animation-timeline: view(); animation-range: entry cover 30%; }
}

Gotcha: only compositor-friendly properties (opacity, transform) stay off the main thread; animating width/top/height forces main-thread layout every scroll frame and reintroduces the jank you were avoiding. Also, an animation with a scroll timeline but *no* animation-range defaults to the full timeline — set the range explicitly or the effect feels off. animation-fill-mode: both keeps the start state before the range begins.

3.2 @starting-style + transition-behavior

dialog {
  opacity: 0;
  transition: opacity 0.2s, display 0.2s allow-discrete;
  transition-behavior: allow-discrete;   /* enables display: none transitions */
}
dialog[open] { opacity: 1; }
@starting-style {
  dialog[open] { opacity: 0; }   /* entry state */
}
  • Animate from display:none to visible without JS choreography.

Mechanism. Browsers can't transition *into existence* — an element appearing from display:none has no "before" value to interpolate from. @starting-style supplies that initial value used only for the first style change after the element becomes rendered. transition-behavior: allow-discrete lets *discrete* properties (display, visibility, overlay) flip at the appropriate end of the transition instead of instantly, so display stays block through the fade-out then snaps to none. The overlay property (for top-layer elements like dialog/popover) must also be in the transition so the element stays in the top layer while exiting.

[popover] {
  opacity: 0;
  transform: scale(0.95);
  transition: opacity .2s, transform .2s, display .2s allow-discrete, overlay .2s allow-discrete;
}
[popover]:popover-open {
  opacity: 1;
  transform: scale(1);
}
/* The "from" state for the ENTRY transition only: */
@starting-style {
  [popover]:popover-open { opacity: 0; transform: scale(0.9); }
}

Gotcha: @starting-style rules must have at least the specificity of the target rule or they're ignored; nest them or match selectors exactly. And remember allow-discrete flips display at the *end* of an exit transition but at the *start* of an entry — so entry animations work without @starting-style for the discrete prop, but the *animatable* props still need the starting style to have something to animate from.

3.3 View Transitions — cross-document (MPA)

<meta name="view-transition" content="same-origin">
@view-transition { navigation: auto; }
.hero { view-transition-name: hero; }
/* Different page; same view-transition-name → animated morph */
  • Native MPA navigation animations across pages — same-origin only.
  • Shopify, GitHub use it for instant-feel multi-page apps.

Mechanism. On a same-origin navigation, the browser snapshots the old page, captures the new page after it loads, and cross-fades the ::view-transition-group pseudo-tree. Elements sharing a view-transition-name across the two documents are *paired* and morphed (position/size interpolated) instead of fading — that's the "hero image flies into place" effect. You opt in with @view-transition { navigation: auto; } in both pages' CSS. The pseudo-element tree (::view-transition-old(name) / ::view-transition-new(name)) is fully styleable.

@view-transition { navigation: auto; }

/* Pair the hero across pages; give it a distinct animation. */
.product-image { view-transition-name: hero; }

::view-transition-old(hero),
::view-transition-new(hero) { animation-duration: 0.3s; }

/* Customize the default root cross-fade: slide instead of fade. */
::view-transition-old(root) { animation: slide-out 0.25s ease both; }
::view-transition-new(root) { animation: slide-in  0.25s ease both; }

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  ::view-transition-group(*) { animation: none !important; } /* a11y: respect reduced motion */
}

Gotcha: a view-transition-name must be unique per document at transition time — two visible elements with the same name abort the transition with an error. For lists, generate per-item names (view-transition-name: post-{id}). Cross-document transitions are *same-origin only* and require the new document to render quickly; a slow LCP delays the whole transition, so they pair best with prerendering/Speculation Rules.

3.4 Container style queries

.theme-dark { --bg: black; }
@container style(--bg: black) {
  .card { border-color: white; }
}
  • Style based on a custom property of an ancestor — replaces some Sass workarounds.

Mechanism. Container *style* queries match against the computed value of a custom property on the nearest container ancestor, letting a component restyle itself based on an inherited token rather than a media/size query. This is genuinely new capability: you can theme a subtree by setting one variable and have descendants react in CSS, no JS, no class plumbing. (Container *size* queries — @container (min-width: 400px) — are the better-known sibling; both require an ancestor with container-type.)

.surface { container-name: surface; /* style queries don't need container-type */ }

/* A toolbar that inverts its icons when the surface declares a dark intent. */
.surface { --intent: light; }
.surface[data-mode="dark"] { --intent: dark; }

@container surface style(--intent: dark) {
  .toolbar-icon { fill: white; }
  .divider { border-color: oklch(1 0 0 / 0.2); }
}

Gotcha: style queries currently only support querying registered or custom properties, and equality is exact-match on the computed value — style(--intent: dark) won't match Dark or a fallback. Range syntax (style(--x > 10)) needs the property registered via @property with a numeric syntax. Don't put container-type: inline-size on the element you're style-querying unless you also need size queries — it establishes a layout containment context that can collapse intrinsic sizing.

3.5 Anchor positioning advanced

.tooltip {
  position: absolute;
  position-anchor: --btn;
  position-area: top span-all;
  position-try: flip-block;   /* flip below if not enough room above */
  position-try-fallbacks: --custom-flip-option;
}
@position-try --custom-flip-option {
  position-area: bottom span-all;
}
  • Native tooltip/popover positioning with automatic collision detection.

Mechanism. Anchor positioning lets an absolutely-positioned element tether to another element (the *anchor*) without JS measurement. anchor-name: --btn names the anchor; the positioned element references it via position-anchor and places itself with position-area (a 3×3 grid relative to the anchor) or the anchor() function (top: anchor(bottom)). The browser does collision detection: position-try-fallbacks lists alternative placements to try when the preferred one would overflow the viewport, swapping to the first that fits.

.menu-button { anchor-name: --menu-btn; }

.menu {
  position: fixed;
  position-anchor: --menu-btn;
  /* Preferred: below, left-aligned. */
  top: anchor(bottom);
  left: anchor(left);
  /* If it would overflow, try these in order: */
  position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline, --shift-up;
  /* Size to the anchor's width: */
  width: anchor-size(--menu-btn width);
}
@position-try --shift-up {
  top: auto;
  bottom: anchor(top);   /* open upward as a last resort */
}

Gotcha: the anchor must be a valid anchor scope for the positioned element — they must share a common ancestor and the positioned element generally must come *after* the anchor in the DOM (or use anchor-scope). Also: anchor positioning only kicks in for position: absolute|fixed; a position: static element silently ignores position-anchor. Pair with the Popover API so the menu lives in the top layer and isn't clipped by overflow:hidden ancestors.

3.6 Color spaces (oklch, lab, lch)

  • oklch is perceptually uniform — equal numeric changes look equal.
  • Use for design tokens; better for generating palettes (lighten/darken/shift).
:root {
  --primary: oklch(0.7 0.18 250);
  --primary-hover: oklch(from var(--primary) calc(l - 0.05) c h);
}

Mechanism. oklch(L C H) is lightness (0–1), chroma (0–unbounded), hue (0–360°) in the OKLab perceptual space. Because it's perceptually uniform, fixed lightness steps *look* evenly spaced — unlike HSL, where hsl(60 100% 50%) (yellow) looks far brighter than hsl(240 100% 50%) (blue) at the same "lightness." The relative color syntax oklch(from <color> L C H) decomposes any color into its OKLCH channels (l, c, h keywords) so you can derive variants with calc(). This is how you build a whole token ramp from one seed.

:root {
  --brand: oklch(0.65 0.2 264);
  /* Derive a 5-step ramp by stepping lightness, keeping chroma + hue: */
  --brand-100: oklch(from var(--brand) 0.95 c h);
  --brand-300: oklch(from var(--brand) 0.85 c h);
  --brand-500: var(--brand);
  --brand-700: oklch(from var(--brand) 0.45 c h);
  --brand-900: oklch(from var(--brand) 0.30 c h);
  /* Shift hue for a complementary accent without touching L/C: */
  --accent: oklch(from var(--brand) l c calc(h + 180));
}

Gotcha: high-chroma OKLCH colors can fall outside the sRGB gamut — the browser gamut-maps them, and on a P3 display they render more saturated than on sRGB, so two devices show different colors. Clamp chroma for sRGB targets or wrap wide-gamut values in @media (color-gamut: p3). Also, calc(l - 0.05) in the original is correct, but l is 0–1 — subtracting 0.05 is a real perceptual step, whereas the same number in lab() (L is 0–100) would be invisible.

3.7 color-mix() patterns

background: color-mix(in oklch, var(--primary), white 12%);
/* dynamic theming without a preprocessor */

Mechanism. color-mix(in <space>, c1 p1, c2 p2) interpolates two colors in a chosen space. The *space matters*: mixing in oklch/oklab keeps perceived lightness sane and avoids the muddy grays you get mixing through sRGB. Percentages are optional and normalized; omit one and it fills the remainder. This replaces Sass mix(), lighten(), darken(), and transparentize() entirely — and it works with currentColor and CSS variables, so it's *runtime* dynamic.

:root { --primary: oklch(0.6 0.18 255); }

.btn {
  background: var(--primary);
  /* Tints/shades derived live — change --primary, everything updates. */
  border-color: color-mix(in oklch, var(--primary), black 15%);
}
.btn:hover  { background: color-mix(in oklch, var(--primary), white 12%); }
.btn:active { background: color-mix(in oklch, var(--primary), black 12%); }
.btn:disabled {
  /* Fade to transparent without knowing the base color: */
  background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--primary) 40%, transparent);
}
/* Automatic translucent text via mixing toward transparent: */
.chip { color: color-mix(in oklch, currentColor 85%, transparent); }

Gotcha: when mixing through hue-bearing spaces (oklch, hsl), hue interpolation takes the *shorter arc* by default and can pass through an unexpected hue; add hue shorter|longer to control it. And mixing with transparent in srgb premultiplies alpha differently than in oklab — pick srgb for predictable opacity fades, oklch for color blends.

3.8 Native CSS nesting

.card {
  padding: 1rem;
  & h2 { color: var(--primary); }
  &:hover { background: var(--surface-2); }
  @media (min-width: 600px) { padding: 2rem; }
}
  • Sass-like nesting natively. No build tool needed.

Mechanism. Native nesting is parsed by the browser's CSS engine, not a preprocessor. The & is the *nesting selector* and refers to the enclosing rule's full selector list. A nested rule that doesn't start with a combinator/& is implicitly relative (the browser inserts a descendant &), so h2 {} inside .card {} means .card h2. Crucially, nesting does not flatten at build time — specificity is computed differently from Sass: & h2 has the specificity of :is(.card) h2, and a nested compound like &.active keeps both classes' specificity.

.menu {
  --gap: 8px;
  display: flex; gap: var(--gap);

  & > li { padding: 4px; }          /* .menu > li */
  &:focus-within { outline: 2px solid; }  /* .menu:focus-within */

  /* & can appear in the middle → useful for parent-state styling: */
  .theme-dark & { background: black; }    /* .theme-dark .menu */

  @media (width >= 600px) { gap: 16px; }  /* media nesting, range syntax */
}

Gotcha: the :is()-based specificity of nested selectors bites you — & .foo where the parent is #id .bar gives the nested rule #id-level specificity, which can unexpectedly win or lose. When in doubt, check computed specificity in DevTools. Also, an element-type selector as the *first* token after & historically needed care; modern browsers accept & h2, and a bare h2 {} (no &) also works now since the relaxed nesting spec — both mean .card h2.

3.9 @property (typed custom properties)

@property --angle {
  syntax: "<angle>"; inherits: false; initial-value: 0deg;
}
/* Now --angle can be animated/transitioned */

Mechanism. A plain custom property is an *untyped token* — the browser treats it as a string and cannot interpolate it, so transition: --angle 1s does nothing. @property (or the JS CSS.registerProperty) registers a type via syntax, an inherits flag, and an initial-value. Once typed, the browser knows how to interpolate it, enabling animated gradients, counters, and number tweens that were previously impossible in pure CSS. The initial-value is mandatory for non-universal syntaxes and provides a guaranteed-valid fallback.

@property --angle {
  syntax: "<angle>";
  inherits: false;
  initial-value: 0deg;
}
@property --pct {
  syntax: "<percentage>";
  inherits: false;
  initial-value: 0%;
}

.spinner {
  background: conic-gradient(from var(--angle), #f0f, #0ff, #f0f);
  animation: rotate 2s linear infinite;
}
@keyframes rotate { to { --angle: 360deg; } } /* animatable BECAUSE it's typed */

.bar { background: linear-gradient(90deg, green var(--pct), #eee 0); transition: --pct .4s; }
.bar:hover { --pct: 100%; }

Gotcha: syntax strings are restrictive — "<color>", "<length>", "<number>", "<percentage>", "<angle>", "<length-percentage>", etc., plus "*" (universal, but universal stays non-animatable). A value that doesn't match syntax falls back to initial-value *silently*, which can mask bugs. And inherits: true on a heavily-used property forces recomputation down the subtree — keep inherits: false unless you actually need cascade inheritance.

3.10 contain / content-visibility

  • contain: layout — promises layout does not affect outside; browser can skip layout passes.
  • contain: paint — promises element does not paint outside its box.
  • content-visibility: auto — skip rendering offscreen entirely; massive scroll perf win.
  • contain-intrinsic-size — size hint so skipped content does not collapse the page.

Mechanism. CSS containment is a *promise to the browser* that an element's internals don't affect the outside, which lets the engine skip work. contain: layout isolates the layout subtree (a child's reflow can't dirty siblings/ancestors). contain: paint clips painting to the box and lets the browser skip painting it entirely when offscreen. content-visibility: auto is the big one: the browser skips layout, paint, and style of the element's subtree while it's off-screen, rendering it only when it scrolls near the viewport — turning a 10,000-item list into near-O(visible) work. contain-intrinsic-size gives a placeholder size so the scrollbar and page height stay stable for not-yet-rendered content.

/* Each feed card pays rendering cost only when near the viewport. */
.feed-item {
  content-visibility: auto;
  /* Reserve estimated size so skipped items don't collapse the scroll height
     and cause scrollbar jumping / anchor drift. */
  contain-intrinsic-size: auto 320px;  /* 'auto' remembers the real size once measured */
}

/* Isolate an animating widget so its repaints don't invalidate the page. */
.live-chart { contain: layout paint style; }

Gotcha: content-visibility: auto skipped content was historically invisible to in-page find (Ctrl+F) and to anchor links — modern browsers handle find-in-page and :target by force-rendering, but verify, and never apply it to content that must be immediately accessible (e.g. above-the-fold or print). Also, a wrong contain-intrinsic-size causes scroll-anchoring jumps as estimates correct themselves; use the auto <size> form so the browser caches the last real measurement.

Part 4 — Modern JavaScript (2026)

4.1 Temporal (stable in 2026)

const now = Temporal.Now.zonedDateTimeISO("America/New_York");
const lunch = now.with({ hour: 12, minute: 30, second: 0, millisecond: 0 });
const diff = lunch.until(now);
lunch.add({ days: 7 });   // safe DST handling
  • Replaces Date — immutable, time-zone aware, never silently wrong.
  • Polyfill: @js-temporal/polyfill until browser support is universal.

Mechanism. Temporal models distinct concepts as distinct types instead of overloading one mutable Date: Temporal.Instant (an exact moment, ns precision), Temporal.ZonedDateTime (instant + time zone + calendar), Temporal.PlainDate/PlainTime/PlainDateTime (wall-clock with no zone), and Temporal.Duration. Everything is immutable — .add()/.with() return new objects. Arithmetic on ZonedDateTime is DST-aware: adding "1 day" lands on the same wall-clock time even across a DST jump (which may be 23 or 25 hours of real elapsed time), whereas adding to an Instant adds exact nanoseconds.

// The classic Date bug Temporal fixes: "same time tomorrow" across DST.
const z = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from('2026-03-08T09:00[America/New_York]'); // DST starts 3/8
const tomorrow = z.add({ days: 1 });        // 2026-03-09T09:00 (still 9am, though 23h elapsed)
const exact   = z.toInstant().add({ hours: 24 }).toZonedDateTimeISO('America/New_York');
// exact => 2026-03-09T10:00  (24 real hours lands at 10am because the clock sprang forward)

// Parsing + formatting stay explicit; no ambiguous "new Date(string)" timezone guessing:
const d = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-06-05');
d.toLocaleString('en-US', { dateStyle: 'long' }); // "June 5, 2026"

Gotcha: Temporal.Now.zonedDateTimeISO() uses the ISO 8601 calendar; for non-Gregorian calendars pass a calendar id. And you cannot compare types across kinds — comparing a PlainDateTime to a ZonedDateTime throws, by design, forcing you to decide whether you mean wall-clock or exact time. When persisting, store the Instant (or RFC 9557 string with zone), never a PlainDateTime, or you lose the zone.

4.2 Iterator helpers

const evens = [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9].values().filter(x => x % 2 === 0).map(x => x * 10).take(3).toArray();
// [20, 40, 60]
// Lazy: only consumes what is needed

Mechanism. Iterator helpers add .map/.filter/.take/.drop/.flatMap/.reduce/.toArray/.some/.every/.find directly to the Iterator prototype, so they work on *any* iterator — generators, Map.keys(), Set.values(), DOM iterators — and are lazy: nothing is computed until the chain is pulled. .take(3) short-circuits the source, so chaining over an infinite generator is fine. This is the native answer to Lodash chains without materializing intermediate arrays.

function* naturals() { let i = 1; while (true) yield i++; } // infinite

// Lazy: pulls exactly 5 values from an infinite source, builds 0 intermediate arrays.
const result = naturals()
  .filter((n) => n % 2 === 1)   // odds
  .map((n) => n * n)            // squares
  .take(5)
  .toArray();                   // [1, 9, 25, 49, 81]

// Works on any iterator, e.g. transform a Map's entries lazily:
const m = new Map([['a', 1], ['b', 2], ['c', 3]]);
const big = m.entries().filter(([, v]) => v > 1).map(([k]) => k.toUpperCase()).toArray(); // ['B','C']

Gotcha: helpers consume the underlying iterator — after it.take(2).toArray(), it is partially drained; you can't reuse it. And .map/.filter return *iterator helpers*, not arrays, so console.log(it.map(...)) shows an opaque object; call .toArray() or spread it. Don't confuse these with array methods: [].values() gives you the lazy iterator, while [].map() is eager and array-returning.

4.3 Set methods

a.intersection(b);
a.union(b);
a.difference(b);
a.symmetricDifference(b);
a.isSubsetOf(b);
a.isSupersetOf(b);
a.isDisjointFrom(b);

Mechanism. These are now native Set.prototype methods (no more new Set([...a].filter(x => b.has(x)))). They return new Sets (or booleans for the predicate methods) and are optimized internally — the engine iterates the smaller set and probes the larger, so they're faster than the manual array round-trip. The argument can be any set-like object (has size, has(), keys()), not just a Set.

const enrolled = new Set(['math', 'cs', 'art']);
const required = new Set(['cs', 'math', 'pe']);

const both    = enrolled.intersection(required);        // Set { 'math', 'cs' }
const missing = required.difference(enrolled);          // Set { 'pe' }
const either  = enrolled.union(required);               // Set { 'math','cs','art','pe' }
const xor     = enrolled.symmetricDifference(required); // Set { 'art', 'pe' }

const ok = new Set(['cs']).isSubsetOf(enrolled);        // true
const clash = enrolled.isDisjointFrom(new Set(['pe'])); // true (no overlap)

Gotcha: these methods don't mutate a or b — assign the result. The argument must be set-like; passing a plain array throws (required.intersection(['cs']) → TypeError) because an array has no .has/.size. Wrap arrays in new Set(arr) first. Element identity uses SameValueZero (so NaN is found, +0/-0 are the same).

4.4 Object.groupBy / Map.groupBy

const byKind = Object.groupBy(items, it => it.kind);
// { fruit: [...], veg: [...] }
const map = Map.groupBy(items, it => it.kind);  // returns Map

Mechanism. Both take an iterable and a callback (item, index) => key and bucket items into arrays. Object.groupBy returns a null-prototype object (so no __proto__/constructor collisions) keyed by String(key) — keys are coerced to strings/symbols. Map.groupBy returns a real Map, preserving key *identity* — essential when grouping by an object reference or a non-string key.

const orders = [
  { id: 1, status: 'paid', total: 50 },
  { id: 2, status: 'pending', total: 20 },
  { id: 3, status: 'paid', total: 30 },
];

// String keys → Object.groupBy (null-proto, safe to iterate):
const byStatus = Object.groupBy(orders, (o) => o.status);
// { __proto__: null, paid: [ {id:1...},{id:3...} ], pending: [ {id:2...} ] }

// Non-string / object keys → Map.groupBy (preserves identity):
const tiers = { lo: {}, hi: {} };
const byTier = Map.groupBy(orders, (o) => (o.total >= 40 ? tiers.hi : tiers.lo));
byTier.get(tiers.hi); // [ {id:1, total:50} ]

Gotcha: Object.groupBy stringifies keys — grouping by a numeric key gives string properties (byKind[1] works via coercion, but Object.keys() returns "1"). If your grouping key is an object or you need numeric keys preserved, use Map.groupBy. Neither dedupes — an item appears once in its bucket, in source order. The result object's null prototype means byStatus.hasOwnProperty is *undefined*; use Object.hasOwn(byStatus, 'paid').

4.5 Promise.withResolvers

const { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers();
// Useful for deferred patterns (event-driven libs, signaling)

Mechanism. Before this, exposing a promise's resolve/reject outside the executor required the "deferred" boilerplate (let resolve; const p = new Promise(r => resolve = r)). Promise.withResolvers() returns { promise, resolve, reject } in one call — ideal for bridging callback/event APIs into promises, request/response correlation over a socket, and one-shot signals.

// Bridge an event-driven API (e.g. a WebSocket request/response) to a promise.
class RpcClient {
  #pending = new Map<string, (v: unknown) => void>();
  constructor(private ws: WebSocket) {
    ws.addEventListener('message', (e) => {
      const { id, result } = JSON.parse(e.data);
      this.#pending.get(id)?.(result);
      this.#pending.delete(id);
    });
  }
  call(method: string, params: unknown): Promise<unknown> {
    const id = crypto.randomUUID();
    const { promise, resolve } = Promise.withResolvers<unknown>();
    this.#pending.set(id, resolve);
    this.ws.send(JSON.stringify({ id, method, params }));
    return promise;     // resolved later, from the message handler
  }
}

Gotcha: the returned promise is unhandled until *someone* awaits/.catches it — if you store it and reject() before anyone attaches a handler, you get an unhandledrejection. Always attach handling (or a .catch(() => {})) when you create long-lived deferreds, and clean up the pending-map entry on timeout to avoid leaks.

4.6 using declaration + Symbol.dispose

class TempFile {
  open() { /* … */ }
  [Symbol.dispose]() { this.close(); }
}
function process() {
  using file = new TempFile();
  // file.dispose() runs automatically when scope ends
}
  • TS 5.2+ supports it; great for AbortControllers, locks, transactions.

Mechanism. using x = resource registers resource in the enclosing block's disposal stack; when the block exits by any path (return, throw, break), the engine calls resource[Symbol.dispose]() in reverse order of acquisition — deterministic, synchronous cleanup, like C#'s using or RAII. await using calls the async [Symbol.asyncDispose]() and awaits it. This is the *deterministic* counterpart to FinalizationRegistry (§1.6): use using for locks, file handles, spans, and transactions; use WeakRef only for caches.

// Async disposal: a DB transaction that always rolls back on early exit.
class Transaction {
  constructor(private db: DB) {}
  static async begin(db: DB) { await db.query('BEGIN'); return new Transaction(db); }
  committed = false;
  async commit() { await this.db.query('COMMIT'); this.committed = true; }
  async [Symbol.asyncDispose]() {
    if (!this.committed) await this.db.query('ROLLBACK'); // runs on throw OR early return
  }
}

async function transfer(db: DB, from: string, to: string, amt: number) {
  await using tx = await Transaction.begin(db);
  await db.query('UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - ? WHERE id = ?', [amt, from]);
  if (amt > 10_000) throw new Error('limit');  // ROLLBACK fires automatically here
  await db.query('UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + ? WHERE id = ?', [amt, to]);
  await tx.commit();                            // no throw → COMMIT, dispose is a no-op
}

Gotcha: using is block-scoped, not function-scoped — disposal happens at the } of the enclosing block, so don't wrap a resource you need to outlive the block. Use DisposableStack/AsyncDisposableStack to *aggregate* and conditionally hand off ownership (stack.move()). Requires the Symbol.dispose polyfill on older runtimes; TS downlevels the syntax but the symbols must exist (Symbol.dispose ??= Symbol('dispose')).

4.7 structuredClone (built-in)

  • Deep-clones Maps, Sets, Dates, ArrayBuffers, TypedArrays, cyclic structures.
  • Cannot clone: functions, DOM nodes, class instances, Symbols.
  • Replaces JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) for safe deep clone.

Mechanism. structuredClone runs the structured clone algorithm — the same serializer used by postMessage, IndexedDB, and the History API. It walks the graph, preserves cyclic references and shared subgraphs, and handles Map, Set, Date, RegExp, ArrayBuffer, TypedArray, Blob, File, and Error — none of which survive JSON.parse(JSON.stringify()) (which silently turns Date into a string, drops undefined/functions, and throws on cycles). The optional transfer list moves ownership of buffers instead of copying them (zero-copy).

const original: any = { when: new Date(), tags: new Set(['a', 'b']), buf: new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3]) };
original.self = original;                 // cycle → JSON.stringify would throw

const copy = structuredClone(original);
copy.when instanceof Date;                // true (JSON would give a string)
copy.tags.has('a');                       // true (JSON would give {})
copy.self === copy;                       // true (cycle preserved, points to the clone)

// Zero-copy transfer of a big buffer to a worker (buffer detached in main thread):
const big = new ArrayBuffer(64 * 1024 * 1024);
const moved = structuredClone({ big }, { transfer: [big] });
big.byteLength;                           // 0 — ownership moved, not copied

Gotcha: it throws DataCloneError on functions, Symbols, DOM nodes, and (by default) class instances — it copies *data*, dropping the prototype, so a cloned class User becomes a plain object losing its methods. For class instances, clone the fields and re-wrap, or implement a serializer. It's also synchronous and can block on huge graphs — clone in a worker for multi-MB structures.

4.8 RegExp v flag

  • Unicode property escapes + set notation: /[\p{Emoji}--\p{Emoji_Component}]/v.
  • Cleaner emoji handling without manual surrogate pairs.

Mechanism. The v flag (unicodeSets) is a superset of u that enables set operations inside character classes: intersection &&, difference --, and nested classes [[...][...]]. It also makes character classes match multi-code-point grapheme strings via \q{...} (string literals in a class) and \p{...} properties of strings like \p{RGI_Emoji}. This replaces brittle surrogate-pair regexes and manual emoji range lists.

// Match emoji but EXCLUDE skin-tone modifiers and ZWJ components (set difference):
const emoji = /[\p{Emoji}--\p{Emoji_Component}]/v;

// Match whole emoji sequences (flags, families) as single units — needs string properties:
const rgi = /\p{RGI_Emoji}/v;
'👨‍👩‍👧'.match(rgi);          // matches the whole family glyph, not 3 pieces

// Set INTERSECTION: ASCII letters that are also vowels.
const asciiVowel = /[[a-z]&&[aeiou]]/v;
'crwth'.replace(asciiVowel, '_'); // 'crwth' (no vowels)

// Literal multi-char alternatives inside a class via \q{}:
const yesNo = /^[\q{yes|no|maybe}]$/v;
yesNo.test('maybe');  // true

Gotcha: v and u are mutually exclusive — you can't combine them, and v is *stricter* (more characters require escaping, e.g. (, ), {, } inside classes). Some patterns valid under u throw a SyntaxError under v. Feature-detect (try { new RegExp('', 'v'); }) before using it in code that must run on older engines, since there's no graceful degradation.

4.9 Top-level await

  • Allowed at module top level (not in CommonJS).
  • Use for: config loaded from network, ESM dynamic imports, conditional polyfills.
  • Caveat: blocks the importing module from resolving.

Mechanism. Top-level await makes the *module itself* asynchronous: a module that uses TLA becomes a node in the module graph that the loader awaits before any importer's evaluation completes. The runtime topologically evaluates the graph, suspending importers until awaited modules settle — so TLA serializes part of startup. It's only legal in ES modules (type: "module", .mjs, or <script type="module">); CommonJS require is synchronous and throws.

// config.ts — an async module: importers wait until this settles.
const res = await fetch('/runtime-config.json');
export const config = await res.json();

// feature.ts — conditional polyfill loaded before the module's exports are usable.
if (!('Temporal' in globalThis)) {
  await import('@js-temporal/polyfill').then((m) => {
    (globalThis as any).Temporal = m.Temporal;
  });
}
export function schedule() { return Temporal.Now.instant(); }

Gotcha: TLA can serialize and stall your startup — if config.ts does a slow fetch and ten modules import it, all ten block. Keep TLA off the critical render path; prefer lazy import() inside a function for non-essential async work. Also, a circular dependency where both modules use TLA can deadlock; the loader detects some cases but not all. Bundlers (Vite/esbuild) support TLA but may warn if a target environment lacks it.

4.10 Pipeline operator (stage 2 — coming)

  • |> for fluent chaining without library: value |> double(%) |> increment(%).
  • Track in your TC39 watch list.

Mechanism. The pipeline operator threads a value through a sequence of expressions left-to-right, where % (the *topic reference* in the current Hack-style proposal) marks where the previous result is inserted. It lets you write deeply-nested calls as a readable pipeline without method-chaining or a pipe() utility, and unlike methods it works with *any* function (free functions, await, ternaries).

// Hypothetical (Stage 2/3, syntax may shift). Today, do this with a tiny pipe():
const pipe = (x, ...fns) => fns.reduce((v, f) => f(v), x);
const result = pipe(
  '  Hello World  ',
  (s) => s.trim(),
  (s) => s.toLowerCase(),
  (s) => s.replaceAll(' ', '-'),
);                              // 'hello-world'

// Future native form (Hack-style %):
// const result = '  Hello World  '
//   |> %.trim()
//   |> %.toLowerCase()
//   |> %.replaceAll(' ', '-');

Gotcha: it's not shipped — don't put it in production; the topic-token syntax (% vs ^^ vs F#-style |> fn) has churned across committee revisions, so anything you write today may break. Use a pipe() helper or method chaining now; if you want the ergonomics with types, libraries like Effect/remeda offer a typed pipe. Track it on your TC39 watch list rather than adopting early.

Part 5 — TypeScript at production scale

5.1 Project references (monorepo)

// tsconfig.json
{
  "files": [],
  "references": [
    { "path": "./packages/ui" },
    { "path": "./packages/api" },
    { "path": "./packages/app" }
  ]
}
// Each package has "composite": true; build emits .d.ts + .tsbuildinfo
// tsc --build is incremental, parallel, monorepo-aware

Mechanism. Project references turn one giant type-check into a build graph of small, independently-checked projects. Each referenced project sets "composite": true, which forces declaration: true and writes a .tsbuildinfo file recording input hashes and output state. tsc --build (the "build mode") reads the graph, builds dependencies first, and skips any project whose inputs are unchanged — so a one-line edit in app doesn't re-check ui. Downstream projects consume each dependency's emitted .d.ts, not its source, which is why type-checking parallelizes.

// packages/ui/tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "composite": true,          // required for referenced projects
    "declaration": true,        // implied by composite, emit .d.ts
    "declarationMap": true,     // go-to-def jumps to .ts source, not .d.ts
    "outDir": "dist",
    "rootDir": "src"
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}
// packages/app references ui:
// { "references": [{ "path": "../ui" }] }   then  `tsc --build`  (or `tsc -b -w` watch)

Gotcha: a referenced project must emit declarations — you can't reference a project that another tool (Vite/esbuild) transpiles without tsc emitting .d.ts. The common 2026 pattern is tsc -b for *type-checking + .d.ts* and a fast bundler for *JS output*. Also, deleting outputs without --clean leaves stale .tsbuildinfo claiming work is done; run tsc -b --clean when builds go weird. Circular references between projects are forbidden.

5.2 isolatedModules + verbatimModuleSyntax

  • Required for Vite, esbuild, swc — single-file transpile.
  • Forces explicit type-only imports (import type { X }).
  • Catches: cannot re-export a type as a runtime value.

Mechanism. Single-file transpilers (esbuild/swc) compile each file *without type information* — they don't know whether import { Foo } refers to a type (erase it) or a value (keep it). isolatedModules makes tsc flag constructs that can't be safely compiled per-file. verbatimModuleSyntax (the 2026 replacement for the old importsNotUsedAsValues/preserveValueImports) enforces a simple rule: import type is fully erased, everything else is emitted verbatim — so what you write is what ships, no surprise elision. This makes type-only imports explicit and prevents accidental runtime side-effect loss.

import { type User, getUser } from './user'; // mixed: User erased, getUser kept
import type { Config } from './config';      // entirely erased at compile time

export type { User };          // OK: type-only re-export, erased
// export { User };            // ERROR under verbatimModuleSyntax: User is a type,
                               // emitting it as a value import would crash at runtime.

// A side-effect-only import is preserved verbatim (not dropped):
import './polyfills';

Gotcha: verbatimModuleSyntax breaks some CommonJS interop — you can't mix import x = require() freely, and export = needs care. It also surfaces a real bug class: re-exporting a type as a value (export { SomeType }) now errors instead of silently emitting a dead import. Migrating a large codebase usually means a codemod to add type modifiers; @typescript-eslint/consistent-type-imports with --fix does most of it automatically.

5.3 Strictness ratchet

  • strict: true (gateway).
  • noUncheckedIndexedAccess — arr[0] is T | undefined.
  • exactOptionalPropertyTypes — { x?: string } excludes { x: undefined }.
  • noImplicitOverride — explicit override keyword.
  • noFallthroughCasesInSwitch — each case has break / return / throw.
  • Senior pattern: ratchet up one flag per quarter; fix the new errors.

Mechanism. strict is an umbrella for strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, etc. The "ratchet" flags above are *not* in strict — they're opt-in correctness upgrades you enable incrementally so each one's error wave is digestible. The most impactful, noUncheckedIndexedAccess, changes every indexed access (arr[i], record[key]) to include | undefined, forcing you to handle the out-of-bounds/missing-key case that's the source of countless runtime cannot read property of undefined crashes.

// With noUncheckedIndexedAccess:
function first<T>(arr: T[]): T {
  const x = arr[0];          // type is T | undefined now
  if (x === undefined) throw new RangeError('empty');
  return x;                  // narrowed to T
}

// With exactOptionalPropertyTypes, presence vs value-undefined are distinct:
interface Opts { timeout?: number }
const a: Opts = {};                 // OK (absent)
const b: Opts = { timeout: 1000 };  // OK
// const c: Opts = { timeout: undefined }; // ERROR: explicit undefined not allowed

Gotcha: noUncheckedIndexedAccess is *aggressive* — it also flags for (let i...) arr[i] loops where you "know" the index is valid, producing noise. Mitigate with iterators (for..of), .at(), or a checked-access helper. exactOptionalPropertyTypes interacts badly with spreads and some libraries that pass { x: undefined } intentionally; enable it last. Ratchet one flag per quarter, gate it in CI, and never enable several at once or the error count buries the team.

5.4 Schema-driven dev (Zod / Valibot / Effect Schema / TypeBox)

LibBundleStrengthNote
Zod~50 KBMature, broad ecosystemDefault for most apps
Valibot~5 KBModular, tree-shakeableBetter for bundle-sensitive SPAs
Effect Schema~80 KBComposable, integrates with Effect-TSWhen you use Effect
TypeBox~12 KBJSON Schema-firstBest for OpenAPI / strict JSON Schema needs
ArkType~10 KBType-level inference faster than ZodNewer; large schemas faster

Mechanism. These libraries unify *runtime validation* and *static types* from a single schema: you define the shape once, infer the TS type, and parse at runtime boundaries. The architectural difference is how they're packaged. Zod (v4 in 2026) is a fluent builder where each method exists on a chainable object — ergonomic but every method is in the import graph. Valibot uses *standalone functions* (object, string, pipe) so unused validators tree-shake away → tiny bundles. TypeBox builds actual JSON Schema objects (great for OpenAPI). They all now implement the Standard Schema spec, so libraries (tRPC, TanStack Form) accept any of them interchangeably.

// Valibot: functional, tree-shakeable — only the validators you use ship.
import * as v from 'valibot';

const UserSchema = v.object({
  id: v.pipe(v.string(), v.uuid()),
  email: v.pipe(v.string(), v.email()),
  age: v.pipe(v.number(), v.minValue(0), v.maxValue(150)),
  role: v.picklist(['admin', 'user']),
});
type User = v.InferOutput<typeof UserSchema>; // static type derived from the schema

// Validate at the boundary; downstream code trusts the type:
const user = v.parse(UserSchema, await res.json()); // throws ValiError on bad data

// Zod v4 equivalent (fluent) — same Standard Schema interface, larger bundle:
// const ZUser = z.object({ email: z.email(), age: z.number().min(0) });

Gotcha: validation runs at runtime, so don't re-parse hot data on every render — parse once at the network/IO boundary and pass the typed object inward (the branded-types idea, §5.7). Zod v4 changed several APIs from v3 (.email() moved, error customization differs); check the version. And infer types can get *very* expensive for the type-checker on huge nested schemas — break large schemas into named sub-schemas (§5.9) so the checker caches them.

5.5 Type-safe routing

  • Next.js typedRoutes: experimental_typedRoutes: true → href is type-checked.
  • TanStack Router: type-safe end-to-end with full param + search inference.
  • Tip: generate route types in CI; ship type-only.d.ts so consumers get autocomplete.

Mechanism. Type-safe routers make the *route table* part of the type system, so <Link to="...">, params, and search params are checked at compile time and autocompleted. TanStack Router goes furthest: each route declares a validateSearch (often a Zod/Valibot schema) and loader, and the router *infers* a global route tree (routeTree.gen.ts, generated by its Vite plugin) so navigate({ to: '/posts/$id', params: { id }, search: { page: 2 } }) is fully typed — a typo in a param name or a missing required search key is a compile error.

import { createRoute } from '@tanstack/react-router';
import * as v from 'valibot';

const postRoute = createRoute({
  path: '/posts/$postId',
  getParentRoute: () => rootRoute,
  // Search params are validated AND typed from this schema:
  validateSearch: (s) => v.parse(v.object({ tab: v.optional(v.picklist(['comments','related']), 'comments') }), s),
  loader: ({ params }) => fetchPost(params.postId), // params.postId is string, typed
});

// Usage is fully checked — wrong/missing fields are compile errors:
// <Link to="/posts/$postId" params={{ postId: id }} search={{ tab: 'related' }} />

Gotcha: TanStack's inference depends on the generated route tree — if codegen is stale, types lie; wire the plugin into dev *and* CI and commit (or gitignore consistently) routeTree.gen.ts. Next.js typedRoutes only covers *static* hrefs well; dynamic string concatenation (` /posts/${id} ) bypasses the check, so prefer the params object form. Ship route *types* (.d.ts`) only — never the generator — to consumers.

5.6 Type-safe env

import { z } from "zod";
const envSchema = z.object({
  NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: z.string().url(),
  NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN: z.string(),
});
export const env = envSchema.parse(process.env);
// Fails build if any required var missing
  • Libraries: @t3-oss/env-nextjs, valibot env helpers.

Mechanism. process.env is Record<string, string | undefined> — every access is unchecked and stringly-typed. An env schema validates once at startup/build, coerces strings to the right types ("true" → boolean, "3000" → number), and exports a typed, frozen object so the rest of the app reads env.PORT as a number with no undefined. @t3-oss/env adds the crucial client/server split: it throws if server-only secrets are referenced in client bundles, preventing accidental secret leakage.

import { createEnv } from '@t3-oss/env-nextjs';
import { z } from 'zod';

export const env = createEnv({
  server: {                                  // never exposed to the browser
    DATABASE_URL: z.string().url(),
    STRIPE_SECRET_KEY: z.string().startsWith('sk_'),
  },
  client: {                                  // must be NEXT_PUBLIC_*
    NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: z.string().url(),
  },
  shared: { NODE_ENV: z.enum(['development', 'test', 'production']) },
  runtimeEnv: {
    DATABASE_URL: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
    STRIPE_SECRET_KEY: process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY,
    NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL,
    NODE_ENV: process.env.NODE_ENV,
  },
});
// Reading env.DATABASE_URL in client code → build-time error (leak prevention).

Gotcha: bundlers inline process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_* by static text replacement, so you must reference them literally (no process.env[dynamicKey]) or they won't be replaced. Validate at build time (import the env module in your config) so a missing var fails CI, not production. Coerce explicitly — z.coerce.number() for ports, z.string().transform(s => s === 'true') for flags — since all env values arrive as strings.

5.7 Branded types in domain layer

  • Distinguish UserId from PostId at the type level.
  • Smart constructors: parseEmail returns Email | Error.
  • Server boundary: validate + brand; downstream code never re-validates.

Mechanism. A branded (a.k.a. nominal/opaque) type is a primitive intersected with a unique phantom tag: type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' }. Structurally it's still a string at runtime (zero cost), but TS treats UserId and PostId as incompatible, so you can't pass a post id where a user id is expected — eliminating a whole class of "passed the wrong id" bugs. You mint branded values only through a smart constructor that validates, so possessing a UserId is a *proof* it was validated — downstream code never re-checks.

declare const brand: unique symbol;
type Brand<T, B> = T & { readonly [brand]: B };

type UserId = Brand<string, 'UserId'>;
type Email  = Brand<string, 'Email'>;

// Smart constructors are the ONLY way to create branded values:
function asUserId(s: string): UserId {
  if (!/^u_[a-z0-9]+$/.test(s)) throw new TypeError('bad user id');
  return s as UserId;                 // the only place a cast is allowed
}
function parseEmail(s: string): Email | null {
  return /^[^@]+@[^@]+$/.test(s) ? (s as Email) : null;
}

function loadUser(id: UserId) { /* ... */ }
const raw = 'p_123';
// loadUser(raw);          // ERROR: string is not UserId
// loadUser('u_1' as any); // bypass requires an explicit, greppable `as any`
loadUser(asUserId('u_1')); // OK

Gotcha: brands are erased at runtime — typeof userId === 'string' and JSON.stringify produce a plain string, so they give *no* runtime protection, only compile-time. Centralize the casts in the constructors and lint against ad-hoc as Brand elsewhere. Validate-and-brand exactly at the trust boundary (deserialize API responses through your schema → brand the ids); if you brand without validating, the "proof" is a lie.

5.8 ts-reset

  • Tightens default lib types: JSON.parse → unknown, fetch().json() → unknown, .filter(Boolean) properly narrows.
  • Cheap import, huge correctness gain.

Mechanism. ts-reset (by Total TypeScript) is a single side-effect import that *augments* the built-in lib types to fix their unsound defaults. The headline fixes: JSON.parse() and Response.json() return unknown instead of any (forcing you to validate, §5.4), .filter(Boolean) correctly narrows out null/undefined/false from the result type, Array.includes accepts wider types, and Set/Map constructors infer better. It's purely type-level — zero runtime, one line in a single entry file.

// reset.d.ts (or top of your app entry), imported once for the whole project:
import '@total-typescript/ts-reset';

// Now these are safer:
const data = JSON.parse(body);        // unknown, not any → must validate before use
const json = await res.json();        // unknown, not any
const validated = UserSchema.parse(data); // forced to go through a schema

// .filter(Boolean) narrows correctly:
const names: (string | null)[] = ['a', null, 'b'];
const clean = names.filter(Boolean); // string[]  (was (string | null)[] without ts-reset)

Gotcha: because JSON.parse/.json() become unknown, existing code that treated them as any will suddenly error — that's the point, but it can be a big initial wave; introduce it on a new package or behind a migration. Import it once (a single .d.ts or entry file), not per-file, and make sure it's included in tsconfig. It changes *global* types, so a shared monorepo should agree to adopt it project-wide rather than per-package.

5.9 Compile-time perf

  • --diagnostics shows where time is spent.
  • Heavy conditional types in hot loops slow check time — cache via intermediate type aliases.
  • Avoid > 100-member literal unions; replace with branded string when possible.
  • Project references parallelize the build.

Mechanism. TS type-checking cost is dominated by *type instantiation count* — each conditional/mapped/recursive type the checker must expand. Deeply recursive conditional types (string-template parsers, deep DeepPartial) and giant unions cause combinatorial instantiation that blows up check time and editor responsiveness. tsc --extendedDiagnostics / --generateTrace reveal the hot spots; the --generateTrace out/ flag emits a Chrome-loadable trace showing which *type* and which *file* cost the most. The fix is to give the checker memoization points (named intermediate aliases) and to avoid pathological constructs.

// SLOW: re-instantiates the deep conditional at every use site.
type DeepReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> };
function f(x: DeepReadonly<HugeConfig>) {} // expensive per call

// FASTER: name the result once so the checker caches the instantiation.
type ReadonlyConfig = DeepReadonly<HugeConfig>;
function g(x: ReadonlyConfig) {}            // reuses the cached type

// Avoid 100+ member literal unions in hot positions — replace with a brand:
// type Country = 'US' | 'GB' | ... 200 more;  // explodes inference combinatorially
type Country = Brand<string, 'Country'>;       // validate at runtime instead

Gotcha: the worst offenders hide in library types — a Zod/Prisma/router type that recursively maps a 300-field schema can add seconds to every keystroke. Use --generateTrace and the @typescript/analyze-trace tool to find the culprit, then break the schema into smaller named pieces or use interface (cached by name) over large inline object types. Project references parallelize *across* packages but don't fix a single slow type — that needs structural simplification.

Part 6 — Browser APIs (deeper)

6.1 OPFS — Origin Private File System

  • Sandboxed per-origin file system; no permission prompt.
  • Read/write at filesystem speed; backed by IDB on most browsers.
  • Use cases: local SQLite (sqlite-wasm), large blob caching, project files for IDE-like apps.
const root = await navigator.storage.getDirectory();
const handle = await root.getFileHandle("doc.json", { create: true });
const writable = await handle.createWritable();
await writable.write(JSON.stringify(data));
await writable.close();

Mechanism. OPFS is a private, origin-scoped filesystem with no user-visible files and no permission prompt. Its superpower is the synchronous access handle available *inside a Web Worker*: createSyncAccessHandle() gives read/write/flush/truncate that operate synchronously on the file — which is exactly what WASM SQLite needs to use the file as a database with real low-latency random access. The async createWritable() API (shown above) is convenient on the main thread but writes to a temp copy that's swapped in on close(), so it's transactional but slower.

// In a Web Worker: synchronous handle → fast random-access I/O (the SQLite-wasm path).
const root = await navigator.storage.getDirectory();
const fh = await root.getFileHandle('db.sqlite', { create: true });
const access = await fh.createSyncAccessHandle();   // Worker-only, synchronous

const header = new Uint8Array(16);
access.read(header, { at: 0 });                     // sync random read
access.write(new TextEncoder().encode('PAGE'), { at: 4096 });
access.flush();
access.close();                                     // MUST close — handle is exclusive

// Estimate quota before writing large blobs:
const { quota, usage } = await navigator.storage.estimate();

Gotcha: a createSyncAccessHandle takes an exclusive lock on the file — a second open (even in another tab) throws NoModificationAllowedError until you close(). This is why SQLite-wasm runs the DB in a single dedicated worker. Also, OPFS storage can be evicted under pressure unless you call navigator.storage.persist(); for IDE-like apps that must not lose data, request persistence and handle the denied case.

6.2 WebTransport (HTTP/3)

  • Bi-directional unreliable datagrams + ordered streams.
  • Lower latency than WebSocket; multiplex streams without head-of-line blocking.
  • Use cases: low-latency games, real-time telemetry, AV streaming.

Mechanism. WebTransport runs over HTTP/3 (QUIC), giving two transport modes on one connection: datagrams (unreliable, unordered, no retransmit — like UDP, perfect for game state where stale data is worthless) and streams (reliable, ordered, but *independently* — because QUIC has no head-of-line blocking, a lost packet on stream A doesn't stall stream B, unlike a single WebSocket/TCP connection where any loss stalls everything). You can open many concurrent streams cheaply.

const wt = new WebTransport('https://example.com:4433/wt');
await wt.ready;

// Unreliable datagrams — fire-and-forget low-latency state:
const writer = wt.datagrams.writable.getWriter();
await writer.write(new TextEncoder().encode(JSON.stringify(playerInput)));

// A reliable bidirectional stream for a request/response that must arrive in order:
const stream = await wt.createBidirectionalStream();
const w = stream.writable.getWriter();
await w.write(new TextEncoder().encode('GET /state'));
const reader = stream.readable.getReader();
const { value } = await reader.read();

// Read incoming datagrams:
const dgReader = wt.datagrams.readable.getReader();
for (;;) { const { value, done } = await dgReader.read(); if (done) break; handle(value); }

Gotcha: WebTransport requires HTTP/3 + valid TLS server-side — it won't fall back to TCP, so you need a QUIC-capable server (and many corporate proxies/firewalls block UDP/QUIC, breaking it). Always implement a WebSocket fallback. Datagrams are *lossy by design* — never send anything you can't afford to lose without an app-level ack; and there's a max datagram size (maxDatagramSize), so chunk larger payloads onto streams instead.

6.3 WebCodecs

  • Direct access to browser's media codecs.
  • Encode/decode H.264, VP9, AV1, AAC, Opus in JS.
  • Use cases: in-browser video editing, screen recording, format conversion.

Mechanism. WebCodecs exposes the browser's hardware-accelerated encoders/decoders as low-level JS objects — VideoEncoder, VideoDecoder, AudioEncoder, AudioDecoder — operating on VideoFrame/AudioData/EncodedVideoChunk. You get raw frames in and encoded chunks out (or vice versa) with no container muxing imposed, so you control the pipeline: capture → encode → mux → upload, or download → demux → decode → render. It's the foundation for in-browser editors and low-latency streaming, replacing slow <canvas>+MediaRecorder hacks.

// Encode canvas frames to H.264 chunks (e.g. for a recorder / uploader).
const chunks: EncodedVideoChunk[] = [];
const encoder = new VideoEncoder({
  output: (chunk) => chunks.push(chunk),           // encoded output callback
  error: (e) => console.error(e),
});
encoder.configure({
  codec: 'avc1.42001f',                            // H.264 baseline
  width: 1280, height: 720,
  bitrate: 2_000_000, framerate: 30,
  hardwareAcceleration: 'prefer-hardware',
});

function captureFrame(canvas: HTMLCanvasElement, tsMicros: number) {
  const frame = new VideoFrame(canvas, { timestamp: tsMicros });
  encoder.encode(frame, { keyFrame: tsMicros % 2_000_000 === 0 });
  frame.close();                                   // CRITICAL: frees the GPU buffer
}
await encoder.flush();                             // drain pending frames before muxing

Gotcha: VideoFrame/AudioData hold GPU/native memory that the GC won't reclaim — you must call .close() on every frame or you exhaust the decoder's buffer pool and the pipeline stalls/crashes within seconds. WebCodecs also gives you *raw codecs, not containers* — you still need a muxer (mp4box.js, webm-muxer) to produce a playable file. Check VideoEncoder.isConfigSupported(config) first; codec/profile support varies by platform and hardware.

6.4 Web Audio API + AudioWorklet

  • Procedural audio, synthesis, real-time effects.
  • AudioWorklet runs on the audio thread — no main-thread blocking.
  • Use for: meeting apps, music tools, gaming, AI voice apps.

Mechanism. Web Audio is a graph of AudioNodes processed on a dedicated, real-time audio rendering thread in 128-sample quantums. ScriptProcessorNode (deprecated) ran your JS on the *main* thread → glitches under load. AudioWorklet moves your DSP into an AudioWorkletProcessor that runs on the audio thread, isolated from main-thread jank, communicating via SharedArrayBuffer/port.postMessage. Its process(inputs, outputs, params) must be fast and allocation-free — it's the hard-real-time core of meeting apps, synths, and voice processors.

// noise-gate.worklet.js — runs on the audio thread, processes 128-sample blocks.
class NoiseGate extends AudioWorkletProcessor {
  static get parameterDescriptors() {
    return [{ name: 'threshold', defaultValue: 0.02, automationRate: 'k-rate' }];
  }
  process(inputs, outputs, params) {
    const inp = inputs[0], out = outputs[0];
    const thr = params.threshold[0];
    for (let ch = 0; ch < inp.length; ch++) {
      const i = inp[ch], o = out[ch];
      for (let n = 0; n < i.length; n++) o[n] = Math.abs(i[n]) > thr ? i[n] : 0; // gate
    }
    return true;            // keep the processor alive
  }
}
registerProcessor('noise-gate', NoiseGate);

// main thread:
const ctx = new AudioContext();
await ctx.audioWorklet.addModule('noise-gate.worklet.js');
const gate = new AudioWorkletNode(ctx, 'noise-gate');
mic.connect(gate).connect(ctx.destination);
gate.parameters.get('threshold').value = 0.05;

Gotcha: an AudioContext starts suspended until a user gesture (autoplay policy) — call await ctx.resume() inside a click handler or audio silently never plays. Inside process(), never allocate (no new, no array literals) — GC on the audio thread causes audible dropouts; pre-allocate buffers in the constructor. And addModule is async — await it before constructing the node.

6.5 File System Access API

  • showOpenFilePicker / showSaveFilePicker / showDirectoryPicker.
  • Persistent handles via IndexedDB — re-acquire across sessions with user permission.
  • Chromium only as of 2026.

Mechanism. Unlike OPFS (private), this API touches the user's real filesystem with explicit permission. The pickers return FileSystemFileHandle/FileSystemDirectoryHandle objects that are serializable into IndexedDB — so you can persist a handle and re-acquire access in a later session by calling queryPermission/requestPermission, enabling "reopen recent project" without re-prompting the full picker each time. Writing goes through a FileSystemWritableFileStream that's transactional (temp file swapped on close).

// Open, edit, and save back to the SAME file the user picked (true "Save", not "Download").
const [handle] = await window.showOpenFilePicker({
  types: [{ description: 'Text', accept: { 'text/plain': ['.txt', '.md'] } }],
});
const file = await handle.getFile();
let text = await file.text();
text += '\nedited';

const writable = await handle.createWritable();
await writable.write(text);
await writable.close();              // atomic swap into the real file

// Persist the handle for next session:
await idbSet('lastFile', handle);    // structured-clone stores the handle
// ...later session...
const saved = await idbGet('lastFile');
if (await saved.queryPermission({ mode: 'readwrite' }) !== 'granted')
  await saved.requestPermission({ mode: 'readwrite' }); // needs a user gesture

Gotcha: it's Chromium-only in 2026 (Safari/Firefox expose only the OPFS subset, no real-FS pickers) — feature-detect and fall back to <input type=file> + download. Re-acquiring a stored handle's permission requires a user gesture, so do it in a click handler, not on load. And you can't access system-sensitive directories; the browser blocks pickers on OS/library folders.

6.6 Web Locks

  • Coordinate across tabs / workers.
  • "single primary tab" pattern — only one tab opens the WebSocket.
navigator.locks.request("primary", { mode: "exclusive" }, async () => {
  // I am the only owner now
  openWebSocket();
  await new Promise(() => {});  // hold for tab lifetime
});

Mechanism. The Web Locks API grants named locks scoped to an origin across all its tabs/workers. A request is queued and the callback runs only when the lock is held; the lock releases when the callback's promise settles. mode: 'exclusive' (default) gives one holder; 'shared' allows many concurrent readers (reader/writer pattern). ifAvailable: true returns immediately with null if it can't be acquired (non-blocking probe), and an AbortSignal can cancel a queued request. This is the right primitive for leader election, cross-tab mutexes, and serializing IndexedDB migrations.

// Leader election: exactly one tab becomes "primary" and opens the socket.
function becomePrimary(onLead: () => void) {
  navigator.locks.request('ws-primary', { mode: 'exclusive' }, () => {
    onLead();                              // this tab is leader now
    return new Promise<void>(() => {});    // never resolves → holds for tab lifetime
  });                                      // when this tab closes, lock frees, next tab wins
}

// Non-blocking probe: "is someone else already the leader?"
async function isLeaderHeldElsewhere() {
  const got = await navigator.locks.request('ws-primary', { ifAvailable: true }, (lock) => !!lock);
  return got === false; // false means we couldn't get it → someone else holds it
}

// Inspect all locks for debugging:
const { held, pending } = await navigator.locks.query();

Gotcha: holding a lock forever (new Promise(() => {})) is the *intended* leader pattern, but if that tab is frozen (bfcache/background) the lock is still held and no other tab can take over until it's evicted — combine with a visibilitychange/heartbeat so a frozen leader yields. Locks are not persisted; they vanish on full navigation. Don't use them for long critical sections that could deadlock other tabs.

6.7 Compute Pressure API

  • Tells you when CPU is under sustained pressure (nominal / fair / serious / critical).
  • Adapt UI quality dynamically — reduce particles, drop animations, downsample video.

Mechanism. The Compute Pressure API delivers debounced, privacy-preserving CPU (and increasingly GPU) pressure states — nominal, fair, serious, critical — via a PressureObserver. The browser computes these from thermal/utilization signals without exposing raw core counts or frequencies (which would be a fingerprinting vector). You react by *degrading gracefully*: a video call drops resolution/framerate, a game cuts particle counts, a viz reduces tick rate — *before* the device thermally throttles and everything janks.

if ('PressureObserver' in globalThis) {
  const observer = new PressureObserver((records) => {
    const state = records.at(-1)!.state;          // latest sample
    switch (state) {
      case 'critical': setQuality('low');  pauseNonEssentialAnimations(); break;
      case 'serious':  setQuality('medium'); break;
      case 'fair':
      case 'nominal':  setQuality('high'); break;
    }
  });
  // sampleInterval is a hint (ms); the browser debounces and may sample less often.
  await observer.observe('cpu', { sampleInterval: 1000 });
}

Gotcha: it's Chromium-only and requires a secure context; some configs gate it behind a permission or focus requirement, so always feature-detect and treat absence as "assume nominal." The states are coarse and debounced — don't expect instantaneous reaction or fine-grained metrics; use it for *coarse* quality tiers, not per-frame decisions. Pair with the actual frame-timing signals (LoAF, requestAnimationFrame deltas) for fine control.

6.8 Screen Wake Lock

  • Keeps screen awake during a workflow (presentation, recipe, navigation).
  • Release on visibility change or timer.

Mechanism. navigator.wakeLock.request('screen') asks the OS to keep the display on, returning a WakeLockSentinel you later .release(). The browser auto-releases the lock when the tab loses visibility (you switch tabs/apps), so you must re-acquire on visibilitychange if the workflow is still active — this is the single most common bug. It requires a secure context and (usually) an active/visible document at request time.

let sentinel: WakeLockSentinel | null = null;

async function keepAwake() {
  try {
    sentinel = await navigator.wakeLock.request('screen');
    sentinel.addEventListener('release', () => console.log('wake lock released'));
  } catch (e) { /* NotAllowedError if backgrounded or low battery */ }
}

// Re-acquire after returning to the tab (the OS dropped it on hide):
document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => {
  if (document.visibilityState === 'visible' && workflowActive) keepAwake();
});

function done() { sentinel?.release(); sentinel = null; }

Gotcha: the auto-release-on-hide behavior means a naïve one-time request silently stops working after the user tabs away and back — always wire the visibilitychange re-acquire. Browsers may also refuse the lock on low battery; never assume success, and never hold it longer than the actual task (a stuck wake lock drains the user's battery and is a poor-citizen pattern).

6.9 Idle Detection

  • Fires when user is idle (no input + tab not focused) — log out securely after N minutes.
  • Requires permission; sensitive workplaces use it for compliance.

Mechanism. The IdleDetector reports two orthogonal signals: user state (active/idle — no input for a threshold) and screen state (locked/unlocked — OS screen lock). It's permission-gated (idle-detection) because it reveals presence; you must request permission and run in a secure context. The threshold has a 60-second minimum. Use it for compliance auto-logout (lock screen → end session) — not for casual UX.

async function startIdleLogout() {
  if (await IdleDetector.requestPermission() !== 'granted') return;

  const controller = new AbortController();
  const detector = new IdleDetector();
  detector.addEventListener('change', () => {
    const { userState, screenState } = detector;
    if (userState === 'idle' || screenState === 'locked') {
      endSensitiveSession();          // e.g. clear in-memory tokens, redirect to lock
    }
  });
  await detector.start({ threshold: 60_000, signal: controller.signal }); // 60s min
}

Gotcha: 60s is the hard minimum threshold — you can't detect sub-minute idleness with this API; for shorter timeouts track input events yourself. It's Chromium-only and permission-gated, so it'll be unavailable for most users — treat it as defense-in-depth on top of a normal server-side session timeout, never the sole mechanism. The permission prompt can feel invasive; reserve it for genuinely sensitive (healthcare/finance) contexts.

6.10 Web Share Level 2

  • Share files (images, PDFs) to native share sheet.
  • navigator.share({ files: [...] }).
  • Mobile-only practical; iOS Safari + Android Chrome.

Mechanism. Web Share Level 2 adds files to navigator.share(), invoking the OS share sheet with actual File objects (images, PDFs, etc.) so users can send to native apps. Crucially you should gate on navigator.canShare({ files }) first — not every platform/file type is shareable — and navigator.share() must be called from a user gesture (a click handler), or it throws NotAllowedError.

async function shareReceipt(pdfBlob: Blob) {
  const file = new File([pdfBlob], 'receipt.pdf', { type: 'application/pdf' });
  // Feature + capability detect before showing the button:
  if (!navigator.canShare?.({ files: [file] })) { fallbackDownload(file); return; }
  try {
    await navigator.share({               // MUST be inside a click handler
      title: 'Your receipt',
      text: 'Receipt for order #1234',
      files: [file],
    });
  } catch (e) {
    if ((e as Error).name !== 'AbortError') fallbackDownload(file); // user cancel ≠ error
  }
}

Gotcha: it's mobile-practical only (desktop support is thin) and requires HTTPS + a user gesture — calling it from a setTimeout or async continuation after the gesture is "consumed" throws. Distinguish a real failure from the user *cancelling* the sheet (AbortError) so you don't show a spurious "share failed" toast. canShare only validates the data shape, not whether any app can actually receive it.

6.11 Web Push + Notifications

  • VAPID-keyed push subscription registered with a push service (FCM, Mozilla's, Apple's).
  • Push payload encrypted (ECDH key agreement) — server cannot read it.
  • Service Worker showNotification on push event.

Mechanism. The browser owns a connection to its vendor push service (FCM/Mozilla/Apple). Your page calls pushManager.subscribe() with your VAPID public key, getting back a PushSubscription containing an endpoint URL + two keys (p256dh, auth). Your server signs requests to that endpoint with the VAPID private key (proving identity) and encrypts the payload (RFC 8291, ECDH-derived key) so the push service relays ciphertext it can't read. On delivery, the browser wakes your Service Worker's push event, which must call showNotification (browsers penalize/forbid silent pushes).

// page: subscribe
const reg = await navigator.serviceWorker.ready;
const sub = await reg.pushManager.subscribe({
  userVisibleOnly: true,                     // required by Chromium
  applicationServerKey: urlBase64ToUint8Array(VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY),
});
await fetch('/api/save-sub', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(sub) });

// service-worker.js: receive
self.addEventListener('push', (event) => {
  const data = event.data?.json() ?? {};
  // MUST show a notification or the browser may revoke push permission:
  event.waitUntil(self.registration.showNotification(data.title ?? 'Update', {
    body: data.body, icon: '/icon.png', data: { url: data.url },
  }));
});
self.addEventListener('notificationclick', (e) => {
  e.notification.close();
  e.waitUntil(clients.openWindow(e.notification.data.url));
});

Gotcha: Chromium requires userVisibleOnly: true and a visible notification per push — "silent" data pushes are not allowed and repeated silent behavior gets your origin's push permission revoked. On iOS, Web Push only works for installed (Add-to-Home-Screen) PWAs, and subscriptions can expire (pushsubscriptionchange event) — handle re-subscription or you'll silently stop delivering.

6.12 Background Sync + Periodic Sync

  • Background Sync: retry a one-shot mutation when next online.
  • Periodic Sync: wake the SW occasionally (Chromium only, requires installed PWA).
  • Use cases: drafts, queued comments, periodic news refresh.

Mechanism. Background Sync lets you register a one-off tag (registration.sync.register('send-comment')); if the device is offline, the browser fires the SW's sync event once connectivity returns, even if the page is closed — ideal for "send this mutation eventually, exactly once." Periodic Background Sync fires a periodicsync event at browser-chosen intervals (gated by a permission, site engagement, and *installed PWA* status) for opportunistic refresh. Both run in the Service Worker and must complete their work inside event.waitUntil.

// page: queue an action that must survive offline + page close
async function queueComment(comment) {
  await idbAdd('outbox', comment);
  const reg = await navigator.serviceWorker.ready;
  if ('sync' in reg) await reg.sync.register('flush-outbox');
  else await flushNow(); // fallback: try immediately
}

// service-worker.js
self.addEventListener('sync', (event) => {
  if (event.tag === 'flush-outbox')
    event.waitUntil(flushOutbox()); // browser retries with backoff if this rejects
});

// Periodic (Chromium + installed PWA + granted permission):
self.addEventListener('periodicsync', (event) => {
  if (event.tag === 'refresh-feed') event.waitUntil(refreshFeedCache());
});

Gotcha: both are Chromium-only and Periodic Sync additionally requires an installed PWA + permission + sufficient site engagement — the browser decides the cadence (you can't demand "every 15 min"), and it may never fire for low-engagement sites. Background Sync retries with its own backoff but gives up after a few attempts, so still keep the outbox in IndexedDB and flush on next page load as a backstop. Never put it on the critical path of a user-visible "sent" confirmation.

Part 7 — Service Worker mastery

7.1 Lifecycle

  • install → activate → fetch (loop).
  • Old SW serves while new SW installs; new takes control on next navigation OR via skipWaiting + clients.claim.

7.2 Precache + Workbox

  • Workbox precache lists files with revision hashes.
  • Atomic update: all precached files swap together at activation.
  • Use cleanupOutdatedCaches() to prune old versions.

7.3 Runtime strategies

StrategyWhen
CacheFirstImmutable static assets (fingerprinted)
NetworkFirstAPI responses where freshness matters
StaleWhileRevalidatePersonalized data — show cached + refresh
CacheOnlyPWA shell after install
NetworkOnlyNever cache (auth flows)

7.4 Navigation preload

  • Service Worker is starting up — let the browser fetch the navigation in parallel.
  • self.registration.navigationPreload.enable() in install.
  • Reduces SW startup penalty by ~100 ms on cold visits.

7.5 Background Sync queue

  • Workbox BackgroundSyncPlugin queues failed POSTs.
  • Replays them when next online (Background Sync event).
  • Perfect for chat send, comment post, optimistic mutations offline.

7.6 Service Worker kill switch

// Allow remote shutdown of a SW
self.addEventListener("message", e => {
  if (e.data === "KILL") {
    self.registration.unregister();
    self.clients.matchAll().then(clients => clients.forEach(c => c.navigate(c.url)));
  }
});
  • Critical: if you ever ship a broken SW, you need a way to recover users.

7.7 Cache versioning

  • Use a CACHE_VERSION constant; new SW activates → delete old caches.
  • Workbox handles this automatically.

Part 8 — Real-time deeper

8.1 Operational Transform algorithm

  • Each op (insert / delete) carries a position; concurrent ops are transformed to apply correctly.
  • Central server orders ops; clients transform local pending ops against incoming.
  • Pros: compact, deterministic. Cons: hard to extend, server is bottleneck.

8.2 CRDT — what they really do

  • Conflict-free replicated data types — commutative, associative, idempotent ops.
  • Y.Text uses Yjs Doubly Linked List with TimeStamped IDs (Yjs YATA).
  • Two clients edit offline → merge gives deterministic result regardless of order.
  • Tradeoff: payload size larger than OT; great for offline + P2P.

8.3 Vector clocks vs Lamport timestamps

  • Lamport: scalar counter; total order; loses concurrency info.
  • Vector: per-node counter; partial order; can detect concurrent updates.
  • Used inside CRDT algorithms (HLC = Hybrid Logical Clock combines wall clock + Lamport).

8.4 Managed real-time platforms

PlatformStrengthWhen
LiveblocksYjs-native, presence + cursors out of the boxCollaborative editors / Figma-like
Pusher ChannelsMature WebSocket fan-outChat, notifications
AblyMulti-protocol (WS, SSE, MQTT)High-reliability messaging
PartyKitCloudflare Durable Objects-basedStateful rooms at the edge
Supabase RealtimePostgres → WebSocket eventsCRUD apps wanting live updates
Cloudflare Workers + Durable ObjectsBuild your own at the edgeCost-conscious teams; full control

8.5 Presence patterns

  • Throttle cursor updates to 30 fps; broadcast deltas.
  • At zoom levels, decimate cursors (sample 1 per N cells).
  • Frustum culling — only render cursors in viewport.
  • Per-user color from stable hash(userId) → HSL.

8.6 Conflict-free editors

  • Slate + Yjs (rich text).
  • Tiptap + Yjs (ProseMirror-based).
  • Lexical + Yjs (Meta's editor).
  • Blocknote (Notion-like blocks + Yjs).

Part 9 — Data layer architectures

9.1 TanStack Query normalized cache

  • Out of the box: per-query cache.
  • Normalize manually via queryClient.setQueryData on individual entity queries.
  • Or layer entity manager (relay-style normalized store).

9.2 Apollo Client (GraphQL)

  • Normalized cache via __typename + id (InMemoryCache).
  • Type policies: define merge functions for paginated lists.
  • Persisted queries: send hash instead of full query string.
  • Fragment colocation: each component declares the fields it needs.

9.3 Relay (Facebook)

  • Compiler-driven; fragments hoisted at build time.
  • Each component declares its own data dependency; Relay batches into one request.
  • Best-in-class for very large GraphQL apps.

9.4 urql + graphcache

  • Lighter Apollo alternative.
  • Document caching by default; graphcache for normalized cache.
  • Sensible defaults; smaller bundle.

9.5 tRPC (no GraphQL)

  • Type-safe end-to-end without code generation — server types flow to client.
  • Built on HTTP; integrates with TanStack Query out of the box.
  • Best when frontend + backend are same monorepo / same TS.
// server
export const appRouter = router({
  user: { byId: publicProcedure.input(z.object({ id: z.string() })).query(({ input }) => db.user(input.id)) },
});
export type AppRouter = typeof appRouter;
// client
const { data } = trpc.user.byId.useQuery({ id: "u_1" });  // fully typed

9.6 BFF (Backend for Frontend)

  • Thin server per client (web / mobile / desktop) that shapes data + aggregates downstream APIs.
  • Avoid over-fetch; provide exactly what the UI needs.
  • Common stacks: Next.js Route Handlers + Server Actions, tRPC, GraphQL Mesh, Hasura.

9.7 Aggregation patterns

  • DataLoader (batch + dedupe) on the BFF — combine N+1 into one call.
  • Persisted GraphQL queries — server stores allow-list of queries by hash; clients send hash only.
  • Edge cache: same query hash + same args = same response cached at edge.

9.8 Optimistic concurrency in the data layer

  • ETag header from server; client sends If-Match on PUT.
  • Conflict response: 412 Precondition Failed → UI shows merge UX.
  • Or version field in the resource — same idea.

9.9 Distributed cache invalidation

  • Server pushes invalidation events (SSE / WebSocket) when data changes.
  • Client receives event → queryClient.invalidateQueries.
  • Pair with TanStack Query refetchOnWindowFocus for belt + suspenders.

Part 10 — Microfrontends in production

10.1 When MFEs actually help

  • 100+ engineers; teams that need to deploy independently.
  • Multiple frameworks (legacy AngularJS + new React) sharing one app.
  • Strong domain boundaries — Spotify's podcast vs music sections.
  • Otherwise: a monolith with feature-folded packages is better.

10.2 Module Federation 3.0 (2026)

  • Native ESM federation using Import Maps; no webpack/rspack runtime needed for the host.
  • Remote manifest endpoint — host fetches latest remoteEntry URL via API.
  • Server-side Module Federation: stitch RSC payloads from multiple origins into one stream.

10.3 Shared dependencies

  • Singleton react / react-dom — must be same major; mismatched versions crash.
  • Shared design system: ship as a separate remote, pin major version.
