  • Force eager loading for tiny deps; lazy for heavy.

10.4 Single-spa orchestration

  • Top-level router routes path → registered application → mount/unmount.
  • Each MFE exports bootstrap / mount / unmount lifecycles.
  • Combine with Module Federation for shared deps.

10.5 Communication between MFEs

  • Events: CustomEvent on window; BroadcastChannel for cross-tab.
  • Shared store: Zustand singleton exposed via Module Federation.
  • Avoid prop drilling across boundaries — events are loose-coupled.

10.6 Versioning + deployment

  • Each MFE is its own build pipeline + CDN deploy.
  • Manifest endpoint controls which version is live (rollback by swapping manifest).
  • Smoke test against a known-good host before flipping the manifest.

10.7 Failure isolation

  • Wrap remote loads in ErrorBoundary; show fallback when remote fails.
  • Timeout remote fetch; if too slow, render without it.
  • Health check at runtime — disable a remote if it errors > N times.

Part 11 — Architecture patterns for FE

11.1 Feature-Sliced Design (FSD)

src/
  app/         # entry, providers, router
  pages/       # routes
  widgets/     # composite UI blocks
  features/    # user-facing features
  entities/    # business entities (User, Post, Order)
  shared/      # reusable libraries, UI kit, utils
  • Strict dependency direction: lower layers don't import higher.
  • Each feature is replaceable + relocatable.

11.2 Hexagonal / Clean Architecture for FE

  • Domain layer (entities + use cases) — framework-agnostic TS.
  • Adapters: HTTP, IDB, WebSocket — interchangeable.
  • UI layer = thin React components calling use cases.
  • Tradeoff: more files, easier testing + migrating.

11.3 Container / Presentational (still useful)

  • Container: data + state + side effects.
  • Presentational: pure rendering from props.
  • Modern React conflates these often, but keeping leaf components pure aids testing.

11.4 Storybook as living docs

  • Every component has stories: default, variants, error, loading.
  • Stories double as visual regression + a11y tests via Chromatic + axe.
  • Designers can review without spinning up a dev server.

11.5 Design tokens pipeline

  • Source of truth = JSON / YAML / Figma tokens.
  • Style Dictionary transforms to CSS, JS, iOS, Android.
  • Locked in CI — designers PR token changes; code rebuilds automatically.

11.6 Publishing a design system

  • Semver: breaking → major; new component → minor; bugfix → patch.
  • Changesets for monorepo version management.
  • Deprecation warnings at runtime + via TS @deprecated.
  • Migration guides + codemods bundled with breaking releases.

Part 12 — Testing deep

12.1 Test pyramid vs trophy

  • Pyramid: many unit, fewer integration, fewest E2E.
  • Trophy (Kent C. Dodds): static, lots of integration, fewer unit + E2E.
  • Reality: depends on your app — UI-heavy apps benefit from more integration tests.

12.2 Mutation testing

  • Stryker mutates source code (flip boolean, change operator) and runs tests.
  • If tests still pass, your test suite is weak there.
  • Reveals "high coverage, low quality" tests.

12.3 Property-based testing

import fc from "fast-check";
test("reverse is involutive", () => {
  fc.assert(fc.property(fc.array(fc.string()), arr =>
    expect(reverse(reverse(arr))).toEqual(arr)));
});
  • Generates many random inputs; finds edge cases humans miss.

12.4 Visual regression at scale

  • Chromatic: stories → screenshots → diff on PR.
  • Sharding for large suites; ignore known unstable elements (data + dates).
  • Tag baselines per branch; auto-approve cosmetic-only diffs.

12.5 Contract tests (Pact / Schemathesis)

  • Consumer defines what it expects; provider tests against that contract.
  • Catches API breaking changes before integration.

12.6 Performance regression

  • Run k6 / Lighthouse CI against staging on every merge.
  • Fail PR on > 10% regression in p95 latency or > 5% LCP regression.
  • Trend chart over time — catch slow creep.

12.7 Flake quarantine + budget

  • Failing-intermittently tests get marked .skip with a Jira ticket.
  • Quarantine list reviewed weekly — fix or delete.
  • Allow N flakes per CI run; > N fails the build (forces investment).

12.8 MSW handlers reusable across test + storybook + dev

  • One handlers.ts; import in vitest setup, Storybook preview, dev API mocking.
  • Tests + UI in dev see identical mock data; no drift.

Part 13 — Security deep

13.1 Cross-origin isolation (COOP + COEP + CORP)

  • Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin → isolates browsing context group.
  • Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp → all resources must opt-in.
  • Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin / same-site / cross-origin per resource.
  • Required to use SharedArrayBuffer + performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory.

13.2 Iframe sandbox attributes

<iframe src="…"
  sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-forms"
  allow="geolocation 'none'; payment 'none'"
/>
  • Default sandbox = maximal restriction.
  • Add explicit allow-* tokens for what you need.

13.3 postMessage origin verification

window.addEventListener("message", e => {
  if (e.origin !== "https://trusted.example.com") return;
  // process e.data
});
  • Always check origin; never trust source.

13.4 WebAuthn / Passkeys

  • Phishing-resistant auth — uses asymmetric crypto bound to the device.
  • navigator.credentials.create({ publicKey: ... }) registers; .get() authenticates.
  • Apple, Google, Microsoft all support passkeys via platform authenticators.
  • Use libraries: SimpleWebAuthn, Hanko, Stytch.

13.5 Web Crypto API

  • Native crypto: subtle.digest, encrypt, decrypt, sign, verify, deriveKey.
  • Use for: client-side encryption (E2EE notes), HMAC verification, password hashing (PBKDF2 / Argon2 via lib).
  • Never roll your own crypto.

13.6 Reporting API

  • Reporting-Endpoints header configures where browser sends violation + intervention + deprecation reports.
  • Catches CSP violations, deprecated API usage, intervention notices.

13.7 Mixed content + insecure links

  • CSP: upgrade-insecure-requests upgrades http:// to https:// automatically.
  • Block: ?utm_source=untrusted_redirect_param — validate redirect URLs against allow-list.

13.8 Threat modeling for FE

  • STRIDE-lite: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
  • Per feature: who can act, what data flows, what assumptions does FE make about backend?
  • Senior tell: cite a real threat-model-driven decision you made in interviews.

Part 14 — Observability deep

14.1 Tail-based sampling

  • Sample after the trace is complete — keep all error traces + slow traces, drop fast successes.
  • OTel Collector + Refinery (Honeycomb).
  • Tradeoff: requires buffering; more infra than head-based sampling.

14.2 Cardinality control

  • Never attach user_id / request_id as a metric label (high cardinality kills metrics backends).
  • Put high-cardinality attributes on traces / logs / events instead.
  • Use exemplar metrics: aggregated metric + sample trace IDs that contributed.

14.3 RUM ↔ APM correlation

  • Browser fetch sends W3C traceparent header.
  • Backend records the same trace ID; you can link a slow user request to its server-side spans.
  • Datadog, Honeycomb, Sentry all support this.

14.4 User-journey reconstruction

  • Stitch traces from one user across sessions using user.id attribute.
  • Find users who hit a bug — replay their session in Sentry / FullStory.
  • Senior win: "we found a 3-step funnel drop-off and fixed it with this telemetry"

14.5 Structured logging

  • JSON logs always. Include: level, timestamp, service, env, deploy SHA, user.id, request_id.
  • Pino (Node), browser-bunyan (FE) emit structured logs.
  • Search by attribute, not regex.

14.6 SLO-based alerting

  • Burn-rate alerts: page when error budget burns > 14.4× normal for 1 h (Google SRE math).
  • Multi-window: 5-min spike + 1-h sustained both required to page.
  • Reduces alert fatigue dramatically.

Part 15 — Edge + Workers patterns

15.1 Durable Objects (Cloudflare)

  • Single-instance stateful actor at the edge — perfect for collab editor rooms, multiplayer game rooms.
  • Persistent storage tied to the object; WebSocket hibernation.
  • Hibernation: object sleeps when no traffic; wakes on next request, no cold start for the user.

15.2 Service Bindings

  • Worker → Worker calls without going through public network.
  • Zero-latency, type-safe, no auth overhead.
  • Use for: BFF that fans out to multiple internal Workers.

15.3 Cron / Queued workloads

  • Cloudflare Cron Triggers / Vercel Cron — scheduled invocations.
  • Cloudflare Queues / AWS SQS for fire-and-forget tasks.
  • Use for: refreshing caches, sending digest emails, periodic syncs.

15.4 KV / D1 / R2 / Vector at the edge

  • KV: eventually consistent key-value, sub-ms reads, ~60 s writes.
  • D1: SQLite at the edge, regional read replicas.
  • R2: S3-compatible blob storage, no egress fees.
  • Vectorize: embeddings + vector search at the edge.

15.5 Geographic redirection at the edge

export default {
  async fetch(req) {
    const country = req.cf?.country;
    if (country === "GB") return Response.redirect("https://uk.example.com");
    return fetch(req);
  },
};

15.6 A/B testing at the edge

  • Bucket via cookie (set by edge); rewrite URL or path to variant.
  • Variant gets cached separately; full edge speed for both.
  • Critical for personalization without sacrificing TTFB.

15.7 AI streaming proxies

  • Edge function authenticates user, applies rate limit, then forwards stream to model provider.
  • Keeps API keys server-side; adds cost control + logging.
  • Vercel AI Gateway / OpenRouter / Helicone do this as a service.

Part 16 — Mobile web in production

16.1 iOS Safari quirks

  • 100vh includes URL bar — use 100dvh (dynamic viewport).
  • Tap delay 300 ms historically — gone with touch-action: manipulation or viewport meta.
  • position: fixed + soft keyboard = quirks; use VisualViewport API.
  • Momentum scroll: -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch needed historically; deprecated.
  • PWA install flow: Safari requires user manual "Add to Home Screen".

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, viewport-fit=cover">
.bottom-nav {

16.3 Adaptive serving

  • Network Information API: navigator.connection.effectiveType (2g/3g/4g) + saveData.
  • Save-Data: on hint → serve smaller images, skip prefetch.
  • navigator.deviceMemory < 2 → reduce feature set.

16.4 Touch + pointer

  • 44 × 44 CSS px minimum (Apple HIG); 24 × 24 WCAG 2.2 absolute floor.
  • touch-action: pan-y disables horizontal native scroll while letting vertical pass.
  • Hover states must not be sole indicator — many mobile users never hover.

16.7 Web vs native (when to push to native)

  • Push to native: hardware integration (NFC, Bluetooth on non-Chrome), advanced gestures, deep OS integration.
  • Stay web: most SaaS, content, e-commerce.

Part 17 — Developer experience (DevX) at scale

17.1 Codemods for safe migrations

  • jscodeshift / ts-morph for AST transforms.
  • Use for: rename hook, migrate API import paths, upgrade a deprecated pattern across thousands of files.
  • Trojan-deploy: codemod + automated PR per package.

17.2 Custom ESLint rules

  • Enforce org conventions: "no direct use of fetch — use ourFetch wrapper".
  • eslint-plugin-local for project-only rules without publishing.
  • @typescript-eslint/utils to read TS types in rules.

17.3 Bundler plugins

  • Vite plugins: virtual modules, code generation, asset transforms.
  • Rollup plugins: tree-shaking-friendly transforms.
  • Use for: generate routes from filesystem, inject env at build, code-split by chunk markers.

17.4 Build-time data generation

  • Sitemap, RSS, OG images at build OR edge.
  • Vercel og-image, satori (HTML → SVG → image) for OG images.
  • Cache aggressively; regenerate on content publish.

17.5 Type-safe boundaries everywhere

  • Forms (RHF + Zod), routes (TanStack Router / typedRoutes), env (T3 env), API (tRPC / GraphQL-codegen).
  • Goal: catch errors at TypeScript level, not at runtime.

17.6 Dev server quality of life

  • Vite HMR < 100 ms.
  • MSW for API mocking — devs unblocked when backend not ready.
  • Storybook for component sandbox.
  • GitHub Codespaces / VS Code Tunnels for cloud dev environments.

17.7 Lint-staged + pre-commit

  • Husky + lint-staged: ESLint --fix + Prettier on staged files only.
  • Fast feedback; never commit unformatted code.
  • Pre-push runs typecheck + tests on affected packages.

Part 18 — AI-assisted FE development (2026)

18.1 Copilot / Cursor / Continue patterns

  • Pin types in scope — AI generates better when types are visible.
  • Write the function signature + JSDoc first; let AI fill the body.
  • Always review AI-generated tests — they often pass without asserting.

18.2 Code-aware AI tools

  • Cursor, Continue, Codeium, Sweep, Aider.
  • Indexed across your repo — context-aware refactors.

18.3 AI in CI

  • PR review bots (Greptile, CodeRabbit) flag risky patterns.
  • Auto-generated changelog from commits + LLM summary.
  • Auto-triage Sentry errors → suggested fix PR.

18.4 Prompt engineering for component generation

  • Provide existing component as example; AI mimics conventions.
  • Reference design tokens by name; AI uses var(--token).
  • Ask for accessibility + edge cases explicitly.

18.5 AI features in your product

  • Tier 1 — autocomplete / suggestion (lowest risk, biggest value).
  • Tier 2 — summarize / explain (medium risk, easy evals).
  • Tier 3 — agent that takes actions (highest risk, needs guardrails).
  • Always: log + replay, eval suite, kill switch.

Part 19 — Design system at production scale

19.1 Component layers

  • Primitives: Button, Input, Checkbox (Radix-style).
  • Compositions: Card, Modal, Toast (built from primitives).
  • Patterns: page layouts, dashboard templates.
  • Each layer has its own tests + docs.

19.2 Polymorphic + asChild

  • asChild prop (Radix) lets consumers swap the rendered element.
  • <Button asChild><Link href="/x">Go</Link></Button> — keeps semantics + styles.

19.3 Compound APIs

  • <Dialog.Root><Dialog.Trigger /><Dialog.Content /></Dialog.Root> — explicit composition.
  • Avoids prop explosion; clearer than a 30-prop monolith.

19.4 Variants via cva / tailwind-variants

const button = cva("btn", {
  variants: {
    intent: { primary: "btn-primary", danger: "btn-danger" },
    size: { sm: "h-8", md: "h-10", lg: "h-12" },
  },
  defaultVariants: { intent: "primary", size: "md" },
});

19.5 Theming layers

  • Tokens (raw values) → semantic tokens (intent.primary) → component tokens (button.primary.bg).
  • Themes swap by changing the middle layer.
  • Tooling: Style Dictionary, Open Props, Tokens Studio.

19.6 Versioning + migration

  • Semver strict.
  • Deprecated props: TS @deprecated + runtime warn once per component.
  • Major release: codemod for breaking changes.
  • Migration guide in changelog; pin to N-2 supported versions.

19.7 Docs site

  • Storybook OR a custom site (Astro Starlight, Docusaurus, Nextra).
  • Each component: live preview, props table, code, a11y notes, do/don't.
  • Search: Algolia DocSearch or built-in.

Part 20 — Staff-level judgment (the soft layer)

20.1 When NOT to use the shiny new thing

  • Just-released frameworks: wait 6 months unless you can absorb breakage.
  • Pre-1.0 libraries in critical paths: only if a maintainer commits to LTS.
  • AI tools that lock you into a vendor: prefer OpenTelemetry / OSS alternatives.

20.2 Tech debt budget

  • 20% of capacity reserved for cleanup.
  • Track debt as Linear tickets with cost estimates.
  • Senior responsibility: argue with PM about debt-vs-feature tradeoff with numbers.

20.3 Migration patterns

  • Strangler fig: new code paths around the old; old shrinks over time.
  • Branch-by-abstraction: introduce an interface; swap implementations.
  • Feature flag per migration phase.
  • Never big-bang rewrite a working system.

20.4 Design doc culture

  • Any change > 1 week of work = design doc first.
  • Sections: problem, goals, non-goals, options considered, decision, risks, rollout.
  • Async review > sync meeting.
  • Archive in a searchable repo (Notion / GitHub wiki).

20.5 Code review at staff level

  • Focus on architecture + tests + edge cases, not style (let linter handle that).
  • Suggest experiments / alternatives; do not demand.
  • Approve fast on small PRs; deeper review on architecture-affecting ones.
  • Tag with severity: nit / suggestion / blocking.

20.6 On-call rotation health

  • Every alert must be actionable; every page must have a runbook.
  • Weekly review of paged incidents; fix top noisemakers.
  • Compensate time-off-in-lieu; otherwise seniors leave.

20.7 Career conversations

  • Senior FE → Staff: focus on cross-team impact, mentorship, technical leadership.
  • Staff → Principal: org-level impact, architecture across multiple teams, hiring + retention.
  • Track concrete artifacts: design docs, mentorship outcomes, postmortems, RFCs.

20.8 The "Senior Test"

You operate at senior level when you can: (1) own a feature end-to-end including reliability + security + a11y, (2) write a design doc someone else can execute, (3) mentor a mid-level to ship, (4) say no to scope creep with data, (5) own a production incident from page → resolution → postmortem.

End of Volume II. Pair Doc 09 + Doc 10 for the full advanced curriculum. The 90/10 rule: most of senior work is 9 covered + 10 covered; the remaining 10% is good judgment in ambiguous moments.

docs.search: 10 — More Advanced Production FE Techniques (Volume II, 2026) V8 + GC · RSC internals · Scroll-driven CSS · Temporal · OPFS · WebTransport · OT internals · Durable Objects · WebAuthn · Mobile · DevX Continuation of Doc 09 with 20 more parts. Everything here is real production patterns that senior engineers at Figma, Linear, Notion, Stripe, Vercel use. Pair with Doc 09. Part 1 — V8 internals + memory management 1.1 Hidden classes + inline caches V8 builds a hidden class per object shape; constant property layout = fast property access. Adding properties after construction creates a new hidden class — slow. Senior pattern: initialize all properties in the constructor, even to null. Inline caches memoize property lookup per call site; polymorphic call sites are slower. Mechanism. V8 represents every object with a Map (internally called a "hidden class" or "Shape") that records the property names, their order, and their storage offsets. When you read obj.x , V8 doesn't do a hash lookup — it checks the object's Map, and if the Map matches the one it cached at this call site, it reads directly from a fixed byte offset. That cache lives at the call site (an *inline cache*, IC). The IC has four states: uninitialized → first run, no info yet. monomorphic → exactly one Map seen; fastest, can be inlined by TurboFan. polymorphic → 2–4 Maps seen; V8 keeps a small list and linear-scans it. megamorphic → >4 Maps; V8 gives up on the per-site cache and falls back to a slow global lookup. This is the silent killer in generic code (loggers, serializers, virtual-DOM differs). Transition chains. Adding properties in a *consistent order* lets many objects share the same transition chain ( {} → {x} → {x,y} ). Adding them in different orders forks the tree and produces distinct Maps that all hit the same call sites → polymorphic/megamorphic. // BAD: shape diverges → two hidden classes, polymorphic ICs downstream function makePointBad(a, b, flag) { const p = {}; if (flag) { p.x = a; p.y = b; } // shape A: x then y else { p.y = b; p.x = a; } // shape B: y then x (DIFFERENT Map!) return p; } // GOOD: one shape, monomorphic. Initialize every field, same order, no conditionals. class Point { constructor(x = 0, y = 0) { this.x = x; // always present this.y = y; // always present, always after x this.label = null; // declare even when unused → no later transition } } const pts = Array.from({ length: 1e6 }, (_, i) => new Point(i, i)); // dist() below sees ONE Map forever → monomorphic IC → TurboFan inlines the field loads. function dist(p) { return Math.hypot(p.x, p.y); } Gotcha: delete p.x demotes the object to *dictionary mode* (slow hash-map backing store) and the whole transition chain is abandoned. To "remove" a field on a hot object, set it to null / undefined , never delete . Diagnose IC state in Node: node --allow-natives-syntax then %HaveSameMap(a, b) and %DebugPrint(obj) (look for map = 0x... — same address = same hidden class). 1.2 Deoptimization patterns Mixing types in a hot loop (sometimes number, sometimes string) → deopt. Arguments object access (use rest parameters). try/catch around hot loops (V8 historically refused to inline; less true now). with statement, delete operator on objects → deopt. Diagnose: --trace-opt --trace-deopt in Node flags (or DevTools "Optimize for Performance"). Mechanism. V8 runs your code in Ignition (bytecode interpreter), collects type feedback, and once a function is "hot" hands it to TurboFan, which compiles *speculative* optimized machine code: "I assume x is always a Smi (small int), so I'll emit integer add." If that assumption is later violated (you pass a string), V8 must *bail out* — discard the optimized code, restore interpreter state mid-frame (a "deopt"), and resume in Ignition. If it re-optimizes and deopts repeatedly, V8 marks the function deoptimized too many times and stops optimizing it entirely — the worst state: permanently slow. Key deopt triggers in 2026 V8: Type instability of fields and arguments (Smi → HeapNumber → String at the same site). arguments aliasing in sloppy mode — use rest (...args) . Holey vs packed arrays. new Array(n) or assigning past length creates a *holey* elements kind ( HOLEY_SMI_ELEMENTS ); V8 must check each slot for holes. Push from empty to stay *packed*. -0 , NaN , and reading out of bounds silently switch elements kinds (Smi → Double). // Observe a deopt. Run: node --trace-deopt --trace-opt deopt.js function sum(arr) { let s = 0; for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) s += arr[i]; // TurboFan assumes Smi elements return s; } const ints = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; for (let i = 0; i < 1e6; i++) sum(ints); // optimizes to integer add sum([1, 2, "3"]); // ← string forces PACKED_SMI → PACKED_ELEMENTS, prints: // [deoptimizing (DEOPT eager): ... reason: wrong map / not a Smi] Gotcha: a try/catch no longer blocks optimization in modern V8, but a try/finally that throws across an inlined frame still can. The bigger real-world trap is keeping *one polymorphic helper* (e.g. clone(x) ) that every type flows through — it goes megamorphic and never optimizes. Specialize hot paths or monomorphize with a type tag. 1.3 Generational GC Young generation (small, scavenge often). Most objects die young. Old generation (mark-sweep + compaction). Promoted after surviving two scavenges. Major GC pauses are the INP killer — minimize allocations in hot loops. Mechanism (Orinoco, V8's GC). The heap is split: Young generation (new space) , a few MB, managed by a semi-space Scavenger (Cheney's algorithm): two equal halves, from and to . Allocation is a pointer bump in from . On scavenge, live objects are copied to to , the spaces flip, and dead objects are reclaimed *for free* (you never touch them). Objects surviving two scavenges are promoted to old space. Old generation (old space) , managed by a Mark-Compact collector: tri-color marking (white/grey/black) traces from roots, then sweeps free space and occasionally compacts to defragment. Modern V8 hides most of this from your frame budget with concurrent marking (marking on a background thread while JS runs) and incremental steps, plus parallel scavenging. But the final "atomic pause" of a major GC still stops the main thread, and that's what shows up as a long task / bad INP. Allocation rate drives GC frequency: the faster you allocate, the more often the scavenger runs and the sooner objects get promoted into the expensive old space. // Measure GC pressure from the page (Chrome). Run with: chrome://flags → enable // "Experimental Web Platform features" for measureUserAgentSpecificMemory. performance.mark('hot-start'); // ...hot path... performance.measure('hot', 'hot-start'); // Node: surface GC pauses on the event loop const { PerformanceObserver } = require('node:perf_hooks'); new PerformanceObserver((list) => { for (const e of list.getEntries()) if (e.entryType === 'gc') console.log(`GC ${e.detail.kind} took ${e.duration.toFixed(2)}ms`); }).observe({ entryTypes: ['gc'] }); Gotcha: a giant long-lived array of small objects forces every minor GC to scan it via the remembered set (old→young pointers). Prefer a Float64Array /struct-of-arrays layout for million-element hot data so the GC has *zero* pointers to trace. 1.4 Reducing allocations in hot paths Reuse arrays/objects via object pools. Prefer typed arrays (Float32Array) for numerical hot loops. Avoid creating closures per render in animation/scroll loops. Use Map for dynamic dictionaries; object literal for static shape. Mechanism. Every object literal, array, closure, bound function, and even {...spread} is a heap allocation that the scavenger must later process. In a 60fps loop (16.6ms budget) or a scroll handler firing at 120Hz, per-frame garbage is what creates the sawtooth memory graph and intermittent GC jank. The fix is structural : hoist allocations out of the loop, reuse buffers, and prefer flat typed-array storage so there are no per-element objects to collect. // Object pool for a particle system — zero allocations per frame. class Vec2Pool { #buf; #n = 0; constructor(cap) { this.#buf = new Float32Array(cap * 2); } acquire(x, y) { const i = this.#n++ * 2; this.#buf[i] = x; this.#buf[i + 1] = y; return i; } reset() { this.#n = 0; } // "free everything" = pointer reset, no GC x(i) { return this.#buf[i]; } y(i) { return this.#buf[i + 1]; } } const pool = new Vec2Pool(10_000); function frame(particles) { pool.reset(); // reuse the same Float32Array forever for (let i = 0; i < particles.length; i++) { pool.acquire(particles[i].x, particles[i].y); } // ...draw from the pool's buffer in one tight loop... } Gotcha: arrow functions you pass to arr.forEach / .map inside a render allocate a fresh closure every call. In hot loops, switch to a plain for loop and call a *hoisted* named function. Also: Map is the right tool for dynamic string keys (no hidden-class churn, no prototype-pollution risk), while a frozen object literal is best for a fixed-shape config the JIT can inline. 1.5 Heap snapshot triage Take baseline snapshot. Reproduce the suspected leak (open + close modal 5×). Take second snapshot. Diff: "Comparison" view, sort by Delta Size. Click retainer chain — find what is holding the object. Common: closure scope, detached DOM, event listeners on window. Mechanism + workflow. A heap snapshot is a graph: nodes (objects) and edges (references). The two metrics that matter: Shallow size — bytes the object itself occupies. Retained size — bytes that would be freed if this object were deleted (it + everything only it keeps alive). A small object with a huge retained size is your leak root. The three-snapshot technique beats two: snapshot → do the action 7× → snapshot → do it 7× more → snapshot. Use the "Objects allocated between snapshot 1 and 2, still alive at 3" filter. Anything that grows linearly with the repetition count is leaking. Then follow Retainers (bottom panel) up the chain to the GC root. The classic culprits: Detached DOM : filter the Summary view by Detached — a removed node still referenced by a JS variable keeps its entire subtree alive. Closures : a long-lived callback (event listener, setInterval , observer) closes over a big object. Forgotten listeners on window / document that were never removeEventListener 'd. // A real leak: each modal open registers a window listener closing over `bigData`. function openModal(bigData /* 5MB */) { const onResize = () => layout(bigData); // closure retains bigData window.addEventListener('resize', onResize); // BUG: no cleanup — bigData survives every close forever. } // Fixed with AbortController (one signal cleans up N listeners atomically): function openModalFixed(bigData) { const ac = new AbortController(); window.addEventListener('resize', () => layout(bigData), { signal: ac.signal }); return () => ac.abort(); // call on modal close → listener + closure GC'd } Gotcha: snapshots themselves pin objects — take them in an Incognito window with extensions disabled, and force a GC (the trash-can icon) before each snapshot so you're not counting collectible garbage. 1.6 WeakRef + FinalizationRegistry WeakRef holds a reference that does not prevent GC. Use for caches where the consumer may keep the object alive elsewhere. const cache = new Map(); function getOrLoad(key) { const ref = cache.get(key); const cached = ref?.deref(); if (cached) return cached; const obj = load(key); cache.set(key, new WeakRef(obj)); return obj; } Mechanism + the gotchas the snippet hides. WeakRef.deref() returns the target *or* undefined if it's been collected. FinalizationRegistry lets you run a cleanup callback *after* an object is collected — but with no timing guarantee and no guarantee it runs at all (e.g. on tab close). The naïve Map<key, WeakRef> above leaks the WeakRef wrapper and the Map entry even after the target dies — the map grows unbounded with dead refs. You need a registry to evict the stale key: class WeakCache<K, V extends object> { #map = new M

11 — FE Tools & Services Catalog (Production Stack 2026)

30 categories · 200+ services · what each does · when to pick · integration · gotchas

A working catalog of services that frontend teams actually integrate with at companies. For each category: top options, when to pick which, how the FE talks to it, and the gotcha you must defend. Use this as a reference, not a study list — pull what your project needs.

Part 1 — Authentication + Identity

1.1 The landscape

ServiceSweet spotPricing modelNote
Auth.js (NextAuth)Next.js apps; OSSFreeMost popular OSS choice; bring your own DB
ClerkB2C + B2B SaaS; great DXPer-MAUDrop-in UI components; expensive at scale
WorkOSB2B SSO/SAML; enterprisePer-active-connectionBest for enterprise SSO + SCIM
StytchPasswordless firstPer-MAUMagic link, passkey, OAuth
KindeMid-market SaaSPer-MAUBuilt-in feature flags + billing
OktaLarge enterprise IDPPer-MAU (steep)Industry standard for IT-managed identity
KeycloakSelf-hosted enterpriseFree (OSS)Heavy to operate; powerful
Supabase AuthSupabase usersIncludedPostgres-backed; tight integration
Firebase AuthFirebase usersFree → usageMobile-first ecosystem
AWS CognitoAWS-nativePer-MAUJanky DX; powerful at scale
FronteggB2B SaaS, multi-tenantPer-tenantBuilt-in admin portal + workspaces

Decision matrix (tool → when to pick):

  • Clerk → B2C/B2B SaaS wanting drop-in UI, organizations, passkeys today; accept per-MAU cost.
  • Auth.js → Next.js app where you own the DB and want zero vendor lock; you build the UI.
  • WorkOS → you sell to enterprise and need SAML/SCIM/Directory Sync without operating an IdP.
  • Stytch → passwordless-first (magic link, passkey) consumer flows.
  • Supabase/Firebase Auth → you already live in that BaaS and want auth bundled with the DB.
  • Cognito → hard AWS mandate and you can stomach the DX.
  • Keycloak → air-gapped/self-host compliance requirement with ops capacity.
// Clerk — server component reading the session + protecting a route (Next.js App Router, 2026)
import { auth, currentUser } from "@clerk/nextjs/server";
import { redirect } from "next/navigation";

export default async function Dashboard() {
  const { userId, orgId, redirectToSignIn } = await auth();
  if (!userId) return redirectToSignIn();      // not authenticated
  if (!orgId) redirect("/select-org");          // multi-tenant: force org context

  const user = await currentUser();
  return <h1>Welcome {user?.firstName} — org {orgId}</h1>;
}

Senior gotcha: auth() is request-scoped — never cache the resolved userId/orgId in a module-level variable, or you leak one user's session into another's request under serverless instance reuse.

1.2 Integration patterns

  • OAuth/OIDC: redirect → callback → exchange code → session cookie. Always PKCE for SPAs.
  • JWT: HttpOnly cookie OR memory + refresh; never localStorage.
  • SAML for enterprise SSO; you usually proxy via WorkOS / Clerk / Auth0.
  • SCIM 2.0 for automated user provisioning; WorkOS + Frontegg shine here.
// PKCE: generate verifier + challenge before redirecting to the IdP
function base64url(buf: ArrayBuffer) {
  return btoa(String.fromCharCode(...new Uint8Array(buf)))
    .replace(/\+/g, "-").replace(/\//g, "_").replace(/=+$/, "");
}
const verifier = base64url(crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32)).buffer);
const challenge = base64url(await crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", new TextEncoder().encode(verifier)));
sessionStorage.setItem("pkce_verifier", verifier); // exchange for tokens at callback
location.assign(`${authorizeUrl}?code_challenge=${challenge}&code_challenge_method=S256&...`);

Senior gotcha: validate state AND the PKCE verifier at callback. Skipping state opens CSRF on the login flow; skipping PKCE lets an intercepted code be redeemed by an attacker.

1.3 Senior gotchas

  • Logout in tab A → tab B must reflect (BroadcastChannel or storage event).
  • Token rotation + theft detection (reuse = kill session).
  • Anonymous → signed-in cart/state migration must be atomic + tested.
  • Multi-org / workspace switching needs cache clear; otherwise stale data leaks across tenants.
// Cross-tab logout sync
const ch = new BroadcastChannel("auth");
export function broadcastLogout() { ch.postMessage({ type: "logout" }); }
ch.onmessage = (e) => { if (e.data.type === "logout") location.assign("/sign-in"); };

Senior gotcha: on org/workspace switch, blow away every query cache keyed by the old tenant before fetching — a stale cache entry rendering tenant A's data inside tenant B is a reportable data-isolation breach, not just a UX bug.

Part 2 — Product Analytics + CDP

2.1 Product analytics

ToolBest atPricing
PostHogOSS, all-in-one (analytics + flags + replay)Generous free tier
MixpanelEvent analytics, funnels, retentionPer-MTU
AmplitudeBehavioral cohorts + journeyPer-MTU
HeapAuto-capture every eventPer-MAU
PendoIn-app guides + analyticsPer-MAU (high)
JuneMid-market SaaS analyticsPer-MTU
Google Analytics 4Free baseline; weak on product analyticsFree
Plausible / FathomPrivacy-first, no cookiesPer-pageview

Decision matrix:

  • PostHog → startup wanting analytics + flags + replay + experiments in one tool, optionally self-hosted.
  • Amplitude → growth org living in behavioral cohorts and journeys.
  • Mixpanel → funnel/retention reporting for PMs without warehouse plumbing.
  • Heap → can't instrument up front, need retroactive auto-capture.
  • Plausible/Fathom → marketing site wanting privacy-first, cookie-less pageviews.
// PostHog — typed capture wrapper (autocapture off for SPAs to control taxonomy)
import posthog from "posthog-js";
posthog.init(process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY!, {
  api_host: "https://us.i.posthog.com",
  autocapture: false,
  capture_pageview: false,
  person_profiles: "identified_only", // don't bill anonymous as MTUs
});
export function track(event: "Order Completed" | "Item Added to Cart", props: Record<string, unknown>) {
  posthog.capture(event, props);
}

Senior gotcha: person_profiles: "always" silently creates a profile per anonymous visitor and can multiply your MTU bill overnight. Default to identified_only and upgrade only when you actually need anonymous-user profiles.

2.2 Customer Data Platforms (CDP)

  • Segment — the original; ship one event, fan-out to N destinations.
  • RudderStack — OSS alternative; warehouse-first model.
  • mParticle / Tealium — enterprise CDPs with deep mobile + IoT support.
  • Twilio Engage — Segment + journey orchestration.
// Segment — identify BEFORE track, single source of truth for the user
analytics.identify(user.id, { email: user.email, plan: user.plan });
analytics.track("Order Completed", { orderId, revenue, currency: "USD" });

Senior gotcha: client-side Segment is blocked by ad-blockers for 30–50% of users. Route revenue-critical events (purchase, signup) through a server-side source so your funnel and billing reconciliation don't silently undercount.

2.3 Integration pattern

// FE → CDP → fans out
analytics.identify(user.id, { email, plan, signup_at });
analytics.track("Item Added to Cart", { item_id, price });
analytics.page();   // implicit on route change
  • Always identify before track; otherwise events are anonymous.
  • Use a consistent event taxonomy (Subject Verb Object: "Order Completed").
// Enforce taxonomy at the type level so CI catches drift
type AnalyticsEvent =
  | { name: "Order Completed"; props: { orderId: string; revenue: number } }
  | { name: "Item Added to Cart"; props: { itemId: string; price: number } };
export const track = <E extends AnalyticsEvent>(e: E) => analytics.track(e.name, e.props);

Senior gotcha: fire page() on usePathname/router change events, not on popstate alone — client-side route transitions in Next/React Router don't emit popstate, so you lose most pageviews if you only listen there.

2.4 Senior gotchas

  • GDPR/CCPA: respect consent before firing analytics; tools like OneTrust / Cookiebot gate this.
  • Ad blockers eat 30–50% of events; use server-side tagging (Segment Server-Side) for critical funnel events.
  • Event taxonomy drift: write it down + enforce in CI via type checks on the wrapper.

Senior gotcha: consent state must gate SDK *initialization*, not just track() calls. Lazy-init the SDK after consent resolves; an SDK that loads pre-consent already dropped cookies and pinged the host, which is the violation regulators cite.

Part 3 — Frontend Observability + Session Replay

3.1 Tool comparison

ToolBest atWhen
SentryErrors + perf + replay; defaultMost teams; free tier generous
Datadog RUMEnd-to-end with backend tracesAlready on Datadog
New Relic BrowserUser-tier pricingMid-market
HoneycombHigh-cardinality debuggingTrace-first culture
LogRocketSession replay + funnel + DOM eventsReplay-heavy support workflows
FullStoryUX + funnels + heatmapsPM-led orgs
HotjarHeatmaps + lightweight replaySMB + marketing
Microsoft ClarityFree replay + heatmapsCost-sensitive teams
Highlight.ioOSS Sentry + LogRocket alternativeSelf-host friendly
Rollbar / BugsnagSentry alternativesMulti-language enterprise
Sentry ReplayBuilt into Sentry, maskedYou already use Sentry
SpeedCurve / Calibre / DebugBearPerf monitoring + benchmarkingMarketing-funnel perf

Decision matrix:

  • Sentry → default for errors + perf + masked replay in one SDK; correlate to releases.
  • Datadog RUM → already on Datadog APM; stitch FE traces to backend spans.
  • Honeycomb → trace-first culture debugging high-cardinality production behavior.
  • LogRocket/FullStory → support/PM workflows that live in session replay.
  • Clarity → free heatmaps + replay when budget is zero.
// Sentry — wired right (Next.js, 2026)
import * as Sentry from "@sentry/nextjs";
Sentry.init({
  dsn: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN,
  release: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_DEPLOY_SHA,
  tracesSampleRate: 0.1,
  replaysSessionSampleRate: 0.01,
  replaysOnErrorSampleRate: 1.0,
  ignoreErrors: [/ResizeObserver loop/, /Non-Error promise rejection/],
  integrations: [Sentry.replayIntegration({ maskAllText: true, blockAllMedia: true })],
});

Senior gotcha: release must equal the value you upload source maps under, byte-for-byte. A mismatch silently leaves every production stack trace minified — invisible until you're paged at 3am with a.b.c is not a function.

3.2 Integration code patterns

// Sentry — wired right
Sentry.init({
  dsn: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN,
  release: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_DEPLOY_SHA,
  tracesSampleRate: 0.1,
  replaysSessionSampleRate: 0.01,
  replaysOnErrorSampleRate: 1.0,
  ignoreErrors: [/ResizeObserver loop/, /Non-Error promise rejection/],
  integrations: [Sentry.replayIntegration({ maskAllText: true, blockAllMedia: true })],
});
// Attach user + tenant context so traces are filterable, not anonymous
Sentry.setUser({ id: user.id });
Sentry.setTag("tenant", orgId);
Sentry.setTag("feature_flag.new_checkout", flagValue ? "on" : "off");

Senior gotcha: never put email/PII in setUser for regulated domains — use an opaque id and resolve identity in your dashboard. The replay mask is irrelevant if you already shipped the email as a tag.

3.3 Senior gotchas

  • Privacy: mask PII in replay (form fields, tokens). Default OFF for medical/finance domains.
  • Source maps must upload on every release; otherwise stack traces are useless.
  • Sampling: 100% errors, 1–10% perf, < 1% replays — tune for cost.
  • Filter noise (third-party ResizeObserver loops, browser extension errors).

Senior gotcha: maskAllText: true still leaks PII rendered into element *attributes* (title, aria-label, image alt, URL query params). Add explicit .sentry-mask/block classes on those and scrub query strings in beforeSend before you trust the masking.

4.1 Integration patterns

  • Front-end via algoliasearch / instantsearch.js or @typesense/instantsearch-adapter.

// Race-condition guard: ignore stale responses from slower in-flight queries
let seq = 0;
async function onInput(q: string) {
  const mine = ++seq;
  const res = await search(q);
  if (mine === seq) render(res); // drop if a newer query already fired
}

Senior gotcha: debounce alone doesn't prevent out-of-order results — a slow request for "ip" can resolve *after* "iphone". The monotonic sequence guard above is mandatory, not optional.

4.2 Senior gotchas

  • Index drift: schema change → reindex everything; have a migration plan.
  • Security: filter by tenant on the server; Algolia has secured API keys per user.
  • Cost: per-record + per-search; can balloon fast on commerce catalogs.

Senior gotcha: reindex into a new alias and atomically swap, never mutate the live index in place. An in-place reindex serves half-old/half-new documents mid-run, surfacing deleted products and broken facets to live users.

// Stripe — Checkout session + webhook verify + idempotency (Next.js route handlers, 2026)
import Stripe from "stripe";
const stripe = new Stripe(process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY!);

// 1) Create a Checkout Session (idempotent against double-clicks)
export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const { priceId, userId } = await req.json();
  const session = await stripe.checkout.sessions.create(
    {
      mode: "subscription",
      line_items: [{ price: priceId, quantity: 1 }],
      success_url: `${process.env.URL}/success?sid={CHECKOUT_SESSION_ID}`,
      cancel_url: `${process.env.URL}/pricing`,
      client_reference_id: userId,
    },

// 2) Webhook: verify signature against the RAW body, then sync state
export async function webhook(req: Request) {
  const body = await req.text(); // raw, un-parsed
  const sig = req.headers.get("stripe-signature")!;
  let event: Stripe.Event;
  try {
    event = stripe.webhooks.constructEvent(body, sig, process.env.STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET!);
  } catch {
    return new Response("bad signature", { status: 400 });
  }
  if (event.type === "customer.subscription.deleted") {
    await db.downgrade(event.data.object.id);
  }
  return new Response("ok"); // 2xx fast, or Stripe retries
}

Senior gotcha: webhook verification needs the raw request body — any middleware that JSON-parses first (express.json(), default body parsers) breaks constructEvent because the signature is computed over exact bytes. Disable body parsing on the webhook route.

5.1 Stripe Checkout vs Stripe Elements

  • Stripe Elements: iframe-isolated fields you embed; full design control; SAQ-A compliance.

// Payment Element: confirm against a server-created PaymentIntent client_secret
const stripe = useStripe(); const elements = useElements();
async function pay() {
  const { error } = await stripe!.confirmPayment({
    elements: elements!, confirmParams: { return_url: `${origin}/order/complete` },
  });
  if (error) setMessage(error.message); // 3DS handled automatically via return_url
}

Senior gotcha: create the PaymentIntent on the server with the amount derived from your DB, never from the client. Trusting a client-sent amount lets a user pay $0.01 for a $100 cart.

5.2 Subscription patterns

  • Customer Portal hosted by Stripe — let users manage their own subs.

  • 3DS / SCA in EU is mandatory; Payment Intents handle it automatically.
// Treat the webhook as the source of truth; the success redirect is just UX
const ENTITLED = new Set(["active", "trialing", "past_due"]);
async function syncSub(sub: Stripe.Subscription) {
  await db.user.update({ where: { stripeCustomerId: sub.customer as string },

Senior gotcha: never grant access on the success_url redirect — users close the tab before it loads, and the URL is forgeable. Grant entitlement only when checkout.session.completed/invoice.paid arrives via verified webhook.

5.3 Senior gotchas

  • Tax: built-in (Stripe Tax / Paddle) or your problem — non-trivial across 100+ countries.

  • Webhook signature verification — never trust the body alone.
  • Sandbox vs prod keys — single set of webhook endpoints; check Stripe-Signature header for which env.

Senior gotcha: webhooks are at-least-once — the same event id can arrive twice. Persist processed event.ids and no-op on replay, or a duplicate invoice.paid double-credits the account.

// On-demand revalidation triggered by a CMS publish webhook (Next.js)
export async function POST(req: Request) {
  if (req.headers.get("x-secret") !== process.env.REVALIDATE_SECRET)
    return new Response("forbidden", { status: 401 });
  const { slug } = await req.json();
  revalidateTag(`post:${slug}`); // surgical, not a full rebuild
  return Response.json({ revalidated: true });
}

Senior gotcha: tag-scope your revalidation (revalidateTag) — calling revalidatePath("/") or full rebuilds on every edit creates a thundering herd of regenerations on a busy editorial team and blows your build minutes.

6.2 Senior gotchas

  • Image transforms: most CMSes pipe through their own CDN; check formats + cropping APIs.
  • Webhook → revalidate flow must be reliable; use a queue (Inngest / Hookdeck) if CMS is flaky.

Senior gotcha: CMS publish webhooks are fire-and-forget and *do* get dropped. Put a queue (Hookdeck/Inngest) with retries in front of your revalidation endpoint, or a missed webhook leaves stale content live with no signal until a human notices.

  store.setQuery(api.todos.list, { workspaceId }, [...cur, { _id: "temp" as any, title }]);

Senior gotcha: never call external APIs (Stripe, OpenAI) from a mutation — mutations run in a deterministic transaction and may be retried, double-firing side effects. Put network calls in an action, then write results back via a mutation.

7.2 Supabase pattern (Postgres-first)

  queryKey: ["todos", workspaceId],

// Realtime
supabase.channel("todos").on("postgres_changes", { event: "*", schema: "public", table: "todos" },
  () => queryClient.invalidateQueries(["todos"])).subscribe();
-- RLS policy: a user only sees rows for workspaces they belong to
alter table todos enable row level security;
create policy "members read" on todos for select
  using (workspace in (select workspace from memberships where user_id = auth.uid()));

Senior gotcha: Realtime broadcasts respect RLS only if you've enabled it on the *replication* path too — without RLS on the table, the Realtime stream happily pushes every tenant's row change to every subscribed client even though the REST .select() is locked down.

7.3 Senior gotchas

  • RLS (Row-Level Security) is your authz on Supabase/Postgres — author + test policies thoroughly.
  • Vendor lock: BaaS APIs are non-standard; migration plan needed.
  • Cost spikes: connection pooling (Supabase PgBouncer / Neon's native pooler) on serverless.
  • Edge runtime + DB: D1 / Turso / Neon HTTP driver handle Worker-style connections.

Senior gotcha: on serverless/edge, every cold function instance opens its own Postgres connection — at scale you exhaust the limit and throw too many connections. Always route through the pooler endpoint (PgBouncer / Neon pooled URL / Supavisor), not the direct DB host.

// Web Push — subscribe in the SW registration, send subscription to your server
const reg = await navigator.serviceWorker.register("/sw.js");
const sub = await reg.pushManager.subscribe({
  userVisibleOnly: true,
  applicationServerKey: urlBase64ToUint8Array(process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY!),
});
await fetch("/api/push/subscribe", { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify(sub) });

Senior gotcha: pushManager.subscribe must be called from an active SW registration *and* after a user gesture — calling it on page load triggers the permission prompt cold, which most users hard-deny, permanently poisoning your opt-in rate for that origin.

10.1 Web Push

  • VAPID keys; subscribe in SW; server pushes via FCM (Chrome), Mozilla Push, Apple Push.
  • Payload encrypted (ECDH); push service cannot read it.
  • iOS 16.4+ supports Web Push only for installed PWAs.
// Server — send an encrypted push with VAPID; prune dead subscriptions
import webpush from "web-push";
webpush.setVapidDetails("mailto:ops@acme.com", PUBLIC_KEY, PRIVATE_KEY);
try {
  await webpush.sendNotification(sub, JSON.stringify({ title: "New message", url: "/inbox" }));
} catch (e: any) {
  if (e.statusCode === 404 || e.statusCode === 410) await db.deleteSubscription(sub.endpoint);
}

Senior gotcha: push endpoints go stale constantly (uninstalled PWAs, expired tokens) and return 404/410 — if you don't prune on those status codes, your subscription table bloats with dead endpoints and every broadcast wastes time/quota retrying them.

10.2 In-app notifications

  • SSE / WebSocket connection delivers events; client renders into a notification center.
  • Read state synced server-side (avoid local-only counts).
// SSE feed → render into the notification center, server owns read state
const es = new EventSource("/api/notifications/stream");
es.onmessage = (e) => store.add(JSON.parse(e.data));
async function markRead(id: string) { await fetch(`/api/notifications/${id}/read`, { method: "POST" }); }

Senior gotcha: unread counts must be server-authoritative — a local-only count desyncs the moment the user opens a second tab or device, showing "3 unread" on the phone after they cleared them on desktop. Reconcile the badge from the server on focus.

10.3 Senior gotchas

  • Permission UX: prompt only after user does X; never on page load.
  • Preferences: per-channel, per-category — give users control or face unsubscribes.
  • Quiet hours + frequency capping — Knock / Customer.io handle this.

Senior gotcha: without frequency capping + cross-channel de-dup, a single backend event fans out to email + push + SMS + in-app simultaneously — the user gets pinged four times for one thing and mass-disables notifications. Centralize routing (Knock/Novu) so one event = one chosen channel.

// OpenFeature — server-evaluate the flag, pass to client to prevent flicker
import { OpenFeature } from "@openfeature/server-sdk";
export default async function Page() {
  const client = OpenFeature.getClient();
  const newCheckout = await client.getBooleanValue("new-checkout", false,

Senior gotcha: OpenFeature is just the spec — you still bind a provider (LaunchDarkly/Flagsmith/etc.). The win is that swapping vendors is a one-line provider change, but if you call vendor-specific APIs around it you re-introduce the lock-in OpenFeature exists to remove.

11.1 SSR flag eval (anti-flicker)

// app/page.tsx (Next.js)
import { cookies } from "next/headers";
import { flagClient } from "@/flags";
export default async function Page() {
  const newCheckout = await flagClient.boolVariation("new-checkout",
    { userId: cookies().get("uid")?.value }, false);
  return newCheckout ? <NewCheckout /> : <OldCheckout />;
}
// Bootstrap client SDK with server-evaluated values so hydration matches
<FlagProvider bootstrap={serverEvaluatedFlags}>{children}</FlagProvider>

Senior gotcha: if the server evaluates a flag one way and the client SDK (fetching fresh) evaluates it another, React throws a hydration mismatch and flashes the wrong variant. Bootstrap the client with the exact server-resolved values so the first client render is identical.

11.2 Senior gotchas

  • Flag debt: every flag has owner + expiry + Linear ticket.
  • Bootstrap server-side for SSR — never flicker.
  • Bucketing: stable hash(userId+expId); never random per request.
  • Exposure logging: log only when variant actually rendered, not when fetched.

Senior gotcha: log the exposure only when the variant is actually *rendered to the user*, not when the flag is fetched. Logging on fetch counts users who bounced before seeing the variant, biasing your experiment toward null and invalidating the readout.

// Edge middleware — geo-route + rewrite before render (Vercel)
import { NextResponse } from "next/server";
export function middleware(req: Request) {
  const country = (req as any).geo?.country ?? "US";
  const url = new URL(req.url);

Senior gotcha: edge middleware runs on *every* matched request — an over-broad matcher adds latency to every image and _next chunk. Exclude static paths explicitly (as above) or you pay middleware cost on the whole page load.

// Durable Object — single-threaded actor for atomic per-room state
export class Room {
  constructor(private state: DurableObjectState) {}
  async fetch() {
    let count = (await this.state.storage.get<number>("c")) ?? 0;
    await this.state.storage.put("c", ++count); // serialized, no race
    return new Response(String(count));
  }
}

Senior gotcha: edge runtimes are not Node — no fs, no raw TCP sockets, tiny CPU budget. Pulling in a Node-only dependency (e.g. a Postgres driver using raw sockets) fails at deploy or runtime; use HTTP-based drivers (Neon HTTP, D1) at the edge.

// Surgical purge by cache tag instead of nuking the whole zone (Cloudflare)
await fetch(`https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/zones/${ZONE}/purge_cache`, {
  method: "POST", headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${CF_TOKEN}` },
  body: JSON.stringify({ tags: [`product:${productId}`] }),
});

Senior gotcha: tag-based purge requires you to *emit* Cache-Tag (Cloudflare) / Surrogate-Key (Fastly) response headers at origin. Without them your only option is "purge everything," which cold-starts your entire cache and hammers origin on every small content change.

// Presigned PUT — client uploads directly, server never proxies the bytes (R2/S3 SDK)
import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";
import { getSignedUrl } from "@aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner";
const s3 = new S3Client({ region: "auto", endpoint: process.env.R2_ENDPOINT });
const url = await getSignedUrl(s3, new PutObjectCommand({
  Bucket: "uploads", Key: `${userId}/${crypto.randomUUID()}`,
  ContentType: contentType, ContentLength: size,
}), { expiresIn: 300 });
return Response.json({ url }); // client PUTs the file to this URL

Senior gotcha: pin ContentType and ContentLength (ideally a content-length-range condition) into the presigned policy. An unconstrained presigned URL lets the client upload a 5GB file or a text/html payload to a path you serve, turning your bucket into a malware/XSS host.

const f = createUploadthing();
export const router = {
  avatar: f({ image: { maxFileSize: "2MB", maxFileCount: 1 } })
    .middleware(async ({ req }) => {
      const user = await auth(req); if (!user) throw new Error("unauthorized");
      return { userId: user.id }; // passed to onUploadComplete
    })

Senior gotcha: enforce auth + size/type limits in the middleware, which runs server-side before the upload is authorized — client-side maxFileSize is cosmetic and bypassed by anyone hitting the endpoint directly.

  • Tagging for cache purge (Cloudflare cache tags, Fastly surrogate keys).

Senior gotcha: after a direct presigned upload, still validate the object server-side (magic-byte sniff, virus scan, dimension check) before exposing it — the client controls the bytes, so a file named avatar.png can be an executable or a polyglot SVG with embedded script.

// Intercom — lazy-load after idle, identify with server-computed HMAC
function bootIntercom(user: { id: string; email: string; hmac: string }) {
  (window as any).intercomSettings = { app_id: APP_ID, user_id: user.id,
    email: user.email, user_hash: user.hmac /* HMAC-SHA256(user.id, secret) on server */ };

Senior gotcha: the user_hash (HMAC) must be computed server-side with your secret and the user's id — never ship the secret to the client. Without identity verification, anyone can impersonate another user's id in the messenger and read their support history.

// MapLibre — render markers via the map API, keep React out of the pan/zoom path
import maplibregl from "maplibre-gl";
useEffect(() => {
  const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: ref.current!, style: STYLE_URL,
    center: [-122.4, 37.8], zoom: 11 });
  points.forEach(p => new maplibregl.Marker().setLngLat([p.lng, p.lat]).addTo(map));
  return () => map.remove(); // critical cleanup
}, []); // do NOT re-run on every render

Senior gotcha: never let React re-render drive the map — recreating the Map on each render leaks WebGL contexts (browsers cap them ~16, then the map silently goes blank). Instantiate once in an effect with an empty dep array, mutate via the imperative API, and always map.remove() on unmount.

Senior gotcha: without a session token, Places bills each keystroke as a separate request — a 12-character search costs 12x. Reuse one session token across the keystrokes of a single search and discard it after the user picks a result.

  • Svix — outbound webhook delivery service (you send webhooks to your users).
  • Hookdeck — webhook ingestion + observability + retries.
  • WebhookRelay — webhook forwarding to localhost.
  • ngrok / Cloudflare Tunnel — local tunnel for dev.
  • Inngest — durable functions + webhook ingestion.
  • Trigger.dev — background jobs + webhooks.
  • Pipedream — workflow automation.

Part 29 — Background Jobs / Queues

  • Inngest — durable functions for TS; perfect for serverless apps.
  • Trigger.dev — V3 OSS background jobs.
  • Hatchet — distributed task queues.
  • BullMQ (OSS) — Redis-based queue for Node.
  • Cloudflare Queues + Workers — edge queue.
  • AWS SQS + Lambda — serverless queue.
  • Temporal — workflow orchestration at scale.
  • Resque / Sidekiq (Ruby), Celery (Python), Faktory — non-JS options.
  • Tembo / Hatchet (Postgres-backed) — when you don't want a Redis dep.

Part 30 — Internal Tools + Docs Sites

30.1 Docs site frameworks

  • Mintlify — modern, AI-powered, fast.
  • Docusaurus — Meta default, React-based.
  • Nextra — Next.js-native.
  • Astro Starlight — fast static docs.
  • VitePress — Vue-flavored.
  • GitBook — managed, all-in-one.
  • ReadMe — API docs focus.

30.2 Knowledge bases

  • Notion — flexible all-purpose.
  • Confluence — enterprise default.
  • Outline (OSS) — self-host Notion.
  • Coda — Notion alternative.
  • Slab — engineering-focused.

30.3 Diagram + design

  • Excalidraw — sketchy, OSS.
  • Tldraw — collaborative whiteboard (also SDK).
  • Miro / Mural — enterprise whiteboards.
  • Figma — design + Figjam for whiteboard.
  • Mermaid / D2 / Graphviz — text → diagram.

Part 31 — Other essentials

31.1 Code quality + review

  • SonarCloud — SAST + code quality.
  • Codacy — code review automation.
  • CodeClimate — coverage + maintainability.
  • Greptile / CodeRabbit / Sweep — AI PR review.
  • Reviewable / Gerrit — alternative PR UIs.

31.2 Security scanning

  • Snyk — deps + container + IaC.
  • Dependabot — GitHub-native.
  • Renovate — flexible bumps.
  • Semgrep — SAST.
  • Trivy / Grype — container scanning.
  • gitleaks / TruffleHog — secret scanning.
  • GitHub Advanced Security — bundled.

31.3 Secret management

  • Doppler — modern secret manager.
  • HashiCorp Vault — enterprise.
  • 1Password — for humans + 1Password Connect for CI.
  • AWS Secrets Manager / Parameter Store.
  • Infisical (OSS).
  • Cloudflare Secrets Store.

31.4 Feature management

  • Sentry Releases — track releases + commits.
  • LinearB — engineering ops insights.
  • Swarmia — engineering analytics.
  • Jellyfish — engineering effectiveness.

31.5 Misc dev tools

  • Mintlify — docs.
  • Devbox / Devcontainers / Nix — reproducible dev envs.
  • Gitpod / GitHub Codespaces — cloud dev.
  • Replit — collaborative IDE.
  • Linear / Jira — project management.
  • Slack / Discord / Microsoft Teams — comms.

Part 32 — Real production stacks (case studies)

Stripe-like SaaS (B2B mid-market)

  • Hosting: Vercel.
  • Auth: Clerk or WorkOS.
  • DB: Neon Postgres + Drizzle ORM.
  • Analytics: PostHog (flags + analytics + replay).
  • Email: Resend + React Email.
  • Monitoring: Sentry.
  • Payments: Stripe.
  • Feature flags: PostHog.
  • Support: Plain.
  • Notifications: Knock.

Figma-like collab editor

  • Hosting: Cloudflare Pages + Workers + Durable Objects.
  • Auth: WorkOS (SSO heavy).
  • DB: PlanetScale / D1.
  • Real-time: PartyKit (Durable Objects) or Liveblocks.
  • Storage: R2.
  • Search: Algolia / Typesense.
  • Monitoring: Sentry + Honeycomb traces.

Netflix-like content platform

  • Hosting: AWS CloudFront + Lambda@Edge.
  • Video: HLS via internal pipeline (Mux for smaller orgs).
  • Image CDN: Cloudinary / internal.
  • Auth: internal OIDC.
  • Search: Elastic.
  • Monitoring: Datadog + custom RUM.

Linear-like project management

  • Hosting: Vercel or self-host.
  • Sync engine: custom (Replicache / their own).
  • DB: Postgres + Yjs CRDT.
  • Auth: WorkOS.
  • Real-time: WebSocket + sync engine.
  • Search: Typesense.

Notion-like docs + DB

  • Hosting: AWS / Vercel.
  • DB: PostgreSQL + custom block store.
  • Auth: Auth0.
  • Real-time: WebSocket + their own sync.
  • Search: Elastic.
  • AI: OpenAI for AI features.

Indie SaaS bootstrap stack (cheap, fast)

  • Hosting: Vercel (free tier) → Cloudflare Pages as you scale.
  • Auth: Clerk free tier OR Lucia (OSS).
  • DB: Turso / Neon (generous free tier).
  • Analytics: PostHog Cloud free tier.
  • Email: Resend free tier.
  • Payments: Stripe.
  • Monitoring: Sentry free tier.
  • Status: Better Stack free tier.
  • Feature flags: PostHog or GrowthBook self-host.

Part 33 — Build vs Buy + Decision Frameworks

33.1 When to buy

  • Not your core competency (auth, payments, search, video).
  • Compliance pre-built (SOC 2, HIPAA, PCI).
  • Engineering team < 50 — cannot afford the headcount.
  • Time-to-market is the bottleneck.

33.2 When to build

  • Differentiating capability (your product's unique value).
  • Vendor pricing is > 30% of revenue.
  • Existing solutions miss critical features your customers need.
  • You can credibly build it in 1–2 months.

33.3 Migration cost framework

  • Estimated engineering weeks to migrate.
  • Lost productivity during migration.
  • Risk of regression (data loss, customer churn).
  • Pricing delta (annual) × 3 (expected life).
  • If (engineering cost + risk + opportunity cost) < (pricing delta × 3), migrate.

33.4 Vendor evaluation checklist

  • SLA + uptime history (request 12 months).
  • Pricing transparency (no hidden overage surprises).
  • Data export (can you leave?).
  • Multi-region presence + data residency.
  • SOC 2 + GDPR + HIPAA as needed.
  • SDK quality + docs + community.
  • Roadmap alignment (do they ship?).
  • Acquisition / shutdown risk (founder-led? funding?).

End of catalog. Pair with Doc 09 (advanced techniques) + Doc 10 (Vol II). When the question is "what tool would you reach for here?", this is your answer key.

For each category: top options, when to pick which, how the FE talks to it, and the gotcha you must defend. Use this as a reference, not a study list — pull what your project needs. Part 1 — Authentication + Identity 1.1 The landscape Service Sweet spot Pricing model Note Auth.js (NextAuth) Next.js apps; OSS Free Most popular OSS choice; bring your own DB Clerk B2C + B2B SaaS; great DX Per-MAU Drop-in UI components; expensive at scale WorkOS B2B SSO/SAML; enterprise Per-active-connection Best for enterprise SSO + SCIM Stytch Passwordless first Per-MAU Magic link, passkey, OAuth Kinde Mid-market SaaS Per-MAU Built-in feature flags + billing Okta Large enterprise IDP Per-MAU (steep) Industry standard for IT-managed identity Keycloak Self-hosted enterprise Free (OSS) Heavy to operate; powerful Supabase Auth Supabase users Included Postgres-backed; tight integration Firebase Auth Firebase users Free → usage Mobile-first ecosystem AWS Cognito AWS-native Per-MAU Janky DX; powerful at scale Frontegg B2B SaaS, multi-tenant Per-tenant Built-in admin portal + workspaces Decision matrix (tool → when to pick): Clerk → B2C/B2B SaaS wanting drop-in UI, organizations, passkeys today; accept per-MAU cost. Auth.js → Next.js app where you own the DB and want zero vendor lock; you build the UI. WorkOS → you sell to enterprise and need SAML/SCIM/Directory Sync without operating an IdP. Stytch → passwordless-first (magic link, passkey) consumer flows. Supabase/Firebase Auth → you already live in that BaaS and want auth bundled with the DB. Cognito → hard AWS mandate and you can stomach the DX. Keycloak → air-gapped/self-host compliance requirement with ops capacity. // Clerk — server component reading the session + protecting a route (Next.js App Router, 2026) import { auth, currentUser } from "@clerk/nextjs/server"; import { redirect } from "next/navigation"; export default async function Dashboard() { const { userId, orgId, redirectToSignIn } = await auth(); if (!userId) return redirectToSignIn(); // not authenticated if (!orgId) redirect("/select-org"); // multi-tenant: force org context const user = await currentUser(); return <h1>Welcome {user?.firstName} — org {orgId}</h1>; } Senior gotcha: auth() is request-scoped — never cache the resolved userId / orgId in a module-level variable, or you leak one user's session into another's request under serverless instance reuse. 1.2 Integration patterns OAuth/OIDC: redirect → callback → exchange code → session cookie. Always PKCE for SPAs. JWT: HttpOnly cookie OR memory + refresh; never localStorage. SAML for enterprise SSO; you usually proxy via WorkOS / Clerk / Auth0. SCIM 2.0 for automated user provisioning; WorkOS + Frontegg shine here. // PKCE: generate verifier + challenge before redirecting to the IdP function base64url(buf: ArrayBuffer) { return btoa(String.fromCharCode(...new Uint8Array(buf))) .replace(/\+/g, "-").replace(/\//g, "_").replace(/=+$/, ""); } const verifier = base64url(crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32)).buffer); const challenge = base64url(await crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", new TextEncoder().encode(verifier))); sessionStorage.setItem("pkce_verifier", verifier); // exchange for tokens at callback location.assign(`${authorizeUrl}?code_challenge=${challenge}&code_challenge_method=S256&...`); Senior gotcha: validate state AND the PKCE verifier at callback. Skipping state opens CSRF on the login flow; skipping PKCE lets an intercepted code be redeemed by an attacker. 1.3 Senior gotchas Logout in tab A → tab B must reflect (BroadcastChannel or storage event). Token rotation + theft detection (reuse = kill session). Anonymous → signed-in cart/state migration must be atomic + tested. Multi-org / workspace switching needs cache clear; otherwise stale data leaks across tenants. // Cross-tab logout sync const ch = new BroadcastChannel("auth"); export function broadcastLogout() { ch.postMessage({ type: "logout" }); } ch.onmessage = (e) => { if (e.data.type === "logout") location.assign("/sign-in"); }; Senior gotcha: on org/workspace switch, blow away every query cache keyed by the old tenant before fetching — a stale cache entry rendering tenant A's data inside tenant B is a reportable data-isolation breach, not just a UX bug. Part 2 — Product Analytics + CDP 2.1 Product analytics Tool Best at Pricing PostHog OSS, all-in-one (analytics + flags + replay) Generous free tier Mixpanel Event analytics, funnels, retention Per-MTU Amplitude Behavioral cohorts + journey Per-MTU Heap Auto-capture every event Per-MAU Pendo In-app guides + analytics Per-MAU (high) June Mid-market SaaS analytics Per-MTU Google Analytics 4 Free baseline; weak on product analytics Free Plausible / Fathom Privacy-first, no cookies Per-pageview Decision matrix: PostHog → startup wanting analytics + flags + replay + experiments in one tool, optionally self-hosted. Amplitude → growth org living in behavioral cohorts and journeys. Mixpanel → funnel/retention reporting for PMs without warehouse plumbing. Heap → can't instrument up front, need retroactive auto-capture. Plausible/Fathom → marketing site wanting privacy-first, cookie-less pageviews. // PostHog — typed capture wrapper (autocapture off for SPAs to control taxonomy) import posthog from "posthog-js"; posthog.init(process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY!, { api_host: "https://us.i.posthog.com", autocapture: false, capture_pageview: false, person_profiles: "identified_only", // don't bill anonymous as MTUs }); export function track(event: "Order Completed" | "Item Added to Cart", props: Record<string, unknown>) { posthog.capture(event, props); } Senior gotcha: person_profiles: "always" silently creates a profile per anonymous visitor and can multiply your MTU bill overnight. Default to identified_only and upgrade only when you actually need anonymous-user profiles. 2.2 Customer Data Platforms (CDP) Segment — the original; ship one event, fan-out to N destinations. RudderStack — OSS alternative; warehouse-first model. mParticle / Tealium — enterprise CDPs with deep mobile + IoT support. Twilio Engage — Segment + journey orchestration. // Segment — identify BEFORE track, single source of truth for the user analytics.identify(user.id, { email: user.email, plan: user.plan }); analytics.track("Order Completed", { orderId, revenue, currency: "USD" }); Senior gotcha: client-side Segment is blocked by ad-blockers for 30–50% of users. Route revenue-critical events (purchase, signup) through a server-side source so your funnel and billing reconciliation don't silently undercount. 2.3 Integration pattern // FE → CDP → fans out analytics.identify(user.id, { email, plan, signup_at }); analytics.track("Item Added to Cart", { item_id, price }); analytics.page(); // implicit on route change Always identify before track; otherwise events are anonymous. Use a consistent event taxonomy (Subject Verb Object: "Order Completed"). // Enforce taxonomy at the type level so CI catches drift type AnalyticsEvent = | { name: "Order Completed"; props: { orderId: string; revenue: number } } | { name: "Item Added to Cart"; props: { itemId: string; price: number } }; export const track = <E extends AnalyticsEvent>(e: E) => analytics.track(e.name, e.props); Senior gotcha: fire page() on usePathname /router change events, not on popstate alone — client-side route transitions in Next/React Router don't emit popstate , so you lose most pageviews if you only listen there. 2.4 Senior gotchas GDPR/CCPA: respect consent before firing analytics; tools like OneTrust / Cookiebot gate this. Ad blockers eat 30–50% of events; use server-side tagging (Segment Server-Side) for critical funnel events. Event taxonomy drift: write it down + enforce in CI via type checks on the wrapper. Senior gotcha: consent state must gate SDK *initialization*, not just track() calls. Lazy-init the SDK after consent resolves; an SDK that loads pre-consent already dropped cookies and pinged the host, which is the violation regulators cite. Part 3 — Frontend Observability + Session Replay 3.1 Tool comparison Tool Best at When Sentry Errors + perf + replay; default Most teams; free tier generous Datadog RUM End-to-end with backend traces Already on Datadog New Relic Browser User-tier pricing Mid-market Honeycomb High-cardinality debugging Trace-first culture LogRocket Session replay + funnel + DOM events Replay-heavy support workflows FullStory UX + funnels + heatmaps PM-led orgs Hotjar Heatmaps + lightweight replay SMB + marketing Microsoft Clarity Free replay + heatmaps Cost-sensitive teams Highlight.io OSS Sentry + LogRocket alternative Self-host friendly Rollbar / Bugsnag Sentry alternatives Multi-language enterprise Sentry Replay Built into Sentry, masked You already use Sentry SpeedCurve / Calibre / DebugBear Perf monitoring + benchmarking Marketing-funnel perf Decision matrix: Sentry → default for errors + perf + masked replay in one SDK; correlate to releases. Datadog RUM → already on Datadog APM; stitch FE traces to backend spans. Honeycomb → trace-first culture debugging high-cardinality production behavior. LogRocket/FullStory → support/PM workflows that live in session replay. Clarity → free heatmaps + replay when budget is zero. // Sentry — wired right (Next.js, 2026) import * as Sentry from "@sentry/nextjs"; Sentry.init({ dsn: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN, release: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_DEPLOY_SHA, tracesSampleRate: 0.1, replaysSessionSampleRate: 0.01, replaysOnErrorSampleRate: 1.0, ignoreErrors: [/ResizeObserver loop/, /Non-Error promise rejection/], integrations: [Sentry.replayIntegration({ maskAllText: true, blockAllMedia: true })], }); Senior gotcha: release must equal the value you upload source maps under, byte-for-byte. A mismatch silently leaves every production stack trace minified — invisible until you're paged at 3am with a.b.c is not a function . 3.2 Integration code patterns // Sentry — wired right Sentry.init({ dsn: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN, release: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_DEPLOY_SHA, tracesSampleRate: 0.1, replaysSessionSampleRate: 0.01, replaysOnErrorSampleRate: 1.0, ignoreErrors: [/ResizeObserver loop/, /Non-Error promise rejection/], integrations: [Sentry.replayIntegration({ maskAllText: true, blockAllMedia: true })], }); // Attach user + tenant context so traces are filterable, not anonymous Sentry.setUser({ id: user.id }); Sentry.setTag("tenant", orgId); Sentry.setTag("feature_flag.new_checkout", flagValue ? "on" : "off"); Senior gotcha: never put email/PII in setUser for regulated domains — use an opaque id and resolve identity in your dashboard. The replay mask is irrelevant if you already shipped the email as a tag. 3.3 Senior gotchas Privacy: mask PII in replay (form fields, tokens). Default OFF for medical/finance domains. Source maps must upload on every release; otherwise stack traces are useless. Sampling: 100% errors, 1–10% perf, < 1% replays — tune for cost. Filter noise (third-party ResizeObserver loops, browser extension errors). Senior gotcha: maskAllText: true still leaks PII rendered into element *attributes* ( title , aria-label , image alt , URL query params). Add explicit .sentry-mask / block classes on those and scrub query strings in beforeSend before you trust the masking. Part 4 — Search (in-app) Service Strength Tradeoff Algolia Best DX, fast, federated Pricey at scale; vendor lock Typesense OSS, fast, Algolia-like API Self-host or managed cloud Meilisearch OSS, dead-simple, instant search Smaller scale ceiling than Algolia Elastic / OpenSearch Heavy data, complex queries Complex to operate Pinecone / Weaviate / Qdrant Vector / semantic search Different use case (RAG, similarity) Coveo Enterprise commerce search + AI Expensive Ves
